```markdown
- the only place we need to update an issue file when the issue is partially complete is the "current behavior" section. We don't need to add append-logs to the end, it's better to update the main body to align with the current design, and the current behavior with the current status.

```

### feedback_comprehensive_first_pass.md

```markdown
---
name: Don't tier work into cheap / medium / expensive
description: For new features, do every fold of the work in one comprehensive slice rather than splitting into easy-now / hard-later tiers
type: feedback
originSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa
---
When scoping a new feature, resist the instinct to propose a
"slice 1 covers cheap fields; slice 2 covers expensive fields"
split unless the user explicitly asks for it.

**Why:** The user's framing: "they should all be configurable
with the same interface, so... don't split up the work in that
way. Just do it comprehensively the first time so we don't
forget anything on the return trip." Tiered work means coming
back, and round-trips are where details get forgotten —
especially the cross-cutting plumbing that connects the easy
and hard paths.

**How to apply:** When writing an issue file, if a feature
spans cheap-and-hard variations of the same surface (e.g. all
fields of a schema, all kinds of a polymorphic type), describe
slice 1 as covering the whole surface. The implementation may
still ship incrementally on a per-commit basis, but the issue
should not encode a "we'll do the rest later" plan unless the
user has explicitly asked for that staging.

```

### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

### project_yarq_and_third_ring.md

```markdown
---
name: YARQ and the third input ring (issue 320)
description: Per-port third ring carries box-JSON reconfigure messages; YARQ (yield-and-requeue) is the project name for the cooperative-with-scheduler barrier that protects in-place box mutation
type: project
originSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa
---
Issue 320 introduces two pieces of project vocabulary that
recur in other code-paths:

**YARQ** (yield-and-requeue) — the synchronization primitive
that protects in-place box mutation. Acquire is a CAS from 0
to 1 on a per-box atomic word. On acquire failure, the
contended worker does NOT busy-wait — it re-submits its own
task to the **tail** of the pool queue and returns, letting
the scheduler drain other work first. Same barrier is acquired
by every path that mutates a box's record (reconfigure,
runtime_connect from 319d). The point: synchronization
*cooperative with the scheduler*, not adversarial to it.
The user named it; the joke is that they want to name a dog
YARQ too.

**The third input ring** — every input slot grows a third ring
alongside the native + JSON pair from issue 312. Carries
box-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages. Per-PORT placement (not
per-box) — any input port can receive reconfigure cells, and
the per-cell ring-selector tag from issue 312/318a grows a
third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`). When the consumer's
input-gather encounters a reconfigure cell, it retains
already-popped values, acquires YARQ, applies the reconfigure,
releases YARQ, and resumes gathering under the new config.

**Why:** Together with issue 319 (create_box / connect),
issue 320 gives the runtime its full "graph as a living
artifact" surface: 319 grows the graph (additive), 320
mutates what's already there (in-place). Many future features
will read or write these primitives — runtime DSLs, planner
boxes, the editor's live-mutation feedback path.

**How to apply:** When other issues touch box mutation,
slot rings, or per-cell ordering, treat YARQ and the third
ring as established vocabulary — don't reinvent the
primitive or the name. When the user mentions "reconfigure,"
"the third ring," or YARQ, they mean these specific pieces
of the design.

```

### reference_strategems.md

```markdown
---
name: Strategems directory

**Location:** `/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/`

**What it is:** Files in this directory are **distilled design rules** the user has named after a pattern that recurs in many places. They're shorter than docs/, longer than a one-line CLAUDE.md instruction, and load-bearing for design judgment. Each file is one strategem — a rule with a memorable phrase as the filename. The phrase-as-filename is the strategem's name; use it as shared vocabulary.

**Current strategems (as of 2026-05-23):**
- `commit-language-is-runtime-language.md`
- `contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md`
- `redesigns-change-the-surface-too.md`

**How to apply (the user's preference is encouragement, not force):**
- **Re-list the directory once per context** (`ls strategems/`) so the current set is in my working memory. Don't auto-read each one — let the filenames sit there as triggers.
- When a filename *feels* relevant to the task at hand, read it before proceeding. Relevance signals: I'm about to propose a contract, a redesign, a language-spec change, or anything where a recurring principle might apply. If nothing feels relevant, don't force a reach.
- Re-list at session start (or first time the project surfaces) — new strategems land here without ceremony and the list above may be stale across sessions.
- When a strategem does apply, name it explicitly to the user using its filename phrase. That's the shared vocabulary the naming is for.
- If during a session the user expresses a rule in the form "X must always Y because Z" and the rule generalizes beyond the current task, suggest writing it as a strategem rather than only as a memory.

**Recent commit pattern:** strategem files are committed individually (e.g. `c57c719 strategems: contracts must fit every implementer, not just the simplest`), so `git log -- strategems/` is the fastest way to see what's been added lately and the reasoning that prompted it.
```

```json
        "content":"1\t# 248 — Encapsulated map as box\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\tin progress · input-side load-time inlining shipped; output-side\n5\t(ext-consumed write boxes), editor UI, and recursion across mixed\n6\text-consumed wires deferred\n7\t\n8\t## Current behavior\n9\t\n10\tInput-side encapsulation runs at graph load. The loader recognizes\n11\t`kind: \"map\"` with a `ref` to a sub-map directory. A new pass between\n12\t`load_boxes` and `resolve_topology` walks every BOX_MAP record,\n13\tloads the sub-map's boxes into the parent's arena, prefix-renames\n14\ttheir ids with `<encap_id>__<sub_id>`, splices them into the parent's\n15\tflat box list, then rewires each parent producer's connection that\n16\ttargeted the encapsulating box. The rewire splices THROUGH the\n17\texternally-supplied data box: each parent wire to `encap.port` is\n18\treplaced with copies pointing to the matching data box's\n19\tdownstreams, preserving each from_branch tag. Externally-supplied\n20\tdata boxes are matched to the encapsulating box's input ports by\n21\tthe issue's three binding kinds (positional / numbered by index,\n22\tnamed by string).\n23\t\n24\tAfter inlining, the encap box stays in the index but is inert\n25\t(connections cleared, `ref` stripped — the loader skips it on\n26\tsubsequent passes, dispatch's BOX_MAP case is a logged no-op). The\n27\text-supplied data box is also orphaned (its outgoing connections\n28\twere absorbed into the parent producer; the cache pass skips it so\n29\tthe \"neither value nor path\" check doesn't reject the value-less\n30\tshape).\n31\t\n32\tThe end-to-end fixture `tests/maps/248-encap-input-only/` proves\n33\tthe splice reaches disk: a parent read box wires\n34\t`\"encapsulated-greeting\"` to a BOX_MAP whose sub-map has one\n35\texternally-supplied data box feeding a write box; the parent's\n36\tbytes land in `/tmp/soramech-248-encap-out.txt`.\n37\t\n38\tOutput-side encapsulation (externally-consumed write boxes\n39\tsurfacing as the encap's output ports) is not yet wired. Wires\n40\tthe user drew from `encap.port_x` to a parent consumer don't fire\n41\tin this slice. The editor toggles, file-browser Encapsulate\n42\taction, and the multi-output exception to issue 218 also remain\n43\tahead.\n44\t\n45\t## Concept\n46\t\n47\tA map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\n48\ttop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\n49\topen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\n50\ton the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\n51\tsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`\n52\tboxes inside the sub-map that have been marked\n53\t**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes\n54\tinside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.\n55\tThe two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from \"file\n56\ton disk\" to \"wire from parent,\" the other redirects an output\n57\tfrom \"file on disk\" to \"wire to parent.\"\n58\t\n59\tEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\n60\tThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\n61\twith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\n62\tsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\n63\tparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n64\t\n65\t**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's\n66\t\"single output per box\" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly\n67\tone output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one\n68\toutput). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one\n69\tper `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the\n70\tmap is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),\n71\tor many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's\n72\toutputs are independent values produced by independent\n73\t`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier\n74\tdesign in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing\n75\tmachinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:\n76\t`write` boxes should keep their semantics (\"terminate a value\")\n77\tand the destination kind (\"file vs. parent wire\") should be a\n78\tmode toggle, not a substitution.\n79\t\n80\t## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n81\t\n82\tA **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing\n83\tlanguage-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as\n84\t**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's\n85\tinspector. Toggling declares: \"this data box's value comes from\n86\tthe encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`\n87\tfield.\"\n88\t\n89\tThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are\n90\tthe natural entry points for external values into a map. Call\n91\tboxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which\n92\tkeeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each\n93\texternal input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by\n94\tthe encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from\n95\tthat chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value\n96\tloaded from disk.\n97\t\n98\tThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n99\t\n100\t```json\n101\t{\n102\t    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n103\t    \"kind\": \"data\",\n104\t    \"external\": {\n105\t        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n106\t        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n107\t        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n108\t    },\n109\t    \"...\": \"...\"\n110\t}\n111\t```\n112\t\n113\tThree binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input\n114\tmaps to this internal port:\n115\t\n116\t- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n117\t  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the\n118\t  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually\n119\t  matches positional function arguments.\n120\t- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape\n121\t  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave\n122\t  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).\n123\t- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n124\t  input port has a label; the matching internal box's\n125\t  `external.name` is the same string.\n126\t\n127\tA single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some\n128\tpositional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box\n129\texposes the union as its input ports.\n130\t\n131\t## Marked output ports inside the sub-map\n132\t\n133\tA **write** box inside the sub-map (kind: `write`, issue 229's\n134\tfile-write kind) can be marked as **externally-consumed** via a\n135\tsmall toggle on the box's inspector — the mirror of the\n136\texternally-supplied toggle on data boxes. Toggling declares:\n137\t\"this write box's value goes to the encapsulating context, not\n138\tto its `path` field.\"\n139\t\n140\tThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `write` boxes — those are\n141\tthe natural exit points for values out of a map. Each\n142\texternally-consumed write box surfaces as one **distinct output\n143\tport** on the encapsulating box. The port carries that one\n144\tvalue, on its own wire, to whichever downstream box(es) the\n145\tparent wires it to.\n146\t\n147\tThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON, in\n148\tthe same shape as the input-side toggle:\n149\t\n150\t```json\n151\t{\n152\t    \"id\": \"result_value\",\n153\t    \"kind\": \"write\",\n154\t    \"external\": {\n155\t        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n156\t        \"name\": \"result\",           // for named\n157\t        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n158\t    },\n159\t    \"...\": \"...\"\n160\t}\n161\t```\n162\t\n163\tThree binding kinds — same vocabulary as the input side:\n164\t\n165\t- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n166\t  box's *k*th output port is the externally-consumed write box\n167\t  whose `external.index` is *k*.\n168\t- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index, allowing\n169\t  gaps and reordering.\n170\t- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n171\t  output port carries that label.\n172\t\n173\tA write box marked externally-consumed **also** writes to its\n174\t`path` if one is set — the two destinations are independent. The\n175\twrite box can opt out of the file write (set `path: null`) if it\n176\texists solely to surface a value to the parent.\n177\t\n178\tEach externally-consumed write box's emitted value becomes an\n179\tindependent output wire on the encapsulating box. The earlier\n180\tdesign in this issue packed all write-box outputs into a single\n181\tbyte-blob with a leading size index; that design is rejected —\n182\tsee the \"Concept\" section for why. No packing, no unpacking\n183\tlibrary; the wire format is the same per-port wire format every\n184\tother box uses.\n185\t\n186\t## File layout in the parent map\n187\t\n188\t**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the\n189\teditor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other\n190\tcall box — `kind: \"call\"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,\n191\t`connections`, `routing`. What makes it an encapsulation is\n192\tthat its `lang` is `map` and its `ref` points to a sub-map\n193\tdirectory rather than a source file. The map-language spec\n194\t(`langs/map/spec.so`) is responsible for the \"behind the\n195\tscenes\" processing — running the sub-graph and packing the\n196\toutputs.\n197\t\n198\t```json\n199\t{\n200\t    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n201\t    \"kind\": \"call\",\n202\t    \"lang\": \"map\",\n203\t    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n204\t    \"fn\": null,                                  // unused for map kind\n205\t    \"inputs\": [\n206\t        { \"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"int\" },\n207\t        { \"name\": \"label\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n208\t    ],\n209\t    \"outputs\": [\n210\t        { \"name\": \"mean\",  \"type\": \"float\" },\n211\t        { \"name\": \"stdev\", \"type\": \"float\" },\n212\t        { \"name\": \"n\",     \"type\": \"int\" }\n213\t    ],\n214\t    \"...\": \"...\"\n215\t}\n216\t```\n217\t\n218\tThe `outputs` array on the encapsulating box JSON is the\n219\tdocumented exception to the single-output-per-box rule. The\n220\tgraph loader treats each entry as a distinct output slot,\n221\tallocates one ring buffer per output port (same machinery as\n222\tinput slots, but on the producer side), and lets the parent\n223\twire each output independently.\n224\t\n225\tThe map-language spec is registered in the spec registry the\n226\tsame way `lua` / `c` / `bash` are. Its `file_ext` is `.map`\n227\t(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph\n228\tloader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)\n229\tloads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and\n230\tpacks the outputs. From the dispatch layer's view, an\n231\tencapsulating call is just another spec invocation.\n232\t\n233\tThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked data boxes)\n234\tand output ports (derived from its marked write boxes) are\n235\texposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as `inputs` and `outputs`\n236\tarrays. The user doesn't write either array themselves — the\n237\teditor generates them from the sub-map on first encapsulation\n238\tand re-syncs them when the sub-map changes.\n239\t\n240\t## Editor UI\n241\t\n242\t### File browser\n243\t\n244\tThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\n245\tdescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\n246\tfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\n247\tgraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:\n248\t\n249\t- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the\n250\t  existing map-select behaviour).\n251\t- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: \"map\"` box to the\n252\t  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the\n253\t  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any\n254\t  other box.\n255\t\n256\t### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)\n257\t\n258\tThe inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small\n259\ttoggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a\n260\t`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it\n261\texternally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:\n262\t\n263\t```\n264\t  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n265\t  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n266\t  │   kind:    named            │\n267\t  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n268\t  └─────────────────────────────┘\n269\t```\n270\t\n271\tWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n272\t(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\n273\tWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on\n274\tthe data box; `path` write on the write box).\n275\t\n276\tA map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box\n277\t(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed\n278\twrite boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting\n279\tonly — legal but unusual; useful for \"fire and forget\"\n280\tsub-pipelines).\n281\t\n282\t### Visual on the canvas\n283\t\n284\tThe encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,\n285\tmaybe a small \"sub-map\" badge — so the user sees at a glance\n286\tthat this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name\n287\tand a small thumbnail of its graph.\n288\t\n289\t## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n290\t\n291\tTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\n292\tnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\n293\tbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\n294\tdoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\n295\tpipeline does at build time.\n296\t\n297\t### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n298\t\n299\tThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\n300\tboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\n301\tSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n302\t\n303\t1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n304\t2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n305\t   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n306\t3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n307\t4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n308\t   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n309\t   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n310\t5. For each externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map:\n311\t   route its emitted value to the matching output port on the\n312\t   encapsulating box (so downstream consumers in the parent map\n313\t   see the value on a distinct wire per write box). The write\n314\t   box still performs its disk-write if `path` is set.\n315\t6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n316\t\n317\tAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\n318\tThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\n319\texists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\n320\tthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n321\t\n322\t**Pros:**\n323\t\n324\t- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n325\t  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n326\t- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n327\t  nested dispatch.\n328\t- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n329\t  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n330\t  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n331\t- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n332\t  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n333\t\n334\t**Cons:**\n335\t\n336\t- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n337\t  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n338\t- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n339\t  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n340\t  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n341\t- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n342\t  encapsulations.\n343\t- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n344\t  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n345\t- The multi-output exception to issue 218 has to be carried\n346\t  through compile-time inlining as well: after expansion, the\n347\t  parent's flat graph has wires going from internal sub-graph\n348\t  boxes directly to whichever parent consumers were wired to\n349\t  the encapsulating box's output ports. The compile-time\n350\t  artifact loses the \"encapsulated box\" identity entirely but\n351\t  preserves the per-output routing.\n352\t\n353\t### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n354\t\n355\tThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\n356\tgraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\n357\tcall time:\n358\t\n359\t1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n360\t   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n361\t   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n362\t   dispatch context).\n363\t2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., outputs, ...)`** —\n364\t   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n365\t   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n366\t   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n367\t   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n368\t   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk each\n369\t   externally-consumed write box and push its emitted value onto\n370\t   the matching output port of the encapsulating box. Each output\n371\t   port surfaces on its own wire to the parent — no packing.\n372\t\n373\tThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\n374\tparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\n375\tparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\n376\tjust box-id prefix.\n377\t\n378\t**Pros:**\n379\t\n380\t- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n381\t  invocations and across many parent maps.\n382\t- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n383\t  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n384\t- The multi-output boundary is clean — each externally-consumed\n385\t  write box pushes onto its own output port wire as it would\n386\t  if it were a leaf box in the parent graph, no packing or\n387\t  unpacking required.\n388\t- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n389\t  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n390\t- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n391\t  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n392\t\n393\t**Cons:**\n394\t\n395\t- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n396\t  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n397\t  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n398\t  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n399\t- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n400\t  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n401\t  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n402\t- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n403\t  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n404\t  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n405\t  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n406\t  a separate design.)\n407\t- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n408\t  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n409\t  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n410\t  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n411\t\n412\t### What to weigh\n413\t\n414\tThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\n415\tabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\n416\tor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\n417\tlibrary)**.\n418\t\n419\tPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\n420\thow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\n421\tflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\n422\tthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n423\t\n424\tPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\n425\treal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\n426\tas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\n427\thot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\n428\tloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n429\t\n430\tA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\n431\tbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n432\t\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\n433\truntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\n434\tencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\n435\tbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\n436\tfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n437\t\n438\tRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\n439\teither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\n440\tload-time, under B) error.\n441\t\n442\t## Relationship to existing issues\n443\t\n444\t- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n445\t  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n446\t- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n447\t  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n448\t  input-port row.\n449\t- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** —\n450\t  encapsulation adds an \"externally-supplied\" toggle to data\n451\t  boxes and an \"externally-consumed\" toggle to write boxes. The\n452\t  boxes' default behaviour (read from / write to disk) is\n453\t  unchanged; the toggles route the value through a parent-wire\n454\t  instead of (or in addition to) the disk file.\n455\t\n456\t- **Issue 218 (single output per box)** — the encapsulated\n457\t  `kind: \"map\"` box is the documented exception. Every other box\n458\t  has exactly one output; an encapsulated box has one per\n459\t  externally-consumed write box (zero or more).\n460\t- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the\n461\t  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the\n462\t  pipeline with an \"encapsulation expansion\" step.\n463\t- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes\n464\t  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-\n465\t  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they\n466\t  were always part of one map.\n467\t\n468\t## Relevant files\n469\t\n470\t- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: \"map\"` box,\n471\t  the per-input-port external-binding state.\n472\t- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /\n473\t  Encapsulate actions.\n474\t- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding\n475\t  toggle.\n476\t- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map\n477\t  paths, validating bindings.\n478\t- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise\n479\t  `kind: \"map\"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated\n480\t  shape.\n481\t- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime\n482\t  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).\n483\t- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the\n484\t  compile-time path wins.\n485\t\n486\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n487\t\n488\t1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n489\t   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n490\t   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n491\t2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes\n492\t   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);\n493\t   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for\n494\t   both.\n495\t3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n496\t   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n497\t   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new\n498\t   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n499\t4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n500\t   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n501\t   marked-output lists on the parent box record.\n502\t5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets\n503\t   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the\n504\t   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot\n505\t   store accept this shape only for `lang: \"map\"` boxes.\n506\t6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n507\t   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n508\t   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n509\t7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n510\t   compile (or load) time.\n511\t8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n512\t   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n513\t\n514\t## Open questions\n515\t\n516\t- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n517\t  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n518\t  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.\n519\t  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and\n520\t  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to\n521\t  live inside the parent's map directory tree.\n522\t- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user\n523\t  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's\n524\t  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely\n525\t  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the\n526\t  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs\n527\t  fixing.\n528\t- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are\n529\t  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)\n530\t  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;\n531\t  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.\n532\t- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same\n533\t  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The\n534\t  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds\n535\t  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether\n536\t  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —\n537\t  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.\n538\t- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as\n539\t  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating\n540\t  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If\n541\t  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the\n542\t  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth\n543\t  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of\n544\t  the existing dispatch model.\n545\t\n546\t## Design history\n547\t\n548\tThe original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into\n549\ta single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and\n550\tthe encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:\n551\t\n552\t> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n553\t> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n554\t> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n555\t> of data...\" — 2026-05-21\n556\t\n557\tThat design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the\n558\tself-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:\n559\tboxes never \"return\" values to the outside world under the\n560\texisting model — they push values onto wires that other boxes\n561\tconsume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to\n562\tfiles. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings\n563\tinto wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for\n564\tanother. The symmetric design — mark write boxes\n565\texternally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —\n566\tpreserves the `write` box's semantics (\"terminate a value\") and\n567\ttreats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes\n568\texist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs\n569\tcleanly.\n570\t",
```
