    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    # Per-map env opt-in: a map may set SORAMECH_TEST_WORKERS to\n    # pin worker count for tests that depend on per-worker state\n    # (e.g. issue 318's $lang_opaque, which lives in the producer's\n    # Lua registry and can only be reconstructed by a consumer on\n    # the same worker).\n    local workers_env=\"\"\n    if [[ -f \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers\" ]]; then\n        workers_env=$(cat \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers\")\n    fi\n    if [[ -n \"$workers_env\" ]]; then\n        output=$(SORAMECH_WORKERS=\"$workers_env\" \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    else\n        output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    fi\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\ncheck_map \"319a-many-inputs\" \\\n    \"combine → count=20 sum=210\"\n\ncheck_map \"319d-runtime-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"auto_\" \\\n    \"echo_dyn-received:trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\ncheck_map \"319e-c-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → c-trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"c-echo-received:c-trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\ncheck_map \"246-c-shim\" \\\n    \"echo → seen:HELLO-FROM-SEED\"\n\ncheck_map \"246-lua-shim\" \\\n    \"echo → seen:REV-fedcba\"\n\n# Issue 318 — the producer's output proves the emit side works\n# end-to-end (Lua function → $lang_opaque sentinel in JSON). A read box emits a box spec; a\n# create_box-kind box consumes it; the new box's id is captured\n# downstream. No per-language wrapper involved — same shape works\n# for Lua, C, and Bash producers.\ncheck_map \"319-box-kind-create\" \\\n    \"creator → auto_\"\n\n# 319 auto-init follow-on: a C trigger creates a Lua box at\n# runtime; the Lua spec wasn't in the static graph's language set,\n# so the worker's Lua handle was NULL at pool startup. The\n# dispatch's lazy-init populates the handle on demand and the new\n# box fires.\ncheck_map \"319-cross-lang-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → c-trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"lua-echo-from-runtime-init:c-trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\n# Issue 248 input-side encapsulation. The parent's read box wires\n# a value into a BOX_MAP whose sub-map has one externally-supplied\n# data box; the graph loader splices the parent's wire through to\n# the sub-map's write box at load time. Verification is split: the\n# stdout check confirms the renamed write box fires; the disk file\n# check confirms the parent's bytes actually arrived through the\n# splice (the only path that produces the file's content).\ncheck_map \"248-encap-input-only\" \\\n    \"encap__writer → true\"\n\n# Issue 248 output-side encapsulation. The encap declares an output\n# port; the sub-map's externally-consumed write box emits its\n# `value` bytes downstream (rather than the usual \"true\" success\n# string) and the encapsulation pass appends the parent's downstream\n# wire onto that write box's connections. The renamed sub-writer\n# emits the payload value, and the parent's writer then reports\n# \"true\" after writing that value to disk.\ncheck_map \"248-encap-output-only\" \\\n    \"encap__external_writer → round-trip-through-encap\" \\\n    \"parent_writer → true\"\n\n# {{{ encap_input_only_file_check() — input-side encap reaches disk\nencap_input_only_file_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/248-encap-input-only\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"encap input-only write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"encapsulated-greeting\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected 'encapsulated-greeting', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"encap-input file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"encap-input: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\nencap_input_only_file_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

    "type":"edited_text_file",
    "snippet":"1\t# 250 — Routing kind: nonlinearity (squash)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen · design carried forward from issues 240 / 241 / 242 / 243\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\t\n8\tThe routing kinds shipped or queued so far — `plain`, `comparator`,\n9\t`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241), `distributor`\n10\t(242), `multi-band-comparator` (243) — all pick a **branch** and\n11\tforward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**. The\n12\tschema (`src/001-schema.lua`) and the dispatch picker\n13\t(`src/012-dispatch.c`) treat the wire payload as opaque on the\n14\tway out; routing has only ever decided *where* a value goes, never\n15\t*what* it is.\n16\t\n17\tThere is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the way\n18\tthrough. A user who wants the producer's output remapped into a\n19\tnew numeric range — for feeding a UI slider, an audio level, a\n20\theat-map cell — has to insert a dedicated call box that runs a\n21\tLua / C function whose entire job is one arithmetic expression.\n22\tThat's a lot of box for one knob.\n23\t\n24\t## Intended behavior\n25\t\n26\tA new routing kind, **`nonlinearity`** (working name; \"squash\"\n27\tis the alternative — see open questions), maps each numeric value\n28\tthat flows through the box into a bounded output range via a\n29\tchosen unary function (default: logistic sigmoid). The input is\n30\tnormalised against either:\n31\t\n32\t- **`auto`** — the running min and max observed on this wire\n33\t  during the current run, OR\n34\t- **`fixed`** — two user-supplied numeric bounds (`min`, `max`).\n35\t\n36\tAfter normalisation the value lands in `[0, 1]` (or `[-1, 1]` for\n37\ttanh — see open questions), the chosen non-linearity is applied,\n38\tand the result is forwarded on the box's single output port. The\n39\trouting kind has exactly one output — fan-out happens the same\n40\tway every other single-output box's fan-out happens (multiple\n41\twires leaving one port).\n42\t\n43\t-- to switch between auto and fixed, the user just needs to supply one or two\n44\t   values - if they supply one, the minimum / maximum is set (the slots in the\n45\t   editor and json are specified as \"min\" or \"max\" so there's no ambiguity about\n46\t   which is which) if they supply both then it's set to \"fixed\" mode as specified.\n47\t   I want there to be only one mode, and auto is the fallback if no fixed values\n48\t   are specified. C treats NULL as zero, so if we wanted to switch back to auto\n49\t   after specifying a value then we'd need to have two separate flags on-top of\n50\t   the min and max value - they basically say \"is this a fixed value or is it\n51\t   an auto value?\" - if the flag is set to fixed, then the value won't change if\n52\t   we receive a higher/lower value. If the flag is unset to auto, then we will\n53\t   adjust the min/max value depending on the min/max value we've received.\n54\t\n55\t-- I don't know the math very well so you'll have to take the lead on this part,\n56\t   but we need a function that will work equally well without normalization.\n57\t   The vision I had, which might be more / less useful for AI purposes than some\n58\t   other kind of function, is essentially an S curve with the minimum and max\n59\t   set to certain values, and whatever inputs come in will get fairly mid value\n60\t   unless they're very clearly a \"strong\" value one way or the other. This is\n61\t   why 0 is selected as the midpoint usually, I think, so that values close to\n62\t   mid, or perhaps a fairly even mixture of two values, can be multiplied and\n63\t   the result will be close to 0. So, maybe we need three - one that has the\n64\t   midpoint at 0, one that has the midpoint at 1, and one that scales? I'm not\n65\t   sure, can you picture why I would want such a thing? If so, can you offer any\n66\t   ideas about how to create intelligent behavior with this structure?\n67\t\n68\t### Schema\n69\t\n70\t```json\n71\t\"routing\": {\n72\t  \"kind\":     \"nonlinearity\",\n73\t  \"shape\":    \"sigmoid\",        // or \"tanh\" / \"linear\" / \"softsign\"\n74\t  \"mode\":     \"auto\",           // or \"fixed\"\n75\t  \"min\":      0,                // present only when mode == \"fixed\"\n76\t  \"max\":      100,              // present only when mode == \"fixed\"\n77\t  \"out_range\":\"unit\"            // or \"signed\" — see open questions\n78\t}\n79\t```\n80\t\n81\t`mode: \"auto\"` requires no bounds — the dispatch picker maintains\n82\ta running min and max in two slot-store cells (issue 302) per\n83\tnonlinearity box, updated atomically on each fire. `mode:\n84\t\"fixed\"` requires both `min` and `max`; schema rejects either\n85\tmissing or `min >= max`.\n86\t\n87\t### Branch picker (dispatch layer)\n88\t\n89\tThere is no branch to pick — the kind always emits on the single\n90\toutput. The dispatch code path differs from the existing\n91\trouting kinds in that it **mutates the value** rather than\n92\t**selecting an index**. Pseudocode:\n93\t\n94\t```c\n95\tdouble x = coerce_to_number(value_in);     // hard-error path on failure\n96\t\n97\tdouble lo, hi;\n98\tif (mode == AUTO) {\n99\t    lo = slot_min_load(min_slot);\n100\t    hi = slot_max_load(max_slot);\n101\t    slot_min_cas_update(min_slot, x);      // best-effort widen\n102\t    slot_max_cas_update(max_slot, x);\n103\t} else {\n104\t    lo = box->fixed_min;\n105\t    hi = box->fixed_max;\n106\t}\n107\t\n108\tdouble t = (hi == lo) ? 0.5 : (x - lo) / (hi - lo);   // bootstrap case\n109\t\n110\tdouble y;\n111\tswitch (shape) {\n112\t    case SIGMOID:  y = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k * (t - 0.5))); break;\n113\t    case TANH:     y = tanh(k * (t - 0.5));               break;\n114\t    case LINEAR:   y = t;                                 break;\n115\t    case SOFTSIGN: y = (t - 0.5) / (1.0 + fabs(t - 0.5)); break;\n116\t}\n117\t\n118\temit_number(out_port, y);\n119\t```\n120\t\n121\t`k` is a steepness constant (see open questions). The bootstrap\n122\tcase (`hi == lo`, true on the very first value seen under `auto`\n123\tmode) maps to `t = 0.5` so the sigmoid emits 0.5 — a defensible\n124\t\"no information yet\" value.\n125\t\n126\t### Coercion and the hard-error path\n127\t\n128\tThe kind operates on numbers only. The dispatch picker tries to\n129\tcoerce the inbound value:\n130\t\n131\t- **number on the wire** — used directly.\n132\t- **string** — parsed as a number (`strtod`). On parse failure,\n133\t  the box raises a hard error matching the project's \"errors over\n134\t  fallbacks\" rule. The error names the box id, the offending\n135\t  string, and the wire it arrived on.\n136\t- **other types** (boolean, blob, sentinel) — hard error,\n137\t  unconditional. No silent coercion.\n138\t\n139\tHard errors stop the box from emitting. No \"skip on bad input\"\n140\tfallback — that's a warning shape this project treats as an\n141\terror.\n142\t\n143\t### Inspector UI\n144\t\n145\tMode dropdown on the routing inspector gains a `nonlinearity`\n146\toption (same row as the other routing kinds). When selected, the\n147\tinspector body shows:\n148\t\n149\t- **Shape** dropdown: sigmoid / tanh / linear / softsign.\n150\t- **Bounds mode** dropdown: auto / fixed.\n151\t- **Min** and **Max** number inputs (visible only when bounds\n152\t  mode is fixed).\n153\t- A small **live preview** plot — the chosen shape rendered into\n154\t  a thumbnail SVG so the user sees what they're picking. (Stretch\n155\t  goal; not blocking the first slice.)\n156\t\n157\tThe box's single output port keeps the plain-routing name\n158\t(`out`) so wires drawn before the kind was changed don't need\n159\trenaming.\n160\t\n161\t## Suggested implementation steps\n162\t\n163\t1. `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `kind: \"nonlinearity\"`; validate\n164\t   `shape`, `mode`, the `min` / `max` pair when `mode == fixed`,\n165\t   and the `out_range` choice.\n166\t2. `src/302-wire-value-slot-store.*` — add `SLOT_MIN_DOUBLE` and\n167\t   `SLOT_MAX_DOUBLE` slot kinds with CAS-update semantics\n168\t   (compare-and-swap loop that retries if another worker widened\n169\t   the slot between the load and the store). Reuse if such slots\n170\t   already exist; otherwise extend.\n171\t3. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — read the nonlinearity routing\n172\t   fields into the box record; allocate the two slot cells when\n173\t   `mode == auto`.\n174\t4. `src/012-dispatch.c` — implement the value-transform path.\n175\t   This is the first routing kind that **writes a new value** to\n176\t   the output wire instead of forwarding the input unchanged; the\n\n...     "snippet":"1\t/* src/010-graph-loader.h — C graph loader (phase 3), public API.\n2\t *\n3\t * What it is, in a sentence: reads a map directory off disk, parses\n4\t * every JSON file in it, and produces an in-memory graph_t that the\n5\t * dispatch layer (issue 304) and the pool runner (issue 301) walk\n6\t * to drive a run.\n7\t *\n8\t * Designed in issue 305. Aligned to the unified routing schema\n9\t * from issue 233 — every call box carries a routing.kind, and the\n10\t * legacy `comparand` / `iterator_outputs` fields are gone. The data\n11\t * and file_write box kinds from issue 229 are dispatch-layer\n12\t * primitives — they have no function to invoke.\n13\t *\n14\t * Memory model: every string the graph_t holds (box ids, refs,\n15\t * function names, branch tags, paths, input port names) lives in a\n16\t * single json_arena_t owned by the graph_t. graph_destroy frees the\n17\t * arena, the box / connection / input arrays, and the graph_t in\n18\t * one call.\n19\t *\n20\t * Errors: graph_load returns NULL on failure and sets *err to a\n21\t * malloc'd diagnostic of the form \"<file>:<line>: <message>\". The\n22\t * caller frees *err. The hard-crash policy of the rest of phase 3\n23\t * (issue 303) applies upstream — graph_load's caller decides\n24\t * whether to abort or surface the error.\n25\t *\n26\t * Pipeline: directory walk, JSON parse, per-box schema validation,\n27\t * topology resolution (string refs → integer indices), non-iterator\n28\t * cycle rejection, per-edge same-language classification (issue 312),\n29\t * entry-box detection. graph_attach_runtime then allocates input\n30\t * slots sized per the feeders' declared output_capacity, resolves\n31\t * each call box's language spec, and enumerates the distinct\n32\t * languages and slot size classes the map uses.\n33\t *\n34\t * Errors out of any phase abort the load and return NULL with a\n35\t * diagnostic via *err.\n36\t */\n37\t\n38\t#ifndef SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n39\t#define SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n40\t\n41\t#include <stddef.h>\n42\t#include <stdatomic.h>\n43\t\n44\t#ifdef __cplusplus\n45\textern \"C\" {\n46\t#endif\n47\t\n48\t/* {{{ Box kinds */\n49\ttypedef enum {\n50\t    BOX_CALL,        /* runs a function via a language spec                */\n51\t    BOX_READ,        /* value source — inline literal or file at `path`    */\n52\t    BOX_WRITE,       /* file sink — writes one input, emits \"true\" downstream */\n53\t    /* Runtime self-construction (issue 319, design-correction follow-on\n54\t     * to 319d/319e). These are language-agnostic box kinds — the same\n55\t     * shape as read/write boxes, no `lang` field. Their `do_*`\n56\t     * implementations live in the dispatch layer and call\n57\t     * runtime_create_box / runtime_connect internally.\n58\t     *\n59\t     * The per-language wrappers (langs/lua/spec.c's\n60\t     * `soramech.create_box`, langs/c/soramech.h's\n61\t     * `soramech_create_box`) remain as backwards-compatible\n62\t     * convenience entry points; the box-kind path is the new idiomatic\n63\t     * way and the only path that works uniformly across every\n64\t     * language (including Bash, which has no per-language wrapper). */\n65\t    BOX_CREATE_BOX,  /* construct a new box from a spec on the input wire  */\n66\t    BOX_CONNECT,     /* attach a wire described by a connection-entry input */\n67\t    /* Issue 248: encapsulated map. A box of this kind names a\n68\t     * sub-map directory via `ref`; at graph load the loader\n69\t     * recursively loads the sub-map's boxes, splices them into\n70\t     * the parent with id prefixes, and rewires the parent's\n71\t     * wires that reach this box to instead reach the sub-map's\n72\t     * externally-marked data / write boxes. After inlining the\n73\t     * box itself becomes inert — it never dispatches. */\n74\t    BOX_MAP,\n75\t} box_kind_t;\n76\t/* }}} */\n77\t\n78\t/* {{{ Routing kinds (issue 233 unified schema) */\n79\ttypedef enum {\n80\t    ROUTING_PLAIN,\n81\t    ROUTING_COMPARATOR,\n82\t    ROUTING_ITERATOR,\n83\t    ROUTING_RANDOMIZER,\n84\t    ROUTING_WEIGHTED,\n85\t    ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR,\n86\t} routing_kind_t;\n87\t\n88\ttypedef struct {\n89\t    routing_kind_t kind;\n90\t    int            n_outputs;   /* iterator / randomizer / weighted / distributor */\n91\t    double         comparand;   /* comparator */\n92\t    /* Weighted routing: arena-owned double array of n_outputs\n93\t     * entries. When non-NULL,\n105\t     * names a file relative to the map dir that contains a\n106\t     * user-written shim.           "old_string":"## Status\nin progress · input-side load-time inlining shipped; output-side\n(ext-consumed write boxes), editor UI, and recursion across mixed\next-consumed wires deferred\n\n## Current behavior\n\nInput-side encapsulation runs at graph load. The loader recognizes\n`kind: \"map\"` with a `ref` to a sub-map directory. A new pass between\n`load_boxes` and `resolve_topology` walks every BOX_MAP record,\nloads the sub-map's boxes into the parent's arena, prefix-renames\ntheir ids with `<encap_id>__<sub_id>`, splices them into the parent's\nflat box list, then rewires each parent producer's connection that\ntargeted the encapsulating box. The rewire splices THROUGH the\nexternally-supplied data box: each parent wire to `encap.port` is\nreplaced with copies pointing to the matching data box's\ndownstreams, preserving each from_branch tag. Externally-supplied\ndata boxes are matched to the encapsulating box's input ports by\nthe issue's three binding kinds (positional / numbered by index,\nnamed by string).\n\nAfter inlining, the encap box stays in the index but is inert\n(connections cleared, `ref` stripped — the loader skips it on\nsubsequent passes, dispatch's BOX_MAP case is a logged no-op). The\next-supplied data box is also orphaned (its outgoing connections\nwere absorbed into the parent producer; the cache pass skips it so\nthe \"neither value nor path\" check doesn't reject the value-less\nshape).\n\nThe end-to-end fixture `tests/maps/248-encap-input-only/` proves\nthe splice reaches disk: a parent read box wires\n`\"encapsulated-greeting\"` to a BOX_MAP whose sub-map has one\nexternally-supplied data box feeding a write box; the parent's\nbytes land in `/tmp/soramech-248-encap-out.txt`.\n\nOutput-side encapsulation (externally-consumed write boxes\nsurfacing as the encap's output ports) is not yet wired. Wires\nthe user drew from `encap.port_x` to a parent consumer don't fire\nin this slice. The editor toggles, file-browser Encapsulate\naction, and the multi-output exception to issue 218 also remain\nahead.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Status\nin progress · input-side AND output-side load-time inlining\nshipped; editor UI (inspector toggles + file-browser Encapsulate\naction) and the recursion-across-mixed-ext-consumed-wires\nverification still deferred\n\n## Current behavior\n\nEncapsulation runs at graph load in both directions. The loader\nrecognizes `kind: \"map\"` with a `ref` to a sub-map directory. A\nnew pass between `load_boxes` and `resolve_topology` walks every\nBOX_MAP record, loads the sub-map's boxes into the parent's arena,\nprefix-renames their ids with `<encap_id>__<sub_id>`, splices them\ninto the parent's flat box list, then rewrites the wires in both\ndirections:\n\n**Input side.** Each parent producer's connection that targets the\nencapsulating box is replaced with copies pointing to the matching\nexternally-supplied read box's downstreams — preserving each\nfrom_branch tag. The binding follows the issue's three kinds\n(positional / numbered by index, named by string). The ext-supplied\nread box itself is orphaned (its outgoing connections were absorbed\ninto the parent producer; the cache pass skips it so the \"neither\nvalue nor path\" check doesn't reject the value-less shape).\n\n**Output side.** Each wire the parent drew leaving the encap box\ngets matched (by `from_branch` against the encap's declared\n`outputs` array) to an externally-consumed write box inside the\nsub-map and appended to that write box's connections array. The\nexternally-consumed write box's dispatch path emits its `value`\ninput bytes downstream rather than the literal `\"true\"` success\nstring, so the spliced wire carries the actual computed value to\nthe parent's consumer. The disk write at `path` still happens —\nthe two destinations are independent. The \"set path:null to opt\nout of the disk write\" path described above lands with the editor\nschema slice once the path input is allowed to be optional.\n\nAfter both splices, the encap box stays in the index but is inert\n(connections cleared, `ref` stripped — the loader skips it on\nsubsequent passes, dispatch's BOX_MAP case is a logged no-op).\n\nTwo end-to-end fixtures prove the splices reach disk:\n\n- `tests/maps/248-encap-input-only/` — input-side only. A parent\n  read box wires `\"encapsulated-greeting\"` to a BOX_MAP whose\n  sub-map has one externally-supplied read box feeding a write\n  box; the parent's bytes land in `/tmp/soramech-248-encap-out.txt`.\n- `tests/maps/248-encap-output-only/` — both sides. A parent\n  read box wires `\"round-trip-through-encap\"` into the encap;\n  the sub-map's externally-consumed write box surfaces the value\n  back onto the encap's output port; a parent-side write box\n  receives the value and lands it on disk. Both the sub-map's\n  write and the parent's write produce identical files,\n  confirming the value flowed through the encapsulation in\n  both directions.\n\nMulti-output (more than one externally-consumed write box per\nencap) is supported by the schema — `outputs` is an array — but\nisn't covered by a fixture yet.\n\nThe editor toggles, file-browser Encapsulate action, and a\nrecursion fixture (sub-maps that themselves encapsulate sub-maps)\nremain ahead.",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Two of the three 248 sub-tasks landed in this stretch, with the suite now at 21 passed / 4 pre-existing failed.\n\n**What changed**\n- `src/010-graph-loader.h` — new `n_outputs` / `outputs` fields on the box struct, scoped to encapsulated-map records.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — `parse_outputs` for the encap's port declarations; `find_output_port_index` + `find_ext_consumed_for_port` lookups; output-side rewrite pass inside the encapsulation splice; deferred the `sub_boxes` array free until after the splice (that was a one-shot UB that segfaulted the first dry run).\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — externally-consumed write boxes push their `value` bytes downstream instead of the literal `\"true\"` so the spliced wire carries the actual computed value to the parent's consumer; the disk write at `path` still runs.\n- Three fixtures: `tests/maps/248-encap-output-only/` (output-side splice), `tests/maps/248-encap-output-sub/` (its sub-map), `tests/maps/248-encap-recursive/` + `…-outer/` + `…-inner/` (nested encapsulations).\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — two new substring assertions and two new on-disk file checks.\n- `issues/248-encapsulated-map-as-box.md` — status + current-behavior rewritten to describe what shipped.\n\n**Result**\n- Output-side: the parent's writer reports `parent_writer → true` after the sub-map's `encap__external_writer → round-trip-through-encap` lands, and both disk files hold identical bytes.\n- Recursion: `encap_outer__encap_inner__inner_writer` shows the double-namespace prefix in action; all three writers in the two-level nest hold the same bytes.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The `inline_encapsulations` outer loop already handled recursion correctly — it iterates up to 1024 times picking up any `BOX_MAP` with a non-NULL `ref` until none remain. Once an outer sub-map gets inlined, its inner BOX_MAP appears as a fresh entry in the parent's flat box list with the right ref, and the next iteration handles it. No code change needed; only a fixture to prove it.\n- The most interesting bug today was the dangling `sub_boxes` array. The pointer-array I allocated locally got `free()`d as soon as the records inside were copied into `g->boxes` — but my new output-side splice still needed the original `sub_boxes[i]` indexing to find the ext-consumed write box. The records are still alive (they migrated to the graph), but reading them through the freed *pointer array* is UB and crashed on the first dry run. Moving the `free` after the splice fixed it. The lesson is that \"the records are still owned\" doesn't mean \"every container I held them in is still valid\" — separate lifetimes.\n- The `do_write_box` change is genuinely small — three lines of new behavior inside one `if (rc == 0 && out_buf)` — because the externally-consumed semantics fit naturally into the existing return path. The write box already wrote the file and the disk-write/wire-emit pair is independent; only the bytes copied into `out_buf` had to change.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n**Where to go next?** Three options on the todo, in increasing implementation effort:\n\n1. **315 — reference-counted compiled artifacts** (release blocker). Backend, concrete: change `soramech-compile.sh`'s destructive `rm -rf` startup to either skip-the-clobber-when-refs-exist or build-a-sibling-directory. Self-contained, no UI, testable from the shell.\n2. **319 — built-in library for map self-construction** (release blocker). The issue is `open — planning stub` with several open design questions needing your resolution before code lands. Probably needs a pre-implementation conversation, not solo dive.\n3. **248 editor toggles + file-browser Encapsulate action**. JS/HTML work in `assets/`. I can read the existing inspector code and make changes, but I can't browser-test from here — would need you to run the dev server and click around to verify.\n\nMy read: **315 next** is the cleanest stretch — concrete, backend, end-to-end testable, and it's a real release blocker. Want me to go? Or would you rather I pause so you can review what's landed for 248 first (and maybe commit it before the diff grows)?"
      }],

    "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via third input ring\n\n## Status\nopen · design draft; several open questions need user resolution\nbefore implementation can begin\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses the\nbox's JSON once (`parse_box_file` in `src/010-graph-loader.c`),\nfills in every field — `kind`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, the routing\nshape, the input port list, the connections array — and the\ndispatch layer (`src/012-dispatch.c`) walks that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes those fields.\n\nThe two paths the runtime already has to \"change the graph\nwhile it's running\" — issue 319's `create_box` / `connect`\nprimitives, and issue 248's load-time encapsulation splice —\nboth **add** to the graph; they never **rewrite** a box that\nalready exists. A box is the box it was born as.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\n**reconfigured** mid-run. A new configuration arrives as a JSON\nmessage in a per-box auxiliary inbox; the next worker that picks\nthe box up consumes the message instead of running the function,\nre-parses the box's identity, and either fires under the new\nconfig (if inputs are satisfied) or quietly exits.\n\n## Concept\n\nEvery box gains a **third input channel** (alongside the per-port\nnative + JSON rings from issue 312). It carries one kind of\nmessage only — a JSON object **exactly matching the box's own\nJSON schema**, the same shape a `boxes/<id>.json` file holds at\nload. When the dispatch scheduler picks this channel to consume\nnext (instead of one of the box's normal input ports), the worker:\n\n1. Acquires the box's reconfigure barrier (the \"not-quite-a-\n   spinlock\" — see below).\n2. Pops the config message off the third ring.\n3. Re-parses it through the same machinery that parsed the box\n   at load time, applying the result to the live box record in\n   place.\n4. Releases the barrier.\n5. Re-checks the box's input readiness against the new schema:\n   - If inputs are now satisfied → fire the box normally.\n   - If not → quietly exit. The next push to a real input port\n     (or another reconfigure) will spawn the next task.\n\nThe point is to make **mutation a first-class scheduling event**.\nReconfigures interleave with fires in the same FIFO the scheduler\nalready uses; a producer that wants to change a downstream box's\nbehavior on a given step just pushes config to the third ring at\nthe right moment, and the change lands before the next fire.\n\nThis is the symmetric counterpart to issue 319's `create_box` /\n`connect` primitives: 319 grows the graph, this issue mutates\nwhat's already there. Together they cover the full \"graph as a\nliving artifact\" surface.\n\n## The \"not-quite-a-spinlock\" yield-and-requeue barrier\n\nThe reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers\nfiring the same box. While a worker is rewriting the box's\nrecord, no other worker may read inconsistent state — half the\nnew `inputs` array with the old `routing.kind`, etc.\n\nA spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing\ncaptures the intended shape:\n\n> \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back\n> at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n\nMechanism: the barrier is a single atomic word on the box record\n(`box->reconfigure_in_flight`, or similar). Acquire = CAS from 0\nto 1. If the CAS fails, the worker does NOT spin — it re-submits\nits own task to the pool's queue and returns. The task lands at\nthe tail (or head — see open questions) and gets picked up later,\nby which time the reconfigure is likely done. Release = atomic\nstore of 0.\n\nThe cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for the contended\nworker, but no busy-waiting and no priority inversion. The\nscheduler does what it does best — manage many small units of\nwork fairly. The reconfiguring worker holds the barrier for as\nlong as the JSON parse + record rewrite takes, which is bounded\nby the box's complexity, not by other workers.\n\nThe barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the box —\nnot just reconfigure but also `connect` (319's runtime wire\nattachment), which already does its own copy-and-publish atomic\ndance on the connections array. Folding those into the same\nbarrier means the two mutation paths can't interleave dangerously\nwhen both fire at once.\n\n## Schema for the third-ring message\n\nA message on the third ring is a JSON object identical in shape\nto what `parse_box_file` parses today:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\":      \"my_box\",          // must match the target box\n    \"kind\":    \"call\",            // any kind, including a kind change\n    \"lang\":    \"lua\",\n    \"ref\":     \"lib/new_impl.lua\",\n    \"fn\":      \"new_handler\",\n    \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n    \"inputs\":  [\n        { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n        { \"name\": \"y\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true }\n    ],\n    \"connections\": [\n        { \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"value\" }\n    ]\n}\n```\n\nThe `id` field MUST match the target box (a safety check; mixed\nids hard-error). Every other field is the new state. Fields that\nare absent get default treatment (same as a freshly-parsed box\nfile). The schema validator runs in full so a malformed\nreconfigure can't half-apply.\n\n## Reconfigure semantics — which fields can change\n\nThis is the most consequential design choice; the answer\ndetermines how much surgery the dispatch layer has to grow.\n\nCheap fields (one pointer assignment, no slot-store interaction):\n- `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `routing.kind`, `routing.comparand`,\n  `routing.weights`, `output_capacity`, the per-box compile hints\n  (cflags / link_libs / headers), `returns`.\n\nMedium-cost fields (require revalidating, but no slot growth):\n- `routing.n_outputs` — the box's output ports rename. Existing\n  connections' `from_branch` tags may stop matching.\n- The `external` binding block (issue 248) — but the\n  encapsulation pass already ran at load time, so changing this\n  mid-run is meaningless unless re-running the splice is supported.\n- `connections[]` array — issue 319 already grows this via\n  `box_add_connection`. Reconfigure can SET the array wholesale,\n  which is the natural complement.\n\nExpensive fields (require slot store growth / shrink):\n- `inputs[]` array — adding a port means the slot store has to\n  allocate a new input slot (issue 319b's slot growth). Removing\n  a port means draining and releasing a slot. Renaming a port\n  means re-resolving every producer's connection `to_input_idx`.\n\nInfeasible (probably never supported):\n- `id` — the field is the lookup key for the whole graph.\n- `kind` change between BOX_CALL and BOX_MAP — would require\n  re-running the encapsulation pass on this single box, which\n  is structurally a load-time pass.\n\nA reasonable first slice: support every **cheap** field and\n**connections[]**; reject changes to `id`, `kind`, `inputs[]`\nwith a precise diagnostic; defer the expensive and infeasible\ncases to follow-on issues.\n\n## How the third ring gets fed\n\nA reconfigure message needs a producer. Two complementary\nmechanisms:\n\n1. **A `reconfigure` box kind** (analogous to `create_box` and\n   `connect` from issue 319's design-correction follow-on). One\n   input port `spec` carries the box-JSON; one declared field\n   (or an additional input port) carries the target box id. On\n   fire, the box pushes the message onto the target's third ring.\n\n2. **A runtime API** — `runtime_reconfigure(target_id, json,\n   size, err)` — that any language spec's invoke can call. Same\n   shape as `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` from\n   319d.\n\nA box can also reconfigure itself by pushing onto its own third\nring; the next dispatch picks it up after this one exits.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Add the third ring to the slot store** (`src/009-slot-store.*`).\n   One per box (not per port), small fixed capacity (8? 16?). The\n   ring carries variable-length JSON blobs; use the\n   large-value-heap (issue 015) for the bytes.\n2. **Add the yield-and-requeue barrier** to `box_t`\n   (`src/010-graph-loader.h`). One `_Atomic int` field;\n   acquire/release helpers in `src/012-dispatch.c`.\n3. **Extend `box_add_connection`** to acquire the barrier so\n   reconfigure and `connect` can't interleave.\n4. **Add a `reconfigure_apply` function** in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c` that takes a JSON blob and a target\n   box, runs the parse through the same `parse_box_file` machinery\n   on an in-memory buffer, and rewrites the box record in place\n   (only the cheap-field set; reject the others).\n5. **Teach the dispatch scheduler** (`dispatch_spawn_if_ready`?\n   `dispatch_action`?) to peek the third ring first; if non-empty,\n   acquire the barrier, pop, call `reconfigure_apply`, release\n   the barrier, then re-check readiness.\n6. **Implement the `reconfigure` box kind** in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c` and parse-side support in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`.\n7. **Add `runtime_reconfigure`** to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.\n8. **Fixture**: `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-routing/` — a box\n   starts with comparator routing, a reconfigure flips it to\n   iterator routing mid-run, the downstream connections fire on\n   the new branches.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — third-ring storage.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` reuse,\n  reconfigure-apply function, barrier field on box_t.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch scheduler check, reconfigure\n  task path, yield-and-requeue logic, `reconfigure` box kind.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_reconfigure` entry\n  point for language specs.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` — emit a reconfigure event so\n  the JSONL transcript records every mutation.\n- `issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md` —\n  sister issue; create_box / connect are the additive\n  primitives, this is the mutative primitive.\n- `issues/318a-per-call-output-format-threads-to-push.md` —\n  per-cell ordering tags; the third ring may want to participate\n  in the same ordering scheme so reconfigures land at the right\n  moment relative to in-flight values.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Per-box vs per-port ring placement.** A box-level config\n  ring (one per box) reads cleanest because the message\n  concerns the whole box. A per-port \"third ring\" would mirror\n  the native/JSON pairing exactly but raises \"which port's\n  config wins?\" questions. The proposal above is per-box; flag\n  this for confirmation before the slot-store work lands.\n- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and config-pops.**\n  When the box has BOTH pending values on input ports AND a\n  pending reconfigure, which does the dispatch consume next?\n  Options:\n    1. Strict FIFO across all four channels (port-native, port-\n       JSON, port-config-not-applicable, box-config) using\n       issue 318a's per-cell ordering tags.\n    2. Reconfigures get priority — drain them before any fire,\n       so a fire always runs under the latest config.\n    3. Reconfigures get NO priority — they wait their turn in\n       the same FIFO, so values already in flight get processed\n       under the old config they were generated against.\n   Option 2 is \"configuration is always current\"; option 3 is\n   \"values keep their original interpretation.\"\n- **Yield-and-requeue target end.** The user described it as\n  \"put yourself back at the end\" *and* \"the beginning\" in the\n  same sentence. End-of-queue is fairer (other tasks get to\n  run before this one retries); beginning is faster recovery\n  (this task retries soonest). End is probably the right\n  default but worth confirming.\n- **Scope of reconfigurable fields in slice 1.** The proposal\n  is \"cheap fields + connections[]; reject changes to id /\n  kind / inputs[] with a clean diagnostic.\" Confirm or expand.\n- **What if the reconfigure JSON is invalid?** Hard-error\n  (box dies and dispatches a failure event), or silently\n  reject the reconfigure and continue with the old config?\n  Lean toward hard-error — matches the project's \"errors over\n  fallbacks\" rule.\n- **Recursive reconfigure / loop guard.** A box reconfigures\n  itself, the new config has a `reconfigure` step that pushes\n  another config, etc. Should the runtime cap reconfigure\n  depth per box per run, or trust the user?\n- **Visibility of in-flight values when port shape changes.**\n  If a future slice supports adding/removing/renaming input\n  ports, what happens to values already sitting in the\n  affected port's ring? Drain and discard, drain and re-queue\n  on the renamed port, hard-error if drain reveals values?\n- **Interaction with the compile pipeline.** The compile\n  artifact (issue 309) currently bakes the box JSONs into the\n  built program. If a box can be reconfigured at runtime,\n  the compiled artifact has to either (a) emit reconfigure\n  hooks for every box, or (b) be opt-in per box. Option (b)\n  feels right but means a per-box `reconfigurable: true` flag\n  in the JSON.\n- **Connections array swap-and-replace.** A reconfigure that\n  rewrites `connections[]` wholesale means the existing array\n  goes away and a new one takes its place. issue 319d\n  established the copy-and-publish atomic pattern for\n  growing the array — does the wholesale-replace use the\n  same pattern (allocate new, atomic-store, park the old on\n  the stale list), or a different one?\n- **Reconfigure event in the JSONL transcript.** The transcript\n  is the run's audit log; a reconfigure that changes box\n  behavior mid-run should be visible there. Event shape:\n  `{kind: \"reconfigure\", box: \"<id>\", before: {...}, after:\n  {...}, at_task: <id>}` — full before/after? Diff only? Just\n  the id and timestamp?\n- **Composability with issue 248 encapsulation.** Could a\n  reconfigure change a box from BOX_CALL to BOX_MAP, requiring\n  the encapsulation pass to re-run on that one box?\n  Structurally hard — the load-time pass assumes single-pass\n  flat-graph construction. Flag this as out-of-scope unless\n  there's a compelling use case.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe user's original phrasing for the yield-and-requeue\nmechanism, preserved verbatim because it captures the intent\nbetter than any rephrase:\n\n> \"I'm thinking we'll need to put an atomic spinlock on the\n> entire box that, instead of spinning, will ask the waiting\n> thread to re-add the box to the end of the thread pool queue.\n> When we're done re-configuring the box, the spinlock is\n> removed. It's not quite a spinlock actually... but you get\n> the idea, it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\n> yourself back at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n\nThe \"end\" / \"beginning\" choice in the same sentence is the\nopen question above; both are defensible. The deeper signal —\nthat the synchronization primitive is *cooperative with the\nscheduler* rather than *adversarial to it* — is the design\nnote that should carry through to the implementation.\n",

    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/320-box-reconfigure-via-third-input-ring.md"
  },

}

Two complementary\nmechanisms:\n\n1. **A `reconfigure` box kind** (analogous to `create_box` and\n   `connect` from issue 319's design-correction follow-on). One\n   input port `spec` carries the box-JSON; one declared field\n   (or an additional input port) carries the target box id. On\n   fire, the box pushes the message onto the target's third ring.\n\n2. **A runtime API** — `runtime_reconfigure(target_id, json,\n   size, err)` — that any language spec's invoke can call. Same\n   shape as `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` from\n   319d.\n\nA box can also reconfigure itself by pushing onto its own third\nring; the next dispatch picks it up after this one exits.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Add the third ring to the slot store** (`src/009-slot-store.*`).\n   One per box (not per port), small fixed capacity (8? 16?). The\n   ring carries variable-length JSON blobs; use the\n   large-value-heap (issue 015) for the bytes.\n2. **Add the yield-and-requeue barrier** to `box_t`\n   (`src/010-graph-loader.h`). One `_Atomic int` field;\n   acquire/release helpers in `src/012-dispatch.c`.\n3. **Extend `box_add_connection`** to acquire the barrier so\n   reconfigure and `connect` can't interleave.\n4. **Add a `reconfigure_apply` function** in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c` that takes a JSON blob and a target\n   box, runs the parse through the same `parse_box_file` machinery\n   on an in-memory buffer, and rewrites the box record in place\n   (only the cheap-field set; reject the others).\n5. **Teach the dispatch scheduler** (`dispatch_spawn_if_ready`?\n   `dispatch_action`?) to peek the third ring first; if non-empty,\n   acquire the barrier, pop, call `reconfigure_apply`, release\n   the barrier, then re-check readiness.\n6. **Implement the `reconfigure` box kind** in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c` and parse-side support in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`.\n7. **Add `runtime_reconfigure`** to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.\n8. **Fixture**: `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-routing/` — a box\n   starts with comparator routing, a reconfigure flips it to\n   iterator routing mid-run, the downstream connections fire on\n   the new branches.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — third-ring storage.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` reuse,\n  reconfigure-apply function, barrier field on box_t.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch scheduler check, reconfigure\n  task path, yield-and-requeue logic, `reconfigure` box kind.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_reconfigure` entry\n  point for language specs.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` — emit a reconfigure event so\n  the JSONL transcript records every mutation.\n- `issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md` —\n  sister issue; create_box / connect are the additive\n  primitives, this is the mutative primitive.\n- `issues/318a-per-call-output-format-threads-to-push.md` —\n  per-cell ordering tags; the third ring may want to participate\n  in the same ordering scheme so reconfigures land at the right\n  moment relative to in-flight values.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Per-box vs per-port ring placement.** A box-level config\n  ring (one per box) reads cleanest because the message\n  concerns the whole box. A per-port \"third ring\" would mirror\n  the native/JSON pairing exactly but raises \"which port's\n  config wins?\" questions. The proposal above is per-box; flag\n  this for confirmation before the slot-store work lands.\n- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and config-pops.**\n  When the box has BOTH pending values on input ports AND a\n  pending reconfigure, which does the dispatch consume next?\n  Options:\n    1. Strict FIFO across all four channels (port-native, port-\n       JSON, port-config-not-applicable, box-config) using\n       issue 318a's per-cell ordering tags.\n    2. Reconfigures get priority — drain them before any fire,\n       so a fire always runs under the latest config.\n    3. Reconfigures get NO priority — they wait their turn in\n       the same FIFO, so values already in flight get processed\n       under the old config they were generated against.\n   Option 2 is \"configuration is always current\"; option 3 is\n   \"values keep their original interpretation.\"\n- **Yield-and-requeue target end.** The user described it as\n  \"put yourself back at the end\" *and* \"the beginning\" in the\n  same sentence. End-of-queue is fairer (other tasks get to\n  run before this one retries); beginning is faster recovery\n  (this task retries soonest). End is probably the right\n  default but worth confirming.\n- **Scope of reconfigurable fields in slice 1.** The proposal\n  is \"cheap fields + connections[]; reject changes to id /\n  kind / inputs[] with a clean diagnostic.\" Confirm or expand.\n- **What if the reconfigure JSON is invalid?** Hard-error\n  (box dies and dispatches a failure event), or silently\n  reject the reconfigure and continue with the old config?\n  Lean toward hard-error — matches the project's \"errors over\n  fallbacks\" rule.\n- **Recursive reconfigure / loop guard.** A box reconfigures\n  itself, the new config has a `reconfigure` step that pushes\n  another config, etc. Should the runtime cap reconfigure\n  depth per box per run, or trust the user?\n- **Visibility of in-flight values when port shape changes.**\n  If a future slice supports adding/removing/renaming input\n  ports, what happens to values already sitting in the\n  affected port's ring? Drain and discard, drain and re-queue\n  on the renamed port, hard-error if drain reveals values?\n- **Interaction with the compile pipeline.** The compile\n  artifact (issue 309) currently bakes the box JSONs into the\n  built program. If a box can be reconfigured at runtime,\n  the compiled artifact has to either (a) emit reconfigure\n  hooks for every box, or (b) be opt-in per box. Option (b)\n  feels right but means a per-box `reconfigurable: true` flag\n  in the JSON.\n- **Connections array swap-and-replace.** A reconfigure that\n  rewrites `connections[]` wholesale means the existing array\n  goes away and a new one takes its place. issue 319d\n  established the copy-and-publish atomic pattern for\n  growing the array — does the wholesale-replace use the\n  same pattern (allocate new, atomic-store, park the old on\n  the stale list), or a different one?\n- **Reconfigure event in the JSONL transcript.** The transcript\n  is the run's audit log; a reconfigure that changes box\n  behavior mid-run should be visible there. Event shape:\n  `{kind: \"reconfigure\", box: \"<id>\", before: {...}, after:\n  {...}, at_task: <id>}` — full before/after? Diff only? Just\n  the id and timestamp?\n- **Composability with issue 248 encapsulation.** Could a\n  reconfigure change a box from BOX_CALL to BOX_MAP, requiring\n  the encapsulation pass to re-run on that one box?\n  Structurally hard — the load-time pass assumes single-pass\n  flat-graph construction. Flag this as out-of-scope unless\n  there's a compelling use case.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe user's original phrasing for the yield-and-requeue\nmechanism, preserved verbatim because it captures the intent\nbetter than any rephrase:\n\n> \"I'm thinking we'll need to put an atomic spinlock on the\n> entire box that, instead of spinning, will ask the waiting\n> thread to re-add the box to the end of the thread pool queue.\n> When we're done re-configuring the box, the spinlock is\n> removed. It's not quite a spinlock actually... but you get\n> the idea, it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\n> yourself back at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n\nThe \"end\" / \"beginning\" choice in the same sentence is the\nopen question above; both are defensible. The deeper signal —\nthat the synchronization primitive is *cooperative with the\nscheduler* rather than *adversarial to it* — is the design\nnote that should carry through to the implementation.\n",

          "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via third input ring\n\n## Status\nopen · design draft; a handful of open questions remain but the\nshape is settled enough to scope an implementation slice\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses the\nbox's JSON once (`parse_box_file` in `src/010-graph-loader.c`),\nfills in every field — `kind`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, the routing\nshape, the input port list, the connections array — and the\ndispatch layer (`src/012-dispatch.c`) walks that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes those fields.\n\nThe two paths the runtime already has to \"change the graph while\nit's running\" — issue 319's `create_box` / `connect` primitives,\nand issue 248's load-time encapsulation splice — both **add** to\nthe graph; they never **rewrite** a box that already exists. A\nbox is the box it was born as.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\n**reconfigured** mid-run. A new configuration arrives as a\nJSON-shaped message inside the normal input stream, on any input\nport; the worker that's gathering inputs for the next fire\nencounters the reconfigure tag, applies it, and continues\ngathering under the new config before firing.\n\n## Concept\n\nEvery input slot grows a **third ring** alongside the native +\nJSON pair from issue 312. The third ring carries one kind of\nmessage only — a JSON object **exactly matching the box's own\nJSON schema**, the same shape a `boxes/<id>.json` file holds at\nload. Any input port can carry reconfigure messages; producers\npush to whichever port makes sense for their fan-in topology, and\nthe dispatch layer treats reconfigure cells as a peer to native\nand JSON cells.\n\nThe per-cell **ring-selector tag** (the bookkeeping that already\ntells the consumer \"this cell came in on the native ring, or the\nJSON ring\" — issue 312's dual-ring `which_ring` flag, extended\nthrough issue 318a's per-call ordering) grows a third value:\n**reconfigure**. When the consumer's input-gathering walks a port\nand sees the next cell tagged `reconfigure`, it doesn't push the\nbytes into an input buffer for the box function; it interprets\nthem as a re-parse of the box's own JSON.\n\n### The mixed-stream scenario\n\nImagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The\ndispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells\nin turn:\n\n```\nport_a → native value (popped, retained)\nport_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)\nport_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)\nport_c → RECONFIGURE\n```\n\nThe worker:\n\n1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.\n2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second\n   in worker-local stack buffers.\n3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails\n   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker\n   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;\n   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is\n   done.\n4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the\n   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory\n   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in\n   place.\n5. Releases the YARQ barrier.\n6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more\n   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port\n   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.\n7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained\n   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the\n   new config expects.\n\nThe fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure\nis a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering\nand the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.\n\n### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?\n\nThe retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the\nnew config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,\nremove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the\nretained values still map by port name. If the new config renames\na port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the\nrename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence\nrecorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port\nremoval mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get\ndropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.\n\n## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier\n\nA reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers\nfiring the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,\nno other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new\n`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.\n\nA spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing\ncaptures the intended shape exactly:\n\n> \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back\n> at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n\n**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this\nprimitive. Mechanism:\n\n- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).\n- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the\n  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker\n  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue\n  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.\n  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from\n  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately\n  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other\n  pending work runs first.\n- **Release**: atomic store of 0.\n\nThe cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each\ncontended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization\nprimitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than\n*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does\nbest (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the\nbox record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue\n319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own\ncopy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding\nthose into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't\ninterleave dangerously when both fire at once.\n\n## Schema for the third-ring message\n\nA message on the third ring is a JSON object identical in shape\nto what `parse_box_file` parses today:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\":      \"my_box\",          // must match the target box\n    \"kind\":    \"call\",            // any kind, including a kind change\n    \"lang\":    \"lua\",\n    \"ref\":     \"lib/new_impl.lua\",\n    \"fn\":      \"new_handler\",\n    \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n    \"inputs\":  [\n        { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n        { \"name\": \"y\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true }\n    ],\n    \"connections\": [\n        { \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"value\" }\n    ]\n}\n```\n\nThe `id` field MUST match the target box (a safety check; mixed\nids hard-error). Every other field is the new state. Fields\nabsent get default treatment (same as a freshly-parsed box file).\nThe schema validator runs in full — a malformed reconfigure\ncan't half-apply.\n\n## Reconfigure semantics — what changes\n\n**Slice 1 supports every field comprehensively.** No \"cheap vs\nmedium vs expensive\" split; the same machinery that parses a box\nat load time runs against the in-memory reconfigure buffer and\napplies the result wholesale. Splitting the work into easy /\nhard tiers means coming back later to finish, and round-trips\nare where details get forgotten.\n\nThat means slice 1 has to handle, in one pass:\n\n- **Cheap-field rewrites** (lang / ref / fn / routing.kind /\n  routing.comparand / routing.weights / output_capacity /\n  returns / cflags / link_libs / headers) — pointer assignments\n  on the live record. The arena holds the strings; the rewrite\n  swaps pointers.\n- **Connections array swap** — uses the same copy-and-publish\n  pattern issue 319d established for `box_add_connection`,\n  except wholesale-replace instead of append. Old array goes to\n  the graph's stale list and is freed at graph_destroy.\n- **Input port shape changes** — adding, removing, renaming\n  ports. Triggers:\n  - Slot-store growth or shrink (issue 319b's slot growth in\n    the additive case; symmetric drain-and-release in the\n    removal case).\n  - Re-resolution of every producer's connection\n    `to_input_idx` against the new port names.\n  - Rebinding of retained pre-pop values via the old-name →\n    new-name correspondence (rename allowed; removal of a\n    retained port drops its values to the JSONL transcript).\n- **Kind changes** (BOX_CALL ↔ BOX_WRITE, etc.) — the dispatch\n  table is already keyed off kind; flipping the field flips\n  which branch runs next. BOX_MAP is the special case (would\n  re-trigger the encapsulation pass) — see open questions.\n\nA reconfigure that hands in an invalid spec is a hard error: the\nbox dies, the JSONL transcript records the failure with the\noffending JSON, the run terminates. No silent reject-and-continue\n— matches the project's \"errors over fallbacks\" rule.\n\n## How the third ring gets fed\n\nTwo complementary mechanisms, symmetric with issue 319's\ncreate_box / connect:\n\n1. **A `reconfigure` box kind** — one input port `spec` carries\n   the box-JSON, one field (or a second input port) names the\n   target box id and the target's input port to push the message\n   onto. On fire, the box pushes the reconfigure-tagged cell onto\n   the target slot's third ring.\n\n2. **A runtime API** —\n   `runtime_reconfigure(target_id, target_port, json, size, err)`\n   — that any language spec's invoke can call. Same shape as\n   `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` from issue 319d.\n\nA box can reconfigure itself by pushing onto its own third ring;\nthe next time the dispatch gathers inputs for this box, the\nreconfigure lands.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Extend the per-cell ring-selector tag** in\n   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. The dual-ring slot's `which_ring`\n   field grows a third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`).\n2. **Add the third ring to every input slot.** Same shape as the\n   JSON ring (variable-size cells, large-value-heap backed). Cell\n   capacity per slot is small (8? 16?) — reconfigures shouldn't\n   pile up faster than the box can apply them.\n3. **Add the YARQ barrier field** to `box_t`\n   (`src/010-graph-loader.h`). One `_Atomic int`;\n   acquire / release / yield-and-requeue helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.\n4. **Fold issue 319d's `box_add_connection` into YARQ.** Today\n   it has its own copy-and-publish atomic dance; sharing the\n   barrier keeps mutation paths from racing.\n5. **Refactor `parse_box_file`** so the JSON-parsing core\n   accepts an in-memory buffer (not just a file path). The\n   reconfigure path uses the same parser; one schema, one\n   validator, two entry points.\n6. **Add a `reconfigure_apply` function** in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c` that takes a parsed box record and\n   merges it into a live box, handling port-rename via name\n   correspondence, slot growth / shrink, connection array swap,\n   and producer re-resolution.\n7. **Teach the dispatch's input-gather loop** to peek the\n   ring-selector tag and, on `RING_RECONFIGURE`, acquire YARQ,\n   retain pre-popped values, apply the reconfigure, release\n   YARQ, then resume gathering under the new shape.\n8. **Implement the `reconfigure` box kind** in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c` and add parse-side support in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`.\n9. **Add `runtime_reconfigure`** to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.\n10. **JSONL event** for every reconfigure: full before / after\n    (or at least the changed fields), task id, worker id.\n    Reconfigures change behaviour mid-run; the audit log must\n    show them.\n11. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-routing/` — comparator routing\n      flipped to iterator routing mid-run; downstream\n      connections fire on the new branches.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn/` — same box, different\n      function on the same lang; output changes mid-stream.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape/` — input port\n      added (slot store growth) and renamed (producer\n      re-resolution); pre-popped retained values still land on\n      the right inputs.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind/` — BOX_CALL flipped to\n      BOX_WRITE; subsequent fires write to disk instead of\n      invoking a function.\n    - `tests/maps/320-yarq-contended/` — two reconfigure-feeders\n      race on the same target; both reconfigures land, neither\n      is lost, the box behaves correctly after both apply.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — ring-selector tag, third ring\n  storage per slot.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` refactor,\n  `reconfigure_apply`, YARQ field on box_t.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch input-gather changes, YARQ\n  acquire / release / yield-and-requeue, `reconfigure` box kind.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_reconfigure` entry\n  point for language specs.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` — reconfigure event emission.\n- `issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md` —\n  sister issue: create_box / connect are the additive\n  primitives, this is the mutative primitive.\n- `issues/318a-per-call-output-format-threads-to-push.md` and\n  `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the per-cell\n  ring-selector mechanism the third ring extends.\n- `issues/319b-slot-store-growth.md` — slot growth in the\n  additive port-add direction; symmetric shrink is new.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and reconfigure-pops.**\n  The mixed-stream scenario above shows reconfigure cells\n  interleaved with value cells on the same input port; the\n  consumer encounters them in producer-push order. Is that\n  ordering strict per port, or strict across all ports of the\n  box (so a reconfigure on port A blocks pops from port B until\n  it's applied)? The cleanest reading of \"ordered same as all\n  the other inputs\" is **strict per port**, with the consumer\n  applying reconfigures as it hits them. Across-port ordering\n  would need a per-box sequence number on every cell, which is\n  more bookkeeping than the user described.\n- **Slot growth and shrink for input port changes.** Issue 319b\n  defined slot growth in the create_box direction; this issue\n  extends it to the within-a-box direction (adding a new port\n  to an existing box). Shrink — releasing a slot when a port\n  goes away — is genuinely new and needs an issue of its own,\n  or rolled in here as part of slice 1.\n- **Port-rename correspondence.** When a reconfigure renames\n  port `x` to `y`, the rename is unambiguous if both\n  configurations declare the same number of ports in the same\n  position-order. When the port count or order changes too,\n  the correspondence isn't obvious — fall back to name match\n  (ports keeping their names get rebound by name; ports\n  whose names no longer exist get dropped). Worth documenting\n  precisely so the implementation behaves consistently.\n- **Recursive reconfigure / loop guard.** A box reconfigures\n  itself, the new config includes a producer that pushes\n  another reconfigure, etc. Cap per-box reconfigure depth per\n  run? Or trust the user and rely on integration tests to\n  surface infinite loops?\n- **BOX_MAP as a reconfigure target / source.** Changing a\n  BOX_CALL to a BOX_MAP would require re-running the\n  encapsulation pass on just this one box. The load-time pass\n  assumes single-pass flat-graph construction; running it\n  per-box at runtime is structurally awkward. Probably\n  out-of-scope unless a clear use case appears. Hard-error\n  the BOX_MAP transition in slice 1.\n- **Reconfigure visible in the compile artifact.** Issue 309's\n  compile pipeline bakes the box JSONs into the built program.\n  Reconfigure machinery is runtime-only by nature, but the\n  compile artifact needs to keep the YARQ barrier field, the\n  third ring per slot, and the in-memory parser path linked in\n  regardless. Probably means slice 1 ships always-on; the\n  per-box opt-out flag (`reconfigurable: false`) is a future\n  refinement if anyone needs the slot-store savings.\n- **JSONL event shape.** Full before/after JSON is the most\n  faithful audit trail; diff-only is smaller; \"just record\n  the new state\" loses the before. Default: full before/after\n  so the transcript is self-describing without cross-event\n  reasoning.\n- **Pre-popped retained values that don't fit the new schema.**\n  Reconfigure renames port `x` → `y` and adds port `z`; the\n  worker had already popped a value for `x` before hitting\n  the reconfigure cell. Rebind by name correspondence? If\n  the new config has no port `y` after a removal-rename\n  (effectively a delete), the retained value goes to the\n  JSONL transcript as a discard event and the box still fires\n  with whatever the new shape requires.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across two passes. The first\ndraft (now discarded) proposed a per-box config inbox treated as\na separate scheduling unit — i.e. reconfigure as its own task,\ndistinct from any fire. The user redirected to **per-port**\nplacement, with reconfigure cells riding the same ring-selector\ntag mechanism that already distinguishes native from JSON cells\non each port. The mixed-stream scenario described in the\n\"Concept\" section is the user's clarifying example.\n\nThe YARQ name landed in the same conversation. The user's\nphrasing:\n\n> \"yield and requeue works. yarq for short. YARQ what a weird\n> name!! I want to name my dog yarq. BARK BARK says yarq, haha\n> what a cute puppy ^_^\"\n\nSo: YARQ in the code, YARQ in the docs, and somewhere out there\na dog who answers to the same name. Both kinds of YARQ go where\nthe scheduler tells them — that's the joke and that's the\nmechanism.\n\nOn the YARQ requeue target (tail vs head of the pool queue),\nthe user's instruction was:\n\n> \"put it at the part of the queue that has the longest time\n> until running again. I think that's the end of the queue, but\n> you can decide. The tip of the tail maybe? snakes move\n> forward after all...\"\n\nEnd-of-queue (the \"tip of the tail\") is the chosen default.\nThe contended worker won't immediately re-collide with whoever\nis inside the barrier; the scheduler gets a chance to drain\nother pending work first.\n\nOn scoping, the user's direction was decisive:\n\n> \"they should all be configurable with the same interface,\n> so... don't split up the work in that way. Just do it\n> comprehensively the first time so we don't forget anything\n> on the return trip.\"\n\nSlice 1 covers every reconfigurable field — including the\nport-shape changes that require slot store growth / shrink and\nproducer re-resolution. No tiered \"cheap then medium then\nexpensive\" split; one comprehensive pass.\n",
