    "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via third input ring\n\n## Status\nopen · design draft; a handful of open questions remain but the\nshape is settled enough to scope an implementation slice\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses the\nbox's JSON once (`parse_box_file` in `src/010-graph-loader.c`),\nfills in every field — `kind`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, the routing\nshape, the input port list, the connections array — and the\ndispatch layer (`src/012-dispatch.c`) walks that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes those fields.\n\nThe two paths the runtime already has to \"change the graph while\nit's running\" — issue 319's `create_box` / `connect` primitives,\nand issue 248's load-time encapsulation splice — both **add** to\nthe graph; they never **rewrite** a box that already exists. A\nbox is the box it was born as.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\n**reconfigured** mid-run. A new configuration arrives as a\nJSON-shaped message inside the normal input stream, on any input\nport; the worker that's gathering inputs for the next fire\nencounters the reconfigure tag, applies it, and continues\ngathering under the new config before firing.\n\n## Concept\n\nEvery input slot grows a **third ring** alongside the native +\nJSON pair from issue 312. The third ring carries one kind of\nmessage only — a JSON object **exactly matching the box's own\nJSON schema**, the same shape a `boxes/<id>.json` file holds at\nload. Any input port can carry reconfigure messages; producers\npush to whichever port makes sense for their fan-in topology, and\nthe dispatch layer treats reconfigure cells as a peer to native\nand JSON cells.\n\nThe per-cell **ring-selector tag** (the bookkeeping that already\ntells the consumer \"this cell came in on the native ring, or the\nJSON ring\" — issue 312's dual-ring `which_ring` flag, extended\nthrough issue 318a's per-call ordering) grows a third value:\n**reconfigure**. When the consumer's input-gathering walks a port\nand sees the next cell tagged `reconfigure`, it doesn't push the\nbytes into an input buffer for the box function; it interprets\nthem as a re-parse of the box's own JSON.\n\n### The mixed-stream scenario\n\nImagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The\ndispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells\nin turn:\n\n```\nport_a → native value (popped, retained)\nport_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)\nport_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)\nport_c → RECONFIGURE\n```\n\nThe worker:\n\n1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.\n2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second\n   in worker-local stack buffers.\n3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails\n   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker\n   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;\n   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is\n   done.\n4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the\n   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory\n   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in\n   place.\n5. Releases the YARQ barrier.\n6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more\n   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port\n   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.\n7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained\n   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the\n   new config expects.\n\nThe fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure\nis a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering\nand the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.\n\n### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?\n\nThe retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the\nnew config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,\nremove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the\nretained values still map by port name. If the new config renames\na port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the\nrename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence\nrecorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port\nremoval mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get\ndropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.\n\n## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier\n\nA reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers\nfiring the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,\nno other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new\n`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.\n\nA spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing\ncaptures the intended shape exactly:\n\n> \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back\n> at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n\n**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this\nprimitive. Mechanism:\n\n- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).\n- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the\n  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker\n  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue\n  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.\n  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from\n  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately\n  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other\n  pending work runs first.\n- **Release**: atomic store of 0.\n\nThe cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each\ncontended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization\nprimitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than\n*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does\nbest (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the\nbox record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue\n319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own\ncopy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding\nthose into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't\ninterleave dangerously when both fire at once.\n\n## Schema for the third-ring message\n\nA message on the third ring is a JSON object identical in shape\nto what `parse_box_file` parses today:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\":      \"my_box\",          // must match the target box\n    \"kind\":    \"call\",            // any kind, including a kind change\n    \"lang\":    \"lua\",\n    \"ref\":     \"lib/new_impl.lua\",\n    \"fn\":      \"new_handler\",\n    \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n    \"inputs\":  [\n        { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n        { \"name\": \"y\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true }\n    ],\n    \"connections\": [\n        { \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"value\" }\n    ]\n}\n```\n\nThe `id` field MUST match the target box (a safety check; mixed\nids hard-error). Every other field is the new state. Fields\nabsent get default treatment (same as a freshly-parsed box file).\nThe schema validator runs in full — a malformed reconfigure\ncan't half-apply.\n\n## Reconfigure semantics — what changes\n\n**Slice 1 supports every field comprehensively.** No \"cheap vs\nmedium vs expensive\" split; the same machinery that parses a box\nat load time runs against the in-memory reconfigure buffer and\napplies the result wholesale. Splitting the work into easy /\nhard tiers means coming back later to finish, and round-trips\nare where details get forgotten.\n\nThat means slice 1 has to handle, in one pass:\n\n- **Cheap-field rewrites** (lang / ref / fn / routing.kind /\n  routing.comparand / routing.weights / output_capacity /\n  returns / cflags / link_libs / headers) — pointer assignments\n  on the live record. The arena holds the strings; the rewrite\n  swaps pointers.\n- **Connections array swap** — uses the same copy-and-publish\n  pattern issue 319d established for `box_add_connection`,\n  except wholesale-replace instead of append. Old array goes to\n  the graph's stale list and is freed at graph_destroy.\n- **Input port shape changes** — adding, removing, renaming\n  ports. Triggers:\n  - Slot-store growth or shrink (issue 319b's slot growth in\n    the additive case; symmetric drain-and-release in the\n    removal case).\n  - Re-resolution of every producer's connection\n    `to_input_idx` against the new port names.\n  - Rebinding of retained pre-pop values via the old-name →\n    new-name correspondence (rename allowed; removal of a\n    retained port drops its values to the JSONL transcript).\n- **Kind changes** (BOX_CALL ↔ BOX_WRITE, etc.) — the dispatch\n  table is already keyed off kind; flipping the field flips\n  which branch runs next. BOX_MAP is the special case (would\n  re-trigger the encapsulation pass) — see open questions.\n\nA reconfigure that hands in an invalid spec is a hard error: the\nbox dies, the JSONL transcript records the failure with the\noffending JSON, the run terminates. No silent reject-and-continue\n— matches the project's \"errors over fallbacks\" rule.\n\n## How the third ring gets fed\n\nTwo complementary mechanisms, symmetric with issue 319's\ncreate_box / connect:\n\n1. **A `reconfigure` box kind** — one input port `spec` carries\n   the box-JSON, one field (or a second input port) names the\n   target box id and the target's input port to push the message\n   onto. On fire, the box pushes the reconfigure-tagged cell onto\n   the target slot's third ring.\n\n2. **A runtime API** —\n   `runtime_reconfigure(target_id, target_port, json, size, err)`\n   — that any language spec's invoke can call. Same shape as\n   `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` from issue 319d.\n\nA box can reconfigure itself by pushing onto its own third ring;\nthe next time the dispatch gathers inputs for this box, the\nreconfigure lands.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Extend the per-cell ring-selector tag** in\n   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. The dual-ring slot's `which_ring`\n   field grows a third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`).\n2. **Add the third ring to every input slot.** Same shape as the\n   JSON ring (variable-size cells, large-value-heap backed). Cell\n   capacity per slot is small (8? 16?) — reconfigures shouldn't\n   pile up faster than the box can apply them.\n3. **Add the YARQ barrier field** to `box_t`\n   (`src/010-graph-loader.h`). One `_Atomic int`;\n   acquire / release / yield-and-requeue helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.\n4. **Fold issue 319d's `box_add_connection` into YARQ.** Today\n   it has its own copy-and-publish atomic dance; sharing the\n   barrier keeps mutation paths from racing.\n5. **Refactor `parse_box_file`** so the JSON-parsing core\n   accepts an in-memory buffer (not just a file path). The\n   reconfigure path uses the same parser; one schema, one\n   validator, two entry points.\n6. **Add a `reconfigure_apply` function** in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c` that takes a parsed box record and\n   merges it into a live box, handling port-rename via name\n   correspondence, slot growth / shrink, connection array swap,\n   and producer re-resolution.\n7. **Teach the dispatch's input-gather loop** to peek the\n   ring-selector tag and, on `RING_RECONFIGURE`, acquire YARQ,\n   retain pre-popped values, apply the reconfigure, release\n   YARQ, then resume gathering under the new shape.\n8. **Implement the `reconfigure` box kind** in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c` and add parse-side support in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`.\n9. **Add `runtime_reconfigure`** to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.\n10. **JSONL event** for every reconfigure: full before / after\n    (or at least the changed fields), task id, worker id.\n    Reconfigures change behaviour mid-run; the audit log must\n    show them.\n11. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-routing/` — comparator routing\n      flipped to iterator routing mid-run; downstream\n      connections fire on the new branches.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn/` — same box, different\n      function on the same lang; output changes mid-stream.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape/` — input port\n      added (slot store growth) and renamed (producer\n      re-resolution); pre-popped retained values still land on\n      the right inputs.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind/` — BOX_CALL flipped to\n      BOX_WRITE; subsequent fires write to disk instead of\n      invoking a function.\n    - `tests/maps/320-yarq-contended/` — two reconfigure-feeders\n      race on the same target; both reconfigures land, neither\n      is lost, the box behaves correctly after both apply.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — ring-selector tag, third ring\n  storage per slot.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` refactor,\n  `reconfigure_apply`, YARQ field on box_t.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch input-gather changes, YARQ\n  acquire / release / yield-and-requeue, `reconfigure` box kind.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_reconfigure` entry\n  point for language specs.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` — reconfigure event emission.\n- `issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md` —\n  sister issue: create_box / connect are the additive\n  primitives, this is the mutative primitive.\n- `issues/318a-per-call-output-format-threads-to-push.md` and\n  `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the per-cell\n  ring-selector mechanism the third ring extends.\n- `issues/319b-slot-store-growth.md` — slot growth in the\n  additive port-add direction; symmetric shrink is new.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and reconfigure-pops.**\n  The mixed-stream scenario above shows reconfigure cells\n  interleaved with value cells on the same input port; the\n  consumer encounters them in producer-push order. Is that\n  ordering strict per port, or strict across all ports of the\n  box (so a reconfigure on port A blocks pops from port B until\n  it's applied)? The cleanest reading of \"ordered same as all\n  the other inputs\" is **strict per port**, with the consumer\n  applying reconfigures as it hits them. Across-port ordering\n  would need a per-box sequence number on every cell, which is\n  more bookkeeping than the user described.\n- **Slot growth and shrink for input port changes.** Issue 319b\n  defined slot growth in the create_box direction; this issue\n  extends it to the within-a-box direction (adding a new port\n  to an existing box). Shrink — releasing a slot when a port\n  goes away — is genuinely new and needs an issue of its own,\n  or rolled in here as part of slice 1.\n- **Port-rename correspondence.** When a reconfigure renames\n  port `x` to `y`, the rename is unambiguous if both\n  configurations declare the same number of ports in the same\n  position-order. When the port count or order changes too,\n  the correspondence isn't obvious — fall back to name match\n  (ports keeping their names get rebound by name; ports\n  whose names no longer exist get dropped). Worth documenting\n  precisely so the implementation behaves consistently.\n- **Recursive reconfigure / loop guard.** A box reconfigures\n  itself, the new config includes a producer that pushes\n  another reconfigure, etc. Cap per-box reconfigure depth per\n  run? Or trust the user and rely on integration tests to\n  surface infinite loops?\n- **BOX_MAP as a reconfigure target / source.** Changing a\n  BOX_CALL to a BOX_MAP would require re-running the\n  encapsulation pass on just this one box. The load-time pass\n  assumes single-pass flat-graph construction; running it\n  per-box at runtime is structurally awkward. Probably\n  out-of-scope unless a clear use case appears. Hard-error\n  the BOX_MAP transition in slice 1.\n- **Reconfigure visible in the compile artifact.** Issue 309's\n  compile pipeline bakes the box JSONs into the built program.\n  Reconfigure machinery is runtime-only by nature, but the\n  compile artifact needs to keep the YARQ barrier field, the\n  third ring per slot, and the in-memory parser path linked in\n  regardless. Probably means slice 1 ships always-on; the\n  per-box opt-out flag (`reconfigurable: false`) is a future\n  refinement if anyone needs the slot-store savings.\n- **JSONL event shape.** Full before/after JSON is the most\n  faithful audit trail; diff-only is smaller; \"just record\n  the new state\" loses the before. Default: full before/after\n  so the transcript is self-describing without cross-event\n  reasoning.\n- **Pre-popped retained values that don't fit the new schema.**\n  Reconfigure renames port `x` → `y` and adds port `z`; the\n  worker had already popped a value for `x` before hitting\n  the reconfigure cell. Rebind by name correspondence? If\n  the new config has no port `y` after a removal-rename\n  (effectively a delete), the retained value goes to the\n  JSONL transcript as a discard event and the box still fires\n  with whatever the new shape requires.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across two passes. The first\ndraft (now discarded) proposed a per-box config inbox treated as\na separate scheduling unit — i.e. reconfigure as its own task,\ndistinct from any fire. The user redirected to **per-port**\nplacement, with reconfigure cells riding the same ring-selector\ntag mechanism that already distinguishes native from JSON cells\non each port. The mixed-stream scenario described in the\n\"Concept\" section is the user's clarifying example.\n\nThe YARQ name landed in the same conversation. The user's\nphrasing:\n\n> \"yield and requeue works. yarq for short. YARQ what a weird\n> name!! I want to name my dog yarq. BARK BARK says yarq, haha\n> what a cute puppy ^_^\"\n\nSo: YARQ in the code, YARQ in the docs, and somewhere out there\na dog who answers to the same name. Both kinds of YARQ go where\nthe scheduler tells them — that's the joke and that's the\nmechanism.\n\nOn the YARQ requeue target (tail vs head of the pool queue),\nthe user's instruction was:\n\n> \"put it at the part of the queue that has the longest time\n> until running again. I think that's the end of the queue, but\n> you can decide. The tip of the tail maybe? snakes move\n> forward after all...\"\n\nEnd-of-queue (the \"tip of the tail\") is the chosen default.\nThe contended worker won't immediately re-collide with whoever\nis inside the barrier; the scheduler gets a chance to drain\nother pending work first.\n\nOn scoping, the user's direction was decisive:\n\n> \"they should all be configurable with the same interface,\n> so... don't split up the work in that way. Just do it\n> comprehensively the first time so we don't forget anything\n> on the return trip.\"\n\nSlice 1 covers every reconfigurable field — including the\nport-shape changes that require slot store growth / shrink and\nproducer re-resolution. No tiered \"cheap then medium then\nexpensive\" split; one comprehensive pass.\n",

        "input":{
          "content":"---\nname: YARQ and the third input ring (issue 320)\ndescription: Per-port third ring carries box-JSON reconfigure messages; YARQ (yield-and-requeue) is the project name for the cooperative-with-scheduler barrier that protects in-place box mutation\ntype: project\n---\n\nIssue 320 introduces two pieces of project vocabulary that\nrecur in other code-paths:\n\n**YARQ** (yield-and-requeue) — the synchronization primitive\nthat protects in-place box mutation. Acquire is a CAS from 0\nto 1 on a per-box atomic word. On acquire failure, the\ncontended worker does NOT busy-wait — it re-submits its own\ntask to the **tail** of the pool queue and returns, letting\nthe scheduler drain other work first. Same barrier is acquired\nby every path that mutates a box's record (reconfigure,\nruntime_connect from 319d). The point: synchronization\n*cooperative with the scheduler*, not adversarial to it.\nThe user named it; the joke is that they want to name a dog\nYARQ too.\n\n**The third input ring** — every input slot grows a third ring\nalongside the native + JSON pair from issue 312. Carries\nbox-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages. Per-PORT placement (not\nper-box) — any input port can receive reconfigure cells, and\nthe per-cell ring-selector tag from issue 312/318a grows a\nthird value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`). When the consumer's\ninput-gather encounters a reconfigure cell, it retains\nalready-popped values, acquires YARQ, applies the reconfigure,\nreleases YARQ, and resumes gathering under the new config.\n\n**Why:** Together with issue 319 (create_box / connect),\nissue 320 gives the runtime its full \"graph as a living\nartifact\" surface: 319 grows the graph (additive), 320\nmutates what's already there (in-place). Many future features\nwill read or write these primitives — runtime DSLs, planner\nboxes, the editor's live-mutation feedback path.\n\n**How to apply:** When other issues touch box mutation,\nslot rings, or per-cell ordering, treat YARQ and the third\nring as established vocabulary — don't reinvent the\nprimitive or the name. When the user mentions \"reconfigure,\"\n\"the third ring,\" or YARQ, they mean these specific pieces\nof the design.\n",
          "file_path":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/project_yarq_and_third_ring.md"
        },

    "structuredPatch":[],
    "userModified":false,
    "content":"---\nname: YARQ and the third input ring (issue 320)\ndescription: Per-port third ring carries box-JSON reconfigure messages; YARQ (yield-and-requeue) is the project name for the cooperative-with-scheduler barrier that protects in-place box mutation\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa\n---\nIssue 320 introduces two pieces of project vocabulary that\nrecur in other code-paths:\n\n**YARQ** (yield-and-requeue) — the synchronization primitive\nthat protects in-place box mutation. Acquire is a CAS from 0\nto 1 on a per-box atomic word. On acquire failure, the\ncontended worker does NOT busy-wait — it re-submits its own\ntask to the **tail** of the pool queue and returns, letting\nthe scheduler drain other work first. Same barrier is acquired\nby every path that mutates a box's record (reconfigure,\nruntime_connect from 319d). The point: synchronization\n*cooperative with the scheduler*, not adversarial to it.\nThe user named it; the joke is that they want to name a dog\nYARQ too.\n\n**The third input ring** — every input slot grows a third ring\nalongside the native + JSON pair from issue 312. Carries\nbox-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages. Per-PORT placement (not\nper-box) — any input port can receive reconfigure cells, and\nthe per-cell ring-selector tag from issue 312/318a grows a\nthird value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`). When the consumer's\ninput-gather encounters a reconfigure cell, it retains\nalready-popped values, acquires YARQ, applies the reconfigure,\nreleases YARQ, and resumes gathering under the new config.\n\n**Why:** Together with issue 319 (create_box / connect),\nissue 320 gives the runtime its full \"graph as a living\nartifact\" surface: 319 grows the graph (additive), 320\nmutates what's already there (in-place). Many future features\nwill read or write these primitives — runtime DSLs, planner\nboxes, the editor's live-mutation feedback path.\n\n**How to apply:** When other issues touch box mutation,\nslot rings, or per-cell ordering, treat YARQ and the third\nring as established vocabulary — don't reinvent the\nprimitive or the name. When the user mentions \"reconfigure,\"\n\"the third ring,\" or YARQ, they mean these specific pieces\nof the design.\n",
    "type":"create",
    "filePath":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/project_yarq_and_third_ring.md"
  },

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Issue 320 rewritten and two memories saved (YARQ + third-ring vocabulary, and the no-tier scoping preference). 250 left untouched.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The per-port placement is conceptually stronger than per-box because it preserves the **single ordering scheme** that already governs value cells: if the producer pushes \"value, value, reconfigure, value\" onto a port, the consumer sees them in exactly that order. A per-box config inbox would have been a parallel scheduling channel, requiring its own ordering rules to interleave with port pops. Per-port means \"one fewer thing to coordinate\" — same scheduler, same FIFO, just one extra tag value.\n- YARQ being **cooperative with the scheduler** rather than blocking is the move that unlocks per-cell reconfigure interleaving. A traditional lock would have meant \"while reconfiguring, every other worker that touches this box stalls a thread\"; YARQ means \"while reconfiguring, every other worker that touches this box returns to the pool and gets used for other work.\" The barrier holder doesn't pay a coordination cost; the contended workers each pay one extra scheduler trip. That's a much friendlier accounting for a runtime where thousands of tiny tasks compete for tens of workers.\n- The comprehensive-first-slice preference is the right call **because the cross-cutting plumbing IS the work**. Splitting \"cheap fields now, port-shape changes later\" would mean writing the input-gather → YARQ → reconfigure-apply pipeline twice (once for the easy case, once again with slot-store growth/shrink threaded through). Doing both in one pass means the plumbing is shaped correctly from the start — slot store calls live next to JSON parse calls live next to producer re-resolution calls, all in one function, one mental model.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nThe original todo (315 next, or editor toggles for 248, or pause for review) is still open — pick whichever and I'll keep going. And I'll leave 250 alone until you say it's ready."
      }],

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# Strategem — when a worker can't make progress, return the work to the scheduler, not the worker\n\n## The pattern\n\nIn a runtime where many small tasks compete for a small pool of\nworkers, synchronization primitives that *hold workers* (locks,\nspinlocks, parked threads) silently flip the cost model. The\nworker is the scarce resource; the scheduler is the abundant\ncoordinator. When a worker hits a contended boundary and can't\nmake progress, the cooperative move is to **hand the task back\nto the scheduler** — not to camp on the worker until the\nboundary clears.\n\nYARQ — yield-and-requeue, the primitive that protects in-place\nbox mutation in issue 320 — is the project's name for this\npattern in one specific place. The shape is general: any time a\nworker realises \"I can't finish this task right now,\" it should\nre-submit the task to the pool queue and return its body to the\nscheduler for the next ready unit of work.\n\nThe trap is that locks read as \"the right tool\" because they\nwork fine in the textbook setting where threads are heavyweight\nand tasks are large. Spinlock or mutex, every contended worker\neither burns CPU or parks; either way, the worker is committed\nto that task until it can proceed. When tasks are tiny and\nworkers are few, that commitment is expensive — the worker\ncould have done five other things in the time it spent waiting.\n\nSymptoms that suggest the wrong primitive:\n\n- Many short tasks per second, few workers, occasional bursts\n  of contention. The contended workers stall, throughput\n  collapses for the duration of the burst, then recovers.\n- Priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a lock, a\n  high-priority task can't proceed, the scheduler's careful\n  ordering is silently overridden by the lock contract.\n- Workers parked on locks that other parked workers depend on\n  — the deadlock-prevention dance grows around the locks\n  because the locks themselves don't compose.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen you reach for a lock to protect shared mutable state:\n\n- Ask: **is the worker the scarce resource, or is the lock\n  contract genuinely needed?** If workers are cheap (one per\n  CPU, OS threads, the system is throughput-bounded by CPU),\n  a lock is fine. If workers are scarce (a fixed-size pool\n  smaller than the task fanout, the system is latency-bounded\n  by scheduler trips), prefer YARQ.\n- Express acquire as a non-blocking CAS that **returns failure\n  instead of waiting**. On failure, the worker re-submits the\n  task to the scheduler (usually at the queue tail — see below)\n  and exits the task body. No spin, no park, no waiting.\n- Release is a plain atomic store. The contended worker's\n  re-submission lands later by virtue of scheduler progress,\n  not because the holder signalled.\n- Pick the requeue end thoughtfully. **Tail** is fairer (other\n  pending work runs first, the contended task doesn't\n  immediately re-collide with the holder, the system as a\n  whole keeps draining). **Head** is faster recovery for one\n  task (it retries soonest) at the cost of unfairness to\n  whatever else is queued. Default to tail; choose head only\n  when latency on this one task dominates.\n- Fold every mutation path that touches the shared state into\n  the same YARQ barrier — not just the path you noticed first.\n  If `connect` and `reconfigure` both mutate a box, they share\n  YARQ. The barrier is \"no concurrent mutator,\" not \"no\n  concurrent reconfigure.\"\n\n## Adjacent pattern — async/await is YARQ at the language level\n\nThe async-await primitive in modern runtimes is the same shape\ngeneralised: a coroutine returns `Pending` instead of blocking,\nthe executor reschedules the coroutine when its waker fires.\nThe worker (the executor thread) is freed for other coroutines\nin the meantime. The pattern's name varies — green threads,\nfibers, futures, tasks — but the core invariant is identical:\n**when a unit of work can't proceed, hand the unit back, not\nthe worker.**\n\nYARQ is the lower-level version: no waker, no future. The\ncontended task just re-submits itself and trusts the scheduler\nto eventually try again. Coarser-grained than async-await, but\nstrictly simpler to implement and reason about — there's no\nwaker chain to keep coherent, no `Poll` state machine, just\n\"try, fail, re-submit.\"\n\n## Why this happens\n\nLock-style primitives carry a hidden assumption: *workers are\ninterchangeable units of capacity, plentiful enough that\nholding one is cheap.* That assumption is right for OS threads\non big servers and wrong for almost every other context — task\npools, async executors, embedded runtimes, the actor model. In\nthe wrong context, locks turn the scheduler's careful work\ndistribution into a coordination bottleneck.\n\nThe strategem is to notice which side of that assumption the\nsystem actually lives on. If the scheduler is the load-bearing\npiece — the thing making the system fast — then synchronization\nshould be **expressed in scheduler vocabulary**: re-submit,\nyield, requeue. Locks express it in thread vocabulary: park,\nspin, wake. Mixing the two means the lock's parked workers are\ninvisible to the scheduler, and the scheduler's careful\nordering is broken by waits the lock owns.\n\n## Related issues\n\n- Issue 320 — the box reconfigure path that introduces YARQ to\n  this project.\n- Issue 319d — `box_add_connection`'s copy-and-publish atomic\n  dance; the comprehensive YARQ-folded design subsumes it\n  under the same barrier.\n- Issue 301 / 304 — the pool runner and dispatch layer whose\n  scheduler-vocabulary YARQ speaks. The fact that the pool\n  already routes tasks by re-submission is what makes YARQ\n  cheap to add — the machinery is there.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/yarq-return-the-work-not-the-worker.md"

    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# Strategem — when a worker can't make progress, return the work to the scheduler, not the worker\n\n## The pattern\n\nIn a runtime where many small tasks compete for a small pool of\nworkers, synchronization primitives that *hold workers* (locks,\nspinlocks, parked threads) silently flip the cost model. The\nworker is the scarce resource; the scheduler is the abundant\ncoordinator. When a worker hits a contended boundary and can't\nmake progress, the cooperative move is to **hand the task back\nto the scheduler** — not to camp on the worker until the\nboundary clears.\n\nYARQ — yield-and-requeue, the primitive that protects in-place\nbox mutation in issue 320 — is the project's name for this\npattern in one specific place. The shape is general: any time a\nworker realises \"I can't finish this task right now,\" it should\nre-submit the task to the pool queue and return its body to the\nscheduler for the next ready unit of work.\n\nThe trap is that locks read as \"the right tool\" because they\nwork fine in the textbook setting where threads are heavyweight\nand tasks are large. Spinlock or mutex, every contended worker\neither burns CPU or parks; either way, the worker is committed\nto that task until it can proceed. When tasks are tiny and\nworkers are few, that commitment is expensive — the worker\ncould have done five other things in the time it spent waiting.\n\nSymptoms that suggest the wrong primitive:\n\n- Many short tasks per second, few workers, occasional bursts\n  of contention. The contended workers stall, throughput\n  collapses for the duration of the burst, then recovers.\n- Priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a lock, a\n  high-priority task can't proceed, the scheduler's careful\n  ordering is silently overridden by the lock contract.\n- Workers parked on locks that other parked workers depend on\n  — the deadlock-prevention dance grows around the locks\n  because the locks themselves don't compose.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen you reach for a lock to protect shared mutable state:\n\n- Ask: **is the worker the scarce resource, or is the lock\n  contract genuinely needed?** If workers are cheap (one per\n  CPU, OS threads, the system is throughput-bounded by CPU),\n  a lock is fine. If workers are scarce (a fixed-size pool\n  smaller than the task fanout, the system is latency-bounded\n  by scheduler trips), prefer YARQ.\n- Express acquire as a non-blocking CAS that **returns failure\n  instead of waiting**. On failure, the worker re-submits the\n  task to the scheduler (usually at the queue tail — see below)\n  and exits the task body. No spin, no park, no waiting.\n- Release is a plain atomic store. The contended worker's\n  re-submission lands later by virtue of scheduler progress,\n  not because the holder signalled.\n- Pick the requeue end thoughtfully. **Tail** is fairer (other\n  pending work runs first, the contended task doesn't\n  immediately re-collide with the holder, the system as a\n  whole keeps draining). **Head** is faster recovery for one\n  task (it retries soonest) at the cost of unfairness to\n  whatever else is queued. Default to tail; choose head only\n  when latency on this one task dominates.\n- Fold every mutation path that touches the shared state into\n  the same YARQ barrier — not just the path you noticed first.\n  If `connect` and `reconfigure` both mutate a box, they share\n  YARQ. The barrier is \"no concurrent mutator,\" not \"no\n  concurrent reconfigure.\"\n\n## Adjacent pattern — async/await is YARQ at the language level\n\nThe async-await primitive in modern runtimes is the same shape\ngeneralised: a coroutine returns `Pending` instead of blocking,\nthe executor reschedules the coroutine when its waker fires.\nThe worker (the executor thread) is freed for other coroutines\nin the meantime. The pattern's name varies — green threads,\nfibers, futures, tasks — but the core invariant is identical:\n**when a unit of work can't proceed, hand the unit back, not\nthe worker.**\n\nYARQ is the lower-level version: no waker, no future. The\ncontended task just re-submits itself and trusts the scheduler\nto eventually try again. Coarser-grained than async-await, but\nstrictly simpler to implement and reason about — there's no\nwaker chain to keep coherent, no `Poll` state machine, just\n\"try, fail, re-submit.\"\n\n## Why this happens\n\nLock-style primitives carry a hidden assumption: *workers are\ninterchangeable units of capacity, plentiful enough that\nholding one is cheap.* That assumption is right for OS threads\non big servers and wrong for almost every other context — task\npools, async executors, embedded runtimes, the actor model. In\nthe wrong context, locks turn the scheduler's careful work\ndistribution into a coordination bottleneck.\n\nThe strategem is to notice which side of that assumption the\nsystem actually lives on. If the scheduler is the load-bearing\npiece — the thing making the system fast — then synchronization\nshould be **expressed in scheduler vocabulary**: re-submit,\nyield, requeue. Locks express it in thread vocabulary: park,\nspin, wake. Mixing the two means the lock's parked workers are\ninvisible to the scheduler, and the scheduler's careful\nordering is broken by waits the lock owns.\n\n## Related issues\n\n- Issue 320 — the box reconfigure path that introduces YARQ to\n  this project.\n- Issue 319d — `box_add_connection`'s copy-and-publish atomic\n  dance; the comprehensive YARQ-folded design subsumes it\n  under the same barrier.\n- Issue 301 / 304 — the pool runner and dispatch layer whose\n  scheduler-vocabulary YARQ speaks. The fact that the pool\n  already routes tasks by re-submission is what makes YARQ\n  cheap to add — the machinery is there.\n",

        "content":"1\t# 250 — Routing kind: nonlinearity (squash)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen · design carried forward from issues 240 / 241 / 242 / 243\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\t\n8\tThe routing kinds shipped or queued so far — `plain`, `comparator`,\n9\t`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241), `distributor`\n10\t(242), `multi-band-comparator` (243) — all pick a **branch** and\n11\tforward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**. The\n12\tschema (`src/001-schema.lua`) and the dispatch picker\n13\t(`src/012-dispatch.c`) treat the wire payload as opaque on the\n14\tway out; routing has only ever decided *where* a value goes, never\n15\t*what* it is.\n16\t\n17\tThere is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the way\n18\tthrough. A user who wants the producer's output remapped into a\n19\tnew numeric range — for feeding a UI slider, an audio level, a\n20\theat-map cell — has to insert a dedicated call box that runs a\n21\tLua / C function whose entire job is one arithmetic expression.\n22\tThat's a lot of box for one knob.\n23\t\n24\t## Intended behavior\n25\t\n26\tA new routing kind, **`nonlinearity`** (working name; \"squash\"\n27\tis the alternative — see open questions), maps each numeric value\n28\tthat flows through the box into a bounded output range via a\n29\tchosen unary function (default: logistic sigmoid). The input is\n30\tnormalised against either:\n31\t\n32\t- **`auto`** — the running min and max observed on this wire\n33\t  during the current run, OR\n34\t- **`fixed`** — two user-supplied numeric bounds (`min`, `max`).\n35\t\n36\tAfter normalisation the value lands in `[0, 1]` (or `[-1, 1]` for\n37\ttanh — see open questions), the chosen non-linearity is applied,\n38\tand the result is forwarded on the box's single output port. The\n39\trouting kind has exactly one output — fan-out happens the same\n40\tway every other single-output box's fan-out happens (multiple\n41\twires leaving one port).\n42\t\n43\t-- to switch between auto and fixed, the user just needs to supply one or two\n44\t   values - if they supply one, the minimum / maximum is set (the slots in the\n45\t   editor and json are specified as \"min\" or \"max\" so there's no ambiguity about\n46\t   which is which) if they supply both then it's set to \"fixed\" mode as specified.\n47\t   I want there to be only one mode, and auto is the fallback if no fixed values\n48\t   are specified. C treats NULL as zero, so if we wanted to switch back to auto\n49\t   after specifying a value then we'd need to have two separate flags on-top of\n50\t   the min and max value - they basically say \"is this a fixed value or is it\n51\t   an auto value?\" - if the flag is set to fixed, then the value won't change if\n52\t   we receive a higher/lower value. If the flag is unset to auto, then we will\n53\t   adjust the min/max value depending on the min/max value we've received.\n54\t\n55\t-- I don't know the math very well so you'll have to take the lead on this part,\n56\t   but we need a function that will work equally well without normalization.\n57\t   The vision I had, which might be more / less useful for AI purposes than some\n58\t   other kind of function, is essentially an S curve with the minimum and max\n59\t   set to certain values, and whatever inputs come in will get fairly mid value\n60\t   unless they're very clearly a \"strong\" value one way or the other. This is\n61\t   why 0 is selected as the midpoint usually, I think, so that values close to\n62\t   mid, or perhaps a fairly even mixture of two values, can be multiplied and\n63\t   the result will be close to 0. So, maybe we need three - one that has the\n64\t   midpoint at 0, one that has the midpoint at 1, and one that scales? I'm not\n65\t   sure, can you picture why I would want such a thing? If so, can you offer any\n66\t   ideas about how to create intelligent behavior with this structure?\n67\t\n68\t-- what if, for the scaling one, we also added a \"dampening\" effect where each\n69\t   time the function is run, it reduces the min/max a little toward an equilibrium.\n70\t   it doesn't necessarily have to be 0 or 1 or whatever, it should just adjust so\n71\t   that the values become normalized over time. How would we ensure that there's\n72\t   a decent enough gap between the min and max? How would the input values which\n73\t   expand the min/max be considered? We'd re-calculate the curve, probably, right?\n74\t\n75\t### Schema\n76\t\n77\t```json\n78\t\"routing\": {\n79\t  \"kind\":     \"nonlinearity\",\n80\t  \"shape\":    \"sigmoid\",        // or \"tanh\" / \"linear\" / \"softsign\"\n81\t  \"mode\":     \"auto\",           // or \"fixed\"\n82\t  \"min\":      0,                // present only when mode == \"fixed\"\n83\t  \"max\":      100,              // present only when mode == \"fixed\"\n84\t  \"out_range\":\"unit\"            // or \"signed\" — see open questions\n85\t}\n86\t```\n87\t\n88\t`mode: \"auto\"` requires no bounds — the dispatch picker maintains\n89\ta running min and max in two slot-store cells (issue 302) per\n90\tnonlinearity box, updated atomically on each fire. `mode:\n91\t\"fixed\"` requires both `min` and `max`; schema rejects either\n92\tmissing or `min >= max`.\n93\t\n94\t### Branch picker (dispatch layer)\n95\t\n96\tThere is no branch to pick — the kind always emits on the single\n97\toutput. The dispatch code path differs from the existing\n98\trouting kinds in that it **mutates the value** rather than\n99\t**selecting an index**. Pseudocode:\n100\t\n101\t```c\n102\tdouble x = coerce_to_number(value_in);     // hard-error path on failure\n103\t\n104\tdouble lo, hi;\n105\tif (mode == AUTO) {\n106\t    lo = slot_min_load(min_slot);\n107\t    hi = slot_max_load(max_slot);\n108\t    slot_min_cas_update(min_slot, x);      // best-effort widen\n109\t    slot_max_cas_update(max_slot, x);\n110\t} else {\n111\t    lo = box->fixed_min;\n112\t    hi = box->fixed_max;\n113\t}\n114\t\n115\tdouble t = (hi == lo) ? 0.5 : (x - lo) / (hi - lo);   // bootstrap case\n116\t\n117\tdouble y;\n118\tswitch (shape) {\n119\t    case SIGMOID:  y = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k * (t - 0.5))); break;\n120\t    case TANH:     y = tanh(k * (t - 0.5));               break;\n121\t    case LINEAR:   y = t;                                 break;\n122\t    case SOFTSIGN: y = (t - 0.5) / (1.0 + fabs(t - 0.5)); break;\n123\t}\n124\t\n125\temit_number(out_port, y);\n126\t```\n127\t\n128\t`k` is a steepness constant (see open questions). The bootstrap\n129\tcase (`hi == lo`, true on the very first value seen under `auto`\n130\tmode) maps to `t = 0.5` so the sigmoid emits 0.5 — a defensible\n131\t\"no information yet\" value.\n132\t\n133\t-- what if we take the midpoint of the min/max and we say \"if above, then do\n134\t   this branch. If below, then this branch.\" That way, we're saying which path\n135\t   the value takes while also including a \"strength\" or \"magnitude\" value in the\n136\t   modified output value. Is that a good idea?\n137\t\n138\t### Coercion and the hard-error path\n139\t\n140\tThe kind operates on numbers only. The dispatch picker tries to\n141\tcoerce the inbound value:\n142\t\n143\t- **number on the wire** — used directly.\n144\t- **string** — parsed as a number (`strtod`). On parse failure,\n145\t  the box raises a hard error matching the project's \"errors over\n146\t  fallbacks\" rule. The error names the box id, the offending\n147\t  string, and the wire it arrived on.\n148\t- **other types** (boolean, blob, sentinel) — hard error,\n149\t  unconditional. No silent coercion.\n150\t\n151\t-- C treats 1 and 0 as true and false, so keep an eye out for that... Make sure\n152\t   there's a test case for that.\n153\t\n154\tHard errors stop the box from emitting. No \"skip on bad input\"\n155\tfallback — that's a warning shape this project treats as an\n156\terror.\n157\t\n158\t### Inspector UI\n159\t\n160\tMode dropdown on the routing inspector gains a `nonlinearity`\n161\toption (same row as the other routing kinds).       "content":"# 250 — Routing kind: nonlinearity (squash)\n\n## Status\nopen · design carried forward from issues 240 / 241 / 242 / 243\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe routing kinds shipped or queued so far — `plain`, `comparator`,\n`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241), `distributor`\n(242), `multi-band-comparator` (243) — all pick a **branch** and\nforward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**. The\nschema (`src/001-schema.lua`) and the dispatch picker\n(`src/012-dispatch.c`) treat the wire payload as opaque on the\nway out; routing has only ever decided *where* a value goes, never\n*what* it is.\n\nThere is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the way\nthrough. A user who wants the producer's output remapped into a\nnew numeric range — for feeding a UI slider, an audio level, a\nheat-map cell — has to insert a dedicated call box that runs a\nLua / C function whose entire job is one arithmetic expression.\nThat's a lot of box for one knob.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA new routing kind, **`nonlinearity`** (working name; \"squash\"\nis the alternative — see open questions), maps each numeric value\nthat flows through the box into a bounded output range via a\nchosen unary function (default: logistic sigmoid). The input is\nnormalised against either:\n\n- **`auto`** — the running min and max observed on this wire\n  during the current run, OR\n- **`fixed`** — two user-supplied numeric bounds (`min`, `max`).\n\nAfter normalisation the value lands in `[0, 1]` (or `[-1, 1]` for\ntanh — see open questions), the chosen non-linearity is applied,\nand the result is forwarded on the box's single output port. The\nrouting kind has exactly one output — fan-out happens the same\nway every other single-output box's fan-out happens (multiple\nwires leaving one port).\n\n-- to switch between auto and fixed, the user just needs to supply one or two\n   values - if they supply one, the minimum / maximum is set (the slots in the\n   editor and json are specified as \"min\" or \"max\" so there's no ambiguity about\n   which is which) if they supply both then it's set to \"fixed\" mode as specified.\n   I want there to be only one mode, and auto is the fallback if no fixed values\n   are specified. C treats NULL as zero, so if we wanted to switch back to auto\n   after specifying a value then we'd need to have two separate flags on-top of\n   the min and max value - they basically say \"is this a fixed value or is it\n   an auto value?\" - if the flag is set to fixed, then the value won't change if\n   we receive a higher/lower value. If the flag is unset to auto, then we will\n   adjust the min/max value depending on the min/max value we've received.\n\n-- I don't know the math very well so you'll have to take the lead on this part,\n   but we need a function that will work equally well without normalization.\n   The vision I had, which might be more / less useful for AI purposes than some\n   other kind of function, is essentially an S curve with the minimum and max\n   set to certain values, and whatever inputs come in will get fairly mid value\n   unless they're very clearly a \"strong\" value one way or the other. This is\n   why 0 is selected as the midpoint usually, I think, so that values close to\n   mid, or perhaps a fairly even mixture of two values, can be multiplied and\n   the result will be close to 0. So, maybe we need three - one that has the\n   midpoint at 0, one that has the midpoint at 1, and one that scales? I'm not\n   sure, can you picture why I would want such a thing? If so, can you offer any\n   ideas about how to create intelligent behavior with this structure?\n\n-- what if, for the scaling one, we also added a \"dampening\" effect where each\n   time the function is run, it reduces the min/max a little toward an equilibrium.\n   it doesn't necessarily have to be 0 or 1 or whatever, it should just adjust so\n   that the values become normalized over time. How would we ensure that there's\n   a decent enough gap between the min and max? How would the input values which\n   expand the min/max be considered? We'd re-calculate the curve, probably, right?\n\n### Schema\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":     \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"shape\":    \"sigmoid\",        // or \"tanh\" / \"linear\" / \"softsign\"\n  \"mode\":     \"auto\",           // or \"fixed\"\n  \"min\":      0,                // present only when mode == \"fixed\"\n  \"max\":      100,              // present only when mode == \"fixed\"\n  \"out_range\":\"unit\"            // or \"signed\" — see open questions\n}\n```\n\n`mode: \"auto\"` requires no bounds — the dispatch picker maintains\na running min and max in two slot-store cells (issue 302) per\nnonlinearity box, updated atomically on each fire. `mode:\n\"fixed\"` requires both `min` and `max`; schema rejects either\nmissing or `min >= max`.\n\n### Branch picker (dispatch layer)\n\nThere is no branch to pick — the kind always emits on the single\noutput. The dispatch code path differs from the existing\nrouting kinds in that it **mutates the value** rather than\n**selecting an index**. Pseudocode:\n\n```c\ndouble x = coerce_to_number(value_in);     // hard-error path on failure\n\ndouble lo, hi;\nif (mode == AUTO) {\n    lo = slot_min_load(min_slot);\n    hi = slot_max_load(max_slot);\n    slot_min_cas_update(min_slot, x);      // best-effort widen\n    slot_max_cas_update(max_slot, x);\n} else {\n    lo = box->fixed_min;\n    hi = box->fixed_max;\n}\n\ndouble t = (hi == lo) ? 0.5 : (x - lo) / (hi - lo);   // bootstrap case\n\ndouble y;\nswitch (shape) {\n    case SIGMOID:  y = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k * (t - 0.5))); break;\n    case TANH:     y = tanh(k * (t - 0.5));               break;\n    case LINEAR:   y = t;                                 break;\n    case SOFTSIGN: y = (t - 0.5) / (1.0 + fabs(t - 0.5)); break;\n}\n\nemit_number(out_port, y);\n```\n\n`k` is a steepness constant (see open questions). The bootstrap\ncase (`hi == lo`, true on the very first value seen under `auto`\nmode) maps to `t = 0.5` so the sigmoid emits 0.5 — a defensible\n\"no information yet\" value.\n\n-- what if we take the midpoint of the min/max and we say \"if above, then do\n   this branch. If below, then this branch.\" That way, we're saying which path\n   the value takes while also including a \"strength\" or \"magnitude\" value in the\n   modified output value. Is that a good idea?\n\n### Coercion and the hard-error path\n\nThe kind operates on numbers only. The dispatch picker tries to\ncoerce the inbound value:\n\n- **number on the wire** — used directly.\n- **string** — parsed as a number (`strtod`). On parse failure,\n  the box raises a hard error matching the project's \"errors over\n  fallbacks\" rule. The error names the box id, the offending\n  string, and the wire it arrived on.\n- **other types** (boolean, blob, sentinel) — hard error,\n  unconditional. No silent coercion.\n\n-- C treats 1 and 0 as true and false, so keep an eye out for that... Make sure\n   there's a test case for that.\n\nHard errors stop the box from emitting. No \"skip on bad input\"\nfallback — that's a warning shape this project treats as an\nerror.\n\n### Inspector UI\n\nMode dropdown on the routing inspector gains a `nonlinearity`\noption (same row as the other routing kinds). When selected, the\ninspector body shows:\n\n- **Shape** dropdown: sigmoid / tanh / linear / softsign.\n- **Bounds mode** dropdown: auto / fixed.\n- **Min** and **Max** number inputs (visible only when bounds\n  mode is fixed).\n- A small **live preview** plot — the chosen shape rendered into\n  a thumbnail SVG so the user sees what they're picking. (Stretch\n  goal; not blocking the first slice.)\n\n-- the svg is cute ^_^\n\nThe box's single output port keeps the plain-routing name\n(`out`) so wires drawn before the kind was changed don't need\nrenaming.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `kind: \"nonlinearity\"`; validate\n   `shape`, `mode`, the `min` / `max` pair when `mode == fixed`,\n   and the `out_range` choice.\n2. `src/302-wire-value-slot-store.*` — add `SLOT_MIN_DOUBLE` and\n   `SLOT_MAX_DOUBLE` slot kinds with CAS-update semantics\n   (compare-and-swap loop that retries if another worker widened\n   the slot between the load and the store). Reuse if such slots\n   already exist; otherwise extend.\n3. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — read the nonlinearity routing\n   fields into the box record; allocate the two slot cells when\n   `mode == auto`.\n4. `src/012-dispatch.c` — implement the value-transform path.\n   This is the first routing kind that **writes a new value** to\n   the output wire instead of forwarding the input unchanged; the\n   dispatch code currently passes the input slot pointer through.\n   Generalise so a routing kind can supply a transformed value.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — add `nonlinearity` to the mode\n   dropdown; render the shape / mode / min / max controls.\n6. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — single output port named `out`,\n   same as plain routing.\n7. Fixture: `tests/maps/nonlinearity-route/` — feed a sequence of\n   integers 1..100 into a sigmoid box, assert the outputs are\n   monotonic, bounded in `[0, 1]`, and the midpoint is near 0.5.\n   A second fixture exercises `mode: \"fixed\"` with bounds\n   tighter than the input range to confirm the box does **not**\n   clamp (it lets sigmoid saturate naturally) — or does, per the\n   open-questions decision.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/240-routing-kind-randomizer.md`,\n  `issues/241-routing-kind-weighted.md`,\n  `issues/242-routing-kind-distributor.md`,\n  `issues/243-routing-multi-band-comparator.md` — sibling\n  routing-kind issues; copy the schema-and-inspector shape.\n- `issues/completed/233-unified-routing-schema.md` — the parent\n  schema this kind plugs into.\n- `src/001-schema.lua`, `src/010-graph-loader.c`,\n  `src/012-dispatch.c` — runtime side.\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js`, `assets/js/002-boxes.js` —\n  editor side.\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot kinds the running\n  min/max cells live in.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Name of the kind.** `nonlinearity` is descriptive but long\n  and abstract. `squash` is shorter and matches the\n  neural-network vocabulary the user invoked when proposing it.\n  `remap` is the most boring and most discoverable. Pick one\n  before the schema lands — once it's on disk in fixture maps,\n  renaming is a migration.\n- **Default shape.** Sigmoid is the user's suggestion. Tanh\n  centres around zero (useful when the consumer wants signed\n  output). Linear (i.e. just the normalisation, no curve) is\n  the \"I only want the rescaling, not the bend\" case. Softsign\n  is a cheaper sigmoid-shaped alternative that doesn't need\n  `exp`. All they'd have\n   to do is take the upstream box, wire it to both the non-linearity box, and\n   also to the downstream multiplication box - the scaling would start running\n   it's processing, and it wouldn't get scaled until it finished because the\n   input value, also inputted to the downstream box, would sit and wait in the\n   queue until the non-linearity finished and supplied it's output downstream.\n\n- **Steepness `k`.** A sigmoid with `k = 1` is gentle; the\n  middle 80% of the input range maps to roughly `[0.27, 0.73]`.\n  `k = 6` gives a much sharper S-curve, with the middle 80%\n  mapping to roughly `[0.05, 0.95]`. Expose `k` as an inspector\n  control? Pick a sensible default and hide it? The latter is\n  cleaner UI but less expressive.\n\n-- I say sensible default, and let the user provide json values when reconfiguring\n   (see issue 320 I think?) if they want a different steepness K or whatever.\n   if it's a common operation then we can expose it in the editor. I think\n   k = 1 sounds better, 0.27 and 0.73 are more forgiving. But, I also don't\n   want to be opinionated... well, I can be opinionated in structure, but not in\n   methodology. So ahhhhh screw it let's just expose it in the editor. Just make\n   sure we both show the graph as an svg, and we show those 80% values you specified\n   because those are both useful.\n\n- **Bootstrap behaviour under `auto`.** The first value seen\n  has no min/max to normalise against (`hi == lo`). Suppressing is appealing on theoretical grounds but\n  breaks the \"every fire emits\" contract every other routing\n  kind upholds.\n- **`auto` mode is non-deterministic across runs.** The same\n  input sequence produces different outputs depending on what\n  was seen earlier in the run. Users debugging a downstream\n  consumer will see drift. Worth documenting; maybe surface a\n  \"freeze observed bounds\" inspector action that snapshots the\n  current `auto` bounds into `fixed` bounds on save.\n\n-- It's expected to be non-deterministic.         "content":"1\t# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\t\n8\t`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the\n9\ttop:\n10\t\n11\t```bash\n12\trm -rf \"$COMPILED\"\n13\tmkdir -p \"$COMPILED\" \"$COMPILED/boxes\" \"$COMPILED/src\" ...\n14\t```\n15\t\n16\tWhatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If\n17\tanother process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a\n18\tsibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to\n19\tthat exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a\n20\tparticular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C\n21\tboxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,\n22\tsilently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new\n23\tfiles mid-flight.\n24\t\n25\tThis is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the\n26\tmoment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs\n27\thold onto across time.\n28\t\n29\t## Intended behavior\n30\t\n31\tA compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other\n32\tprograms that depend on a particular build of a map are expected\n33\tto *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.\n34\tWhen `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any\n35\tlive references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.\n36\tInstead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the\n37\treferenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.\n38\t\n39\tThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing\n40\tholder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that\n41\tdrops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the\n42\tcommon case, not the exception — every reference entry carries\n43\tenough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)\n44\treaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a\n45\tguarantee.\n46\t\n47\tThis is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled\n48\tartifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers\n49\texist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;\n50\tgenerations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still\n51\tpoints at them.\n52\t\n53\t## Concept\n54\t\n55\tA compiled directory contains a `.refs` file (hidden, dot-prefixed\n56\tso it doesn't clutter directory listings). It's append-only by\n57\tdesign — concurrent acquires never need to take a lock; concurrent\n58\treleases write a separate marker without rewriting the file.\n59\t\n60\tEach reference has three parts:\n61\t\n62\t1. **A date.** When the reference was acquired. Lets a janitor\n63\t   prune references older than some threshold even if their back\n64\t   pointer can't be validated.\n65\t2. **A back-pointer.** The identity of the holder — enough\n66\t   information that an outside observer can ask \"is this holder\n67\t   still alive, and does it still want this reference?\" without\n68\t   trusting the count alone. Concrete candidates:\n69\t   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs\n70\t     recycle)\n71\t   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of\n72\t     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the\n73\t     ref)\n74\t   - some combination (PID + a marker path)\n75\t3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later\n76\t   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it\n77\t   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.\n78\t\n79\tA release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.\n80\tNet live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.\n81\t\n82\t## Reference file format\n83\t\n84\tA line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:\n85\t\n86\t```\n87\tacquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>\n88\trelease <id> <iso8601-date>\n89\t```\n90\t\n91\tAppend-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line\n92\tper operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in\n93\t`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short\n94\trecords.\n95\t\n96\tReading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,\n97\tsubtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then\n98\tvalidate each survivor's back pointer.\n99\t\n100\tA `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the\n101\tlog to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the\n102\tfork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /\n103\twrites don't lock.\n104\t\n105\t## Acquire / release API\n106\t\n107\tA small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability\n108\tsince holders are written in many languages:\n109\t\n110\t```\n111\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]\n112\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\n113\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts\n114\tscripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs\n115\t```\n116\t\n117\t`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is\n118\tresponsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call\n119\trelease. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one\n120\t(timestamp + random suffix).\n121\t\n122\t`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,\n123\tholder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's\n124\tliveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file\n125\texists).\n126\t\n127\t`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries\n128\twhose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never\n129\tautomatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state\n130\tits caller might care about).\n131\t\n132\t## Compile-time fork logic\n133\t\n134\t`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any\n135\tsibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding\n136\twhere to write:\n137\t\n138\t1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.\n139\t2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after\n140\t   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.\n141\t3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling\n142\t   directory name (see below) and build there. The original\n143\t   `compiled/` stays intact.\n144\t\n145\tAfter a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`\n146\tin the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`\n147\tfield pointing at the previous generation's path).\n148\t\n149\t### Sibling directory naming\n150\t\n151\tTwo reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:\n152\t\n153\t- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...\n154\t  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest\n155\t  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build\n156\t  order.\n157\t- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601\n158\t  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself\n159\t  tells the operator when it was built.\n160\t\n161\tWhichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink\n162\tpointing at the newest generation, so callers who want \"the\n163\tlatest\" don't have to enumerate.\n164\t\n165\t## Stale reference handling\n166\t\n167\tA reference is stale if any of the following hold:\n168\t\n169\t- The PID no longer exists on the system.\n170\t- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)\n171\t  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled\n172\t  PID.\n173\t- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now\n174\t  missing.\n175\t\n176\tStale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if\n177\tANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run\n178\t`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The\n179\tphilosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers\n180\tuntil proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is\n181\ttrivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.\n182\t\n183\t## Gitignore considerations\n184\t\n185\tEvery generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,\n186\t`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived\n187\tartifact and should never be tracked. The existing\n188\t`.gitignore` line `tests/maps/*/compiled/` covers the canonical\n189\tname; add a sibling pattern to cover generations:\n190\t\n191\t```\n192\ttests/maps/*/compiled/\n193\ttests/maps/*/compiled.*/\n194\t```\n195\t\n196\tThe `.refs` file itself lives *inside* the compiled directory,\n197\tso it inherits the same gitignore.\n198\t\n199\t## Suggested implementation steps\n200\t\n201\t1. Pick the back-pointer format. Recommend PID + start time +\n202\t   optional marker path. Document the choice with a comment at\n203\t   the top of the ref helper.\n204\t2. Write `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` with `acquire`, `release`,\n205\t   `list`, `reap`. Append-only writes for the first two, log\n206\t   rewrite under `.refs.lock` for the last.\n207\t3. Add a small `tests/315-refs-test.sh` that exercises:\n208\t   acquire → list (1 entry, valid) → release → list (0 valid) →\n209\t   acquire → kill the holder process → list (1 entry, stale) →\n210\t   reap → list (0).\n211\t4. Teach `soramech-compile.sh` to read `.refs` and pick the\n212\t   target directory. Implement the sibling-naming scheme.\n213\t   `compiled` becomes a symlink to the newest generation.\n214\t5. Add a `forked_from` field to `manifest.json` when forking.\n215\t6. Update `.gitignore` for the new generation pattern.\n216\t7. Integration check in `scripts/run-tests.sh`: compile the\n217\t   pipeline fixture twice — second time with a live `acquire` —\n218\t   assert a sibling generation was created and the original\n219\t   pinned generation still runs unchanged.\n220\t\n221\t## Open questions\n222\t\n223\t- Should the runner (`soramech-pool`) itself acquire a reference\n224\t  when it opens a compiled directory? On the one hand, yes —\n225\t  it's the canonical case the system protects against. On the\n226\t  other, soramech-pool runs are usually short-lived and the\n227\t  acquire/release overhead per run is unwelcome. Possible\n228\t  compromise: only acquire if pool runs longer than N seconds.\n229\t- How does a fork chain end? If `compiled.5` is built while\n230\t  `compiled.4` had live refs but `compiled.4`'s refs are now all\n231\t  stale (caller never released, then died), do we ever prune\n232\t  `compiled.4`? Probably yes, via `soramech-ref.sh reap-all\n233\t  <map>` which walks every generation and drops the ones whose\n234\t  refs all validate as dead.\n235\t- Is the `.refs` log itself something that should be versioned\n236\t  (`.refs.v1`)? If we ever change the line format, in-flight\n237\t  holders won't know how to read it. Versioning the filename\n238\t  avoids the problem.\n239\t- Does the editor (`maps/<x>/` user-facing) want the same\n240\t  mechanism? Probably yes eventually, but out of scope for this\n241\t  issue — start with `compiled/` artifacts only.\n242\t\n243\t## Relevant files\n244\t\n245\t- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — issue 309's compile pipeline,\n246\t  modified here to fork on live references\n247\t- `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` — new helper for acquire / release /\n248\t  list / reap\n249\t- `tests/315-refs-test.sh` — new\n250\t- `.gitignore` — extended pattern for generation directories\n251\t- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — new integration check\n252\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — parent issue; references this\n253\t  one's fork behavior\n254\t\n255\t## Notes (philosophy)\n256\t\n257\tThe unreliability is a feature, not a bug. A reliable reference\n258\tcount would require a kernel-level mechanism (file locks held\n259\tfor the lifetime of the holder), and that's a tower of\n260\toperational complexity for marginal value. By accepting that\n261\tholders sometimes lie and sometimes vanish, we get a system\n262\tthat's robust to crashes, network drops, and SIGKILL — at the\n263\tcost of needing a \"reap\" pass to catch up with reality\n264\toccasionally.
