The parent's read box wires\n219\t# a value into a BOX_MAP whose sub-map has one externally-supplied\n220\t# data box; the graph loader splices the parent's wire through to\n221\t# the sub-map's write box at load time. The C dispatch picker, the\nloader-side parse, and the counter-slot allocation have all\nbeen on the floor since issue 233's groundwork; this commit\nlights up the schema acceptance, the editor surface, and a\nfixture so the kind is reachable end-to-end.\n\nThe Lua schema (src/001-schema.lua) accepts the three\ncounter-driven kinds (randomizer / weighted / distributor) and\nthe multi-band comparator's thresholds array shape — those\nsibling 241 / 242 / 243 commits land their fixtures and\ncloseouts separately but share the schema validation block\nlanded here.\n\nEditor surface: the inspector's routing-kind dropdown grows\nthree new options (randomizer / weighted / distributor); the\ndefault_routing helper learns the minimum-viable starting\nshape for each so flipping the dropdown leaves the box\nschema-valid without further input; set_n_outputs accepts the\nthree n_outputs-driven kinds so the +/− port-count control\nworks uniformly; weighted gets its own weights text-input with\na set_weights helper that severs outgoing wires on edit\n(weights.length is the port count); the comparator panel grows\na thresholds text-input (issue 243's multi-band path) with\nset_thresholds that flips the box between single-comparand and\nmulti-band modes by setting / clearing the array. Canvas\n(assets/js/002-boxes.js) extends box_height and port_positions\nso randomizer / weighted / distributor render out_<i> ports\nper n_outputs (weighted reads weights.length) and the\ncomparator renders below_<t> / between_<a>_<b> / above_<t>\n(plus eq_<t> for doubled adjacent thresholds) when in\nmulti-band mode.\n\nFixture: tests/maps/randomizer-route/ exercises the\ndeterministic first-call shape — the counter starts at 0,\nhash(0) is 0, and the picker lands on branch 0 reliably. The\nfixture's three taggers expose which branch fired by tagging\nthe input string with their port index.\n\nPhase-2 progress table gains a row for 240; the issue file\nmoves to completed/ with a status note recording the editor +\nschema work this commit landed.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",

phase 2 mirror skipped per teardown) |\n| 230  | required inputs and the optional flag           | complete (compile-time; runtime arg-list shortening deferred) |\n| 231  | move signature parsers into langs/              | complete |\n| 232  | test coverage map (parser tests landed; tracks gaps) | ongoing |\n| 233  | unified routing schema (comparator+iterator)    | complete |\n| 234  | middle-click duplicates the selected box        | complete |\n| 235  | literal value replaces port name on the canvas  | complete |\n| 236  | box header = filename, output label = `fn()`    | complete |\n| 237  | string-manipulation library expansion           | complete |\n| 238  | editor HTTP server config file                  | complete |\n| 239  | literal-bound input port shrinks to a nodule, name moves to the gutter | complete |\n| 216  | read-file box                                  | complete |\n| 217  | variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape | complete |\n| 218  | enforce single-output driver contract          | complete |\n| 220  | root run script and entry point cleanup        | complete |\n| 221  | iterator box (editor surface only)             | complete |\n| 222  | compile button and assets directory            | complete |\n| 248  | encapsulated map as a box (sub-maps via load-time inlining) | complete · input + output splice + recursion across nested encaps + full editor surface (kind dropdown, external bindings on read/write, file-browser encapsulate action); three on-disk fixtures green |\n| 240  | routing kind: randomizer (hash-of-counter mod n_outputs) | complete · schema + editor dropdown + n_outputs control + canvas out_<i> rendering + fixture |\n\n## Phase goal checklist\n\n- [x] Boxes render on map load\n- [x] Clicking a box opens the inspector\n- [x] Ref/fn set by browsing src/ files; ports auto-derived\n- [x] Map loads centered on screen (fit-to-view)\n- [x] Map can be switched from a list, not a text prompt\n- [x] Empty canvas shows interaction hints\n- [—] Entry box marker (won't implement — phase 3 auto-detects, see 305)\n- [ ] Comparator routing replaces the old branch box (issue 210)\n- [x] Iterator box with auto-grow output slots (editor; runtime in phase 3 / issue 304)\n- [x] Compile button (issue 222) — placeholder UI for the phase 3 build\n\n## Notes on graph model changes during phase 2\n\nThese are not new features so much as model corrections that shape\nwhat phase 3 will consume:\n\n- **Single-output rule** (218, complete): every box has exactly one\n  output wire. The driver contract emits one JSON value, not an\n  array.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (210, complete): the old `branch`\n  box kind with named ports is removed.     "originalFile":"# Phase 2 Progress\n\nGoal: an editor you can actually use to build maps, plus the graph\nmodel the phase 3 runtime will consume.\n\n## Issues\n\n| ID   | Title                                          | Status   |\n|------|------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| 201  | fix box rendering closure bug                  | complete |\n| 202  | fit-to-view on map load                        | complete |\n| 203  | map picker panel                               | complete |\n| 204  | visible interaction hints                      | complete |\n| 206  | entry box designation                          | won't implement |\n| 207  | source file browser and port auto-population   | complete |\n| 208  | port literal values                            | complete |\n| 209  | ollama query library                           | complete |\n| 210  | comparator wire branching                      | complete |\n| 211  | file browser library directories               | complete |\n| 211a | unify src/ into same directory pipeline        | complete |\n| 212  | editor interaction modes                       | complete |\n| 213  | queued inputs and task model                   | won't implement |\n| 219  | map compiler                                   | won't implement (folded into 309) |\n| 214  | tmp symlink recreation on reboot               | complete |\n| 215  | view source button                             | complete |\n| 223  | syntax highlighting via user-written lexers    | complete |\n| 224  | editable port names (canvas) — values stay in inspector | complete |\n| 225  | dir picker shows files and dir/file icons      | complete |\n| 226  | hide output controls for no-return functions   | complete |\n| 227  | hide view button when box has no ref           | complete |\n| 228  | self-loop wires routed around the box body     | complete |\n| 229  | `read` / `write` box kinds (language-agnostic IO) | complete (phase 3 + editor; phase 2 mirror skipped per teardown) |\n| 230  | required inputs and the optional flag           | complete (compile-time; runtime arg-list shortening deferred) |\n| 231  | move signature parsers into langs/              | complete |\n| 232  | test coverage map (parser tests landed; tracks gaps) | ongoing |\n| 233  | unified routing schema (comparator+iterator)    | complete |\n| 234  | middle-click duplicates the selected box        | complete |\n| 235  | literal value replaces port name on the canvas  | complete |\n| 236  | box header = filename, output label = `fn()`    | complete |\n| 237  | string-manipulation library expansion           | complete |\n| 238  | editor HTTP server config file                  | complete |\n| 239  | literal-bound input port shrinks to a nodule, name moves to the gutter | complete |\n| 216  | read-file box                                  | complete |\n| 217  | variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape | complete |\n| 218  | enforce single-output driver contract          | complete |\n| 220  | root run script and entry point cleanup        | complete |\n| 221  | iterator box (editor surface only)             | complete |\n| 222  | compile button and assets directory            | complete |\n| 248  | encapsulated map as a box (sub-maps via load-time inlining) | complete · input + output splice + recursion across nested encaps + full editor surface (kind dropdown, external bindings on read/write, file-browser encapsulate action); three on-disk fixtures green |\n| 240  | routing kind: randomizer (hash-of-counter mod n_outputs) | complete · schema + editor dropdown + n_outputs control + canvas out_<i> rendering + fixture |\n| 241  | routing kind: weighted (cumulative-band lookup over weights) | complete · schema + editor dropdown + weights text input + canvas out_<i> rendering per weights.length + fixture |\n\n## Phase goal checklist\n\n- [x] Boxes render on map load\n- [x] Clicking a box opens the inspector\n- [x] Ref/fn set by browsing src/ files; ports auto-derived\n- [x] Map loads centered on screen (fit-to-view)\n- [x] Map can be switched from a list, not a text prompt\n- [x] Empty canvas shows interaction hints\n- [—] Entry box marker (won't implement — phase 3 auto-detects, see 305)\n- [ ] Comparator routing replaces the old branch box (issue 210)\n- [x] Iterator box with auto-grow output slots (editor; runtime in phase 3 / issue 304)\n- [x] Compile button (issue 222) — placeholder UI for the phase 3 build\n\n## Notes on graph model changes during phase 2\n\nThese are not new features so much as model corrections that shape\nwhat phase 3 will consume:\n\n- **Single-output rule** (218, complete): every box has exactly one\n  output wire. The driver contract emits one JSON value, not an\n  array.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (210, complete): the old `branch`\n  box kind with named ports is removed. A box may carry a\n  `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `lt` / `eq` / `gt`.\n- **Iterator routing** (221): a box with `iterator_outputs` is a\n  pure routing primitive; the dispatch layer rotates through the\n  declared output names. Iterators have no `ref` / `fn`.\n- **Connection schema**: `from_branch` field replaces the old\n  `from_output` / `from_port` dual-field design.\n",

The 319 issue file got a corrected postscript: what I'd flagged as a latent visibility race turned out to be a partial-rebuild trap in the Makefile, now closed by `-MMD -MP` auto-deps.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The Make bug had been **silently corrupting struct reads for three or four sessions** every time we extended `box_t` or `routing_t`. Every \"intermittent\" 319 failure I saw, every \"fixed by adding traces\" mystery, every \"clean rebuild made it work\" — all the same root cause. Auto-header-deps is the kind of infrastructure that pays for itself the first time it prevents a wild-goose chase, and the diagnostic JSONL events from 311's earlier commit are what made it diagnosable at all (the push event's `result=to-input-out-of-range` was the breadcrumb that pointed at field-offset corruption rather than memory ordering).\n- The `DIR := $(abspath ...)` immediate-assignment fix is the kind of make footgun that bites quietly: with `?=` recursive, `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` changes every time `-include` pulls in another file, so `$(dir lastword ...)` silently mutates between expansions. The compile command's `-I/.../build/src/langs` (a path that doesn't exist) was the only visible symptom — and only when a header search actually missed. The dry-run `make -n` caught it immediately because it printed the actual cc command; without that the error message blamed lang-spec.h.\n- Splitting four interleaved routing-kind issues into separate commits while the work was actually done in parallel needed pragmatic compromise. The infrastructure landed under whichever issue introduced the most schema/canvas/inspector machinery (240, since it added the multi-kind dropdown + n_outputs control + set_n_outputs extension all in one logical step). The other three issues' commits stay thin because their per-issue work is genuinely small — just a fixture, a test entry, and the closeout. \"One commit per issue\" as a rule scales when the work is per-issue separable; when it isn't, biasing toward \"first-numbered issue carries the shared infrastructure\" reads honestly in git log because the commit message says so.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nAll four routing kinds shipped end-to-end: schema, runtime, editor, fixture, closeout. Phase-2 progress now has rows for 240/241/242/243. Working tree clean of my work, only your pre-existing untracked WIP left (247, 249, readme.md). Done."
      }],

  "message":{
    "content":"Can we make an issue file to make a box that's a timer? All it does is have a \"tick-tock rate\" that is either defined in the editor or given as an input value. The map shouldn't compile if there's no wires attached to this box AND there's no value defined in the editor. If there's a wire attached but no value has come in yet, it shouldn't run, but every time it runs it emits a single \"true\" boolean as it's output. When it receives a value, it should add itself to the thread pool queue as any other box, and then when it finishes it re-adds itself. If the timer value is ever set to 0, then when it re-adds itself it instead just stops. It can be restarted by adding another timer value as input, because when input slots are filled they are also added to the task queue as part of the normal operating procedure for any box.\n\nhow can we implement this without endlessly spinning with an otherwise empty queue, and without locking a thread in a sleep, and without a single timer thread running in the background?",
    "role":"user"
  },

          "content":"# 251 — Timer box: tick-tock emitter\n\n## Status\nopen · design draft; the load-bearing open question is how to\nschedule the inter-tick wait without spinning, without locking\na worker in a sleep, and without a dedicated timer thread\n\n## Concept\n\nA new box kind, **`timer`**, that emits a single boolean `true`\non its output once per \"tick-tock rate.\" The rate is set either\nas a literal in the editor (a number of milliseconds) or as an\ninput value arriving on a wire. The timer's body is small: each\nfire emits `true` and re-arms itself; setting the rate to zero\nstops the chain; pushing a fresh rate restarts it.\n\nThe compelling shape is the **fire-then-respawn loop**. The\ntimer box's invoke does almost nothing — push one `true`\ndownstream, request a re-spawn at `now + rate_ms`. The runtime\nthen has to deliver that re-spawn at the right time without\nburning a worker waiting for it.\n\n## Concrete behavior\n\n### Schema\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"every_second\",\n  \"kind\": \"timer\",\n  \"rate_ms\": 1000,\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"rate_ms\", \"type\": \"number\", \"optional\": true }\n  ],\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"to_box\": \"consumer\", \"to_input\": \"tick\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n- **`rate_ms`** literal field: the default tick interval in\n  milliseconds. May be absent if a wire-fed `rate_ms` input is\n  present.\n- **`rate_ms`** input port: optional; when present and a value\n  arrives, that value overrides the literal and re-arms the\n  loop. Sending `0` stops the loop; sending a positive number\n  restarts (or speeds up / slows down) it.\n\n### Compile-time check\n\nThe graph loader rejects a timer box that has **neither** a\nliteral `rate_ms` **nor** a wire feeding its `rate_ms` input.\nA pure unwired timer has no way to ever start; failing loud at\nload is the project's preferred shape (CLAUDE.md \"errors over\nfallbacks\").\n\n### Output\n\nSingle output port, plain routing. Emits the string `\"true\"`\nonce per tick. Same shape as a write box's success boolean —\ndownstream consumers can treat it as a clock event without\ncaring about the bytes.\n\n### Dispatch behavior\n\n1. On graph load, if the timer has a literal `rate_ms`, the\n   loader queues the first tick at `now + rate_ms` (or\n   immediately at `now` — see open questions).\n2. On task fire, the timer's body:\n   a. Pushes `\"true\"` to every outgoing connection.\n   b. Reads the current effective rate (literal, possibly\n      overridden by a recently-arrived input value).\n   c. If `rate == 0`: stop. Do not re-arm.\n   d. If `rate > 0`: schedule a respawn at `now + rate_ms`.\n3. When the `rate_ms` input slot receives a new value, the\n   value is captured into the timer box's \"current rate\" cell\n   AND the timer is re-added to the task queue immediately (so\n   a stopped timer can be restarted; a running timer's next\n   fire uses the new rate).\n\nThe \"input arrival schedules a task\" hook is the same one every\nother box uses — the dispatch's `spawn_if_ready` on a push. The\ntimer box's first task on graph load is queued by the loader;\nall subsequent tasks come from the fire-and-respawn loop.\n\n## Open questions\n\n### Q1 — How to wait for the next tick (the load-bearing one)\n\nThe user's constraints:\n- No endless spinning with an otherwise-empty queue.\n- No locking a pool worker in a sleep.\n- No dedicated timer thread running in the background.\n\nFour candidate shapes, with the trade-offs as I see them:\n\n**Option A — `pthread_cond_timedwait` on the existing pool\nidle-wait.** The pool's worker threads already block on a\ncondvar when no work is queued. Today that wait is\n\"infinite-until-signalled.\" We extend it to \"wait until either\nnew work arrives OR the next-scheduled-timer's deadline.\"\n\nImplementation:\n- The dispatch maintains a small priority queue of\n  `(deadline, box_idx)` pairs — the pending timer respawns.\n- When the work queue is empty, the worker about to sleep peeks\n  the timer queue's head (the earliest deadline).\n- `pthread_cond_timedwait(condvar, mutex, earliest_deadline)`\n  blocks until the deadline or until another worker signals\n  new work.\n- On wake, the worker checks the timer queue for any deadlines\n  that have passed and pushes those box_idx values onto the\n  task queue, then proceeds with its normal pull.\n\nThis satisfies every constraint:\n- No spin: the worker is in a blocking system call.\n- No locked-in-sleep worker: the worker that's waiting is\n  ALREADY the idle worker the pool always has. We're not adding\n  a wait, we're tightening the existing one's timeout.\n- No dedicated timer thread: any idle worker handles it,\n  whichever one happens to be in the idle slot.\n\nThe \"one worker is in cond_timedwait\" claim is the subtle one\n— is that \"locking a thread in a sleep\"? My read: no, because\nthat worker would be in `pthread_cond_wait` anyway (idle pool),\nand a worker waiting on the work-queue condvar IS the pool's\ncorrect idle behavior. We're not adding a thread; we're adding\na deadline to the wait it already does. If a new task arrives\nbefore the deadline, the condvar signal wakes it just as today.\n\n**Option B — `timerfd` + `epoll` integration.** Linux's\n`timerfd_create` gives each timer a file descriptor that\nbecomes readable after a specified timeout. The pool grows an\nepoll set; the idle worker calls `epoll_wait` with the same\ndeadline as Option A, but the kernel handles the timer\nexpiration via the timerfd's readability.\n\nMore machinery, but two real advantages:\n- Multiple timers coalesce in one epoll_wait — the kernel does\n  the \"earliest deadline\" pick for free.\n- Generalises naturally to any future async-I/O box (a network\n  socket box, a file-watcher box) — the epoll set is the right\n  pattern for those too.\n\nCost: Linux-specific (kqueue equivalent on BSD/macOS); slightly\nmore code than Option A.\n\n**Option C — Pure YARQ requeue at scheduler frequency.** The\ntimer box's fire always re-queues itself immediately, and on\nre-pull the worker checks if `now >= deadline`. If not, YARQ\n(per issue 320's primitive) puts it back at the tail. Workers\nkeep round-robining through the empty queue until enough\nreal-time has passed.\n\nSatisfies the no-thread / no-sleep constraints but VIOLATES the\nno-spinning one: an otherwise-empty queue with one pending\ntimer becomes a CPU-burning loop of YARQ requeue cycles.\nRejected unless there's a way to gate the requeue rate.\n\n**Option D — Hybrid: timer wheel inside the dispatch.** A small\ndata structure (hashed wheel, sorted list, whatever) holds\npending timer deadlines. Same idle-wait extension as Option A,\nbut the data structure is built-in to the dispatch rather than\npiggy-backing on the pool's condvar via priority queue.\n\nEffectively the same as Option A; the question is just whether\nthe structure lives in the pool layer or the dispatch layer.\nThe pool layer feels right — the pool already owns the idle\ncondvar.\n\n**Recommendation:** Option A is the simplest shape that\nsatisfies every constraint, and the work is bounded:\n- One small priority queue inside the pool (or dispatch).\n- One `pthread_cond_timedwait` extension to the worker's idle\n  loop.\n- A `pool_schedule_at(deadline, box_idx)` API.\n\nOption B is the right shape if we ever build network / file\nboxes that need async I/O; defer until that drives the\ndecision.\n\n### Q2 — Drift accumulation\n\nA timer with rate 1000ms takes 5ms inside the dispatch to fire\nand re-arm. Does the next deadline measure from the START of\nthe previous fire (drift-free, periodic) or from the END\n(drift accumulates, but each interval is honest)?\n\n- **Periodic** (`next_deadline = previous_deadline + rate_ms`):\n  predictable cadence; if a fire takes longer than the rate\n  (system load, slow downstream consumers blocking the push),\n  the timer \"catches up\" by firing immediately on next idle —\n  potentially producing back-to-back fires.\n- **Interval** (`next_deadline = now + rate_ms`): no catch-up;\n  the timer's actual rate slows under load.\n\nThe standard `setitimer` / Go ticker pattern is periodic. I'd\ndefault to periodic; document the catch-up behaviour.\n\n### Q3 — Rate changes mid-run\n\nWhen a new `rate_ms` input value arrives, three behaviours are\npossible:\n- **Re-arm from now.** The currently-scheduled tick (if any)\n  gets cancelled; the next tick is `now + new_rate_ms`.\n- **Apply to NEXT cycle.** The currently-scheduled tick still\n  fires on its original deadline; subsequent ticks use the new\n  rate.\n- **Re-arm preserving phase.** The next tick's deadline gets\n  adjusted to match the new period offset.\n\nOption 1 (re-arm from now) is the simplest and matches \"input\narrival schedules a task\" — the input arrival immediately\nfires the timer with the new rate, then the fire body schedules\nthe next at `now + new_rate_ms`. Default to this.\n\n### Q4 — Stopping cleanly\n\nWhen `rate_ms = 0` arrives, the next fire's body sees\n`rate == 0` and skips the re-arm. But:\n- Should any in-flight scheduled deadline for this box be\n  cancelled, or does the next pull just become a no-op?\n- Does the timer emit one final `true` when stopping, or skip\n  the push too?\n\nLean toward: the value=0 push triggers one final fire (so the\ndownstream sees the \"I'm stopping\" event), and the re-arm step\nis the explicit skip. The scheduled-deadline-cancellation\nquestion is moot if Option 1 above is chosen (the input arrival\ncancels the scheduled deadline as part of re-arm).\n\n### Q5 — Editor surface\n\n- Number input for `rate_ms` literal.\n- The `rate_ms` input port renders as a normal input dot\n  (wires connectable; if a literal is set the dot becomes the\n  nodule per issue 239).\n- Header colour: needs a fresh entry in `KIND_COLOR` — yellow\n  or amber reads as \"active / pulsing\" without colliding with\n  call (blue), read (green), write (cheddar), or map (violet).\n- A small \"•\" badge that pulses in the editor canvas at the\n  configured rate is a fun stretch goal — not blocking.\n\n### Q6 — Interaction with quiescence\n\nA timer that keeps re-arming prevents the pool from ever\nreaching quiescence (no tasks queued, no in-flight work). Two\noptions:\n- **Timer prevents quiescence.** A long-running map with a\n  steady tick simply runs forever; the user terminates with\n  Ctrl-C. This is the natural shape for a long-running event\n  pipeline.\n- **Timer counts as \"background\" work.** Quiescence ignores\n  the pending-timer queue, so a map with only timers and\n  consumers waiting on them quiesces. Wrong for a real-time\n  pipeline; right for tests.\n\nDefault to the first; introduce a `background: true` flag if\nthe second becomes useful.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Schema**: `src/001-schema.lua` accepts `kind: \"timer\"`\n   with optional numeric `rate_ms` field and the optional\n   `rate_ms` input port. Validates the\n   neither-literal-nor-input compile-time check.\n2. **Box kind enum**: `src/010-graph-loader.h` adds\n   `BOX_TIMER`; loader maps `\"timer\"` to it.\n3. **Pool extension**: add a small priority queue of\n   `(deadline, box_idx)` to the pool layer, plus a\n   `pool_schedule_at(deadline, box_idx)` API.\n4. **Idle-wait change**: when the pool's worker is about to\n   block on the work-queue condvar, peek the timer queue and\n   pass the earliest deadline as the condvar timeout. On wake,\n   drain any expired timers into the work queue.\n5. **Dispatch**: `do_timer_box` is tiny — push `\"true\"`, read\n   current rate (from the literal-or-input-cached cell), call\n   `pool_schedule_at` if rate > 0.\n6. **Rate-input plumbing**: an arriving `rate_ms` input value\n   updates a per-box atomic cell, then triggers\n   `spawn_if_ready` like any other input (which queues the\n   timer for immediate fire under the new rate).\n7. **Loader hook**: at graph load, every timer with a literal\n   `rate_ms` gets one initial `pool_schedule_at(now + rate_ms,\n   timer_box_idx)` so the loop starts.\n8. **Editor**: kind dropdown grows `timer`; inspector renders\n   `rate_ms` number input; canvas KIND_COLOR entry for timer.\n9. **Fixture**: `tests/maps/timer-tick/` — a timer at 100ms\n   feeds a counter box; assert the counter sees N fires across\n   a fixed test run duration (loose tolerance for scheduler\n   jitter).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — kind acceptance\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — BOX_TIMER, compile-time check\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — `do_timer_box`, the fire-and-schedule body\n- `libs/task-pool/pool.{c,h}` — priority queue, scheduled-deadline\n  API, condvar-timeout idle wait\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — KIND_COLOR + KIND_HEADER for timer\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — `rate_ms` editor control\n- `tests/maps/timer-tick/` — fixture\n\n## Notes\n\n- The timer box is the first one whose firing schedule isn't\n  driven entirely by data arrival on its inputs. Every other\n  box fires when its inputs are ready; the timer fires when\n  the wall clock crosses a deadline. That's a new\n  scheduling-source category for the dispatch — worth being\n  explicit about so future categories (signal-driven, fd-\n  readable, etc.) inherit the same machinery.\n- Multiple timers in one map all coalesce naturally into the\n  same priority queue. The idle wait blocks until the earliest\n  deadline across all of them.\n- This issue is the prerequisite for any future \"every N\n  minutes, run this pipeline\" cron-like pattern at the SoraMech\n  layer. The cron primitive is just a timer with a much larger\n  rate — same mechanism.\n",

Same idle-wait extension as Option A,\nbut the data structure is built-in to the dispatch rather than\npiggy-backing on the pool's condvar via priority queue.\n\nEffectively the same as Option A; the question is just whether\nthe structure lives in the pool layer or the dispatch layer.\nThe pool layer feels right — the pool already owns the idle\ncondvar.\n\n**Recommendation:** Option A is the simplest shape that\nsatisfies every constraint, and the work is bounded:\n- One small priority queue inside the pool (or dispatch).\n- One `pthread_cond_timedwait` extension to the worker's idle\n  loop.\n- A `pool_schedule_at(deadline, box_idx)` API.\n\nOption B is the right shape if we ever build network / file\nboxes that need async I/O; defer until that drives the\ndecision.\n\n### Q2 — Drift accumulation\n\nA timer with rate 1000ms takes 5ms inside the dispatch to fire\nand re-arm. Does the next deadline measure from the START of\nthe previous fire (drift-free, periodic) or from the END\n(drift accumulates, but each interval is honest)?\n\n- **Periodic** (`next_deadline = previous_deadline + rate_ms`):\n  predictable cadence; if a fire takes longer than the rate\n  (system load, slow downstream consumers blocking the push),\n  the timer \"catches up\" by firing immediately on next idle —\n  potentially producing back-to-back fires.\n- **Interval** (`next_deadline = now + rate_ms`): no catch-up;\n  the timer's actual rate slows under load.\n\nThe standard `setitimer` / Go ticker pattern is periodic. I'd\ndefault to periodic; document the catch-up behaviour.\n\n### Q3 — Rate changes mid-run\n\nWhen a new `rate_ms` input value arrives, three behaviours are\npossible:\n- **Re-arm from now.** The currently-scheduled tick (if any)\n  gets cancelled; the next tick is `now + new_rate_ms`.\n- **Apply to NEXT cycle.** The currently-scheduled tick still\n  fires on its original deadline; subsequent ticks use the new\n  rate.\n- **Re-arm preserving phase.** The next tick's deadline gets\n  adjusted to match the new period offset.\n\nOption 1 (re-arm from now) is the simplest and matches \"input\narrival schedules a task\" — the input arrival immediately\nfires the timer with the new rate, then the fire body schedules\nthe next at `now + new_rate_ms`. Default to this.\n\n### Q4 — Stopping cleanly\n\nWhen `rate_ms = 0` arrives, the next fire's body sees\n`rate == 0` and skips the re-arm. But:\n- Should any in-flight scheduled deadline for this box be\n  cancelled, or does the next pull just become a no-op?\n- Does the timer emit one final `true` when stopping, or skip\n  the push too?\n\nLean toward: the value=0 push triggers one final fire (so the\ndownstream sees the \"I'm stopping\" event), and the re-arm step\nis the explicit skip. The scheduled-deadline-cancellation\nquestion is moot if Option 1 above is chosen (the input arrival\ncancels the scheduled deadline as part of re-arm).\n\n### Q5 — Editor surface\n\n- Number input for `rate_ms` literal.\n- The `rate_ms` input port renders as a normal input dot\n  (wires connectable; if a literal is set the dot becomes the\n  nodule per issue 239).\n- Header colour: needs a fresh entry in `KIND_COLOR` — yellow\n  or amber reads as \"active / pulsing\" without colliding with\n  call (blue), read (green), write (cheddar), or map (violet).\n- A small \"•\" badge that pulses in the editor canvas at the\n  configured rate is a fun stretch goal — not blocking.\n\n### Q6 — Interaction with quiescence\n\nA timer that keeps re-arming prevents the pool from ever\nreaching quiescence (no tasks queued, no in-flight work). Two\noptions:\n- **Timer prevents quiescence.** A long-running map with a\n  steady tick simply runs forever; the user terminates with\n  Ctrl-C. This is the natural shape for a long-running event\n  pipeline.\n- **Timer counts as \"background\" work.** Quiescence ignores\n  the pending-timer queue, so a map with only timers and\n  consumers waiting on them quiesces. Wrong for a real-time\n  pipeline; right for tests.\n\nDefault to the first; introduce a `background: true` flag if\nthe second becomes useful.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Schema**: `src/001-schema.lua` accepts `kind: \"timer\"`\n   with optional numeric `rate_ms` field and the optional\n   `rate_ms` input port. Validates the\n   neither-literal-nor-input compile-time check.\n2. **Box kind enum**: `src/010-graph-loader.h` adds\n   `BOX_TIMER`; loader maps `\"timer\"` to it.\n3. **Pool extension**: add a small priority queue of\n   `(deadline, box_idx)` to the pool layer, plus a\n   `pool_schedule_at(deadline, box_idx)` API.\n4. **Idle-wait change**: when the pool's worker is about to\n   block on the work-queue condvar, peek the timer queue and\n   pass the earliest deadline as the condvar timeout. On wake,\n   drain any expired timers into the work queue.\n5. **Dispatch**: `do_timer_box` is tiny — push `\"true\"`, read\n   current rate (from the literal-or-input-cached cell), call\n   `pool_schedule_at` if rate > 0.\n6. **Rate-input plumbing**: an arriving `rate_ms` input value\n   updates a per-box atomic cell, then triggers\n   `spawn_if_ready` like any other input (which queues the\n   timer for immediate fire under the new rate).\n7. **Loader hook**: at graph load, every timer with a literal\n   `rate_ms` gets one initial `pool_schedule_at(now + rate_ms,\n   timer_box_idx)` so the loop starts.\n8. **Editor**: kind dropdown grows `timer`; inspector renders\n   `rate_ms` number input; canvas KIND_COLOR entry for timer.\n9. **Fixture**: `tests/maps/timer-tick/` — a timer at 100ms\n   feeds a counter box; assert the counter sees N fires across\n   a fixed test run duration (loose tolerance for scheduler\n   jitter).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — kind acceptance\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — BOX_TIMER, compile-time check\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — `do_timer_box`, the fire-and-schedule body\n- `libs/task-pool/pool.{c,h}` — priority queue, scheduled-deadline\n  API, condvar-timeout idle wait\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — KIND_COLOR + KIND_HEADER for timer\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — `rate_ms` editor control\n- `tests/maps/timer-tick/` — fixture\n\n## Notes\n\n- The timer box is the first one whose firing schedule isn't\n  driven entirely by data arrival on its inputs. Every other\n  box fires when its inputs are ready; the timer fires when\n  the wall clock crosses a deadline. That's a new\n  scheduling-source category for the dispatch — worth being\n  explicit about so future categories (signal-driven, fd-\n  readable, etc.) inherit the same machinery.\n- Multiple timers in one map all coalesce naturally into the\n  same priority queue. The idle wait blocks until the earliest\n  deadline across all of them.\n- This issue is the prerequisite for any future \"every N\n  minutes, run this pipeline\" cron-like pattern at the SoraMech\n  layer. The cron primitive is just a timer with a much larger\n  rate — same mechanism.\n",
    "type":"create",

        "text":"Wrote `issues/251-timer-box-tick-tock-emitter.md` with the full design + open questions + suggested implementation steps.\n\nNow your tough question directly: **how to wait between ticks without spinning, without locking a worker in sleep, and without a dedicated timer thread.**\n\nMy read of the design space — four options, with my pick at the end:\n\n**Option A — extend the pool's idle-wait with a deadline.** The pool's worker threads already block on a condvar when no work is queued. Today that wait is \"infinite until signalled by a new task.\" Change it to \"wait until either new work arrives OR the next-scheduled-timer's deadline.\" A small priority queue inside the pool holds `(deadline, box_idx)` pairs; the idle worker uses `pthread_cond_timedwait` with the head's deadline as its timeout. On wake, drain expired deadlines into the work queue, then proceed normally.\n\n**Option B — `timerfd_create` + `epoll`.** Each timer gets a kernel-managed file descriptor that becomes readable after its deadline. The pool's idle worker calls `epoll_wait`; kernel coalesces N timers into one wait. More machinery, but generalises to network / file boxes later.\n\n**Option C — pure YARQ requeue at scheduler frequency.** The fire always re-queues itself immediately; on re-pull the worker checks if `now >= deadline` and YARQs back to the tail if not. **This violates your no-spinning constraint** — an otherwise-empty queue burns CPU round-robining a single non-ready timer task. Reject.\n\n**Option D — same as A but with the priority queue inside the dispatch layer rather than the pool layer.** Functionally identical to A; the question is just which layer owns it. The pool owns the idle condvar, so the pool feels like the right home.\n\n**My recommendation is A.** It satisfies every constraint cleanly:\n\n- **No spin:** the worker is in a blocking system call (`pthread_cond_timedwait`).\n- **No locked-in-sleep worker:** the worker doing the wait is *already* the idle worker the pool has when there's no queued work. You're not adding a new wait, you're tightening the timeout on the existing one. A new task arriving signals the condvar and wakes it just like today.\n- **No dedicated timer thread:** whichever worker happens to be idle does it. If 14 workers are busy, none is doing the wait — the timer just fires when the next idle moment arrives, possibly slightly late. That graceful degradation is the right behaviour for a real-time pipeline that's overcommitted.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The subtle bit in your three constraints: **the pool already has an idle worker waiting on a condvar.** That's not \"locking a thread in a sleep\" in the sense you meant — it's the pool's correct idle behaviour. The trick is that we're not *adding* a wait; we're *parameterising* the wait the pool already does. The cost of the timer feature is zero additional threads, zero additional condvars, just a `+deadline` argument to one existing call site.\n- A question back to you: **do you want the timer's first tick to fire at `now + rate_ms` (one-rate-of-wait before the first event) or at `now` (fire immediately on graph load, then tick every rate_ms after)?** Standard cron-style schedulers default to the first; \"kick off a chain at startup\" use cases want the second. I left it as an open question on the issue with a slight lean toward \"fire at `now + rate_ms`\" because that's what `setitimer` does, but either is defensible.\n- Another question: **when a timer is still pending and the map quiesces around it** (no other tasks queued, all consumers done), does the run terminate or wait for the next tick? The natural answer for a long-running event pipeline is \"wait\" — the timer prevents quiescence. The natural answer for a test fixture is \"terminate\" — quiescence ignores pending timers. A `background: true` flag would let the user pick per timer, but adds schema surface. Lean toward \"always prevents quiescence; introduce the flag if a test fixture asks for it.\"\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nThe issue is sitting at `issues/251-timer-box-tick-tock-emitter.md`. Want me to draft any of the open-question answers more concretely, or pause for your design pass on it?"

        "content":"1\t# 232 — Test coverage map\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\tongoing (test inventory; updated each time tests are added or\n5\tremoved)\n6\t\n7\t## Why this exists\n8\t\n9\tThis issue is the project-wide answer to \"what's tested, what\n10\tisn't, and what runs the tests.\" It folds together two earlier\n11\tthreads:\n12\t\n13\t- **316** (now folded in here) — a cheap, build-free unit-test\n14\t  runner script. Its scope lives under \"Test runners → Planned\"\n15\t  below.\n16\t- The parser-test work that opened this issue (Node-side tests\n17\t  for `langs/<name>/parser.js`).\n18\t\n19\tA related but separate issue is **311** — phase-3 integration\n20\ttests and the JSONL run-output format. 311's scope is the JSONL\n21\twriter + the `tests/maps/<name>/` fixtures driven through\n22\t`soramech-pool`; the coverage of those fixtures shows up in the\n23\t\"End-to-end fixtures\" section below, but the writer/format work\n24\tstays in 311.\n25\t\n26\tWithout a coverage view, gaps accumulate silently: tests get\n27\twritten for the area someone happens to be touching, and the rest\n28\tdrifts uncovered. The checklist below is that view, updated every\n29\ttime tests are added or removed.\n30\t\n31\tEvery time a new test file lands or a test gap is closed, the\n32\tchecklist below is updated. the move-parsers-into-langs work made it optional |\n| `langs/lua/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/bash/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/c/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/lua/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `langs/bash/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `langs/c/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/001-canvas.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/002-boxes.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/003-api.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/004-inspector.js` | `[ ]` | — (variadic helpers are pure functions, prime unit-test candidates) |\n| `assets/js/005-app.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/006-wires.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/008-source-view.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n\n**Highest-value next targets:** the variadic-slot helpers in\n`004-inspector.js` (pure functions, no DOM dependency) and the\nlexer registries in each language directory.\n\n## Lua libraries — `libs/*.lua`\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `libs/soramech-data.lua` | `[x]` | `tests/003-data-test.lua` |\n| `libs/text.lua` | `[ ]` | — (concat, split, upper, lower, trim, replace, replace_first, contains, starts_with, ends_with, length, substring) |\n| `libs/files.lua` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `libs/ollama.lua` | `[—]` | requires a live Ollama endpoint; integration-level only |\n| `libs/dkjson.lua` | `[—]` | vendored third-party |\n\n`libs/text.lua` is the most important gap — every function is a\npure string operation with obvious edge cases (empty input, nil\ninput, no match, plain vs. pattern), exactly the shape unit tests\ncatch best.\n\n## Lua server side — `src/*.lua`\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/001-schema.lua` | `[ ]` | — (validates box JSON; deserves direct accept/reject tests) |\n| `src/002-validate-map.lua` | `[ ]` | — (CLI map validator; only exercised via integration fixtures) |\n| `src/003-loader.lua` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `src/004-executor.lua` | `[~]` | exercised end-to-end via `tests/004-driver-test-runner.lua` and integration maps; no unit-level coverage |\n| `src/005-http-server.lua` | `[ ]` | — (GET/PUT boxes, connections, files, source) |\n| `src/006-server-main.lua` | `[—]` | thin entrypoint |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua` | `[—]` | thin entrypoint |\n\nSchema and validator are the highest-value gaps — they are the\nlast line of defense against malformed map files and they're pure\nfunctions over JSON-shaped tables, very testable.\n\n## C runtime — `src/*.c`\n\nBest-covered area of the project; phase 3 was built test-first.\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/008-pool-runner.c` | `[x]` | `tests/301-pool-test.c`, `tests/303-pool-spec-init-test.c` |\n| `src/009-slot-store.c` | `[x]` | `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` |\n| `src/010-graph-loader.c` | `[x]` | `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c` |\n| `src/011-spec-registry.c` | `[x]` | `tests/011-spec-registry-test.c` |\n| `src/012-dispatch.c` | `[x]` | `tests/012-dispatch-test.c` |\n| `src/013-jsonl-events.c` | `[x]` | `tests/013-jsonl-events-test.c` |\n| `src/014-event-queue.c` | `[x]` | `tests/014-event-queue-test.c` |\n| `src/015-large-value-heap.c` | `[x]` | `tests/015-large-value-heap-test.c` |\n| `src/016-unified-allocator.c` | `[x]` | `tests/016-unified-allocator-test.c` |\n| `src/017-box-id.c` | `[x]` | `tests/017-box-id-test.c` |\n| `src/018-runtime-builtins.c` | `[~]` | exercised through `tests/012-dispatch-test.c` and the runtime-create integration fixtures |\n| `src/020-sentinels.c` | `[x]` | `tests/020-sentinels-test.c` |\n| `libs/json/json.c` | `[x]` | `tests/314-json-test.c` |\n\n## Language specs — `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n\n| Spec | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `langs/lua/spec.c` | `[x]` | `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c`, `tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c` |\n| `langs/c/spec.c` | `[x]` | `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` |\n| `langs/bash/spec.c` | `[x]` | `tests/308-bash-spec-test.c`, `tests/317-text-bridge-test.c` |\n\n## End-to-end fixtures — `tests/maps/`\n\nIntegration coverage that runs via `scripts/run-tests.sh`. Each\nfixture is a real map driven through `soramech-pool`; the script\nasserts expected output substrings appear in stderr.\n\n| Fixture | What it exercises |\n|---|---|\n| `calc` | single Lua box |\n| `hello` | data → Lua, string output |\n| `comparator` | comparator branching (lt/eq/gt) |\n| `iter-route` | iterator + routing |\n| `pipeline` | five-box multilang chain (also covers the compile pipeline) |\n| `read-literal` | inline-value source on a read box |\n| `319a-many-inputs` | dispatch input cap removed; box with 20 inputs |\n| `319d-runtime-create` | Lua box uses runtime self-construction to spawn + wire a downstream Lua box |\n| `319e-c-create` | C-to-C runtime self-construction |\n| `319-box-kind-create` | language-agnostic create_box / connect dispatch box kinds |\n| `319-cross-lang-create` | C trigger creates a Lua box at runtime; lazy spec init |\n| `246-c-shim` | per-port custom translation shim (C side) |\n| `246-lua-shim` | per-port custom translation shim (Lua side) |\n| `318-lang-opaque` | $lang_opaque sentinel emit + dual-ring consumer |\n| `248-encap-input-only` | encapsulated map: input-side splice |\n| `248-encap-output-only` | encapsulated map: output-side splice |\n| `248-encap-recursive` | encapsulated map: two-level nested encapsulation |\n| `randomizer-route` | routing kind: randomizer (hash-of-counter pick) |\n| `weighted-route` | routing kind: weighted (cumulative-band lookup) |\n| `distributor-route` | routing kind: distributor (argmin over downstream fill) |\n| `multi-band-comparator-route` | routing kind: multi-band comparator with thresholds |\n| `pipeline (compile)` | the compile pipeline runs the artifact from `/tmp` |\n\nThe reference-counted-artifact (`315-refs-*`) checks plus the\nJSON-Lines run-output writer also fold into the same suite via\n`scripts/run-tests.sh`.\n\n## Test runners\n\n- **`scripts/run-tests.sh`** — integration fixtures + the JS parser\n  tests + the 315 reference-helper unit suite + the\n  compile-pipeline portable-run check. The single entry point for\n  \"run everything the build doesn't run.\" Folds Node-test results\n  into the same pass/fail counter as the integration checks.\n- **`make test`** — builds the C unit-test binaries, runs them,\n  then invokes `scripts/run-tests.sh`. Slow on a clean tree because\n  it does a full rebuild + spec build before any test runs.\n\nA cheap, build-free unit-test runner that lets you iterate without\npaying for the rebuild is **planned** — see the issue file for\nthat work for design notes.\n\n## Suggested next test additions (ranked)\n\n1. **`libs/text.lua`** — pure-Lua tests next to\n   `tests/003-data-test.lua`. The expanded string surface left a\n   wide untested area and consumers are about to multiply.\n2. **`src/001-schema.lua`** — accept/reject tests for box JSON.\n   Cheap, and the schema gates everything the executor sees.\n3. **Inspector variadic helpers** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) —\n   `parse_variadic_name`, `is_variadic_slot`, `variadic_slots_for`,\n   `last_variadic_index`, `make_variadic`, `unmake_variadic`,\n   `add_variadic_slot`, `remove_variadic_slot`. All pure, all\n   feeding into the variadic-port work.\n4. **Lexer round-trips** for the three shipped languages — feed a\n   known source through `tokenize`, check the token stream.\n5. **`langs/c/parser.js`** — write it and its tests together when\n   a C parser commits to a shape.\n\n## Related documents\n\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — components and data flow.\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — pool runner threading model.\n- `docs/005-language-specs.md` — language-spec contract.\n- `issues/phase-2-progress.md`, `issues/phase-3-progress.md` —\n  per-phase issue index, including the issues whose\n  acceptance-test fixtures appear in the End-to-end section above.\n",

          "content":"# 252 — Cheap, build-free unit-test runner\n\n## Status\nopen — design lifted out of the old 232 issue file when it\nwas converted to `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`. The script\nhasn't been written; this file is the surviving design note.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`make test` builds the C unit-test binaries, runs them, then\ninvokes `scripts/run-tests.sh` for the integration fixtures.\nThat's the right shape for \"ship it\" verification, but it's\nawkward as a development loop:\n\n- The build phase prints `→ src/foo.c` for every file, dozens of\n  lines before the first test runs on a clean tree.\n- Tests run inside a Make recipe; one binary failing aborts the\n  recipe, so later binaries that would have run aren't reported.\n- Unit-test and integration-test output interleave in one stream.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA cheap, build-free runner script — `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`\n— that runs the already-built C unit-test binaries without\nre-invoking Make and without touching the integration fixtures.\n\nGoals:\n\n1. **Cheap.** No make recursion, no spec rebuilds, no integration\n   tests. Under a second on a current build.\n2. **Continues past failures.** Every binary runs; summary at\n   the bottom names what went wrong.\n3. **Pretty by default, mineable on request.** Per-binary\n   one-line status by default; `--quiet` prints only totals;\n   `--verbose` dumps each binary's full output.\n4. **Filterable.** `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009` runs only\n   binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\n## Concept\n\nGlob `build/tests/<name>-test`, sort by filename (which sorts by\nthe project's leading numeric index), run each in turn, capture\nstdout/stderr, parse the binary's trailing `N passed, M failed`\nline for the verdict.\n\nOutput shape:\n\n```\n  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok\n  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok\n  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok\n  ...\n  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)\n```\n\nA failing binary prints its captured output below the summary\nline. Exit code is zero iff every binary passes; non-zero with\nthe count of failing binaries otherwise.\n\nConvention compliance per CLAUDE.md: hard-coded `${DIR}` at top\nwith arg override, all paths under `${DIR}`, each shell command\non its own line, lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Write `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` with the layout above.\n2. Verify it picks up every existing `build/tests/*-test` binary\n   and produces the expected totals.\n3. Verify `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 015` filters to one binary.\n4. Verify `--quiet` and `--verbose` produce useful output.\n5. Provoke a failure (temporarily modify one test) and confirm\n   the failure is reported, exit code non-zero, captured output\n   visible.\n6. Add a `make quicktest` alias or document the script in the\n   Makefile's `help` target.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Stale-binary check.** Should the script warn when a test's\n  source is newer than its built binary? Cheap (`stat` both\n  sides) but the default should be \"just run what's built\" —\n  offer it as `--check-stale`.\n- **Parse format coupling.** Parsing each binary's trailing\n  `N passed, M failed` line couples the runner to the test\n  binaries' output format. Acceptable today (every test uses\n  the same convention) but worth documenting so test authors\n  don't accidentally diverge.\n\n## Related documents\n\n- `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md` — the test inventory this\n  runner exercises.\n- The historical `issues/completed/316-simple-test-runner.md`\n  was the original home of this design; the work folded into\n  the old 232 issue file and now ends up here as its own\n  ticket so the runner script can be tracked independently.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/252-build-free-unit-test-runner.md"

    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# 252 — Cheap, build-free unit-test runner\n\n## Status\nopen — design lifted out of the old 232 issue file when it\nwas converted to `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`. The script\nhasn't been written; this file is the surviving design note.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`make test` builds the C unit-test binaries, runs them, then\ninvokes `scripts/run-tests.sh` for the integration fixtures.\nThat's the right shape for \"ship it\" verification, but it's\nawkward as a development loop:\n\n- The build phase prints `→ src/foo.c` for every file, dozens of\n  lines before the first test runs on a clean tree.\n- Tests run inside a Make recipe; one binary failing aborts the\n  recipe, so later binaries that would have run aren't reported.\n- Unit-test and integration-test output interleave in one stream.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA cheap, build-free runner script — `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`\n— that runs the already-built C unit-test binaries without\nre-invoking Make and without touching the integration fixtures.\n\nGoals:\n\n1. **Cheap.** No make recursion, no spec rebuilds, no integration\n   tests. Under a second on a current build.\n2. **Continues past failures.** Every binary runs; summary at\n   the bottom names what went wrong.\n3. **Pretty by default, mineable on request.** Per-binary\n   one-line status by default; `--quiet` prints only totals;\n   `--verbose` dumps each binary's full output.\n4. **Filterable.** `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009` runs only\n   binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\n## Concept\n\nGlob `build/tests/<name>-test`, sort by filename (which sorts by\nthe project's leading numeric index), run each in turn, capture\nstdout/stderr, parse the binary's trailing `N passed, M failed`\nline for the verdict.\n\nOutput shape:\n\n```\n  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok\n  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok\n  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok\n  ...\n  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)\n```\n\nA failing binary prints its captured output below the summary\nline. Exit code is zero iff every binary passes; non-zero with\nthe count of failing binaries otherwise.\n\nConvention compliance per CLAUDE.md: hard-coded `${DIR}` at top\nwith arg override, all paths under `${DIR}`, each shell command\non its own line, lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Write `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` with the layout above.\n2. Verify it picks up every existing `build/tests/*-test` binary\n   and produces the expected totals.\n3. Verify `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 015` filters to one binary.\n4. Verify `--quiet` and `--verbose` produce useful output.\n5. Provoke a failure (temporarily modify one test) and confirm\n   the failure is reported, exit code non-zero, captured output\n   visible.\n6. Add a `make quicktest` alias or document the script in the\n   Makefile's `help` target.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Stale-binary check.** Should the script warn when a test's\n  source is newer than its built binary? Cheap (`stat` both\n  sides) but the default should be \"just run what's built\" —\n  offer it as `--check-stale`.\n- **Parse format coupling.** Parsing each binary's trailing\n  `N passed, M failed` line couples the runner to the test\n  binaries' output format. Acceptable today (every test uses\n  the same convention) but worth documenting so test authors\n  don't accidentally diverge.\n\n## Related documents\n\n- `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md` — the test inventory this\n  runner exercises.\n- The historical `issues/completed/316-simple-test-runner.md`\n  was the original home of this design; the work folded into\n  the old 232 issue file and now ends up here as its own\n  ticket so the runner script can be tracked independently.\n",
    "type":"create",

    "originalFile":"# Phase 2 Progress\n\nGoal: an editor you can actually use to build maps, plus the graph\nmodel the phase 3 runtime will consume.\n\n## Issues\n\n| ID   | Title                                          | Status   |\n|------|------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| 201  | fix box rendering closure bug                  | complete |\n| 202  | fit-to-view on map load                        | complete |\n| 203  | map picker panel                               | complete |\n| 204  | visible interaction hints                      | complete |\n| 206  | entry box designation                          | won't implement |\n| 207  | source file browser and port auto-population   | complete |\n| 208  | port literal values                            | complete |\n| 209  | ollama query library                           | complete |\n| 210  | comparator wire branching                      | complete |\n| 211  | file browser library directories               | complete |\n| 211a | unify src/ into same directory pipeline        | complete |\n| 212  | editor interaction modes                       | complete |\n| 213  | queued inputs and task model                   | won't implement |\n| 219  | map compiler                                   | won't implement (folded into 309) |\n| 214  | tmp symlink recreation on reboot               | complete |\n| 215  | view source button                             | complete |\n| 223  | syntax highlighting via user-written lexers    | complete |\n| 224  | editable port names (canvas) — values stay in inspector | complete |\n| 225  | dir picker shows files and dir/file icons      | complete |\n| 226  | hide output controls for no-return functions   | complete |\n| 227  | hide view button when box has no ref           | complete |\n| 228  | self-loop wires routed around the box body     | complete |\n| 229  | `read` / `write` box kinds (language-agnostic IO) | complete (phase 3 + editor; phase 2 mirror skipped per teardown) |\n| 230  | required inputs and the optional flag           | complete (compile-time; runtime arg-list shortening deferred) |\n| 231  | move signature parsers into langs/              | complete |\n| 232  | test coverage map (parser tests landed; tracks gaps) | ongoing |\n| 233  | unified routing schema (comparator+iterator)    | complete |\n| 234  | middle-click duplicates the selected box        | complete |\n| 235  | literal value replaces port name on the canvas  | complete |\n| 236  | box header = filename, output label = `fn()`    | complete |\n| 237  | string-manipulation library expansion           | complete |\n| 238  | editor HTTP server config file                  | complete |\n| 239  | literal-bound input port shrinks to a nodule, name moves to the gutter | complete |\n| 216  | read-file box                                  | complete |\n| 217  | variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape | complete |\n| 218  | enforce single-output driver contract          | complete |\n| 220  | root run script and entry point cleanup        | complete |\n| 221  | iterator box (editor surface only)             | complete |\n| 222  | compile button and assets directory            | complete |\n| 248  | encapsulated map as a box (sub-maps via load-time inlining) | complete · input + output splice + recursion across nested encaps + full editor surface (kind dropdown, external bindings on read/write, file-browser encapsulate action); three on-disk fixtures green |\n| 240  | routing kind: randomizer (hash-of-counter mod n_outputs) | complete · schema + editor dropdown + n_outputs control + canvas out_<i> rendering + fixture |\n| 241  | routing kind: weighted (cumulative-band lookup over weights) | complete · schema + editor dropdown + weights text input + canvas out_<i> rendering per weights.length + fixture |\n| 242  | routing kind: distributor (argmin over downstream fill + counter tiebreaker) | complete · schema + editor dropdown + shared n_outputs control + canvas out_<i> rendering + fixture |\n| 243  | routing kind: multi-band comparator (thresholds array carves N+1 bands) | complete · schema + C loader thresholds parsing + dispatch band picker (below/between/above + eq for doubled) + canvas band-named rendering + inspector thresholds text input + legacy single-comparand still accepted + fixture |\n\n## Phase goal checklist\n\n- [x] Boxes render on map load\n- [x] Clicking a box opens the inspector\n- [x] Ref/fn set by browsing src/ files; ports auto-derived\n- [x] Map loads centered on screen (fit-to-view)\n- [x] Map can be switched from a list, not a text prompt\n- [x] Empty canvas shows interaction hints\n- [—] Entry box marker (won't implement — phase 3 auto-detects, see 305)\n- [ ] Comparator routing replaces the old branch box (issue 210)\n- [x] Iterator box with auto-grow output slots (editor; runtime in phase 3 / issue 304)\n- [x] Compile button (issue 222) — placeholder UI for the phase 3 build\n\n## Notes on graph model changes during phase 2\n\nThese are not new features so much as model corrections that shape\nwhat phase 3 will consume:\n\n- **Single-output rule** (218, complete): every box has exactly one\n  output wire. The driver contract emits one JSON value, not an\n  array.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (210, complete): the old `branch`\n  box kind with named ports is removed. A box may carry a\n  `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `lt` / `eq` / `gt`.\n- **Iterator routing** (221): a box with `iterator_outputs` is a\n  pure routing primitive; the dispatch layer rotates through the\n  declared output names.           "content":"# 250 — Routing kind: nonlinearity (three intent-named variants)\n\n## Status\nopen · design refined with the user-supplied answers from the\nearlier draft's inline comments; remaining open items are\nmostly naming and the choice of default variant\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe routing kinds shipped so far — `plain`, `comparator`,\n`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241),\n`distributor` (242), multi-band-comparator (243's\n`thresholds` extension on comparator) — all pick a **branch**\nand forward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**.\nThe schema and the dispatch picker treat the wire payload as\nopaque on the way out; routing has only ever decided *where* a\nvalue goes, never *what* it is.\n\nThere is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the\nway through. A user who wants a producer's output remapped\ninto a smoothed, bounded \"response\" — for feeding a UI slider,\nan audio level, a heat-map cell, a downstream decision pipeline\n— has to insert a dedicated call box whose entire job is one\narithmetic expression. That's a lot of box for one knob.\n\n## The shape of the new kind — value mutation as routing\n\nThe new routing kind emits a **scoring response** in a bounded\noutput range. The original input value isn't forwarded; the\n**score** (a smoothed, normalised number reflecting how strongly\nthe input falls on one side of the box's bounds) is what travels\non the wire. If the user wants the *scaled input* downstream\nrather than the response itself, they wire the upstream\nproducer to BOTH the nonlinearity AND a multiplication box, and\nmultiply input × response in the multiplier. The nonlinearity\nis composable in this shape — small, single-responsibility, one\noutput port.\n\nThree intent-named **variants** under one routing kind let the\nuser pick the right semantics without having to know what tanh\nor sigmoid is. Each variant is a different smooth function with\na different center and output range:\n\n| Variant | Output range | Midpoint | What it's for | Multiplication composes like |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `decision`    | `[-1, 1]` | `0`   | Agree / disagree / abstain. Signed strength. | Soft AND with sign-tracking (positive×positive→positive, sign agreement reinforces) |\n| `confidence`  | `[0, 1]`  | `0.5` | Probability / belief. Unsigned strength. | Probabilistic conjunction (independence assumption) |\n| `calibration` | `[0, 1]`  | (none) | Pure range remap, no decision semantics. | Linear scaling — no opinion to compose |\n\nUnder the hood the three are tanh, logistic sigmoid, and a\nclamped linear scale, but the user never has to use those names.\nThe dropdown shows `decision / confidence / calibration` with a\nshort tooltip per option.\n\n### Why three variants are the right granularity\n\nThe user identified the underlying insight in their notes: an\nS-curve produces strong outputs only for strongly positive or\nstrongly negative inputs; values close to the midpoint stay\nclose to the midpoint. Multiplying two values that are close to\nthe midpoint produces a value still close to the midpoint —\nweak evidence stays weak, strong evidence reinforces. That's\nhow neural networks compose decisions, and the three variants\nabove are the three primitive neuron types: signed (`decision`,\nlike a perceptron), unsigned probability (`confidence`, like a\nBayesian-belief node), and linear (`calibration`, like a sensor\npreprocessor).\n\n## Bounds mode — auto or fixed, decided by which sides the user pinned\n\nThe bounds (the min and max the input gets normalised against)\nhave an elegant mode-switch from the user: **presence of a\nsupplied bound on each side is the mode for that side**. Two\nfields on the routing block:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":  \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"shape\": \"confidence\",      // decision / confidence / calibration\n  \"min\":   0,                 // omit for auto-tracked low side\n  \"max\":   100                // omit for auto-tracked high side\n}\n```\n\n- **Both `min` and `max` supplied** → fully fixed bounds; auto\n  tracking off on both sides.\n- **Neither supplied** → fully auto; the box tracks the running\n  min and max it has seen so far and normalises against them.\n- **One supplied, the other omitted** → asymmetric. The\n  supplied side is locked; the omitted side keeps tracking.\n  Useful when one bound is known (\"values are always\n  non-negative\") but the other isn't (\"I don't know how big\n  they get\").\n\nC's `NULL` reading as 0 would have made \"omitted\" ambiguous if\nthe fields were raw doubles. The schema treats absence\ndistinctly from presence-of-zero: the JSON-level shape is \"the\nfield IS or IS NOT in the object,\" not \"the field's value is or\nisn't zero.\" On the C side that surfaces as two per-bound\n\"is_fixed\" flags on the routing struct alongside the two\ndoubles.\n\nA second wire-fed input or third ring reconfigure (issue 320)\ncan push a fresh `{min, max}` object at runtime to switch\nmodes; the same presence-vs-absence rule applies.\n\n## Midpoint and dampening — same elegant absence-is-mode pattern\n\nA `midpoint` field follows the same rule:\n\n- **Supplied** → asymmetric mode. The midpoint is anchored at\n  the user's value; the auto-tracked bounds drift TOWARD that\n  midpoint over time (the dampening pulls outliers in without\n  changing the anchor).\n- **Omitted** → symmetric mode. The midpoint is whatever the\n  current `(min + max) / 2` is, computed each fire. The\n  midpoint drifts with the data.\n\nThe dampening for the auto-tracked sides is an exponential\nmoving average (EMA) toward the midpoint:\n\n```\nmid = supplied_midpoint OR (min + max) / 2\nmin = α * min + (1 - α) * mid    // for auto sides only\nmax = α * max + (1 - α) * mid    // for auto sides only\nif value < min:  min = value     // immediate widen on outlier\nif value > max:  max = value\n```\n\nThe decay rate `α` (default `0.99`, i.e. halve toward midpoint\nroughly every 70 fires) lets the bounds settle after the last\noutlier has aged out. A minimum-gap floor (`max - min >= 2ε`)\nkeeps the bounds from collapsing to a degenerate point on\nconstant input.\n\n## Output — emit the response, always as a double\n\nThe output is always a `double` regardless of the input's type.\nSigmoid's image is dense in `[0, 1]`; rounding to int would\ncollapse it to `{0, 1}` and lose the score. Downstream\nconsumers that want an int should hard-error rather than\nsilently truncate.\n\nThe **scoring response** is the wire payload, not the scaled\ninput. If `input = 5` and the confidence variant says \"5 lands\n73% of the way through your bounds,\" the wire carries `0.73`,\nnot `3.65`. The user composes input × score in a downstream\nmultiplier if they want the scaled input.\n\n## Coercion — strict, hard-error on failure\n\nThe kind operates on numbers only. The dispatch picker tries to\ncoerce the inbound value:\n\n- **number on the wire** — used directly.\n- **string** — parsed as a double via `strtod` with the\n  trailing-junk-rejected variant (so `\"3.14abc\"` is a parse\n  failure, not 3.14). Matches the project's strict-over-permissive\n  preference for parsing.\n- **boolean** — `true` becomes `1.0`, `false` becomes `0.0`.\n  Worth a fixture: the C side treats 1 and 0 as true and false,\n  and the routing kind's first-class numeric handling should\n  match that convention so a boolean wire feeding a\n  nonlinearity behaves predictably.\n- **everything else** (blob, sentinel, unknown JSON shape) —\n  hard error, unconditional.\n\nThe earlier draft considered \"extract the first number from a\nstring\" for LLM-output tolerance — the user's own conclusion\ndiscarded that: a model that says `\"2 × 2 = 4\"` would feed `2`\ninto the nonlinearity, not `4`, so the lossiness is wrong-shape\nanyway. Strict parsing it is.\n\n## Out-of-range under fixed — clamp per variant (the certainty-threshold reinterpretation)\n\nThe user reframed the original \"what to do when a value exceeds\nthe user's bounds\" question elegantly: under fixed mode, the\nsupplied bounds **mean** \"past this value, I'm 100% certain.\"\nClamping isn't erasing information — it's the right behaviour\nfor that semantic.\n\nPer-variant defaults:\n\n- **`confidence`**: `input > max` → output = `1.0` (certain\n  yes); `input < min` → output = `0.0` (certain no). Clamp.\n- **`decision`**: `input > max` → output = `+1.0`; `input <\n  min` → output = `-1.0`. Clamp.\n- **`calibration`**: don't clamp — the variant has no\n  certainty semantics. Out-of-range values either extrapolate\n  linearly (output goes past the [0, 1] range) or hard-error\n  per a per-box toggle. Default: extrapolate.\n\nAuto sides (when the bound is being tracked) widen on\nout-of-range automatically, so the clamp doesn't fire on auto\nsides at all. The clamp only applies where the user has\nexplicitly pinned the bound.\n\n## Steepness `k` — sensible default, reconfigurable, inspector-exposed\n\nThe steepness `k` governs how sharp the S-curve is. `k = 1` is\ngentle: the middle 80% of the input range maps to roughly\n`[0.27, 0.73]`. `k = 6` is sharp: the middle 80% maps to\nroughly `[0.05, 0.95]`. Default to `k = 1` (more forgiving,\nbetter for \"let weak signals stay weak\" use cases).\n\nThe inspector exposes `k` as a number input with a small SVG\npreview of the chosen curve, with vertical guide-lines at the\n80% marks so the user sees both the curve shape AND the\n\"middle 80% maps to [low, high]\" numbers update live. The\npreview is cute and informative; both reasons it stays in scope.\n\nA user who wants to change `k` at runtime feeds the box a\nreconfigure message via issue 320's third input ring — the\nsame path that lets any box's JSON shape be updated mid-run.\nThis keeps the inspector knob and the runtime-tunable knob\nworking off the same field.\n\n## Per-box atomic min/max — local to the box, contested by parallel instantiations\n\nThe auto-tracked min and max live in two atomic cells on the\nbox record (not per-worker, not per-thread). If the same box\nfires under N parallel inputs at once (e.g. an upstream\niterator pushes 500 values at once), all N instantiations\ncontend on the same two cells. CAS-update widens the bounds;\nplain reads return whatever's currently stored — no read lock\nso reads stay free.\n\nAuto bounds are **expected to be non-deterministic across runs**\nbecause the order of arrivals depends on the pool's scheduler.\nThis is a feature, not a bug; the kind is for scoring streams\nof data where the recent past defines what \"normal\" looks like.\nA user who wants deterministic behaviour should supply fixed\nbounds. No debugging output for the non-determinism — a user\nwho wants to inspect the running bounds can wire a small log\nbox downstream of the nonlinearity and read the score\ntrajectory.\n\n## Reset across runs — no persistence by default\n\nThe auto bounds reset to \"unseen\" at the start of each run. A\nuser who wants the previous run's bounds carried forward\nsupplies them as fixed values on the current run's box JSON.\nPersistence-by-default would add a hidden file on disk per\nnonlinearity box; explicit-on-request is cleaner.\n\n## Editor surface\n\n- **Variant dropdown**: `decision / confidence / calibration`,\n  with a short tooltip per option (\"Soft +/- with clear\n  neutral\" / \"Soft yes/no with uncertainty\" / \"Range remap, no\n  curve\").\n- **min, max, midpoint** number inputs. Each has a per-field\n  \"auto\" checkbox; checked means \"omit this field, let the box\n  track it.\" Unchecked means the value in the input is the\n  pinned bound.\n- **k (steepness)** number input.\n- **Live preview**: small SVG showing the chosen variant's\n  curve under the current `k`, with vertical guides at the\n  middle-80% input range and horizontal guides at the output\n  values those map to. Numbers updated live as `k` changes.\n- The box's single output port keeps the plain-routing name\n  (`out`) so wires drawn before the kind was switched in don't\n  need renaming.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`): accept `kind:\n   \"nonlinearity\"`; validate `shape` is one of `decision /\n   confidence / calibration`; optional `min`, `max`, `midpoint`,\n   `k`.\n2. **Slot store** (`src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`): add\n   `SLOT_DOUBLE` cells with CAS-update widening semantics —\n   atomic-load returns the current value; widen is a CAS loop\n   that retries until the new value sticks. Two such cells per\n   nonlinearity box that has auto sides (one for each direction\n   that might widen).\n3. **Graph loader** (`src/010-graph-loader.c`): read the\n   nonlinearity routing fields into the box record; allocate\n   the auto-side slot cells; record the per-bound \"is_fixed\"\n   flags.\n4. **Dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`): implement the\n   value-transform branch in `push_routed`. This is the first\n   routing kind that **writes a new value** to the output wire\n   instead of forwarding the input unchanged; the path\n   currently passes the input slot pointer through. The branch\n   reads bounds + midpoint + k, computes the normalised\n   position, applies the variant's curve, clamps per the\n   per-variant rule, writes the double to the output buffer,\n   pushes downstream.\n5. **Inspector** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): variant\n   dropdown, four number inputs each with the auto checkbox, k\n   input, SVG preview component. Reuses the setter pattern from\n   240/241/243 (sever outgoing wires on shape change — though\n   here the output port shape is stable, so wires survive).\n6. **Canvas** (`assets/js/002-boxes.js`): single output port\n   named `out`, same as plain routing. No new port-shape\n   handling needed.\n7. **Fixtures**: at least one per variant.\n   - `nonlinearity-confidence-route/` — feed integers 1..100\n     into a confidence box with fixed bounds [0, 100]; assert\n     output 50 maps to ~0.5, output 100 clamps to 1.0.\n   - `nonlinearity-decision-route/` — feed -10..10 into a\n     decision box with fixed bounds [-10, 10]; assert 0 → 0,\n     +10 → +1, -10 → -1.\n   - `nonlinearity-calibration-route/` — fixed bounds [0, 200],\n     input 50 → 0.25; out-of-range 250 extrapolates to 1.25\n     (not clamped, calibration variant).\n   - `nonlinearity-auto-route/` — no fixed bounds; feed a\n     stream; assert later values get sensible scores once the\n     box has seen enough data.\n   - `nonlinearity-bool-input-route/` — input is `true` /\n     `false` strings; assert the coercion path produces sane\n     scores.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Name of the kind.** `nonlinearity` is precise but\n  intimidating; `squash` matches neural-network vocabulary;\n  `remap` is the most boring and most discoverable. Pick one\n  before the schema lands — once on disk in fixture maps,\n  renaming is a migration. The three intent-named variants\n  inside the kind soften the kind-name's importance somewhat\n  (users pick a variant, not the kind), so the kind-name only\n  has to read sensibly in the dropdown of routing kinds.\n- **Default variant.** Which of the three variants does a\n  freshly-created box land on? `confidence` is the most\n  general-purpose (probability semantics fit most \"score this\"\n  use cases). `calibration` is the most neutral (no curve,\n  pure remap — closest to plain routing for a user who picked\n  the kind by accident). `decision` is the most opinionated.\n  Default to `confidence` unless a use-case-survey says\n  otherwise.\n- **Calibration out-of-range mode.** Extrapolate (default\n  above) vs hard-error vs clamp-to-1. Extrapolate is the most\n  honest for a \"pure remap\" semantics; the other two are\n  defensible too. Settle when a fixture forces a choice.\n\n## Notes on architecture\n\nThe nonlinearity is the first routing kind whose dispatch path\nemits a value that wasn't already on the input wire. The\nexisting `push_routed` machinery passes the input bytes through\nverbatim; the new path produces a fresh `double`, formatted as\nbytes via `snprintf(\"%g\", score)`, and pushes that. Worth being\nexplicit about so future kinds (a hypothetical `square`,\n`log`, `abs`, `quantise`) can follow the same shape — and so\nthe architecture review notices when a third or fourth value-\ntransforming kind appears and considers whether the category\ndeserves a first-class concept rather than per-kind one-offs in\npush_routed.\n\nOne existing routing kind already breaks the \"every output is\nexactly one branch fired\" rule: the iterator. Its fire emits on\none port but the port chosen depends on the counter, not on a\nbranch index baked into a wire. The nonlinearity also has a\nsingle output port; the user picks a variant, the variant\ndecides what to emit. So the \"single output port + variable\noutput value\" shape isn't unprecedented.\n\nThe dump truck on the other side of town is still picking up\ntrash, and the raccoons and the hillbillies are still arguing\nabout whose turn it is to do the dishes. The user's earlier\nnote about playing hard and loose with the users-who-misuse-the-\nbox — \"you're gonna go far but that's because the dump truck\nthat picks up the trash (aka you) has to drive really far to\nget to the dump which is way on the other side of town with\nthe raccoons and the hillbillies\" — stays preserved here\nbecause that's how feedback memory works on this project:\nsometimes the design lives in the comment, not the spec.\n",
