Worth being","+explicit about so future kinds (a hypothetical `square`,","+`log`, `abs`, `quantise`) can follow the same shape — and so","+the architecture review notices when a third or fourth value-","+transforming kind appears and considers whether the category","+deserves a first-class concept rather than per-kind one-offs in","+push_routed."," ","--- what if we accept the first number found in a string, and strip out the rest,","-   both before and after that number? It'll make it a bit easier if an LLM or","-   something outputs something like: \"sure, I can multiply 2x2! The answer is 4.\"","-   wait actually that won't help at all, because it'd output 2. Nuts. I guess","-   that problem should be solved on the user's end with better prompting...","+One existing routing kind already breaks the \"every output is","+exactly one branch fired\" rule: the iterator. Its fire emits on","+one port but the port chosen depends on the counter, not on a","+branch index baked into a wire. The nonlinearity also has a","+single output port; the user picks a variant, the variant","+decides what to emit. So the \"single output port + variable","+output value\" shape isn't unprecedented."," ","-- **Per-worker vs shared min/max.** Auto-mode bounds are","-  best shared across all workers (so the normalisation is","-  consistent regardless of which worker handled which value),","-  which means atomic CAS on a shared slot. Per-worker bounds","-  would be faster but produce per-worker output streams that","-  drift — likely the wrong shape.","-","--- neither per-worker nor per-thread. The value should be local to the box. If","-   there are multiple instantiations of the same box, then only the box that is","-   being run will have the value. If many different instantiations of the same","-   box are being run, like if we supply 500 input values at once, then they'd","-   all contest the same min/max values - atomic spinlocks on them will keep","-   everyone honest, so long as we don't lock it when reading values.","-","-- **Reset across runs.** Auto bounds reset to \"unseen\" at the","-  start of each run. Persisting them across runs (so the","-  second run starts from where the first left off) is a","-  separate feature; flag it for a follow-up if anyone asks.","-","--- we don't want to persist between runs. If the user wants that, they will provide","-   fixed values as instinct.","-","-- **Where the transform lives.** This is the first routing","-  kind that mutates the wire value. The dispatch layer","-  currently treats routing-kind logic as branch selection","-  only — generalising it to \"may also rewrite the value","-  being forwarded\" is a small but real architectural shift.","-  Worth thinking about whether **value-transforming routing**","-  is a category we want more of (square, log, abs,","-  quantise…) — if so, factor the rewrite-the-value path as","-  a first-class concept rather than a special case for this","-  one kind.","-","--- I think the fact that it mutates the value will be obvious by the fact that","-   there's only one output port.     "content":"# 250 — Routing kind: nonlinearity (three intent-named variants)\n\n## Status\nopen · design refined with the user-supplied answers from the\nearlier draft's inline comments; remaining open items are\nmostly naming and the choice of default variant\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe routing kinds shipped so far — `plain`, `comparator`,\n`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241),\n`distributor` (242), multi-band-comparator (243's\n`thresholds` extension on comparator) — all pick a **branch**\nand forward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**.\nThe schema and the dispatch picker treat the wire payload as\nopaque on the way out; routing has only ever decided *where* a\nvalue goes, never *what* it is.\n\nThere is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the\nway through. A user who wants a producer's output remapped\ninto a smoothed, bounded \"response\" — for feeding a UI slider,\nan audio level, a heat-map cell, a downstream decision pipeline\n— has to insert a dedicated call box whose entire job is one\narithmetic expression. That's a lot of box for one knob.\n\n## The shape of the new kind — value mutation as routing\n\nThe new routing kind emits a **scoring response** in a bounded\noutput range. The original input value isn't forwarded; the\n**score** (a smoothed, normalised number reflecting how strongly\nthe input falls on one side of the box's bounds) is what travels\non the wire. If the user wants the *scaled input* downstream\nrather than the response itself, they wire the upstream\nproducer to BOTH the nonlinearity AND a multiplication box, and\nmultiply input × response in the multiplier. The nonlinearity\nis composable in this shape — small, single-responsibility, one\noutput port.\n\nThree intent-named **variants** under one routing kind let the\nuser pick the right semantics without having to know what tanh\nor sigmoid is. Each variant is a different smooth function with\na different center and output range:\n\n| Variant | Output range | Midpoint | What it's for | Multiplication composes like |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `decision`    | `[-1, 1]` | `0`   | Agree / disagree / abstain. Signed strength. | Soft AND with sign-tracking (positive×positive→positive, sign agreement reinforces) |\n| `confidence`  | `[0, 1]`  | `0.5` | Probability / belief. Unsigned strength. | Probabilistic conjunction (independence assumption) |\n| `calibration` | `[0, 1]`  | (none) | Pure range remap, no decision semantics. | Linear scaling — no opinion to compose |\n\nUnder the hood the three are tanh, logistic sigmoid, and a\nclamped linear scale, but the user never has to use those names.\nThe dropdown shows `decision / confidence / calibration` with a\nshort tooltip per option.\n\n### Why three variants are the right granularity\n\nThe user identified the underlying insight in their notes: an\nS-curve produces strong outputs only for strongly positive or\nstrongly negative inputs; values close to the midpoint stay\nclose to the midpoint. Multiplying two values that are close to\nthe midpoint produces a value still close to the midpoint —\nweak evidence stays weak, strong evidence reinforces. That's\nhow neural networks compose decisions, and the three variants\nabove are the three primitive neuron types: signed (`decision`,\nlike a perceptron), unsigned probability (`confidence`, like a\nBayesian-belief node), and linear (`calibration`, like a sensor\npreprocessor).\n\n## Bounds mode — auto or fixed, decided by which sides the user pinned\n\nThe bounds (the min and max the input gets normalised against)\nhave an elegant mode-switch from the user: **presence of a\nsupplied bound on each side is the mode for that side**. Two\nfields on the routing block:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":  \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"shape\": \"confidence\",      // decision / confidence / calibration\n  \"min\":   0,                 // omit for auto-tracked low side\n  \"max\":   100                // omit for auto-tracked high side\n}\n```\n\n- **Both `min` and `max` supplied** → fully fixed bounds; auto\n  tracking off on both sides.\n- **Neither supplied** → fully auto; the box tracks the running\n  min and max it has seen so far and normalises against them.\n- **One supplied, the other omitted** → asymmetric. The\n  supplied side is locked; the omitted side keeps tracking.\n  Useful when one bound is known (\"values are always\n  non-negative\") but the other isn't (\"I don't know how big\n  they get\").\n\nC's `NULL` reading as 0 would have made \"omitted\" ambiguous if\nthe fields were raw doubles. The schema treats absence\ndistinctly from presence-of-zero: the JSON-level shape is \"the\nfield IS or IS NOT in the object,\" not \"the field's value is or\nisn't zero.\" On the C side that surfaces as two per-bound\n\"is_fixed\" flags on the routing struct alongside the two\ndoubles.\n\nA second wire-fed input or third ring reconfigure (issue 320)\ncan push a fresh `{min, max}` object at runtime to switch\nmodes; the same presence-vs-absence rule applies.\n\n## Midpoint and dampening — same elegant absence-is-mode pattern\n\nA `midpoint` field follows the same rule:\n\n- **Supplied** → asymmetric mode. The midpoint is anchored at\n  the user's value; the auto-tracked bounds drift TOWARD that\n  midpoint over time (the dampening pulls outliers in without\n  changing the anchor).\n- **Omitted** → symmetric mode. The midpoint is whatever the\n  current `(min + max) / 2` is, computed each fire. The\n  midpoint drifts with the data.\n\nThe dampening for the auto-tracked sides is an exponential\nmoving average (EMA) toward the midpoint:\n\n```\nmid = supplied_midpoint OR (min + max) / 2\nmin = α * min + (1 - α) * mid    // for auto sides only\nmax = α * max + (1 - α) * mid    // for auto sides only\nif value < min:  min = value     // immediate widen on outlier\nif value > max:  max = value\n```\n\nThe decay rate `α` (default `0.99`, i.e. halve toward midpoint\nroughly every 70 fires) lets the bounds settle after the last\noutlier has aged out. A minimum-gap floor (`max - min >= 2ε`)\nkeeps the bounds from collapsing to a degenerate point on\nconstant input.\n\n## Output — emit the response, always as a double\n\nThe output is always a `double` regardless of the input's type.\nSigmoid's image is dense in `[0, 1]`; rounding to int would\ncollapse it to `{0, 1}` and lose the score. Downstream\nconsumers that want an int should hard-error rather than\nsilently truncate.\n\nThe **scoring response** is the wire payload, not the scaled\ninput. If `input = 5` and the confidence variant says \"5 lands\n73% of the way through your bounds,\" the wire carries `0.73`,\nnot `3.65`. The user composes input × score in a downstream\nmultiplier if they want the scaled input.\n\n## Coercion — strict, hard-error on failure\n\nThe kind operates on numbers only. The dispatch picker tries to\ncoerce the inbound value:\n\n- **number on the wire** — used directly.\n- **string** — parsed as a double via `strtod` with the\n  trailing-junk-rejected variant (so `\"3.14abc\"` is a parse\n  failure, not 3.14). Matches the project's strict-over-permissive\n  preference for parsing.\n- **boolean** — `true` becomes `1.0`, `false` becomes `0.0`.\n  Worth a fixture: the C side treats 1 and 0 as true and false,\n  and the routing kind's first-class numeric handling should\n  match that convention so a boolean wire feeding a\n  nonlinearity behaves predictably.\n- **everything else** (blob, sentinel, unknown JSON shape) —\n  hard error, unconditional.\n\nThe earlier draft considered \"extract the first number from a\nstring\" for LLM-output tolerance — the user's own conclusion\ndiscarded that: a model that says `\"2 × 2 = 4\"` would feed `2`\ninto the nonlinearity, not `4`, so the lossiness is wrong-shape\nanyway. Strict parsing it is.\n\n## Out-of-range under fixed — clamp per variant (the certainty-threshold reinterpretation)\n\nThe user reframed the original \"what to do when a value exceeds\nthe user's bounds\" question elegantly: under fixed mode, the\nsupplied bounds **mean** \"past this value, I'm 100% certain.\"\nClamping isn't erasing information — it's the right behaviour\nfor that semantic.\n\nPer-variant defaults:\n\n- **`confidence`**: `input > max` → output = `1.0` (certain\n  yes); `input < min` → output = `0.0` (certain no). Clamp.\n- **`decision`**: `input > max` → output = `+1.0`; `input <\n  min` → output = `-1.0`. Clamp.\n- **`calibration`**: don't clamp — the variant has no\n  certainty semantics. Out-of-range values either extrapolate\n  linearly (output goes past the [0, 1] range) or hard-error\n  per a per-box toggle. Default: extrapolate.\n\nAuto sides (when the bound is being tracked) widen on\nout-of-range automatically, so the clamp doesn't fire on auto\nsides at all. The clamp only applies where the user has\nexplicitly pinned the bound.\n\n## Steepness `k` — sensible default, reconfigurable, inspector-exposed\n\nThe steepness `k` governs how sharp the S-curve is. `k = 1` is\ngentle: the middle 80% of the input range maps to roughly\n`[0.27, 0.73]`. `k = 6` is sharp: the middle 80% maps to\nroughly `[0.05, 0.95]`. Default to `k = 1` (more forgiving,\nbetter for \"let weak signals stay weak\" use cases).\n\nThe inspector exposes `k` as a number input with a small SVG\npreview of the chosen curve, with vertical guide-lines at the\n80% marks so the user sees both the curve shape AND the\n\"middle 80% maps to [low, high]\" numbers update live. The\npreview is cute and informative; both reasons it stays in scope.\n\nA user who wants to change `k` at runtime feeds the box a\nreconfigure message via issue 320's third input ring — the\nsame path that lets any box's JSON shape be updated mid-run.\nThis keeps the inspector knob and the runtime-tunable knob\nworking off the same field.\n\n## Per-box atomic min/max — local to the box, contested by parallel instantiations\n\nThe auto-tracked min and max live in two atomic cells on the\nbox record (not per-worker, not per-thread). If the same box\nfires under N parallel inputs at once (e.g. an upstream\niterator pushes 500 values at once), all N instantiations\ncontend on the same two cells. CAS-update widens the bounds;\nplain reads return whatever's currently stored — no read lock\nso reads stay free.\n\nAuto bounds are **expected to be non-deterministic across runs**\nbecause the order of arrivals depends on the pool's scheduler.\nThis is a feature, not a bug; the kind is for scoring streams\nof data where the recent past defines what \"normal\" looks like.\nA user who wants deterministic behaviour should supply fixed\nbounds. No debugging output for the non-determinism — a user\nwho wants to inspect the running bounds can wire a small log\nbox downstream of the nonlinearity and read the score\ntrajectory.\n\n## Reset across runs — no persistence by default\n\nThe auto bounds reset to \"unseen\" at the start of each run. A\nuser who wants the previous run's bounds carried forward\nsupplies them as fixed values on the current run's box JSON.\nPersistence-by-default would add a hidden file on disk per\nnonlinearity box; explicit-on-request is cleaner.\n\n## Editor surface\n\n- **Variant dropdown**: `decision / confidence / calibration`,\n  with a short tooltip per option (\"Soft +/- with clear\n  neutral\" / \"Soft yes/no with uncertainty\" / \"Range remap, no\n  curve\").\n- **min, max, midpoint** number inputs. Each has a per-field\n  \"auto\" checkbox; checked means \"omit this field, let the box\n  track it.\" Unchecked means the value in the input is the\n  pinned bound.\n- **k (steepness)** number input.\n- **Live preview**: small SVG showing the chosen variant's\n  curve under the current `k`, with vertical guides at the\n  middle-80% input range and horizontal guides at the output\n  values those map to. Numbers updated live as `k` changes.\n- The box's single output port keeps the plain-routing name\n  (`out`) so wires drawn before the kind was switched in don't\n  need renaming.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`): accept `kind:\n   \"nonlinearity\"`; validate `shape` is one of `decision /\n   confidence / calibration`; optional `min`, `max`, `midpoint`,\n   `k`.\n2. **Slot store** (`src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`): add\n   `SLOT_DOUBLE` cells with CAS-update widening semantics —\n   atomic-load returns the current value; widen is a CAS loop\n   that retries until the new value sticks. Two such cells per\n   nonlinearity box that has auto sides (one for each direction\n   that might widen).\n3. **Graph loader** (`src/010-graph-loader.c`): read the\n   nonlinearity routing fields into the box record; allocate\n   the auto-side slot cells; record the per-bound \"is_fixed\"\n   flags.\n4. **Dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`): implement the\n   value-transform branch in `push_routed`. This is the first\n   routing kind that **writes a new value** to the output wire\n   instead of forwarding the input unchanged; the path\n   currently passes the input slot pointer through. The branch\n   reads bounds + midpoint + k, computes the normalised\n   position, applies the variant's curve, clamps per the\n   per-variant rule, writes the double to the output buffer,\n   pushes downstream.\n5. **Inspector** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): variant\n   dropdown, four number inputs each with the auto checkbox, k\n   input, SVG preview component. Reuses the setter pattern from\n   240/241/243 (sever outgoing wires on shape change — though\n   here the output port shape is stable, so wires survive).\n6. **Canvas** (`assets/js/002-boxes.js`): single output port\n   named `out`, same as plain routing. No new port-shape\n   handling needed.\n7. **Fixtures**: at least one per variant.\n   - `nonlinearity-confidence-route/` — feed integers 1..100\n     into a confidence box with fixed bounds [0, 100]; assert\n     output 50 maps to ~0.5, output 100 clamps to 1.0.\n   - `nonlinearity-decision-route/` — feed -10..10 into a\n     decision box with fixed bounds [-10, 10]; assert 0 → 0,\n     +10 → +1, -10 → -1.\n   - `nonlinearity-calibration-route/` — fixed bounds [0, 200],\n     input 50 → 0.25; out-of-range 250 extrapolates to 1.25\n     (not clamped, calibration variant).\n   - `nonlinearity-auto-route/` — no fixed bounds; feed a\n     stream; assert later values get sensible scores once the\n     box has seen enough data.\n   - `nonlinearity-bool-input-route/` — input is `true` /\n     `false` strings; assert the coercion path produces sane\n     scores.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Name of the kind.** `nonlinearity` is precise but\n  intimidating; `squash` matches neural-network vocabulary;\n  `remap` is the most boring and most discoverable. Pick one\n  before the schema lands — once on disk in fixture maps,\n  renaming is a migration. The three intent-named variants\n  inside the kind soften the kind-name's importance somewhat\n  (users pick a variant, not the kind), so the kind-name only\n  has to read sensibly in the dropdown of routing kinds.\n- **Default variant.** Which of the three variants does a\n  freshly-created box land on? `confidence` is the most\n  general-purpose (probability semantics fit most \"score this\"\n  use cases). `calibration` is the most neutral (no curve,\n  pure remap — closest to plain routing for a user who picked\n  the kind by accident). `decision` is the most opinionated.\n  Default to `confidence` unless a use-case-survey says\n  otherwise.\n- **Calibration out-of-range mode.** Extrapolate (default\n  above) vs hard-error vs clamp-to-1. Extrapolate is the most\n  honest for a \"pure remap\" semantics; the other two are\n  defensible too. Settle when a fixture forces a choice.\n\n## Notes on architecture\n\nThe nonlinearity is the first routing kind whose dispatch path\nemits a value that wasn't already on the input wire. The\nexisting `push_routed` machinery passes the input bytes through\nverbatim; the new path produces a fresh `double`, formatted as\nbytes via `snprintf(\"%g\", score)`, and pushes that. Worth being\nexplicit about so future kinds (a hypothetical `square`,\n`log`, `abs`, `quantise`) can follow the same shape — and so\nthe architecture review notices when a third or fourth value-\ntransforming kind appears and considers whether the category\ndeserves a first-class concept rather than per-kind one-offs in\npush_routed.\n\nOne existing routing kind already breaks the \"every output is\nexactly one branch fired\" rule: the iterator. Its fire emits on\none port but the port chosen depends on the counter, not on a\nbranch index baked into a wire. The nonlinearity also has a\nsingle output port; the user picks a variant, the variant\ndecides what to emit. So the \"single output port + variable\noutput value\" shape isn't unprecedented.\n\nThe dump truck on the other side of town is still picking up\ntrash, and the raccoons and the hillbillies are still arguing\nabout whose turn it is to do the dishes. The user's earlier\nnote about playing hard and loose with the users-who-misuse-the-\nbox — \"you're gonna go far but that's because the dump truck\nthat picks up the trash (aka you) has to drive really far to\nget to the dump which is way on the other side of town with\nthe raccoons and the hillbillies\" — stays preserved here\nbecause that's how feedback memory works on this project:\nsometimes the design lives in the comment, not the spec.\n",
    "type":"update",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/250-routing-kind-nonlinearity.md"
  },

}

        "text":"250 rewritten. The shape now:\n\n- **Three intent-named variants** (`decision` / `confidence` / `calibration`) replace the old `shape`-by-mathematician-name + `out_range` split. Each carries its own midpoint, output range, and composition semantics. The user never has to know what tanh is.\n- **Bounds-mode is decided by which sides the user pinned.** `min` + `max` both supplied → fixed; neither → auto; one supplied → asymmetric (that side fixed, other auto-tracked). Same presence-is-mode rule applies to `midpoint`.\n- **Dampening as EMA toward the midpoint** for auto sides, with a minimum-gap floor; the supplied-midpoint case anchors the EMA target, the no-midpoint case lets the midpoint follow the data.\n- **Clamping as \"certainty threshold\"** — your reframe. Per-variant defaults: confidence / decision clamp; calibration extrapolates (no certainty semantics).\n- **Output is always a double**, and the wire carries the *response* (the smoothed [0,1] or [-1,1] number) rather than the scaled input. The user composes `input × response` in a downstream multiplier if they want.\n- **Steepness `k`** as a sensible default + inspector knob + reconfigurable via 320. SVG preview with the middle-80% guides stays in scope (cute is justification too).\n- **Per-box atomic min/max cells**, not per-worker or per-thread. Auto bounds non-deterministic across runs, by design; no debug output — wire a log box if you want the trajectory.\n- **No persistence** across runs; user supplies fixed bounds if they want carry-over.\n- **Strict string parsing** (no LLM-output number extraction — your own conclusion); boolean coercion handled per the C-style 1/0 convention with a fixture to lock it.\n\nWhat's still open in the doc: the kind's name (`nonlinearity` / `squash` / `remap`), the default variant for new boxes, and the calibration variant's out-of-range mode (extrapolate vs hard-error vs clamp-to-1).\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The biggest design move here was your **\"presence of a bound IS the mode for that side\"** insight. It collapses three separate flags (`mode`, `fixed_min_flag`, `fixed_max_flag`) into a single JSON-shape rule: a field is either in the object or it isn't, and that's the answer. The C side then mirrors with two `is_fixed` booleans next to the two doubles — same information, two representations, both natural for their respective audiences. The schema becomes self-describing: a reader sees what's set and knows what mode the box is in without having to look up a flag's meaning.\n- The decision to **emit the response, not the scaled input** is the call that makes this kind composable. If the nonlinearity scaled-and-multiplied internally, every consumer would get back a number whose meaning depended on the bounds the nonlinearity happened to be using. Emitting the response gives every consumer the same `[0, 1]` or `[-1, 1]` scale, regardless of what the nonlinearity is scoring against. Then \"I want the scaled input\" is a separate, optional composition the user opts into with a multiplier box. Same pattern as the `write` box keeping its `value` input separate from its `path` input — small box, single responsibility, the user wires together the pipeline they want.\n- The doc preserves your dump-truck-and-raccoons line at the very bottom under \"Notes on architecture.\" It's not just for flavour: that note is the design philosophy for what to do when a user holds the box wrong, and it belongs in the doc that someone reads when they're about to make exactly that choice for their own future kinds.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nThe rewrite is unstaged. Want me to commit it, or hold while you take another read?"
      }],

    "snippet":"1\t# 320 — Box reconfigure via third input ring\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen · design draft; a handful of open questions remain but the\n5\tshape is settled enough to scope an implementation slice\n6\t\n7\t## Current behavior\n8\t\n9\tA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses the\n10\tbox's JSON once (`parse_box_file` in `src/010-graph-loader.c`),\n11\tfills in every field — `kind`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, the routing\n12\tshape, the input port list, the connections array — and the\n13\tdispatch layer (`src/012-dispatch.c`) walks that record on every\n14\tfire. Nothing in the running program changes those fields.\n15\t\n16\tThe two paths the runtime already has to \"change the graph while\n17\tit's running\" — issue 319's `create_box` / `connect` primitives,\n18\tand issue 248's load-time encapsulation splice — both **add** to\n19\tthe graph; they never **rewrite** a box that already exists. A\n20\tbox is the box it was born as.\n21\t\n22\tThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\n23\t**reconfigured** mid-run. A new configuration arrives as a\n24\tJSON-shaped message inside the normal input stream, on any input\n25\tport; the worker that's gathering inputs for the next fire\n26\tencounters the reconfigure tag, applies it, and continues\n27\tgathering under the new config before firing.\n28\t\n29\t## Concept\n30\t\n31\tEvery input slot grows a **third ring** alongside the native +\n32\tJSON pair from issue 312. The third ring carries one kind of\n33\tmessage only — a JSON object **exactly matching the box's own\n34\tJSON schema**, the same shape a `boxes/<id>.json` file holds at\n35\tload. Any input port can carry reconfigure messages; producers\n36\tpush to whichever port makes sense for their fan-in topology, and\n37\tthe dispatch layer treats reconfigure cells as a peer to native\n38\tand JSON cells.\n39\t\n40\tThe per-cell **ring-selector tag** (the bookkeeping that already\n41\ttells the consumer \"this cell came in on the native ring, or the\n42\tJSON ring\" — issue 312's dual-ring `which_ring` flag, extended\n43\tthrough issue 318a's per-call ordering) grows a third value:\n44\t**reconfigure**. When the consumer's input-gathering walks a port\n45\tand sees the next cell tagged `reconfigure`, it doesn't push the\n46\tbytes into an input buffer for the box function; it interprets\n47\tthem as a re-parse of the box's own JSON.\n48\t\n49\t### The mixed-stream scenario\n50\t\n51\tImagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The\n52\tdispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells\n53\tin turn:\n54\t\n55\t```\n56\tport_a → native value (popped, retained)\n57\tport_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)\n58\tport_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)\n59\tport_c → RECONFIGURE\n60\t```\n61\t\n62\t-- this actually will never happen. We only pop one value from each slot per box\n63\t   execution cycle. We should do a quick audit to ensure the design reflects this,\n64\t   updating current or re-opening closed issues if necessary.\n65\t\n66\tThe worker:\n67\t\n68\t1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.\n69\t2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second\n70\t   in worker-local stack buffers.\n71\t3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails\n72\t   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker\n73\t   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;\n74\t   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is\n75\t   done.\n76\t4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the\n77\t   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory\n78\t   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in\n79\t   place.\n80\t5. Releases the YARQ barrier.\n81\t6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more\n82\t   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port\n83\t   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.\n84\t7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained\n85\t   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the\n86\t   new config expects.\n87\t\n88\tThe fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure\n89\tis a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering\n90\tand the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.\n91\t\n92\t### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?\n93\t\n94\tThe retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the\n95\tnew config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,\n96\tremove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the\n97\tretained values still map by port name. If the new config renames\n98\ta port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the\n99\trename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence\n100\trecorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port\n101\tremoval mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get\n102\tdropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.\n103\t\n104\t## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier\n105\t\n106\tA reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers\n107\tfiring the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,\n108\tno other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new\n109\t`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.\n110\t\n111\tA spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing\n112\tcaptures the intended shape exactly:\n113\t\n114\t> \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back\n115\t> at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n116\t\n117\t**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this\n118\tprimitive. Mechanism:\n119\t\n120\t- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).\n121\t- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the\n122\t  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker\n123\t  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue\n124\t  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.\n125\t  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from\n126\t  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately\n127\t  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other\n128\t  pending work runs first.\n129\t- **Release**: atomic store of 0.\n130\t\n131\tThe cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each\n132\tcontended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization\n133\tprimitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than\n134\t*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does\n135\tbest (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\n136\tjust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n137\t\n138\tThe YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the\n139\tbox record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue\n140\t319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own\n141\tcopy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding\n142\tthose into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't\n143\tinterleave dangerously when both fire at once.\n144\t\n145\t-- workers who are just executing the box function should not claim the yarq.\n146\t   they don't need it - they're just reading values, not mutating them.\n147\t\n148\t## Schema for the third-ring message\n149\t\n150\tA message on the third ring is a JSON object identical in shape\n151\tto what `parse_box_file` parses today:\n152\t\n153\t```json\n154\t{\n155\t    \"id\":      \"my_box\",          // must match the target box\n156\t    \"kind\":    \"call\",            // any kind, including a kind change\n157\t    \"lang\":    \"lua\",\n158\t    \"ref\":     \"lib/new_impl.lua\",\n159\t    \"fn\":      \"new_handler\",\n160\t    \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n161\t    \"inputs\":  [\n162\t        { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n163\t        { \"name\": \"y\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true }\n164\t    ],\n165\t    \"connections\": [\n166\t        { \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"value\" }\n167\t    ]\n168\t}\n169\t```\n170\t\n171\tThe `id` field MUST match the target box (a safety check; mixed\n172\tids hard-error). Every other field is the new state. Fields\n173\tabsent get default treatment (same as a freshly-parsed box file).\n174\tThe schema validator runs in full — a malformed reconfigure\n175\tcan't half-apply.\n176\t\n177\t## Reconfigure semantics — what changes\n178\t\n179\t**Slice 1 supports every field comprehensively.** No \"cheap vs\n\n... The Lua schema already validated the\n         * shape string and number types; here we just thread the\n         * fields onto the routing struct.\n         *\n         * Presence vs absence of min / max / midpoint is the\n         * mode-flag for each side — supplied means \"fixed; clamp\n         * past it\"; absent means \"track it via the atomic running\n         * cells, decay toward midpoint via EMA on every fire.\" */\n        out->kind = ROUTING_NONLINEARITY;\n        out->n_outputs = 1;\n        out->nl_shape = NL_CONFIDENCE;     /* default if shape missing/unknown */\n        out->nl_steepness = 1.0;\n        out->nl_min_is_fixed = 0;\n        out->nl_max_is_fixed = 0;\n        out->nl_mid_is_fixed = 0;\n        out->nl_fixed_min = 0.0;\n        out->nl_fixed_max = 1.0;\n        out->nl_fixed_mid = 0.0;\n        /* Running cells initialised so the first observed value\n         * always widens both sides. Using sentinel bit patterns\n         * (+inf for min, -inf for max) makes the first compare\n         * deterministic. */\n        union { double d; uint64_t u; } pos_inf, neg_inf;\n        pos_inf.d =  (double)INFINITY;\n        neg_inf.d = -(double)INFINITY;\n        atomic_init(&out->nl_running_min, pos_inf.u);\n        atomic_init(&out->nl_running_max, neg_inf.u);\n\n        json_node_t *sh = json_object_get(r, \"shape\");\n        if (!sh || json_kind(sh) != JSON_STRING) {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity routing requires \"\n                           \"'shape' string (decision / confidence / calibration)\",\n                           box_id);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        const char *s = json_string_value(sh);\n        if      (strcmp(s, \"confidence\")  == 0) out->nl_shape = NL_CONFIDENCE;\n        else if (strcmp(s, \"decision\")    == 0) out->nl_shape = NL_DECISION;\n        else if (strcmp(s, \"calibration\") == 0) out->nl_shape = NL_CALIBRATION;\n        else {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'shape' = '%s' must be \"\n                           \"'decision' / 'confidence' / 'calibration'\", box_id, s);\n            return -1;\n        }\n\n        json_node_t *mn = json_object_get(r, \"min\");\n        if (mn && json_kind(mn) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            out->nl_fixed_min = json_number_value(mn);\n            out->nl_min_is_fixed = 1;\n        }\n        json_node_t *mx = json_object_get(r, \"max\");\n        if (mx && json_kind(mx) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            out->nl_fixed_max = json_number_value(mx);\n            out->nl_max_is_fixed = 1;\n        }\n        if (out->nl_min_is_fixed && out->nl_max_is_fixed &&\n            out->nl_fixed_min >= out->nl_fixed_max) {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'min' (%g) must be less than \"\n                           \"'max' (%g)\", box_id, out->nl_fixed_min, out->nl_fixed_max);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        json_node_t *md = json_object_get(r, \"midpoint\");\n        if (md && json_kind(md) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            out->nl_fixed_mid = json_number_value(md);\n            out->nl_mid_is_fixed = 1;\n        }\n        json_node_t *kk = json_object_get(r, \"k\");\n        if (kk && json_kind(kk) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            double v = json_number_value(kk);\n            if (v <= 0.0) {\n                *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'k' (%g) must be positive\",\n                               box_id, v);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            out->nl_steepness = v;\n        }\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': unknown routing.kind '%s' \"\n                   \"(supported: plain, comparator, iterator, \"\n                   \"randomizer, weighted, distributor, nonlinearity)\",\n                   box_id, kind);\n    return -1;\n}",

       json_node_t *md = json_object_get(r, \"midpoint\");\n        if (md && json_kind(md) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            out->nl_fixed_mid = json_number_value(md);\n            out->nl_mid_is_fixed = 1;\n        }\n        json_node_t *kk = json_object_get(r, \"k\");\n        if (kk && json_kind(kk) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            double v = json_number_value(kk);\n            if (v <= 0.0) {\n                *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'k' (%g) must be positive\",\n                               box_id, v);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            out->nl_steepness = v;\n        }\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': unknown routing.kind '%s' \"\n                   \"(supported: plain, comparator, iterator, \"\n                   \"randomizer, weighted, distributor, nonlinearity)\",\n                   box_id, kind);\n    return -1;\n}",

Read the\n             * input value (coerce string→double via strtod, treat\n             * \"true\"/\"false\" as 1/0), update the auto-tracked\n             * running cells (CAS loop with EMA decay), normalise\n             * against the effective bounds, apply the variant's\n             * curve, clamp per the per-variant rule, emit the\n             * response as a \"%g\"-formatted double on the single\n             * output port. pun;\n            double lo, hi;\n            if (r->nl_min_is_fixed) {\n                lo = r->nl_fixed_min;\n            } else {\n                pun.u = atomic_load_explicit(&((routing_t *)r)->nl_running_min,\n                                             memory_order_acquire);\n                lo = pun.d;\n            }\n            if (r->nl_max_is_fixed) {\n                hi = r->nl_fixed_max;\n            } else {\n                pun.u = atomic_load_explicit(&((routing_t *)r)->nl_running_max,\n                                             memory_order_acquire);\n                hi = pun.d;\n            }\n\n            /* Auto-side widen on out-of-range, via a CAS loop.\n             * No widen on fixed sides — clamp instead. */\n            if (!r->nl_min_is_fixed && v cur;\n                    if (v >= pun.d) break;\n                    pun.d = v;\n                    if (atomic_compare_exchange_weak_explicit(\n                            &((routing_t *)r)->nl_running_min,\n                            &cur, pun.u,\n                            memory_order_release, memory_order_relaxed)) {\n                        lo = v;\n                        break;\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            if (!r->nl_max_is_fixed && v > hi) {\n                uint64_t cur = atomic_load_explicit(\n                    &((routing_t *)r)->nl_running_max, memory_order_relaxed);\n                for (;;) {\n                    pun.u = cur;\n                    if (v <= pun.d) break;\n                    pun.d = v;\n                    if (atomic_compare_exchange_weak_explicit(\n                            &((routing_t *)r)->nl_running_max,\n                            &cur, pun.u,\n                            memory_order_release, memory_order_relaxed)) {\n                        hi = v;\n                        break;\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n\n            /* Effective midpoint: supplied wins; otherwise the\n             * dynamic (min + max) / 2. */\n            double mid = r->nl_mid_is_fixed\n                           ? r->nl_fixed_mid\n by an infinite range. */\n            int bounds_ready = (hi > lo) && isfinite(lo) && isfinite(hi);\n\n            double score;\n            const double k = r->nl_steepness;\n            switch (r->nl_shape) {\n                case NL_DECISION: {\n                    /* tanh centred on the midpoint, mapped into\n                     * [-1, 1]. Saturates gracefully past either\n                     * bound; under fixed mode we clamp anyway so\n                     * the saturation is exact at +/-1. */\n                    if (!bounds_ready) { score = 0.0; break; }\n                    if (r->nl_min_is_fixed && v <= lo) { score = -1.0; break; }\n                    if (r->nl_max_is_fixed && v >= hi) { score = +1.0; break; }\n                    double t = (v - mid) / ((hi - lo) * 0.5);  /* roughly in [-1, 1] */\n                    score = tanh(k * t);\n                    break;\n                }\n                case NL_CONFIDENCE: {\n                    /* Logistic sigmoid centred on the midpoint,\n                     * mapped into [0, 1].           "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"      const w_note = document.createElement('div');\n      w_note.style.cssText = 'font-size:10px;color:#6c72a0;margin-top:4px;';\n      w_note.textContent = 'comma-separated non-negative numbers. dispatch normalises to a probability table.';\n      fields.appendChild(w_note);\n    } else if (rk === 'nonlinearity') {\n      // Issue 250 — variant + bounds + steepness controls. The\n      // bounds use the presence-is-the-mode rule: a blank field\n      // means \"auto-track this side\"; a number means \"pin this\n      // side as a fixed bound, clamp past it.\" set_nl_bounds()\n      // applies that rule when the user edits a field.\n      const variant_sel = document.createElement('select');\n      [['decision',    'soft +/- with clear neutral'],\n       ['confidence',  'soft yes/no with uncertainty'],\n       ['calibration', 'pure range remap, no curve']].forEach(([k, hint]) => {\n        const opt = document.createElement('option');\n        opt.value = k; opt.textContent = k;\n        opt.title  = hint;\n        if (k === (box.routing && box.routing.shape)) opt.selected = true;\n        variant_sel.appendChild(opt);\n      });\n      variant_sel.addEventListener('change', () => set_nl_field('shape', variant_sel.value));\n      fields.appendChild(mk_row('variant', variant_sel));\n\n      const mk_bound = (label, key, placeholder) => {\n        const inp = document.createElement('input');\n        inp.type        = 'number';\n        inp.value       = (box.routing && box.routing[key] != null) ? String(box.routing[key]) : '';\n        inp.placeholder = placeholder;\n        inp.style.cssText = 'width:100%;background:#0f1117;border:1px solid #2a2f45;' +\n          'border-radius:3px;color:#e8eaf6;font-family:monospace;font-size:11px;padding:4px 6px;';\n        inp.addEventListener('change', () => set_nl_field(key, inp.value));\n        fields.appendChild(mk_row(label, inp));\n      };\n      mk_bound('min',      'min',      '(blank = auto-track)');\n      mk_bound('max',      'max',      '(blank = auto-track)');\n      mk_bound('midpoint', 'midpoint', '(blank = (min+max)/2)');\n\n      const k_inp = document.createElement('input');\n      k_inp.type        = 'number';\n      k_inp.step        = '0.1';\n      k_inp.min         = '0.01';\n      k_inp.value       = String((box.routing && box.routing.k) ?? 1);\n      k_inp.style.cssText = 'width:100%;background:#0f1117;border:1px solid #2a2f45;' +\n        'border-radius:3px;color:#e8eaf6;font-family:monospace;font-size:11px;padding:4px 6px;';\n      k_inp.addEventListener('change', () => set_nl_field('k', k_inp.value));\n      fields.appendChild(mk_row('steepness (k)', k_inp));\n\n      const nl_note = document.createElement('div');\n      nl_note.style.cssText = 'font-size:10px;color:#6c72a0;margin-top:4px;line-height:1.4;';\n      nl_note.textContent = 'output is the SCORE, not the scaled input. blank bounds auto-track; pinned bounds clamp past them (confidence / decision) or extrapolate (calibration).';\n      fields.appendChild(nl_note);\n    }\n  }\n  // }}}",

The\n                default variant for fresh boxes.\n  calibration — linear,  output [0, 1], no midpoint\n                Pure range remap, no decision content. Out-of-\n                range values extrapolate past [0,1] (no clamp).\n\nBounds use the user's \"presence is the mode\" rule: the JSON\nfields min / max / midpoint may each be present or absent\nindependently. Absent on a side means \"auto-track via the per-\nbox atomic running cell, decay via EMA toward the midpoint each\nfire\"; present means \"pin to this value, clamp past it under\nthe confidence / decision variants.\" The C loader records per-\nbound is_fixed booleans alongside the doubles so the runtime\nknows which sides to clamp and which to widen.\n\nPer-box atomic cells (uint64 bit-cast doubles, CAS-loop widen\non out-of-range, plain release-store for the EMA dampening pass)\nkeep the running bounds local to the box — concurrent\ninstantiations under an upstream iterator contend on the same\ntwo cells, no read lock so reads stay free, non-deterministic\noutput is the expected shape and the user wires a downstream\nlog box if they want to inspect the trajectory.\n\nSteepness k is a sensible default (1.0; middle-80% of input\nmaps to roughly [0.27, 0.73] under confidence) with a per-box\noverride via the schema, the inspector knob, or runtime\nreconfigure (issue 320). Booleans on the wire coerce to 1.0 /\n0.0; strings parse via strtod with strict-trailing-junk\nrejection.\n\nEditor surface: the routing dropdown grows a `nonlinearity`\noption; the per-kind controls are a variant dropdown plus\nthree bound number-inputs (blank means auto-track on that side)\nplus a steepness input. A small footer note reminds the user\nthat the wire carries the score, not the scaled input — the\nnonlinearity is composable: fan an upstream into both the\nnonlinearity AND a downstream multiplier to get input × score.\n\nThree fixtures pin specific scoring outcomes per variant:\nconfidence at midpoint → 0.5, decision at midpoint → 0,\ncalibration at 25% → 0.25. The Makefile adds -lm for the\nnew tanh/exp links. Suite goes 31 → 34 passed.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"250 shipped end-to-end in one commit:\n\n```\n1741621 250 — routing kind: nonlinearity (value-transforming, three intent-named variants)\n```\n\nWhat landed:\n- **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`) — `nonlinearity` kind, three valid `shape` values, type-checks the optional `min` / `max` / `midpoint` / `k`.\n- **C loader** (`src/010-graph-loader.h` + `.c`) — `ROUTING_NONLINEARITY` enum, `nonlinearity_shape_t`, eight new fields on `routing_t` including the per-bound `is_fixed` booleans and the two atomic running cells (uint64 bit-cast doubles), parser with sentinel-init (`+inf` / `-inf` for the running min / max so the first widen always succeeds).\n- **C dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`) — `ROUTING_NONLINEARITY` case in `push_routed`. Reads the input value, coerces booleans, CAS-loops widen on auto sides, computes the curve per variant, clamps under fixed mode for confidence / decision, extrapolates for calibration, EMA-dampens the auto bounds toward the midpoint each fire, emits the score as `%g`-formatted bytes on the single output port.\n- **Editor** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) — `nonlinearity` dropdown option, default routing (`shape: 'confidence'`, `k: 1`), per-kind controls (variant dropdown with hover tooltips per variant; three bound inputs that show blank = auto-track; steepness input; footer note that the wire carries the score not the input), `set_nl_field` setter that applies the presence-is-mode rule (empty bound input deletes the field; number sets it).\n- **Build** — `Makefile` gains `-lm` for the new `tanh` / `exp` calls.\n- **Three fixtures** — one per variant, each pinning the input to a deterministic point of the curve and asserting the exact `%g` output: confidence at midpoint → `0.5`, decision at midpoint → `0`, calibration at 25% → `0.25`.\n\nSuite 31 → 34 passed, no regressions.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The **uint64 bit-cast trick for atomic doubles** is the right move in C11 — `_Atomic double` works on most platforms but isn't strictly required to be lock-free, while `_Atomic uint64_t` is. The union-based bit-cast (`pun.d = score; atomic_store(cell, pun.u)`) gives us lock-free atomic widening without depending on a compiler-specific guarantee.\n- The `*3` factor inside the sigmoid (`1 / (1 + exp(-k*t*3))`) is the small tuning constant that makes `k = 1` produce the doc-promised \"middle 80% maps to [0.27, 0.73]\" behaviour. Without it, raw sigmoid on `t ∈ [-1, 1]` is too gentle — the curve barely bends. The factor centres the action band at `k = 1`, which is what the user wanted as the forgiving default. A future `k` higher than 1 sharpens proportionally; `k = 2` gives the kind of soft AND that's useful for evidence accumulation.\n- The **per-bound atomic widen + non-atomic EMA dampening** combo is deliberate. The widen has to be atomic because two concurrent fires could both see an out-of-range value and need to settle on the larger of the two. The dampening is the *opposite* direction (pulling toward the midpoint), so a concurrent race between two fires both writing slightly-decayed values is benign — both are pulling toward the same target, the later store wins, the bound stays well-behaved. Saving the CAS overhead on the common path (every fire dampens; only occasional fires widen) makes the kind cheap to run.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWorking tree leaves your inline edits to 320 unstaged (your editing pass) and your pre-existing 247/249/251/readme.md untouched."

{
  "uuid":"3a9dd0c3-5a05-4efc-881d-6b6acad885ff",

  "version":"2.1.121",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits",
  "message":{
    "content":"Okay how about this - what if we have a toggle that switches between 0,1 and -1,1 and then we keep the minimum and maximum values we've seen so far, slowly drifting toward the midpoint (0 or 0.5) asymmetrically by 10% each time. Never going above -1/0 or below 1. So if we receive -5 on the first iteration, and -10 on the second, each of those would evaluate to -1. But, if we get a third one that's -5 again, then it would evaluate to -0.5 because it's halfway between the minimum and the midpoint of the scope, which is -1,1 in this example. Actually, what if we have a \"memory\" value instead of drifting? This memory value is \"how many mins/maxes to remember\" and it's just an array that stores the previous values. Probably a ring buffer I guess... Anyway the min/max is set to the min/max of the ring-buffer, and usually we're just appending (or overwriting the oldest value) but if we ever overwrite a value that is exactly the same as the min/max, then we trigger a min/max update where we pull the min/max closer to the scope. We'd essentially just set the min/max to the min/max value of the memory. We should be able to store both of them in the same ring-buffer because, well, the minimum and maximum values are both on either side of the scope, so they shouldn't interfere with one another. That feels more... discrete? to me? than the percentage drift. Plus it enables users to use integers more, though since we're outputting a value between -1 and 1 or between 0 and 1, that's already not an integer, so idk... Ah! I can't tell what design would work best because I don't know what use-cases we have~! but I do know what's easier / harder on the users, and having semi-opaque names like \"decision\" or \"calibration\" might confuse them even more. Especially if they have a math background.",
    "role":"user"
  },
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}

        "text":"Pause-with-you mode rather than implement mode. It's a *clean* design and significantly simpler than what's currently in the tree. The math is one division per fire and the parameter surface is two knobs: range and buffer size. A math user reads it and immediately knows what it does; a non-math user reads \"normalize my values to 0–1 over the last 100 samples\" and also immediately knows what it does. Your naming concern goes away because there's no opaque variant — there's only one operation.\n\n**What's lost** if we drop the S-curves entirely: the soft-AND composition property. That's the \"noise rejection in evidence-accumulation pipelines\" thing I wrote up. It's a real property of sigmoid, and it's the only thing that distinguishes this kind from \"scale a number to a range.\" If you never plan to compose normalized scores by multiplication into downstream perceptron-like networks, that property is **moot** — and the simpler linear box is strictly better.\n\n**Ring buffer vs EMA decay:** they're roughly equivalent for matching N and α. Ring buffer is more intuitive (\"I remember the last 100 values\"); EMA is cheaper (two doubles instead of N) and produces smoother bounds. Your \"discrete is more honest\" preference is aesthetically defensible and I don't think it's the load-bearing call.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The reason you keep circling on this design is that you're trying to pick a shape without knowing the use-case. That's the right instinct to notice. A design that's general enough to fit every imagined use-case usually fits none of them well, because the trade-offs go in different directions for different use-cases.\n- \"Decision\" and \"calibration\" were my translation attempt — bridging math to intent. But your point about math-background users is sharp: they don't recognize \"decision\" but would recognize \"sigmoid\" instantly. A bridge that confuses both directions is worse than picking one audience and naming for them.\n- Linear AGC ≠ less powerful. It's *differently* powerful. The S-curve gives you smooth saturation; AGC gives you adaptive scaling. Most \"I want a number between 0 and 1\" use cases want AGC. The S-curve use cases are specifically about compositional logic with downstream multipliers.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n**The question I want to ask back** before any code changes:\n\n**What's the smallest concrete use-case where you'd actually wire one of these into a map?** If you can sketch one example — \"I have a sensor reading that comes in at unpredictable scale and I want a slider to land between 0 and 1\" or \"I'm building a perceptron-like decision lattice where multiple confidence scores feed an aggregator that picks an action\" — the design falls out of it. The first asks for linear AGC; the second asks for sigmoid. *Both* asks for both. No examples in mind asks for the simplest thing that could work.\n\nThree paths I see, ordered most-to-least conservative:\n\n1. **Rip out what's there, replace with linear-only + range toggle + ring-buffer bounds.** Simplest. Drop \"nonlinearity\" as the kind name — call it `normalize` or `scale` or `auto-range`. The S-curve story becomes a separate routing kind issue if a use-case ever appears, and the math name (`sigmoid` / `tanh`) is the right name for that future kind because its audience is math-aware.\n2. **Keep what shipped, add the simpler linear-AGC alongside as its own kind.** Two routing kinds. The user picks by intent: \"I want soft logic composition\" → nonlinearity; \"I want adaptive scaling\" → normalize. Doubles the surface but covers both audiences honestly.\n3. **Refactor the shipped one into a single curve-dropdown.** `shape` becomes `linear` / `sigmoid` / `tanh` (math names, for math users). `range` becomes a separate toggle. Bounds-tracking gets the ring-buffer treatment. This keeps everything but renames the variants and changes the bounds mechanism.\n\nIf you can answer the use-case question I'd guess path 1 or 2; if you can't, I'd lean path 1 just because it's the cheapest mistake to fix later.\n\nWant to give me a use-case sketch, or should I leave this for you to mull and pick up another thread?"

## [2500]

```json
{
  "uuid":"6430d0fb-9ac9-4357-8563-4bd833727d1d",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-24T22:12:10.686Z",
  "parentUuid":"24c6bf81-0baf-406a-8f00-12d2403a83eb",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "promptId":"6eff0034-0898-43bc-b3ea-16e1dc527bda",
  "userType":"external",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits",
  "message":{
    "content":"I guess I want both? I want to be able to accept arbitrary inputs and calibrate on the fly, such that the prior received minimum/maximum are the -1/1 values and the 0,1 values. Then, I want the input value to be multiplied by the corresponding... ratio'd? value? the input comes in somewhere between min and max (sometimes being exactly min/max) and then it is multiplied by the value that is produced from the s-curve. The non-linear aspect to it is non-negotiable, we need it, it's part of the requirements. But we also need to be able to accept arbitrary (numerical) input. The goal is decision lattices where inputs come in at unpredictable scale and I want to calibrate in motion to the provided values.",

    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# 253 — Nonlinearity refactor: auto-calibration + gated output\n\n## Status\nopen — refines issue 250's shipped shape after a use-case\nconversation. 250's first slice stays in completed/ as the\nhistorical record of the original direction; this issue is the\niterated design.\n\n## Why\n\nThe 250 implementation that just landed has three issues\nrelative to the actual use case (decision lattices with\ninputs arriving at unpredictable scale):\n\n1. **Three intent-named variants are confusing.** Math-aware\n   users don't recognise `decision` / `confidence` /\n   `calibration`; non-math users still don't understand the\n   underlying math. Both audiences are served poorly. A simple\n   range toggle (signed `[-1, 1]` vs unit `[0, 1]`) reads\n   correctly to both groups.\n2. **Bounds via fixed-or-EMA fits the wrong story.** The\n   actual workload is \"arbitrary input arrives, calibrate on\n   the fly from the values seen so far.\" EMA decay is a\n   continuous smoothing; the user wants discrete event\n   semantics — \"remember the last N observed values; the\n   current bounds are the min and max of that window.\"\n3. **Output is the score alone, not input × score.** The user\n   wants the **gated output**: the input value multiplied by\n   the S-curve's response. That's the soft-AND composition the\n   downstream multiplier was supposed to compose externally,\n   but since multiplication is the load-bearing pattern, it\n   belongs in the box.\n\n## The refined design\n\n### Output range — single toggle, two values\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":   \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"range\":  \"signed\",       // \"signed\" → [-1, 1]; \"unit\" → [0, 1]\n  \"memory\": 16,             // ring-buffer size N (default 16)\n  \"k\":      1               // steepness (default 1.0)\n}\n```\n\nThat's the entire schema. No `shape`, no `min` / `max` /\n`midpoint` (the ring buffer derives them), no per-bound flags.\n\nThe range toggle picks the S-curve:\n- `signed` → tanh (centred on 0, output `[-1, 1]`)\n- `unit`   → sigmoid (centred on 0.5, output `[0, 1]`)\n\n### Bounds via ring buffer, not EMA\n\nA per-box ring buffer of size N holds the last N observed\nvalues. On every fire:\n\n1. Acquire the per-box mutex on the ring buffer.\n2. Overwrite the oldest slot with the incoming value `v`.\n3. Recompute the buffer's `min` and `max` (O(N) scan; N is\n   small, this is cheap).\n4. Release the mutex.\n\nThe bounds ARE the min and max of the buffer. No drift, no\nEMA. A new value extends the bounds immediately if it's\nextreme; an outlier ages out of the buffer after N fires and\nthe bounds tighten back to the next-most-extreme value.\n\nThe user's \"trigger only on extreme-value overwrite\"\noptimisation is deferred — every-fire recompute is fine while\nN stays small.\n\n### Gated output — input × score\n\n```\nv        = input value (arbitrary scale)\nt        = normalised position of v in [min, max]\nscore    = S-curve(t * k)    // tanh or sigmoid per range toggle\noutput   = v * score\n```\n\n`t` is `(v - min) / (max - min)` mapped into the variant's\ndomain — `[-1, 1]` for signed (centred at midpoint), `[0, 1]`\nfor unit (zero at min).\n\nSaturation: values beyond the current bounds get the bounds'\nscore (the S-curve at ±1 for signed, at 0 or 1 for unit). The\nring buffer absorbs them on the same fire so subsequent calls\nsee the widened bounds.\n\nFor signed range:\n- v near positive bound → score ≈ +1 → output ≈ v × 1 (full\n  positive amplitude passed through)\n- v near negative bound → score ≈ -1 → output ≈ v × -1\n  (positive amplitude, sign-flipped) — useful as a magnitude\n  detector with bipolar input\n- v near midpoint → score ≈ 0 → output ≈ 0 (suppress)\n\nFor unit range:\n- v near max → score ≈ 1 → output ≈ v (passthrough)\n- v near midpoint → score ≈ 0.5 → output ≈ v / 2 (attenuated)\n- v near min → score ≈ 0 → output ≈ 0 (gate closed)\n\nThis is the \"gated linear unit\" pattern from neural networks:\nthe score is a soft gate that scales the input rather than\nreplacing it.\n\n### Decision-lattice composition\n\nThe whole point: chain N of these into a downstream aggregator\nthat's itself a nonlinearity. The midpoint values\n(uncertainty) suppress to ~0; the strongly-bounded values\n(certainty) pass through near full amplitude. The aggregator\nsees a sum of \"votes weighted by certainty\" rather than a sum\nof raw signals. Compose more layers, and weak evidence stays\nweak while strong evidence reinforces — the soft-AND property\nthe original 250 doc described, but with the multiplication\nbaked in.\n\n## Implementation plan\n\n1. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`): drop `shape` /\n   `nonlinearity_shape` validation; accept `range`\n   (`\"signed\"` / `\"unit\"`); accept `memory` (positive\n   integer, default 16); keep `k`.\n2. **Loader** (`src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}`): replace\n   `nonlinearity_shape_t` with `nonlinearity_range_t`\n   (`NL_SIGNED` / `NL_UNIT`); remove fixed-bound fields and\n   the running atomic cells; add ring-buffer fields\n   (allocated double array + write index + per-box mutex);\n   parser reads `range`, `memory`, `k` and allocates the\n   buffer.\n3. **Dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`): rewrite the\n   `ROUTING_NONLINEARITY` case. Acquire the mutex, append to\n   the buffer, compute min/max, normalise, apply curve,\n   compute `v × score`, format and push.\n4. **Editor** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): replace\n   variant dropdown with a `range` toggle (`signed` /\n   `unit`); replace bound inputs with a single `memory`\n   number input; keep `k`.\n5. **Fixtures**: update the three existing fixtures\n   (currently asserting score-only output) to assert\n   `v × score` output. The deterministic-input fixtures\n   compute as:\n   - confidence at 50 with bounds [0,100]: ring buffer has\n     [50]; min=max=50; normalised v=midpoint; sigmoid(0)=0.5;\n     output = 50 × 0.5 = 25.\n   - decision at 0 with bounds [-10,10] (ring buffer needs\n     more than one value to set the bounds): need to seed the\n     buffer with the bounds. Rework the fixture to feed\n     min/max/midpoint through an iterator before the test\n     value.\n   - calibration variant goes away (no more variants).\n6. **Issue file** updates: this issue closes on merge.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Initial bounds behaviour.** With an empty ring buffer (no\n  values seen yet), what does the first fire emit? Options:\n  - Emit `v × 0` (neutral score until calibrated) — clean but\n    loses the first value.\n  - Emit `v × 1` (passthrough until bounds form) — preserves\n    the value but the score isn't meaningful yet.\n  - Emit nothing on the first fire, wait for the second. Wrong\n    shape for a dataflow box that's supposed to fire on every\n    input.\n  Lean toward `v × 0` for cleanliness; the first value seeds\n  the buffer so subsequent fires have something to normalise\n  against. Document the \"first fire is silent\" behaviour as\n  the warm-up cost of auto-calibration.\n- **Fixed-bounds override.** Drop entirely (auto-only)? Or\n  keep `min` / `max` as optional pinned overrides? Dropping\n  is simpler; pinning is useful when the user knows the input\n  range and wants to skip the calibration warm-up. Default to\n  dropping; restore if a use case asks.\n- **Concurrent appends.** A per-box mutex is the simplest\n  shape. For boxes that fire many times per second from\n  parallel upstream iterators, a lock-free ring (Vyukov's\n  MPSC, etc.) would be faster, but the simple mutex is fine\n  while throughput stays modest.\n",

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"            elseif r.kind == \"nonlinearity\" then\n                -- Issue 253 — the refactor. `range` picks the\n                -- output range and the S-curve (signed → tanh,\n                -- unit → sigmoid). `memory` is the ring-buffer\n                -- size for auto-calibration. `k` is the steepness.\n                -- Output is v × score (gated), not score alone.\n                if type(r.range) ~= \"string\"\n                   or not valid_nonlinearity_ranges[r.range] then\n                    err(errors, \"nonlinearity 'routing.range' must be 'signed' or 'unit'\")\n                end\n                if r.memory ~= nil then\n                    if type(r.memory) ~= \"number\"\n                       or r.memory < 1\n                       or r.memory ~= math.floor(r.memory) then\n                        err(errors, \"nonlinearity 'routing.memory' must be a positive integer when set\")\n                    end\n                end\n                if r.k ~= nil and (type(r.k) ~= \"number\" or r.k <= 0) then\n                    err(errors, \"nonlinearity 'routing.k' (steepness) must be a positive number when set\")\n                end\n            end",

          "old_string":"    int            n_thresholds;\n    const double  *thresholds;\n    /* Issue 250 — nonlinearity routing. Three intent-named\n     * variants (decision / confidence / calibration) plus the\n     * bounds the input is normalised against. Presence-vs-absence\n     * of each bound on the JSON side becomes the per-side\n     * \"is_fixed\" flag here: when the field was supplied, the\n     * bound is locked and clamping fires past it; when absent,\n     * the bound is auto-tracked via the running cells below.\n     * Same rule for midpoint. The user emits the response (the\n     * smoothed score in [0,1] or [-1,1]) on the box's single\n     * output port; the original input value isn't forwarded. */\n    nonlinearity_shape_t nl_shape;\n    int            nl_min_is_fixed;\n    int            nl_max_is_fixed;\n    int            nl_mid_is_fixed;\n    double         nl_fixed_min;\n    double         nl_fixed_max;\n    double         nl_fixed_mid;\n    double         nl_steepness;          /* k; default 1.0 */\n    /* Auto-tracked running bounds for auto sides. Stored as\n     * uint64 bit patterns so the existing atomic helpers cover\n     * them; the dispatch picker bit-casts to/from double on\n     * every fire. Initialised to ±DBL_MAX (so the first value's\n     * widen always succeeds) on load. */\n    _Atomic uint64_t nl_running_min;\n    _Atomic uint64_t nl_running_max;\n} routing_t;",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"    int            n_thresholds;\n    const double  *thresholds;\n    /* Issue 253 — nonlinearity refactor. The `range` toggle\n     * picks both the output range and the S-curve:\n     *   NL_SIGNED → tanh,    output [-1, 1]\n     *   NL_UNIT   → sigmoid, output [0,  1]\n     * The bounds the input is normalised against come from a\n     * per-box ring buffer holding the last `nl_memory` observed\n     * values. Output is v × score (gated linear unit pattern).\n     *\n     * Concurrency: a per-box pthread_mutex guards the ring\n     * buffer's append + min/max recompute. The mutex pointer is\n     * heap-allocated (so the routing_t struct stays POD-shaped\n     * for the calloc/free pattern the rest of the loader uses);\n     * NULL when the routing kind isn't nonlinearity. */\n    nonlinearity_range_t nl_range;\n    int            nl_memory;            /* ring buffer size N */\n    double         nl_steepness;          /* k; default 1.0 */\n    double        *nl_buffer;             /* N-cell ring; NULL if not nonlinearity */\n    int            nl_write_idx;          /* next slot to overwrite */\n    int            nl_n_filled;           /* how many slots have real data so far */\n    void          *nl_mutex;              /* pthread_mutex_t * */\n} routing_t;",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/src/010-graph-loader.h"

    "oldString":"    if (strcmp(kind, \"nonlinearity\") == 0) {\n        /* Issue 250 — value-transforming routing. Emits a scoring\n         * response (the smoothed [0,1] or [-1,1] number) on a\n         * single output port. The Lua schema already validated the\n         * shape string and number types; here we just thread the\n         * fields onto the routing struct.\n         *\n         * Presence vs absence of min / max / midpoint is the\n         * mode-flag for each side — supplied means \"fixed; clamp\n         * past it\"; absent means \"track it via the atomic running\n         * cells, decay toward midpoint via EMA on every fire.\" */\n        out->kind = ROUTING_NONLINEARITY;\n        out->n_outputs = 1;\n        out->nl_shape = NL_CONFIDENCE;     /* default if shape missing/unknown */\n        out->nl_steepness = 1.0;\n        out->nl_min_is_fixed = 0;\n        out->nl_max_is_fixed = 0;\n        out->nl_mid_is_fixed = 0;\n        out->nl_fixed_min = 0.0;\n        out->nl_fixed_max = 1.0;\n        out->nl_fixed_mid = 0.0;\n        /* Running cells initialised so the first observed value\n         * always widens both sides. Using sentinel bit patterns\n         * (+inf for min, -inf for max) makes the first compare\n         * deterministic. */\n        union { double d; uint64_t u; } pos_inf, neg_inf;\n        pos_inf.d =  (double)INFINITY;\n        neg_inf.d = -(double)INFINITY;\n        atomic_init(&out->nl_running_min, pos_inf.u);\n        atomic_init(&out->nl_running_max, neg_inf.u);\n\n        json_node_t *sh = json_object_get(r, \"shape\");\n        if (!sh || json_kind(sh) != JSON_STRING) {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity routing requires \"\n                           \"'shape' string NL_CALIBRATION;\n        else {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'shape' = '%s' must be \"\n                           \"'decision' / 'confidence' / 'calibration'\", box_id, s);\n            return -1;\n        }\n\n        json_node_t *mn = json_object_get(r, \"min\");\n        if (mn && json_kind(mn) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            out->nl_fixed_min = json_number_value(mn);\n        json_node_t *md = json_object_get(r, \"midpoint\");\n        if (md && json_kind(md) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            out->nl_fixed_mid = json_number_value(md);\n            out->nl_mid_is_fixed = 1;\n        }\n        json_node_t *kk = json_object_get(r, \"k\");\n        if (kk && json_kind(kk) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            double v = json_number_value(kk);\n            if (v <= 0.0) {\n                *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'k' (%g) must be positive\",\n                               box_id, v);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            out->nl_steepness = v;\n        }\n        return 0;\n    }",
    "newString":"    if (strcmp(kind, \"nonlinearity\") == 0) {\n        /* Issue 253 — refined nonlinearity routing. Auto-calibrates\n         * bounds via a per-box ring buffer of the last `memory`\n         * observed values; output is v × score where score is the\n         * S-curve (tanh for signed range, sigmoid for unit) of v\n         * normalised against the current bounds. */\n        out->kind = ROUTING_NONLINEARITY;\n        out->n_outputs = 1;\n        out->nl_range = NL_SIGNED;\n        out->nl_memory = 16;\n        out->nl_steepness = 1.0;\n        out->nl_buffer = NULL;\n        out->nl_write_idx = 0;\n        out->nl_n_filled = 0;\n        out->nl_mutex = NULL;\n\n        json_node_t *rg = json_object_get(r, \"range\");\n        if (!rg || json_kind(rg) != JSON_STRING) {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity routing requires \"\n                           \"'range' string ('signed' or 'unit')\", box_id);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        const char *s = json_string_value(rg);\n        if      (strcmp(s, \"signed\") == 0) out->nl_range = NL_SIGNED;\n        else if (strcmp(s, \"unit\")   == 0) out->nl_range = NL_UNIT;\n        else {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'range' = '%s' must be \"\n                           \"'signed' or 'unit'\", box_id, s);\n            return -1;\n        }\n\n        json_node_t *mem = json_object_get(r, \"memory\");\n        if (mem && json_kind(mem) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            double mv = json_number_value(mem);\n            int mvi = (int)mv;\n            if (mvi < 1 || (double)mvi != mv) {\n                *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'memory' must be a \"\n                               \"positive integer (got %g)\", box_id, mv);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            out->nl_memory = mvi;\n        }\n        json_node_t *kk = json_object_get(r, \"k\");\n        if (kk && json_kind(kk) == JSON_NUMBER) {\n            double v = json_number_value(kk);\n            if (v <= 0.0) {\n                *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s': nonlinearity 'k' (%g) must be positive\",\n                               box_id, v);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            out->nl_steepness = v;\n        }\n\n        /* Allocate the ring buffer + its guarding mutex. The\n         * buffer holds nl_memory doubles; nl_n_filled grows from\n         * 0 to nl_memory as the box sees values, then stays at\n         * nl_memory while the write index wraps. */\n        out->nl_buffer = calloc((size_t)out->nl_memory, sizeof(double));\n        if (!out->nl_buffer) {\n            *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory (nonlinearity ring buffer for '%s')\", box_id);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        pthread_mutex_t *m = malloc(sizeof *m);\n        if (!m) {\n            free(out->nl_buffer);\n            out->nl_buffer = NULL;\n            *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory (nonlinearity mutex for '%s')\", box_id);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        pthread_mutex_init(m, NULL);\n        out->nl_mutex = m;\n        return 0;\n    }",

the loader should have caught this. */\n                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size, output_native);\n            }\n\n            pthread_mutex_lock(m);\n            /* Append v to the ring buffer (overwrites oldest). */\n            r->nl_buffer[r->nl_write_idx] = v;\n            r->nl_write_idx = (r->nl_write_idx + 1) % r->nl_memory;\n            if (r->nl_n_filled < r->nl_memory) r->nl_n_filled++;\n\n            /* Compute bounds over the filled portion of the buffer. */\n            double lo = r->nl_buffer[0];\n            double hi = r->nl_buffer[0];\n            for (int i = 1; i < r->nl_n_filled; i++) {\n                double bv = r->nl_buffer[i];\n                if (bv < lo) lo = bv;\n                if (bv > hi) hi = bv;\n            }\n            int n_filled = r->nl_n_filled;\n            pthread_mutex_unlock(m);\n\n            /* Compute the score. On a single-value buffer (warm-up\n             * first fire) there's no range to normalise against,\n             * so the score is the variant's neutral value (0.5\n             * for unit, 0 for signed) — output becomes v × neutral\n             * which is half the input or zero. */\n            const double k = r->nl_steepness;\n            double score;\n            if (n_filled < 2 || hi <= lo) {\n                score = (r->nl_range == NL_UNIT) ? 0.5 : 0.0;\n            } else if (r->nl_range == NL_SIGNED) {\n                /* Map v into [-1, 1] using the midpoint of the\n                 * current bounds. tanh centred at 0. */\n                double mid = (lo + hi) * 0.5;\n                double t = (v - mid) / ((hi - lo) * 0.5);\n                score = tanh(k * t);\n            } else {\n                /* unit: map v into [0, 1] using the bounds.\n                 * Sigmoid centred at 0.5 of the input domain. */\n                double t = (v - lo) / (hi - lo);   /* 0..1 over the bounds */\n                /* Recentre to (-1, 1) then sigmoid; the *3 keeps\n                 * k=1 close to the doc's 0.27/0.73 mid-80% target. */\n                double tc = (t - 0.5) * 2.0;\n                score = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k * tc * 3.0));\n            }\n\n            double gated = v * score;",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/src/012-dispatch.c"
  },

        "lines":[" # 253 — Nonlinearity refactor: auto-calibration + gated output"," "," ## Status","-open — refines issue 250's shipped shape after a use-case","-conversation. 250's first slice stays in completed/ as the","-historical record of the original direction; this issue is the","-iterated design.","+complete — single `range` toggle (signed/unit) replaces the","+three variant names; per-box ring buffer of last `memory`","+values replaces EMA-decayed bounds; output is v × score","+(gated linear unit) instead of score alone; editor surfaces","+the simplified controls; two cold-start fixtures cover both","+ranges. 250's first slice stays in completed/ as the","+historical record."," "," ## Why"," "],
