      }],
    "originalFile":"# 253 — Nonlinearity refactor: auto-calibration + gated output\n\n## Status\nopen — refines issue 250's shipped shape after a use-case\nconversation. 250's first slice stays in completed/ as the\nhistorical record of the original direction; this issue is the\niterated design.\n\n## Why\n\nThe 250 implementation that just landed has three issues\nrelative to the actual use case (decision lattices with\ninputs arriving at unpredictable scale):\n\n1. **Three intent-named variants are confusing.** Math-aware\n   users don't recognise `decision` / `confidence` /\n   `calibration`; non-math users still don't understand the\n   underlying math. Both audiences are served poorly. A simple\n   range toggle (signed `[-1, 1]` vs unit `[0, 1]`) reads\n   correctly to both groups.\n2. **Bounds via fixed-or-EMA fits the wrong story.** The\n   actual workload is \"arbitrary input arrives, calibrate on\n   the fly from the values seen so far.\" EMA decay is a\n   continuous smoothing; the user wants discrete event\n   semantics — \"remember the last N observed values; the\n   current bounds are the min and max of that window.\"\n3. **Output is the score alone, not input × score.** The user\n   wants the **gated output**: the input value multiplied by\n   the S-curve's response. That's the soft-AND composition the\n   downstream multiplier was supposed to compose externally,\n   but since multiplication is the load-bearing pattern, it\n   belongs in the box.\n\n## The refined design\n\n### Output range — single toggle, two values\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":   \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"range\":  \"signed\",       // \"signed\" → [-1, 1]; \"unit\" → [0, 1]\n  \"memory\": 16,             // ring-buffer size N (default 16)\n  \"k\":      1               // steepness (default 1.0)\n}\n```\n\nThat's the entire schema. No `shape`, no `min` / `max` /\n`midpoint` (the ring buffer derives them), no per-bound flags.\n\nThe range toggle picks the S-curve:\n- `signed` → tanh (centred on 0, output `[-1, 1]`)\n- `unit`   → sigmoid (centred on 0.5, output `[0, 1]`)\n\n### Bounds via ring buffer, not EMA\n\nA per-box ring buffer of size N holds the last N observed\nvalues. On every fire:\n\n1. Acquire the per-box mutex on the ring buffer.\n2. Overwrite the oldest slot with the incoming value `v`.\n3. Recompute the buffer's `min` and `max` (O(N) scan; N is\n   small, this is cheap).\n4. Release the mutex.\n\nThe bounds ARE the min and max of the buffer. No drift, no\nEMA. A new value extends the bounds immediately if it's\nextreme; an outlier ages out of the buffer after N fires and\nthe bounds tighten back to the next-most-extreme value.\n\nThe user's \"trigger only on extreme-value overwrite\"\noptimisation is deferred — every-fire recompute is fine while\nN stays small.\n\n### Gated output — input × score\n\n```\nv        = input value (arbitrary scale)\nt        = normalised position of v in [min, max]\nscore    = S-curve(t * k)    // tanh or sigmoid per range toggle\noutput   = v * score\n```\n\n`t` is `(v - min) / (max - min)` mapped into the variant's\ndomain — `[-1, 1]` for signed (centred at midpoint), `[0, 1]`\nfor unit (zero at min).\n\nSaturation: values beyond the current bounds get the bounds'\nscore (the S-curve at ±1 for signed, at 0 or 1 for unit). The\nring buffer absorbs them on the same fire so subsequent calls\nsee the widened bounds.\n\nFor signed range:\n- v near positive bound → score ≈ +1 → output ≈ v × 1 (full\n  positive amplitude passed through)\n- v near negative bound → score ≈ -1 → output ≈ v × -1\n  (positive amplitude, sign-flipped) — useful as a magnitude\n  detector with bipolar input\n- v near midpoint → score ≈ 0 → output ≈ 0 (suppress)\n\nFor unit range:\n- v near max → score ≈ 1 → output ≈ v (passthrough)\n- v near midpoint → score ≈ 0.5 → output ≈ v / 2 (attenuated)\n- v near min → score ≈ 0 → output ≈ 0 (gate closed)\n\nThis is the \"gated linear unit\" pattern from neural networks:\nthe score is a soft gate that scales the input rather than\nreplacing it.\n\n### Decision-lattice composition\n\nThe whole point: chain N of these into a downstream aggregator\nthat's itself a nonlinearity. The midpoint values\n(uncertainty) suppress to ~0; the strongly-bounded values\n(certainty) pass through near full amplitude. The aggregator\nsees a sum of \"votes weighted by certainty\" rather than a sum\nof raw signals. Compose more layers, and weak evidence stays\nweak while strong evidence reinforces — the soft-AND property\nthe original 250 doc described, but with the multiplication\nbaked in.\n\n## Implementation plan\n\n1. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`): drop `shape` /\n   `nonlinearity_shape` validation; accept `range`\n   (`\"signed\"` / `\"unit\"`); accept `memory` (positive\n   integer, default 16); keep `k`.\n2. **Loader** (`src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}`): replace\n   `nonlinearity_shape_t` with `nonlinearity_range_t`\n   (`NL_SIGNED` / `NL_UNIT`); remove fixed-bound fields and\n   the running atomic cells; add ring-buffer fields\n   (allocated double array + write index + per-box mutex);\n   parser reads `range`, `memory`, `k` and allocates the\n   buffer.\n3. **Dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`): rewrite the\n   `ROUTING_NONLINEARITY` case. Acquire the mutex, append to\n   the buffer, compute min/max, normalise, apply curve,\n   compute `v × score`, format and push.\n4. **Editor** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): replace\n   variant dropdown with a `range` toggle (`signed` /\n   `unit`); replace bound inputs with a single `memory`\n   number input; keep `k`.\n5. **Fixtures**: update the three existing fixtures\n   (currently asserting score-only output) to assert\n   `v × score` output. The deterministic-input fixtures\n   compute as:\n   - confidence at 50 with bounds [0,100]: ring buffer has\n     [50]; min=max=50; normalised v=midpoint; sigmoid(0)=0.5;\n     output = 50 × 0.5 = 25.\n   - decision at 0 with bounds [-10,10] (ring buffer needs\n     more than one value to set the bounds): need to seed the\n     buffer with the bounds. Rework the fixture to feed\n     min/max/midpoint through an iterator before the test\n     value.\n   - calibration variant goes away (no more variants).\n6. **Issue file** updates: this issue closes on merge.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Initial bounds behaviour.** With an empty ring buffer (no\n  values seen yet), what does the first fire emit? Options:\n  - Emit `v × 0` (neutral score until calibrated) — clean but\n    loses the first value.\n  - Emit `v × 1` (passthrough until bounds form) — preserves\n    the value but the score isn't meaningful yet.\n  - Emit nothing on the first fire, wait for the second. Wrong\n    shape for a dataflow box that's supposed to fire on every\n    input.\n  Lean toward `v × 0` for cleanliness; the first value seeds\n  the buffer so subsequent fires have something to normalise\n  against. Document the \"first fire is silent\" behaviour as\n  the warm-up cost of auto-calibration.\n- **Fixed-bounds override.** Drop entirely (auto-only)? Or\n  keep `min` / `max` as optional pinned overrides? Dropping\n  is simpler; pinning is useful when the user knows the input\n  range and wants to skip the calibration warm-up. Default to\n  dropping; restore if a use case asks.\n- **Concurrent appends.** A per-box mutex is the simplest\n  shape. For boxes that fire many times per second from\n  parallel upstream iterators, a lock-free ring (Vyukov's\n  MPSC, etc.) would be faster, but the simple mutex is fine\n  while throughput stays modest.\n",
    "oldString":"## Status\nopen — refines issue 250's shipped shape after a use-case\nconversation. 250's first slice stays in completed/ as the\nhistorical record of the original direction; this issue is the\niterated design.",
    "newString":"## Status\ncomplete — single `range` toggle (signed/unit) replaces the\nthree variant names; per-box ring buffer of last `memory`\nvalues replaces EMA-decayed bounds; output is v × score\n(gated linear unit) instead of score alone; editor surfaces\nthe simplified controls; two cold-start fixtures cover both\nranges. 250's first slice stays in completed/ as the\nhistorical record.",

        "text":"Refactor shipped. The commit chain reads honestly: 250 → \"first attempt as designed earlier\"; 253 → \"refined after use-case clarified.\"\n\n**What changed in 253 vs 250:**\n\n| Dimension | 250 (shipped first) | 253 (now) |\n|---|---|---|\n| User-facing variants | `decision` / `confidence` / `calibration` | `range`: `signed` or `unit` |\n| Bounds tracking | Fixed-pin OR per-bound EMA-decayed atomic cells | Per-box ring buffer of last N values |\n| Bounds API | `min` / `max` / `midpoint` fields (presence = mode) | `memory` (positive int) |\n| Output | Score alone (in [-1,1] or [0,1]) | `v × score` (gated linear unit) |\n| Cold start | Emit variant-neutral value | Emit `v × neutral` (so first fire passes some signal) |\n| Out-of-range | Clamp per variant (confidence/decision) or extrapolate (calibration) | Auto-extended; new extreme widens the buffer on the same fire |\n| Concurrency | Atomic uint64 bit-cast doubles, CAS-loop widen, plain store EMA | Per-box pthread_mutex on the ring buffer |\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The **gated output** (`v × score`) is the move that makes this composable for decision lattices. When score ∈ [-1, 1] and you multiply N of them through a downstream aggregator, the midpoint-near values multiply toward zero (suppress) and the bound-near values pass through near full amplitude (vote with strength). Without the gating, the user would always need to insert a multiplier box downstream to recover the input — and forget to half the time. Building the multiplication into the box matches the actual use pattern.\n- The **ring buffer is more honest than EMA** for \"remember the last N observed values\" semantics. EMA approximates that with one number that drifts; the buffer literally stores the N. A user who wants to debug \"what's the current min/max?\" can in principle peek the buffer (a follow-up feature) and see the actual values. With EMA, the bound is a smoothed approximation that doesn't correspond to any specific historical event.\n- The 250 → 253 trajectory is a small case study in **why iteration is cheaper than perfection**. The first 250 commit took the design as I understood it at the time; the use-case conversation revealed three substantive shape problems; the 253 commit fixes them. Each piece — schema, loader, dispatch, editor, fixtures — was small enough to refactor in place. If 250 had shipped as a months-long monolith there'd be no room to course-correct; shipping it as a small commit means the second pass is also a small commit.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nSuite holds at 33 / 0. Working tree leaves your inline 320 edits and pre-existing 247/249/251/readme.md untouched."

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-unit-tests.sh — cheap, build-free unit-test runner.\n#\n# What it does, in CEO terms: runs every already-built C unit-test\n# binary under build/tests/, captures pass/fail counts from each\n# binary's trailing \"N passed, M failed\" summary line, and prints\n# one row per binary plus a grand-total footer. No make recursion,\n# no spec rebuilds, no integration tests — strictly an iteration\n# loop for the C unit suite. `make test` remains the gold-standard\n# \"ship it\" verification.\n#\n# Run as:\n#   scripts/run-unit-tests.sh                 # run all built tests\n#   scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009             # only binaries starting with \"009\"\n#   scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 31              # only 31* binaries\n#   scripts/run-unit-tests.sh --quiet         # only totals\n#   scripts/run-unit-tests.sh --verbose       # full output per binary\n#   scripts/run-unit-tests.sh --dir <root>    # override project root\n#\n# Output (default):\n#   009-slot-store-test                          23 /  23  ok\n#   010-graph-loader-test                        13 /  13  ok\n#   ...\n#   N / M tests passed (K binaries)\n#\n# Failing binaries print their captured output below the row.\n# Exit code is zero iff every binary passed, non-zero otherwise\n# with the failing-binary count as the exit value (capped at 125\n# to stay inside the standard exit-code range).\n#\n# Convention compliance per CLAUDE.md: hard-coded ${DIR} with\n# --dir override; one shell command per line; tmp/ for ephemeral\n# per-binary capture so the captures live in RAM rather than\n# polluting the repo.\n\nset -u\n\n# {{{ defaults\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nQUIET=0\nVERBOSE=0\nFILTER=\"\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ argv parse\nwhile [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do\n    case \"$1\" in\n        --dir)\n            DIR=\"$2\"\n            shift 2\n            ;;\n        --quiet|-q)\n            QUIET=1\n            shift\n            ;;\n        --verbose|-v)\n            VERBOSE=1\n            shift\n            ;;\n        --help|-h)\n            grep '^#' \"$0\" | sed 's/^# \\?//'\n            exit 0\n            ;;\n        --*)\n            echo \"run-unit-tests: unknown flag '$1'\" >&2\n            exit 2\n            ;;\n        *)\n            if [[ -z \"$FILTER\" ]]; then\n                FILTER=\"$1\"\n            else\n                echo \"run-unit-tests: only one filter prefix is supported (got '$1' after '$FILTER')\" >&2\n                exit 2\n            fi\n            shift\n            ;;\n    esac\ndone\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ sanity-check paths\nTESTS_DIR=\"$DIR/build/tests\"\nif [[ ! -d \"$TESTS_DIR\" ]]; then\n    echo \"run-unit-tests: no build/tests/ at $TESTS_DIR — run 'make test' once to build the test binaries\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\n\n# Captures live in tmp/ (the project's RAM-backed dir per\n# CLAUDE.md). Fall back to /tmp if the symlink isn't set up.\nCAPTURE_DIR=\"$DIR/tmp/run-unit-tests\"\nif [[ ! -d \"$DIR/tmp\" ]]; then\n    CAPTURE_DIR=\"/tmp/soramech-run-unit-tests\"\nfi\nmkdir -p \"$CAPTURE_DIR\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ collect_binaries — every built *-test executable, sorted\n# The sort by filename also sorts by the project's leading\n# numeric index, which gives a stable, project-meaningful order.\ncollect_binaries() {\n    local b\n    for b in \"$TESTS_DIR\"/*-test; do\n        [[ -x \"$b\" ]] || continue\n        local name\n        name=$(basename \"$b\")\n        if [[ -n \"$FILTER\" ]] && [[ \"$name\" != \"$FILTER\"* ]]; then continue; fi\n        echo \"$b\"\n    done | sort\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run_one — execute one binary, parse its trailing summary\n# The binary's last \"N passed, M failed\" line is the verdict; we\n# look at the LAST such line so a test that prints intermediate\n# summaries (none today, but the format is forgiving) still\n# reports the final tally.       }],
    "originalFile":"# 252 — Cheap, build-free unit-test runner\n\n## Status\nopen — design lifted out of the old 232 issue file when it\nwas converted to `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`. The script\nhasn't been written; this file is the surviving design note.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`make test` builds the C unit-test binaries, runs them, then\ninvokes `scripts/run-tests.sh` for the integration fixtures.\nThat's the right shape for \"ship it\" verification, but it's\nawkward as a development loop:\n\n- The build phase prints `→ src/foo.c` for every file, dozens of\n  lines before the first test runs on a clean tree.\n- Tests run inside a Make recipe; one binary failing aborts the\n  recipe, so later binaries that would have run aren't reported.\n- Unit-test and integration-test output interleave in one stream.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA cheap, build-free runner script — `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`\n— that runs the already-built C unit-test binaries without\nre-invoking Make and without touching the integration fixtures.\n\nGoals:\n\n1. **Cheap.** No make recursion, no spec rebuilds, no integration\n   tests. Under a second on a current build.\n2. **Continues past failures.** Every binary runs; summary at\n   the bottom names what went wrong.\n3. **Pretty by default, mineable on request.** Per-binary\n   one-line status by default; `--quiet` prints only totals;\n   `--verbose` dumps each binary's full output.\n4. **Filterable.** `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009` runs only\n   binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\n## Concept\n\nGlob `build/tests/<name>-test`, sort by filename (which sorts by\nthe project's leading numeric index), run each in turn, capture\nstdout/stderr, parse the binary's trailing `N passed, M failed`\nline for the verdict.\n\nOutput shape:\n\n```\n  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok\n  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok\n  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok\n  ...\n  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)\n```\n\nA failing binary prints its captured output below the summary\nline. Exit code is zero iff every binary passes; non-zero with\nthe count of failing binaries otherwise.\n\nConvention compliance per CLAUDE.md: hard-coded `${DIR}` at top\nwith arg override, all paths under `${DIR}`, each shell command\non its own line, lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Write `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` with the layout above.\n2. Verify it picks up every existing `build/tests/*-test` binary\n   and produces the expected totals.\n3. Verify `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 015` filters to one binary.\n4. Verify `--quiet` and `--verbose` produce useful output.\n5. Provoke a failure (temporarily modify one test) and confirm\n   the failure is reported, exit code non-zero, captured output\n   visible.\n6. Add a `make quicktest` alias or document the script in the\n   Makefile's `help` target.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Stale-binary check.** Should the script warn when a test's\n  source is newer than its built binary? Cheap (`stat` both\n  sides) but the default should be \"just run what's built\" —\n  offer it as `--check-stale`.\n- **Parse format coupling.** Parsing each binary's trailing\n  `N passed, M failed` line couples the runner to the test\n  binaries' output format. Acceptable today (every test uses\n  the same convention) but worth documenting so test authors\n  don't accidentally diverge.\n\n## Related documents\n\n- `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md` — the test inventory this\n  runner exercises.\n- The historical `issues/completed/316-simple-test-runner.md`\n  was the original home of this design; the work folded into\n  the old 232 issue file and now ends up here as its own\n  ticket so the runner script can be tracked independently.\n",
    "oldString":"## Status\nopen — design lifted out of the old 232 issue file when it\nwas converted to `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`. The script\nhasn't been written; this file is the surviving design note.",
    "newString":"## Status\ncomplete — `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` ships with the\npretty-default + `--quiet` + `--verbose` + name-prefix filter\nmodes the design called for. `make quicktest` is the alias;\n`make quicktest ARGS=009` forwards the filter. The runner\nhonestly identifies pre-existing failures (a longstanding\n`307-c-spec-test` failure surfaces immediately when the\nrunner first runs against the built tree).",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/252-build-free-unit-test-runner.md"
  },

    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — Test coverage map\n\nThis document is the project-wide answer to \"what's tested, what\nisn't, and what runs the tests.\" Every time a test file lands or a\ngap is closed, the relevant checklist row gets updated; when a new\nmodule ships, a row goes in showing it has no coverage yet. Without\na single coverage view, gaps accumulate silently — tests get\nwritten for whatever someone happens to be touching, and the rest\ndrifts uncovered.\n\n## Legend\n\n- `[x]` — has a dedicated test file (path in the row).\n- `[ ]` — no dedicated test; may be exercised indirectly through\n  integration fixtures, but not directly verified.\n- `[~]` — partially covered; only some surface area is tested.\n- `[—]` — intentionally untested (vendored library, thin\n  entrypoint, etc.).\n\n## Editor side — JavaScript\n\nThe editor is a browser app served by `src/005-http-server.lua`.\nThe Node-side test runner (Node's built-in `node:test`) was wired\nup alongside the parser tests; other JS modules can follow the same\npattern when they get tests.\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `langs/lua/parser.js` | `[x]` | `tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/bash/parser.js` | `[x]` | `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/c/parser.js` | `[—]` | not written yet; the move-parsers-into-langs work made it optional |\n| `langs/lua/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/bash/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/c/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/lua/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `langs/bash/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `langs/c/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/001-canvas.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/002-boxes.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/003-api.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/004-inspector.js` | `[ ]` | — (variadic helpers are pure functions, prime unit-test candidates) |\n| `assets/js/005-app.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/006-wires.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/008-source-view.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n\n**Highest-value next targets:** the variadic-slot helpers in\n`004-inspector.js` (pure functions, no DOM dependency) and the\nlexer registries in each language directory.\n\n## Lua libraries — `libs/*.lua`\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `libs/soramech-data.lua` | `[x]` | `tests/003-data-test.lua` |\n| `libs/text.lua` | `[ ]` | — (concat, split, upper, lower, trim, replace, replace_first, contains, starts_with, ends_with, length, substring) |\n| `libs/files.lua` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `libs/ollama.lua` | `[—]` | requires a live Ollama endpoint; integration-level only |\n| `libs/dkjson.lua` | `[—]` | vendored third-party |\n\n`libs/text.lua` is the most important gap — every function is a\npure string operation with obvious edge cases (empty input, nil\ninput, no match, plain vs. pattern), exactly the shape unit tests\ncatch best.\n\n## Lua server side — `src/*.lua`\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/001-schema.lua` | `[ ]` | — (validates box JSON; deserves direct accept/reject tests) |\n| `src/002-validate-map.lua` | `[ ]` | — (CLI map validator; only exercised via integration fixtures) |\n| `src/003-loader.lua` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `src/004-executor.lua` | `[~]` | exercised end-to-end via `tests/004-driver-test-runner.lua` and integration maps; no unit-level coverage |\n| `src/005-http-server.lua` | `[ ]` | — (GET/PUT boxes, connections, files, source) |\n| `src/006-server-main.lua` | `[—]` | thin entrypoint |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua` | `[—]` | thin entrypoint |\n\nSchema and validator are the highest-value gaps — they are the\nlast line of defense against malformed map files and they're pure\nfunctions over JSON-shaped tables, very testable.\n\n## C runtime — `src/*.c`\n\nBest-covered area of the project; Each\nfixture is a real map driven through `soramech-pool`; the script\nasserts expected output substrings appear in stderr.\n\n| Fixture | What it exercises |\n|---|---|\n| `calc` | single Lua box |\n| `hello` | data → Lua, string output |\n| `comparator` | comparator branching (lt/eq/gt) |\n| `iter-route` | iterator + routing |\n| `pipeline` | five-box multilang chain (also covers the compile pipeline) |\n| `read-literal` | inline-value source on a read box |\n| `319a-many-inputs` | dispatch input cap removed; box with 20 inputs |\n| `319d-runtime-create` | Lua box uses runtime self-construction to spawn + wire a downstream Lua box |\n| `319e-c-create` | C-to-C runtime self-construction |\n| `319-box-kind-create` | language-agnostic create_box / connect dispatch box kinds |\n| `319-cross-lang-create` | C trigger creates a Lua box at runtime; lazy spec init |\n| `246-c-shim` | per-port custom translation shim (C side) |\n| `246-lua-shim` | per-port custom translation shim (Lua side) |\n| `318-lang-opaque` | $lang_opaque sentinel emit + dual-ring consumer |\n| `248-encap-input-only` | encapsulated map: input-side splice |\n| `248-encap-output-only` | encapsulated map: output-side splice |\n| `248-encap-recursive` | encapsulated map: two-level nested encapsulation |\n| `randomizer-route` | routing kind: randomizer (hash-of-counter pick) |\n| `weighted-route` | routing kind: weighted (cumulative-band lookup) |\n| `distributor-route` | routing kind: distributor (argmin over downstream fill) |\n| `multi-band-comparator-route` | routing kind: multi-band comparator with thresholds |\n| `pipeline (compile)` | the compile pipeline runs the artifact from `/tmp` |\n\nThe reference-counted-artifact (`315-refs-*`) checks plus the\nJSON-Lines run-output writer also fold into the same suite via\n`scripts/run-tests.sh`.\n\n## Test runners\n\n- **`scripts/run-tests.sh`** — integration fixtures + the JS parser\n  tests + the 315 reference-helper unit suite + the\n  compile-pipeline portable-run check. The single entry point for\n  \"run everything the build doesn't run.\" Folds Node-test results\n  into the same pass/fail counter as the integration checks.\n- **`make test`** — builds the C unit-test binaries, runs them,\n  then invokes `scripts/run-tests.sh`. Slow on a clean tree because\n  it does a full rebuild + spec build before any test runs.\n\nA cheap, build-free unit-test runner that lets you iterate without\npaying for the rebuild is **planned** — see the issue file for\nthat work for design notes.\n\n## Suggested next test additions (ranked)\n\n1. **`libs/text.lua`** — pure-Lua tests next to\n   `tests/003-data-test.lua`. To that end, we must\n---\n# SoraMech — Roadmap\n\n## Phase 1 — Foundation (complete)\n\nGoal: a map you can edit in the browser and execute from the\nterminal.\n\nAt the end of phase 1, the user can:\n- Open the editor at `http://localhost:7700/`, see a canvas, create\n  boxes, set their `ref` / `fn` / `inputs`, wire them together\n- Save edits as box files on disk via the HTTP file CRUD server\n- Run `luajit src/007-runner-main.lua <map-dir>` to execute the map\n- Add a custom language driver and have the runner use it\n\nIssues 101–110, all complete and moved to `issues/completed/`.\n\nDemo: `issues/completed/demos/phase-1/`.\n\n## Phase 2 — Editor & graph model (current)\n\n---\n# SoraMech — Language Driver System\n\n## Two systems, one filename\n\nPhase 2 used **driver scripts** — shell wrappers under `drivers/`\nthat the synchronous runner invoked one process per box call.\n\nPhase 3 uses **language specs** — `.so` libraries under `langs/`\nloaded by the C pool runner via `dlopen`, with persistent per-worker\nruntimes.\n\nSame idea, different mechanism. Phase 3 replaces phase 2 wholesale\nwhen it lands. This document covers both, since the project lives in\nphase 2 today and the phase 3 design is fully specified.\n\n## Phase 2 — Driver scripts (current)\n\nA driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one\nlanguage. The synchronous runner looks up the file extension, finds\nthe driver script, and calls it.",

          "description":"Reproduce the test manually to verify gcc/dlopen behaviour"

        "text":"Found it. The two `.so` files have **different checksums** (so the build IS producing different output), but `dlopen` returns the OFF version anyway. That's glibc's well-known same-path cache — even after `dlclose` drops the ref count to zero, `dlopen` of the same path can return the previously-loaded library rather than reading the replaced file from disk. The test exercises a path-reuse scenario that production doesn't hit (real boxes have unique `.so` paths). Fix: use a distinct path per compile in the test, document the limitation. Removing my debug traces first."

(void)sizes; (void)n; (void)out_capacity;\\n\"\n        \"    const char *v =\\n\"\n        \"#ifdef SORAMECH_FLAG_ON\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"on\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#else\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"off\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#endif\\n\"\n        \"    int len = 0;           "new_string":"    char src_path[256], so_off[256], so_on[256];\n    snprintf(src_path, sizeof src_path,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-%d.c\", (int)getpid());\n    /* Use a distinct .so path per build. glibc's dlopen caches by\n     * absolute path even after dlclose drops the ref count to zero,\n     * so two builds at the same path produce the wrong runtime\n     * behaviour the second time (the cached old library wins).\n     * Production code naturally uses unique .so paths per box, so\n     * this never bites at runtime — the test's path-reuse pattern\n     * was the only way to trigger it. */\n    snprintf(so_off, sizeof so_off,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-off-%d.so\", (int)getpid());\n    snprintf(so_on,  sizeof so_on,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-on-%d.so\",  (int)getpid());\n\n    FILE *fp = fopen(src_path, \"w\");\n    ASSERT(fp);\n    fputs(\n        \"int probe(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\\n\"\n        \"          void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size) {\\n\"\n        \"    (void)inputs; (void)sizes; (void)n; (void)out_capacity;\\n\"\n        \"    const char *v =\\n\"\n        \"#ifdef SORAMECH_FLAG_ON\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"on\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#else\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"off\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#endif\\n\"\n        \"    int len = 0; while (v[len]) len++;\\n\"\n        \"    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) ((char *)out_buf)[i] = v[i];\\n\"\n        \"    *out_size = len; return 0;\\n\"\n        \"}\\n\",\n        fp);\n    fclose(fp);\n\n    /* Default build (no cflags): probe returns \"off\". */\n    ASSERT(c->compile(src_path, so_off, NULL) == 0);\n    void *h = c->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    char buf[8]; int n = 0;\n    int rc = c->invoke(h, NULL, so_off, \"probe\", NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, 0,\n                       buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"off\") == 0);\n    c->teardown(h);\n    unlink(so_off);\n\n    /* Build with cflags=\"-DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON\": probe returns \"on\". */\n    box_t hint;\n    memset(&hint, 0, sizeof hint);\n    hint.id     = \"probe\";\n    hint.cflags = \"-DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON\";\n\n    ASSERT(c->compile(src_path, so_on, &hint) == 0);\n    h = c->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    n = 0;\n    rc = c->invoke(h, NULL, so_on, \"probe\", NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, 0,\n                   buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"on\") == 0);\n    c->teardown(h);\n\n    unlink(so_on);\n    unlink(src_path);",

    "oldString":"    char src_path[256], so_path[256];\n    snprintf(src_path, sizeof src_path,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-%d.c\", (int)getpid());\n    snprintf(so_path,  sizeof so_path,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-%d.so\", (int)getpid());\n\n    FILE *fp = fopen(src_path, \"w\");\n    ASSERT(fp);\n    fputs(\n        \"int probe(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\\n\"\n        \"          void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size) {\\n\"\n        \"    (void)inputs; (void)sizes; (void)n; (void)out_capacity;\\n\"\n        \"    const char *v =\\n\"\n        \"#ifdef SORAMECH_FLAG_ON\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"on\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#else\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"off\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#endif\\n\"\n        \"    int len = 0; while (v[len]) len++;\\n\"\n        \"    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) ((char *)out_buf)[i] = v[i];\\n\"\n        \"    *out_size = len; return 0;\\n\"\n        \"}\\n\",\n        fp);\n    fclose(fp);\n\n    /* Default build (no cflags): probe returns \"off\". */\n    ASSERT(c->compile(src_path, so_path, NULL) == 0);\n    void *h = c->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    char buf[8]; int n = 0;\n    int rc = c->invoke(h, NULL, so_path, \"probe\", NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, 0,\n                       buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"off\") == 0);\n    c->teardown(h);\n    unlink(so_path);\n\n    /* Build with cflags=\"-DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON\": probe returns \"on\". */\n    box_t hint;\n    memset(&hint, 0, sizeof hint);\n    hint.id     = \"probe\";\n    hint.cflags = \"-DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON\";\n\n    ASSERT(c->compile(src_path, so_path, &hint) == 0);\n    h = c->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    n = 0;\n    rc = c->invoke(h, NULL, so_path, \"probe\", NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, 0,\n                   buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"on\") == 0);\n    c->teardown(h);\n\n    unlink(so_path);\n    unlink(src_path);",
    "newString":"    char src_path[256], so_off[256], so_on[256];\n    snprintf(src_path, sizeof src_path,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-%d.c\", (int)getpid());\n    /* Use a distinct .so path per build. glibc's dlopen caches by\n     * absolute path even after dlclose drops the ref count to zero,\n     * so two builds at the same path produce the wrong runtime\n     * behaviour the second time (the cached old library wins).\n     * Production code naturally uses unique .so paths per box, so\n     * this never bites at runtime — the test's path-reuse pattern\n     * was the only way to trigger it. */\n    snprintf(so_off, sizeof so_off,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-off-%d.so\", (int)getpid());\n    snprintf(so_on,  sizeof so_on,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflags-on-%d.so\",  (int)getpid());\n\n    FILE *fp = fopen(src_path, \"w\");\n    ASSERT(fp);\n    fputs(\n        \"int probe(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\\n\"\n        \"          void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size) {\\n\"\n        \"    (void)inputs; (void)sizes; (void)n; (void)out_capacity;\\n\"\n        \"    const char *v =\\n\"\n        \"#ifdef SORAMECH_FLAG_ON\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"on\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#else\\n\"\n        \"        \\\"off\\\";\\n\"\n        \"#endif\\n\"\n        \"    int len = 0; while (v[len]) len++;\\n\"\n        \"    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) ((char *)out_buf)[i] = v[i];\\n\"\n        \"    *out_size = len; return 0;\\n\"\n        \"}\\n\",\n        fp);\n    fclose(fp);\n\n    /* Default build (no cflags): probe returns \"off\". */\n    ASSERT(c->compile(src_path, so_off, NULL) == 0);\n    void *h = c->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    char buf[8]; int n = 0;\n    int rc = c->invoke(h, NULL, so_off, \"probe\", NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, 0,\n                       buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"off\") == 0);\n    c->teardown(h);\n    unlink(so_off);\n\n    /* Build with cflags=\"-DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON\": probe returns \"on\". */\n    box_t hint;\n    memset(&hint, 0, sizeof hint);\n    hint.id     = \"probe\";\n    hint.cflags = \"-DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON\";\n\n    ASSERT(c->compile(src_path, so_on, &hint) == 0);\n    h = c->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    n = 0;\n    rc = c->invoke(h, NULL, so_on, \"probe\", NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, 0,\n                   buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"on\") == 0);\n    c->teardown(h);\n\n    unlink(so_on);\n    unlink(src_path);",

Production code uses\n     * box-id-derived paths which are also distinct per box, so the\n     * cache hazard doesn't bite at runtime — this naming just\n     * mirrors the production discipline inside a single test. */\n    long ts = (long)time(NULL);\n    snprintf(src_path, sizeof src_path,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflag-probe-%d-%ld.c\",   (int)getpid(), ts);\n    snprintf(so_off, sizeof so_off,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflag-probe-%d-%ld-default.so\", (int)getpid(), ts);\n    snprintf(so_on,  sizeof so_on,\n             \"/tmp/soramech-cflag-probe-%d-%ld-flagged.so\", (int)getpid(), ts);",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/tests/307-c-spec-test.c"

          "command":"git -C /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech add tests/307-c-spec-test.c && git -C /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\ntests/307: fix cflags test by giving each build its own .so path\n\nThe compile_with_cflags test compiled twice — once without\ncflags (expecting \"off\"), once with -DSORAMECH_FLAG_ON (expecting\n\"on\") — to the SAME .so path. The second invoke then reliably\nreturned \"off\" anyway because glibc's dlopen caches loaded\nlibraries by absolute path even after dlclose drops the ref\ncount to zero. The second dlopen sees the file is \"there\" at the\nsame path it just unloaded, and returns the cached old mapping\nrather than reading the replaced bytes from disk.\n\nThe test's gcc invocation IS correct (the -D flag arrives in the\nargv as designed) and the build produces a genuinely different\n.so on disk (different checksums confirmed). The disagreement is\nentirely between what's on disk and what the in-process dynamic\nlinker cache says is loaded — a well-known glibc behaviour that\nproduction code naturally avoids by giving each box a distinct\n.so path derived from the box id.\n\nThe fix mirrors that production discipline inside the test: each\nbuild writes to its own path (one ending in \"-default.so\", the\nother in \"-flagged.so\"). Path is also stamped with both the test\nprocess's pid AND a timestamp so re-runs within the same second\ncan't share a path either. The src file gets the same scoping\ntreatment.\n\nThree consecutive isolated runs of the test now pass 13/13. The\nfull unit suite goes 178/179 → 179/179; the integration suite\nstays at 33/33.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",

        },

    "structuredPatch":[],
    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# SoraMech — Overview & quickstart\n\n## What SoraMech is\n\nSoraMech is a **visual dataflow runtime**. You build a *map* — a\ngraph of boxes connected by wires — in the browser-based editor.\nEach box runs a function (in Lua, C, or Bash). When you run the\nmap, the runtime fires boxes whose inputs are ready, threads the\noutputs along wires to downstream boxes, and keeps going until\nquiescence. Multiple boxes run in parallel across a thread pool.\n\nThe runtime is structural. It guarantees that wires deliver\nvalues from producers to consumers; that boxes fire when their\ninputs are ready; that values cross language boundaries cleanly.\nIt does not know what your boxes *do* — that's your code. The\nruntime is the apartment building's steel and concrete; box\nauthors and library authors design the rooms.\n\n## When to reach for it\n\nSoraMech fits well when:\n\n- The problem is naturally a dataflow: inputs flow through a\n  sequence of transformations to outputs.\n- You want to mix languages — a Lua planner driving C boxes that\n  feed a Bash post-processor.\n- You want to inspect the wiring visually instead of reading code.\n- The work is naturally parallel — independent boxes should fire\n  on different threads without you orchestrating threads yourself.\n- You want a **JSONL audit trail** of what happened during a run,\n  for debugging, replay, or feeding to a downstream tool.\n\nIt's less useful when the problem isn't dataflow-shaped (long\nsingle-threaded computations, tight tensor math, anything where\nthe box overhead would dominate the work).\n\n## Quickstart\n\n### Install\n\nSoraMech is a small set of C sources, shell scripts, and Lua /\nJavaScript assets. You build it from source.\n\nPrerequisites:\n\n- A C compiler with C11 support (`gcc` or `clang`)\n- `make`\n- `luajit` 2.1 (or compatible) with its headers\n- `bash`\n- `node` (for the editor's JavaScript tests; optional otherwise)\n\nBuild:\n\n```bash\nmake            # builds the pool runner + the three language specs\nmake test       # full ship-it suite (unit tests + integration fixtures)\nmake quicktest  # cheap iteration: just the C unit tests, no rebuild\n```\n\n### Your first map\n\nA map is a directory of JSON files. Boxes live in `boxes/`,\nsource code in `src/`, metadata in `meta.json`. The simplest\nmap is one Lua box wired to one read box.\n\n```\nmy-map/\n  meta.json\n  boxes/\n    seed.json\n    greet.json\n  src/\n    greet.lua\n```\n\n`meta.json`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"my-map\",\n  \"description\": \"Tiny example\",\n  \"entry_box_id\": \"seed\",\n  \"src_dirs\": [\"my-map/src\"]\n}\n```\n\n`boxes/seed.json` (a value source — emits the literal `\"world\"`):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"seed\",\n  \"kind\":  \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"world\",\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"seed\", \"to_box\": \"greet\", \"to_input\": \"name\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`boxes/greet.json` (a Lua call box):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"greet\",\n  \"kind\":  \"call\",\n  \"lang\":  \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":   \"src/greet.lua\",\n  \"fn\":    \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\n`src/greet.lua`:\n\n```lua\nlocal M = {}\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\nreturn M\n```\n\nRun it:\n\n```bash\n./soramech-pool my-map\n```\n\nOutput:\n\n```\nsoramech-pool: 'my-map' — 2 box(es), entry seed, N worker(s)\nsoramech-pool: run log → /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\nsoramech-pool: run complete (1 task(s) in 234 µs).\nsoramech-pool: outputs:\n  greet → Hello, world!\n```\n\nThe seed box pushed `\"world\"` along its wire to `greet.name`.\nThe Lua function ran and returned `\"Hello, world!\"`, which is\nthe output captured for `greet`. The full per-event run log\nsits at `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl` — one JSON event per\nline, ready to feed to whatever downstream tool you like.\n\n### Editing in the browser\n\nFor anything more than a toy, you'll want the editor:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/start-server.sh\n# open http://localhost:7700/ in your browser\n```\n\nThe editor's a canvas-and-inspector view of the same map\ndirectory. Drag to create boxes, click-drag between port dots\nto wire them, click a box to edit its fields in the right\nsidebar. Saves go straight to the JSON files on disk; you can\nrun the map from another terminal at any time.\n\n## What's next\n\n- [`docs/002-map-model.md`](002-map-model.md) — the box kinds,\n  routing kinds, wire semantics, and how encapsulated sub-maps\n  let you compose larger graphs from smaller ones.\n- [`docs/003-editor.md`](003-editor.md) — the canvas + inspector\n  UI walkthrough.\n- [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) — how runs work, what\n  the JSONL log contains, the compile pipeline, the\n  reference-counted artifact system.\n- [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) — per-\n  language quickstarts for Lua, C, and Bash box authors.\n- [`docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`](006-test-coverage-map.md) —\n  the project's test inventory.\n",
    "type":"create",

  },

}

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Overview & quickstart\n\n## What SoraMech is\n\nSoraMech is a **visual dataflow runtime**. You build a *map* — a\ngraph of boxes connected by wires — in the browser-based editor.\nEach box runs a function (in Lua, C, or Bash). When you run the\nmap, the runtime fires boxes whose inputs are ready, threads the\noutputs along wires to downstream boxes, and keeps going until\nquiescence. Multiple boxes run in parallel across a thread pool.\n\nThe runtime is structural. It guarantees that wires deliver\nvalues from producers to consumers; that boxes fire when their\ninputs are ready; that values cross language boundaries cleanly.\nIt does not know what your boxes *do* — that's your code. The\nruntime is the apartment building's steel and concrete; box\nauthors and library authors design the rooms.\n\n## When to reach for it\n\nSoraMech fits well when:\n\n- The problem is naturally a dataflow: inputs flow through a\n  sequence of transformations to outputs.\n- You want to mix languages — a Lua planner driving C boxes that\n  feed a Bash post-processor.\n- You want to inspect the wiring visually instead of reading code.\n- The work is naturally parallel — independent boxes should fire\n  on different threads without you orchestrating threads yourself.\n- You want a **JSONL audit trail** of what happened during a run,\n  for debugging, replay, or feeding to a downstream tool.\n\nIt's less useful when the problem isn't dataflow-shaped (long\nsingle-threaded computations, tight tensor math, anything where\nthe box overhead would dominate the work).\n\n## Quickstart\n\n### Install\n\nSoraMech is a small set of C sources, shell scripts, and Lua /\nJavaScript assets. You build it from source.\n\nPrerequisites:\n\n- A C compiler with C11 support (`gcc` or `clang`)\n- `make`\n- `luajit` 2.1 (or compatible) with its headers\n- `bash`\n- `node` (for the editor's JavaScript tests; optional otherwise)\n\nBuild:\n\n```bash\nmake            # builds the pool runner + the three language specs\nmake test       # full ship-it suite (unit tests + integration fixtures)\nmake quicktest  # cheap iteration: just the C unit tests, no rebuild\n```\n\n### Your first map\n\nA map is a directory of JSON files. Boxes live in `boxes/`,\nsource code in `src/`, metadata in `meta.json`. The simplest\nmap is one Lua box wired to one read box.\n\n```\nmy-map/\n  meta.json\n  boxes/\n    seed.json\n    greet.json\n  src/\n    greet.lua\n```\n\n`meta.json`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"my-map\",\n  \"description\": \"Tiny example\",\n  \"entry_box_id\": \"seed\",\n  \"src_dirs\": [\"my-map/src\"]\n}\n```\n\n`boxes/seed.json` (a value source — emits the literal `\"world\"`):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"seed\",\n  \"kind\":  \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"world\",\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"seed\", \"to_box\": \"greet\", \"to_input\": \"name\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`boxes/greet.json` (a Lua call box):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"greet\",\n  \"kind\":  \"call\",\n  \"lang\":  \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":   \"src/greet.lua\",\n  \"fn\":    \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\n`src/greet.lua`:\n\n```lua\nlocal M = {}\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\nreturn M\n```\n\nRun it:\n\n```bash\n./soramech-pool my-map\n```\n\nOutput:\n\n```\nsoramech-pool: 'my-map' — 2 box(es), entry seed, N worker(s)\nsoramech-pool: run log → /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\nsoramech-pool: run complete (1 task(s) in 234 µs).\nsoramech-pool: outputs:\n  greet → Hello, world!\n```\n\nThe seed box pushed `\"world\"` along its wire to `greet.name`.\nThe Lua function ran and returned `\"Hello, world!\"`, which is\nthe output captured for `greet`. The full per-event run log\nsits at `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl` — one JSON event per\nline, ready to feed to whatever downstream tool you like.\n\n### Editing in the browser\n\nFor anything more than a toy, you'll want the editor:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/start-server.sh\n# open http://localhost:7700/ in your browser\n```\n\nThe editor's a canvas-and-inspector view of the same map\ndirectory. Drag to create boxes, click-drag between port dots\nto wire them, click a box to edit its fields in the right\nsidebar. Saves go straight to the JSON files on disk; you can\nrun the map from another terminal at any time.\n\n## What's next\n\n- [`docs/002-map-model.md`](002-map-model.md) — the box kinds,\n  routing kinds, wire semantics, and how encapsulated sub-maps\n  let you compose larger graphs from smaller ones.\n- [`docs/003-editor.md`](003-editor.md) — the canvas + inspector\n  UI walkthrough.\n- [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) — how runs work, what\n  the JSONL log contains, the compile pipeline, the\n  reference-counted artifact system.\n- [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) — per-\n  language quickstarts for Lua, C, and Bash box authors.\n- [`docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`](006-test-coverage-map.md) —\n  the project's test inventory.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/001-overview.md"
        },

        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Map model\n\nA map is a directed graph of **boxes** connected by **wires**.\nBoxes have **input ports** (left side, where wires arrive) and a\nsingle **output side** (right side, where wires leave). Wires\ncarry values from one box's output to another box's input port.\n\n## Box kinds\n\nEvery box has a `kind` field that tells the runtime what it does.\n\n### `call` — runs a function\n\nThe general-purpose box. Names a function in some language\n(`lua` / `c` / `bash`) and runs it when the inputs are ready.\nThe function's return value becomes the value on the output wire.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"double\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/math.lua\",\n  \"fn\":   \"double\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\n### `read` — emits a value\n\nA pull-on-demand value source. Either a literal (`value` field)\nor the bytes of a file (`path` field). When a downstream box\nneeds a value, the read box's bytes get pulled in.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"config\",\n  \"kind\":  \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"production\",\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"config\", \"to_box\": \"router\", \"to_input\": \"env\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n### `write` — writes to disk\n\nThe sink for \"land this value on the filesystem.\" Reads its\n`value` input and writes it to the `path` input. By default\nemits the string `\"true\"` downstream as a success signal so\nlater boxes can chain off the write.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"save\",\n  \"kind\": \"write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"path\",  \"value\": \"/tmp/result.txt\" },\n    { \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n### `map` — encapsulated sub-map\n\nAn entire sub-graph appearing as one box on the parent canvas.\nSee \"Encapsulation\" below for the full story.\n\n### `create_box` / `connect` — runtime self-construction\n\nA running box can spawn new boxes and wire them up mid-run. The\n`create_box` and `connect` kinds are the language-agnostic\ndispatch primitives; per-language wrappers like Lua's\n`soramech.create_box{...}` are convenience over the same path.\nSee [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) for the\ncalling shape.\n\n## Wires (connections)\n\nA wire lives on the **producer** box's `connections[]` array. Each\nentry names a destination and (when the routing kind has named\nbranches) which branch the wire leaves from.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"from_box\":    \"router\",\n  \"from_branch\": \"lt\",          // optional; depends on routing kind\n  \"to_box\":      \"low_handler\",\n  \"to_input\":    \"value\"\n}\n```\n\nWhen a producer fires, the runtime pushes its output value into\nthe destination box's input slot. The destination fires when all\nits required input slots have values.\n\nA producer can fan out — multiple wires leaving the same output\nport deliver the same value to each consumer. The single-output-\nper-box rule (every kind except `map` has one output port)\nkeeps the wiring discipline simple.\n\n## Routing kinds\n\nThe `routing` field on a `call` box decides *where* the output\ngoes. Seven kinds ship:\n\n### `plain` — fan to every wire\n\nSingle output port (unnamed). Every wire on `connections[]`\nreceives the value. The default for new boxes.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n```\n\n### `comparator` — pick by numeric threshold\n\nTwo flavours. The single-threshold form names three output\nbranches `lt` / `eq` / `gt` and picks the matching one based on\nthe producer's numeric output:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": 5 }\n```\n\nThe multi-band form takes a non-decreasing `thresholds` array\nand carves the number line into N+1 named bands:\n`below_<t0>` / `between_<a>_<b>` / `above_<tN-1>`. Doubled\nadjacent thresholds carve zero-width equality bands named\n`eq_<t>`:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"thresholds\": [3, 7] }\n// → branches: below_3, between_3_7, above_7\n```\n\n### `iterator` — round-robin over N ports\n\nNo function attached — pure routing. Each fire rotates the\noutput among `n_outputs` ports named `out_0` ... `out_<n-1>`.\nMulti-spawn: a single arrival to an iterator's input slot drains\nqueued values one per fire.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n### `randomizer` — hashed pseudo-random pick\n\nSame `out_<i>` port shape as iterator. Each fire hashes the\nper-box counter and takes mod `n_outputs`, so consecutive fires\nspread across branches rather than going to consecutive indices.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n```\n\n### `weighted` — probability-weighted pick\n\nSame `out_<i>` ports. Each fire picks a branch by cumulative-\nband lookup over the user's `weights` array. The dispatch\nnormalises automatically — the weights don't have to sum to 1.0.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"weighted\", \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2] }\n```\n\n### `distributor` — least-busy pick\n\nSame `out_<i>` ports. Each fire samples the downstream slot\nfill on every branch and picks the least-busy one. Ties resolve\nvia a per-box counter so a steady stream rotates across\nequally-empty branches.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n### `nonlinearity` — value-transforming auto-calibrated gate\n\nSingle output port. Reads the producer's numeric output,\nauto-calibrates bounds from a per-box ring buffer of the last\n`memory` observed values, normalises against those bounds,\napplies an S-curve, and emits `input × score` (gated linear\nunit shape) on the wire.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":   \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"range\":  \"signed\",   // \"signed\" → tanh, output [-1, 1]\n                        // \"unit\"   → sigmoid, output [0, 1]\n  \"memory\": 16,         // ring-buffer size for auto-calibration\n  \"k\":      1           // steepness\n}\n```\n\nUseful for decision-lattice composition: chain several into a\ndownstream aggregator and the soft-AND property of multiplying\nscored values bubbles up \"strong evidence reinforces, weak\nevidence stays weak\" behaviour.\n\n## Input port semantics\n\nA `call` box's `inputs[]` array declares its port set. Each port\nhas a name, an optional `type` (`\"string\"` is the convention),\nan optional inline `value` (a literal that supplies the port if\nno wire is attached), and an optional `optional` flag (when\ntrue, the box fires even if this port has no value).\n\nA port can be in one of three states at compile time:\n- **Wired** — a producer's `connections[]` entry targets it.\n- **Literal** — the port carries an inline `value`.\n- **Optional** — neither wired nor literal, but `optional: true`.\n\nAnything else is a hard error at graph load. SoraMech doesn't\nsilently fire a box with a missing required input.\n\n## Encapsulation — sub-maps as boxes\n\nA whole map can appear as a single box on another map's canvas.\nThis is `kind: \"map\"`. The parent's canvas sees one box; the\nruntime expands the sub-map at graph-load time into the parent's\nflat graph, with the sub-map's box ids prefix-renamed.\n\nHow the sub-map exposes ports:\n\n- A **read** box inside the sub-map marked with an `external`\n  block becomes one of the encap box's INPUT ports. Parent\n  wires landing on that port get spliced through to whatever\n  the read box was feeding inside the sub-map.\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"msg_in\", \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"external\": { \"kind\": \"named\", \"name\": \"msg\" } }\n```\n\n- A **write** box marked externally-consumed becomes an OUTPUT\n  port on the encap box. The write still happens to its `path`\n  (when set); additionally the value gets surfaced back to the\n  parent on the wire.\n\nThe encap box itself declares the port shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"stats_pipeline\",\n  \"kind\": \"map\",\n  \"ref\":  \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"msg\",    \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"outputs\": [ { \"name\": \"result\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"stats_pipeline\", \"from_branch\": \"result\",\n      \"to_box\":   \"downstream\",     \"to_input\":    \"value\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nEncapsulation is the documented exception to the single-output-\nper-box rule — an encap can declare any number of output ports\n(one per externally-consumed write box). The runtime treats them\nas independent value sources.\n\nEncaps nest. A sub-map can itself contain a `kind: \"map\"` box,\nand the load-time splice iterates until no encaps remain. Cycle\ndetection runs after the flattening.\n\n## What's next\n\n- [`docs/003-editor.md`](003-editor.md) — using the canvas to\n  build maps visually.\n- [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) — how the runtime\n  executes maps, the JSONL transcript, the compile pipeline.\n- [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) — per-\n  language box-author guides.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/002-map-model.md"
        },

          "type":"direct"
        },

      }],

Each fire samples the downstream slot\nfill on every branch and picks the least-busy one. Ties resolve\nvia a per-box counter so a steady stream rotates across\nequally-empty branches.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n### `nonlinearity` — value-transforming auto-calibrated gate\n\nSingle output port. Reads the producer's numeric output,\nauto-calibrates bounds from a per-box ring buffer of the last\n`memory` observed values, normalises against those bounds,\napplies an S-curve, and emits `input × score` (gated linear\nunit shape) on the wire.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":   \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"range\":  \"signed\",   // \"signed\" → tanh, output [-1, 1]\n                        // \"unit\"   → sigmoid, output [0, 1]\n  \"memory\": 16,         // ring-buffer size for auto-calibration\n  \"k\":      1           // steepness\n}\n```\n\nUseful for decision-lattice composition: chain several into a\ndownstream aggregator and the soft-AND property of multiplying\nscored values bubbles up \"strong evidence reinforces, weak\nevidence stays weak\" behaviour.\n\n## Input port semantics\n\nA `call` box's `inputs[]` array declares its port set. Each port\nhas a name, an optional `type` (`\"string\"` is the convention),\nan optional inline `value` (a literal that supplies the port if\nno wire is attached), and an optional `optional` flag (when\ntrue, the box fires even if this port has no value).\n\nA port can be in one of three states at compile time:\n- **Wired** — a producer's `connections[]` entry targets it.\n- **Literal** — the port carries an inline `value`.\n- **Optional** — neither wired nor literal, but `optional: true`.\n\nAnything else is a hard error at graph load. SoraMech doesn't\nsilently fire a box with a missing required input.\n\n## Encapsulation — sub-maps as boxes\n\nA whole map can appear as a single box on another map's canvas.\nThis is `kind: \"map\"`. The parent's canvas sees one box; the\nruntime expands the sub-map at graph-load time into the parent's\nflat graph, with the sub-map's box ids prefix-renamed.\n\nHow the sub-map exposes ports:\n\n- A **read** box inside the sub-map marked with an `external`\n  block becomes one of the encap box's INPUT ports. Parent\n  wires landing on that port get spliced through to whatever\n  the read box was feeding inside the sub-map.\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"msg_in\", \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"external\": { \"kind\": \"named\", \"name\": \"msg\" } }\n```\n\n- A **write** box marked externally-consumed becomes an OUTPUT\n  port on the encap box. The write still happens to its `path`\n  (when set); additionally the value gets surfaced back to the\n  parent on the wire.\n\nThe encap box itself declares the port shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"stats_pipeline\",\n  \"kind\": \"map\",\n  \"ref\":  \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"msg\",    \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"outputs\": [ { \"name\": \"result\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"stats_pipeline\", \"from_branch\": \"result\",\n      \"to_box\":   \"downstream\",     \"to_input\":    \"value\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nEncapsulation is the documented exception to the single-output-\nper-box rule — an encap can declare any number of output ports\n(one per externally-consumed write box). The runtime treats them\nas independent value sources.\n\nEncaps nest. A sub-map can itself contain a `kind: \"map\"` box,\nand the load-time splice iterates until no encaps remain. Cycle\ndetection runs after the flattening.\n\n## What's next\n\n- [`docs/003-editor.md`](003-editor.md) — using the canvas to\n  build maps visually.\n- [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) — how the runtime\n  executes maps, the JSONL transcript, the compile pipeline.\n- [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) — per-\n  language box-author guides.\n",
    "type":"create",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/002-map-model.md"
  },

        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Editor\n\nThe editor is a browser app. It loads a map directory, draws the\nboxes on a canvas, lets you wire them, and saves every change\nstraight to the JSON files on disk. The runner reads those same\nfiles — there's no \"save and rebuild\" step between editing and\nrunning.\n\n## Starting it\n\n```bash\n./scripts/start-server.sh\n# default: http://localhost:7700/\n```\n\nThe server is a small Lua HTTP server (`src/005-http-server.lua`)\nthat exposes the file CRUD endpoints the editor uses. It serves\nthe map directory you launched it against.\n\nYou can override the port or pick a different map root via\n`config/editor.json` or environment variables — see\n`scripts/start-server.sh` for the knobs.\n\n## The layout\n\nThree regions:\n\n- **Canvas** (centre) — boxes, wires, ports. Pan with click-drag\n  on empty space; zoom with the scroll wheel.\n- **Inspector** (right sidebar) — the selected box's editable\n  fields. Click a box to populate it; click empty canvas to hide.\n- **Map header** (top) — current map name (click to switch maps),\n  compile button, and run status.\n\n## Working with boxes\n\n**Create**: right-click an empty spot on the canvas and pick a\nkind from the menu. Or middle-click an existing box to\nduplicate it at the cursor position.\n\n**Move**: click-drag a box's body.\n\n**Inspect / edit**: click a box. The inspector fills with the\nbox's fields. Editing any field saves to disk on the next\nkeystroke (debounced) or on blur.\n\n**Delete**: click a box to select, then press the delete button\nat the top of the inspector. The wires attached to it get\ncleared automatically.\n\n## Working with wires\n\n**Draw**: click-drag from one box's port dot to another box's\nport dot. Source side is the right edge (an output port);\ndestination side is the left edge (an input port).\n\n**Delete**: click the wire (anywhere along its length) to select\nit, then press Delete.\n\n**Self-loops** route around the box body so they stay readable.\n\n## Inspector by box kind\n\nThe inspector shows only the fields that apply to the current\nbox's kind. The shared header (label, id, kind dropdown, delete\nbutton) is always there.\n\n### Call boxes\n\n- **kind**: dropdown lets you swap between `call` / `read` /\n  `write` / `map`. Changing kind clears the per-kind fields.\n- **routing**: dropdown picks the routing kind. Switching kinds\n  severs any outgoing wires whose port names would no longer\n  exist under the new kind.\n- **ref**: the source file. Click \"browse\" to pick from the\n  attached source directories.\n- **fn**: the function name within that file. Click \"fn\" to\n  pick from the parsed function list.\n- **inputs**: per-port editable rows. Name comes from the\n  parser; you supply the literal value (or leave blank for\n  wired input).\n- **per-routing-kind controls**: comparator gets a `comparand`\n  number input and a `thresholds` text input; iterator /\n  randomizer / distributor get an `n_outputs` number;\n  weighted gets a comma-separated `weights` text input;\n  nonlinearity gets the `range` toggle + `memory` + `k`.\n\n### Read boxes\n\n- **value**: literal text the box emits. When set, the `path`\n  input port hides on the canvas.\n- **external**: toggle to mark this read box as\n  externally-supplied (consumed by the encapsulating sub-map's\n  port shape). When on, a binding-kind selector lets you pick\n  `named` / `positional` / `numbered` plus the matching name or\n  index.\n\n### Write boxes\n\n- **inputs**: `path` (where to write) and `value` (what to\n  write). Either can be wired or carry a literal.\n- **external**: toggle to mark this write box as\n  externally-consumed (the value also surfaces as an output\n  port on the encapsulating sub-map). Same binding-kind shape\n  as read.\n\n### Map boxes (encapsulated sub-maps)\n\n- **ref**: path to the sub-map directory (relative to the\n  current map's directory, or absolute).\n- **inputs / outputs**: editable port lists. Each row is a\n  port name; +/− buttons add and remove rows. The names need to\n  match the externally-supplied read boxes and\n  externally-consumed write boxes inside the sub-map.\n\n## The file browser\n\nThe bottom of the inspector hosts the file browser when you\nclick \"browse\" or \"fn\" on a call box. It lists source files\nacross every attached source directory. Click a directory header\nto collapse / expand; right-click to hide a directory.\n\nThe \"+ library dir\" button at the top lets you attach an\narbitrary directory as another source root for the current map —\nuseful for sharing helpers across maps without copying files.\n\n## The map picker\n\nClick the map name in the header to open the map picker. It\nlists every map known to the current server, plus a recent-maps\nhistory. Selecting one switches the editor to that map.\n\nEach map row also has an **encap** button. Clicking it adds the\nselected map as a `kind: \"map\"` sub-map box on the\ncurrently-edited map's canvas. The new box's port shape is\nderived from the sub-map's externally-marked read and write\nboxes, so the wiring is ready as soon as the box appears.\n\n## Compile\n\nThe compile button at the top of the editor runs\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` against the current map. The\ncompiled artifact lands under `<map>/compiled/` and is portable\n— it bundles the language plugins, pre-compiles every C box,\nand includes the pool runner binary. Copy or symlink the\ndirectory anywhere on the same machine and it runs the map\nstandalone (no source tree required).\n\nSee [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) for the runtime\nside of compilation, including the reference-counted artifacts\nsystem that keeps in-flight runs safe across rebuilds.\n\n## Keyboard shortcuts\n\n- **Delete**: delete the selected box or wire.\n- **Middle-click**: duplicate the box under the cursor at the\n  cursor position.\n- **Scroll**: zoom.\n- **Right-click**: context menu (new box, hide directory in the\n  file browser, etc.).\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/003-editor.md"

    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# SoraMech — Editor\n\nThe editor is a browser app. It loads a map directory, draws the\nboxes on a canvas, lets you wire them, and saves every change\nstraight to the JSON files on disk. The runner reads those same\nfiles — there's no \"save and rebuild\" step between editing and\nrunning.\n\n## Starting it\n\n```bash\n./scripts/start-server.sh\n# default: http://localhost:7700/\n```\n\nThe server is a small Lua HTTP server (`src/005-http-server.lua`)\nthat exposes the file CRUD endpoints the editor uses. It serves\nthe map directory you launched it against.\n\nYou can override the port or pick a different map root via\n`config/editor.json` or environment variables — see\n`scripts/start-server.sh` for the knobs.\n\n## The layout\n\nThree regions:\n\n- **Canvas** (centre) — boxes, wires, ports. Pan with click-drag\n  on empty space; zoom with the scroll wheel.\n- **Inspector** (right sidebar) — the selected box's editable\n  fields. Click a box to populate it; click empty canvas to hide.\n- **Map header** (top) — current map name (click to switch maps),\n  compile button, and run status.\n\n## Working with boxes\n\n**Create**: right-click an empty spot on the canvas and pick a\nkind from the menu. Or middle-click an existing box to\nduplicate it at the cursor position.\n\n**Move**: click-drag a box's body.\n\n**Inspect / edit**: click a box. The inspector fills with the\nbox's fields. Editing any field saves to disk on the next\nkeystroke (debounced) or on blur.\n\n**Delete**: click a box to select, then press the delete button\nat the top of the inspector. The wires attached to it get\ncleared automatically.\n\n## Working with wires\n\n**Draw**: click-drag from one box's port dot to another box's\nport dot. Source side is the right edge (an output port);\ndestination side is the left edge (an input port).\n\n**Delete**: click the wire (anywhere along its length) to select\nit, then press Delete.\n\n**Self-loops** route around the box body so they stay readable.\n\n## Inspector by box kind\n\nThe inspector shows only the fields that apply to the current\nbox's kind. The shared header (label, id, kind dropdown, delete\nbutton) is always there.\n\n### Call boxes\n\n- **kind**: dropdown lets you swap between `call` / `read` /\n  `write` / `map`. Changing kind clears the per-kind fields.\n- **routing**: dropdown picks the routing kind. Switching kinds\n  severs any outgoing wires whose port names would no longer\n  exist under the new kind.\n- **ref**: the source file. Click \"browse\" to pick from the\n  attached source directories.\n- **fn**: the function name within that file. Click \"fn\" to\n  pick from the parsed function list.\n- **inputs**: per-port editable rows. Name comes from the\n  parser; you supply the literal value (or leave blank for\n  wired input).\n- **per-routing-kind controls**: comparator gets a `comparand`\n  number input and a `thresholds` text input; iterator /\n  randomizer / distributor get an `n_outputs` number;\n  weighted gets a comma-separated `weights` text input;\n  nonlinearity gets the `range` toggle + `memory` + `k`.\n\n### Read boxes\n\n- **value**: literal text the box emits. When set, the `path`\n  input port hides on the canvas.\n- **external**: toggle to mark this read box as\n  externally-supplied (consumed by the encapsulating sub-map's\n  port shape). When on, a binding-kind selector lets you pick\n  `named` / `positional` / `numbered` plus the matching name or\n  index.\n\n### Write boxes\n\n- **inputs**: `path` (where to write) and `value` (what to\n  write). Either can be wired or carry a literal.\n- **external**: toggle to mark this write box as\n  externally-consumed (the value also surfaces as an output\n  port on the encapsulating sub-map). Same binding-kind shape\n  as read.\n\n### Map boxes (encapsulated sub-maps)\n\n- **ref**: path to the sub-map directory (relative to the\n  current map's directory, or absolute).\n- **inputs / outputs**: editable port lists. Each row is a\n  port name; +/− buttons add and remove rows. The names need to\n  match the externally-supplied read boxes and\n  externally-consumed write boxes inside the sub-map.\n\n## The file browser\n\nThe bottom of the inspector hosts the file browser when you\nclick \"browse\" or \"fn\" on a call box. It lists source files\nacross every attached source directory. Click a directory header\nto collapse / expand; right-click to hide a directory.\n\nThe \"+ library dir\" button at the top lets you attach an\narbitrary directory as another source root for the current map —\nuseful for sharing helpers across maps without copying files.\n\n## The map picker\n\nClick the map name in the header to open the map picker. It\nlists every map known to the current server, plus a recent-maps\nhistory. Selecting one switches the editor to that map.\n\nEach map row also has an **encap** button. Clicking it adds the\nselected map as a `kind: \"map\"` sub-map box on the\ncurrently-edited map's canvas. The new box's port shape is\nderived from the sub-map's externally-marked read and write\nboxes, so the wiring is ready as soon as the box appears.\n\n## Compile\n\nThe compile button at the top of the editor runs\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` against the current map. The\ncompiled artifact lands under `<map>/compiled/` and is portable\n— it bundles the language plugins, pre-compiles every C box,\nand includes the pool runner binary. Copy or symlink the\ndirectory anywhere on the same machine and it runs the map\nstandalone (no source tree required).\n\nSee [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) for the runtime\nside of compilation, including the reference-counted artifacts\nsystem that keeps in-flight runs safe across rebuilds.\n\n## Keyboard shortcuts\n\n- **Delete**: delete the selected box or wire.\n- **Middle-click**: duplicate the box under the cursor at the\n  cursor position.\n- **Scroll**: zoom.\n- **Right-click**: context menu (new box, hide directory in the\n  file browser, etc.).\n",
    "type":"create",

  },
