        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Runtime\n\nThis doc covers what happens when you run a map: how the runner\nloads the graph, fires boxes, threads values along wires, writes\nthe JSONL transcript, and tears down. Plus the compile pipeline\nand the reference-counted-artifact system that lets long-running\nprocesses hold onto a specific build of a map across rebuilds.\n\n## Running a map\n\n```bash\n./soramech-pool <map-dir>\n```\n\nThe runner reads `<map-dir>/meta.json` + `<map-dir>/boxes/*.json`,\nbuilds the in-memory graph, attaches the slot store (one slot\nper input port), starts a worker pool (one worker per CPU by\ndefault; override with `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`), and submits the\nentry boxes as initial tasks. Workers pick tasks off the pool\nqueue, run the box's spec function (Lua, C, or Bash), and push\nthe output along the producer's outgoing connections.\n\nWhen all consumers are satisfied and no tasks remain, the run\nhits quiescence and the runner exits. The stderr summary prints\neach box's most recent output.\n\n```\nsoramech-pool: 'hello' — 2 box(es), entry seed, 14 worker(s)\nsoramech-pool: run log → /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\nsoramech-pool: run complete (2 task(s) in 1245 µs).\nsoramech-pool: outputs:\n  seed → world\n  greet → Hello, world!\n```\n\n## The JSONL transcript\n\nEvery run writes a JSON-Lines transcript to\n`<map-dir>/tmp/last-run.jsonl` (or\n`/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl` when the map directory has no\n`tmp/` symlink). One line per event, append-only as the run\nproceeds. The file is the authoritative record of what happened\n— the stderr summary is a quick glance; the transcript is the\naudit trail.\n\nDefault events (always emitted):\n\n| Event           | When |\n|-----------------|------|\n| `run_start`     | runner starts |\n| `task_submit`   | a box gets queued to fire |\n| `task_start`    | a worker picks it up |\n| `task_end`      | the box's function returns; carries duration_us, output_size |\n| `run_end`       | every task drained, no more queued |\n\nFor runtime graph mutations (issue 319 self-construction):\n\n| Event         | When |\n|---------------|------|\n| `box_create`  | `create_box` succeeds; records the new box's id + kind + lang + ref + fn |\n| `wire_add`    | `connect` succeeds; records the from→to wire |\n| `slot_alloc`  | a runtime-created box allocates an input slot |\n\nOpt-in verbosity, via env vars:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — adds `task_input` / `task_output`\n  events with the byte payloads (truncated to 4 KB per record).\n  Useful for inspecting what flowed where.\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` — adds the startup slot-layout\n  enumeration AND a per-push event (`push`) for every\n  dispatch-side wire push. The `push` event's `result` field\n  carries either `\"ok\"` or a short skip reason\n  (`\"input-slots-null\"`, `\"to-input-out-of-range\"`, etc.) — the\n  load-bearing diagnostic when a box fires but the value\n  doesn't seem to reach its consumer.\n\nSample (a runtime-create run with `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`):\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",\"ts\":...,\"slot_id\":0,\"cell_capacity\":4,...,\"box\":\"trigger\",\"port\":\"input\"}\n{\"event\":\"run_start\",\"ts\":...,\"map\":\"runtime-planner\",\"n_workers\":14}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"box_id\":\"trigger\",\"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",\"ts\":...,\"slot_id\":1,\"box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"port\":\"x\"}\n{\"event\":\"box_create\",\"ts\":...,\"box_id\":\"auto_00000000\",\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"lua\",...}\n{\"event\":\"wire_add\",\"ts\":...,\"from_box\":\"trigger\",\"to_box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"to_input\":\"x\"}\n{\"event\":\"push\",\"ts\":...,\"from_box\":\"trigger\",\"to_box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"slot_id\":1,\"result\":\"ok\"}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"duration_us\":418,\"output_size\":46}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":1,\"worker_idx\":11}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":1,\"duration_us\":78,\"output_size\":64}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\",\"ts\":...,\"duration_us\":3820,\"n_tasks\":2}\n```\n\nThe transcript is line-oriented and JSON-shaped, so any tool\nthat handles JSON Lines (jq, log aggregators, your own parser)\ningests it directly. The line-per-event shape also means a\ncrash mid-run leaves a recoverable file — the writer just stops\nappending; existing lines are intact.\n\n## The compile pipeline\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` bundles a map into a portable\nartifact:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map-dir>\n```\n\nThe artifact lives at `<map-dir>/compiled/` and contains:\n\n- `meta.json`, `boxes/`, `src/`, `data/` — verbatim copies of\n  the map source\n- `langs/<lang>/spec.so` — the language plugins the map needs\n- `bin/<box>.so` — pre-compiled C boxes (informational; the\n  runner still lazy-compiles from `src/` if a `.so` is missing)\n- `pool-runner` — a copy of `soramech-pool` (a real copy, not a\n  symlink, so the binary discovers its sibling `langs/` via\n  `/proc/self/exe`)\n- `manifest.json` — compile stats and provenance\n\nRun the compiled artifact like the source map:\n\n```bash\n./<map-dir>/compiled/pool-runner <map-dir>/compiled\n```\n\nThe artifact is self-contained — copy or symlink the directory\nanywhere on the same machine and it runs without the source\ntree, the project's `langs/`, or the project's build environment.\n\n## Reference-counted artifacts\n\nA compiled directory carries its own reference log (`.refs`).\nOther programs that hold onto a build of a map across time\n(long-running runners, sibling tools that opened the artifact\nyesterday) **acquire** a reference on startup and **release** on\nshutdown. The compile pipeline checks the log before rebuilding:\n\n- If `compiled/` doesn't exist → build there fresh.\n- If `compiled/` exists with zero live references → wipe and\n  rebuild in place (the destructive case).\n- If `compiled/` exists with **one or more** live references →\n  fork to the next `compiled.N` sibling. The original stays\n  intact for its holders.\n\nEach fork's manifest carries a `forked_from` field naming its\nparent generation, so the lineage is recoverable.\n\nHelper:\n\n```bash\n# acquire a reference (prints the assigned id to stdout)\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir>\n\n# release when you're done\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\n\n# count live references\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh count <compiled-dir>\n\n# inspect — JSON array with per-entry validity\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh list <compiled-dir>\n\n# garbage-collect dead entries (stale PIDs, missing marker files)\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh reap <compiled-dir>\n```\n\nThe back pointer is PID + `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 (start\ntime in clock ticks). PID alone isn't enough — PIDs recycle —\nso the start-time match is what distinguishes \"the original\nholder is still alive\" from \"a different process has the same\nPID now.\" An optional marker file path supplies a second\nliveness signal.\n\nThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable** by design:\na crashing holder doesn't get to release. The back pointer is\nwhat lets `list` and `reap` independently verify whether any\ngiven entry is still meaningful.\n\n## Parallelism\n\nThe runner's thread pool fires independent boxes on different\nworkers. Two boxes whose inputs both become ready at the same\nmoment will run concurrently — there's no global lock on the\ngraph.\n\nSame-box concurrent fires are gated. A box that has been\nspawned but not yet completed won't get spawned again until it\nfinishes (single-spawn invariant). The exception is iterator\nrouting and any box downstream of an iterator: those boxes are\nmarked multi-spawn, and the dispatch re-fires them while their\ninput slots have queued values to drain.\n\nCross-language wires are atomic at the value level. The slot\nstore carries values as native bytes (when both sides share a\nlanguage) or JSON (when the sides differ); the dispatch picks\nthe right format per-wire. Each consumer sees a consistent\nsnapshot of the value, never a partial one.\n\n## Quiescence\n\nThe runner exits when the work queue is empty AND every\nin-flight task has completed AND no boxes have queued values\nwaiting to fire. Long-running maps (e.g., the timer-box design\nin issue 251) prevent quiescence by re-arming after each fire —\nthe runner stays up until you Ctrl-C.\n\n## Running tests\n\n- `make test` — full ship-it suite: builds + runs the C unit\n  tests, then runs the integration fixtures.\n- `make quicktest` — cheap iteration loop: runs only the\n  already-built C unit binaries. Add `ARGS=009` to filter to\n  binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\nSee [`docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`](006-test-coverage-map.md)\nfor the test inventory.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-runtime.md"

    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# SoraMech — Runtime\n\nThis doc covers what happens when you run a map: how the runner\nloads the graph, fires boxes, threads values along wires, writes\nthe JSONL transcript, and tears down. Plus the compile pipeline\nand the reference-counted-artifact system that lets long-running\nprocesses hold onto a specific build of a map across rebuilds.\n\n## Running a map\n\n```bash\n./soramech-pool <map-dir>\n```\n\nThe runner reads `<map-dir>/meta.json` + `<map-dir>/boxes/*.json`,\nbuilds the in-memory graph, attaches the slot store (one slot\nper input port), starts a worker pool (one worker per CPU by\ndefault; override with `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`), and submits the\nentry boxes as initial tasks. Workers pick tasks off the pool\nqueue, run the box's spec function (Lua, C, or Bash), and push\nthe output along the producer's outgoing connections.\n\nWhen all consumers are satisfied and no tasks remain, the run\nhits quiescence and the runner exits. The stderr summary prints\neach box's most recent output.\n\n```\nsoramech-pool: 'hello' — 2 box(es), entry seed, 14 worker(s)\nsoramech-pool: run log → /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\nsoramech-pool: run complete (2 task(s) in 1245 µs).\nsoramech-pool: outputs:\n  seed → world\n  greet → Hello, world!\n```\n\n## The JSONL transcript\n\nEvery run writes a JSON-Lines transcript to\n`<map-dir>/tmp/last-run.jsonl` (or\n`/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl` when the map directory has no\n`tmp/` symlink). One line per event, append-only as the run\nproceeds. The file is the authoritative record of what happened\n— the stderr summary is a quick glance; the transcript is the\naudit trail.\n\nDefault events (always emitted):\n\n| Event           | When |\n|-----------------|------|\n| `run_start`     | runner starts |\n| `task_submit`   | a box gets queued to fire |\n| `task_start`    | a worker picks it up |\n| `task_end`      | the box's function returns; carries duration_us, output_size |\n| `run_end`       | every task drained, no more queued |\n\nFor runtime graph mutations (issue 319 self-construction):\n\n| Event         | When |\n|---------------|------|\n| `box_create`  | `create_box` succeeds; records the new box's id + kind + lang + ref + fn |\n| `wire_add`    | `connect` succeeds; records the from→to wire |\n| `slot_alloc`  | a runtime-created box allocates an input slot |\n\nOpt-in verbosity, via env vars:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — adds `task_input` / `task_output`\n  events with the byte payloads (truncated to 4 KB per record).\n  Useful for inspecting what flowed where.\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` — adds the startup slot-layout\n  enumeration AND a per-push event (`push`) for every\n  dispatch-side wire push. The `push` event's `result` field\n  carries either `\"ok\"` or a short skip reason\n  (`\"input-slots-null\"`, `\"to-input-out-of-range\"`, etc.) — the\n  load-bearing diagnostic when a box fires but the value\n  doesn't seem to reach its consumer.\n\nSample (a runtime-create run with `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`):\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",\"ts\":...,\"slot_id\":0,\"cell_capacity\":4,...,\"box\":\"trigger\",\"port\":\"input\"}\n{\"event\":\"run_start\",\"ts\":...,\"map\":\"runtime-planner\",\"n_workers\":14}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"box_id\":\"trigger\",\"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",\"ts\":...,\"slot_id\":1,\"box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"port\":\"x\"}\n{\"event\":\"box_create\",\"ts\":...,\"box_id\":\"auto_00000000\",\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"lua\",...}\n{\"event\":\"wire_add\",\"ts\":...,\"from_box\":\"trigger\",\"to_box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"to_input\":\"x\"}\n{\"event\":\"push\",\"ts\":...,\"from_box\":\"trigger\",\"to_box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"slot_id\":1,\"result\":\"ok\"}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"duration_us\":418,\"output_size\":46}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":1,\"worker_idx\":11}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":1,\"duration_us\":78,\"output_size\":64}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\",\"ts\":...,\"duration_us\":3820,\"n_tasks\":2}\n```\n\nThe transcript is line-oriented and JSON-shaped, so any tool\nthat handles JSON Lines (jq, log aggregators, your own parser)\ningests it directly. The line-per-event shape also means a\ncrash mid-run leaves a recoverable file — the writer just stops\nappending; existing lines are intact.\n\n## The compile pipeline\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` bundles a map into a portable\nartifact:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map-dir>\n```\n\nThe artifact lives at `<map-dir>/compiled/` and contains:\n\n- `meta.json`, `boxes/`, `src/`, `data/` — verbatim copies of\n  the map source\n- `langs/<lang>/spec.so` — the language plugins the map needs\n- `bin/<box>.so` — pre-compiled C boxes (informational; the\n  runner still lazy-compiles from `src/` if a `.so` is missing)\n- `pool-runner` — a copy of `soramech-pool` (a real copy, not a\n  symlink, so the binary discovers its sibling `langs/` via\n  `/proc/self/exe`)\n- `manifest.json` — compile stats and provenance\n\nRun the compiled artifact like the source map:\n\n```bash\n./<map-dir>/compiled/pool-runner <map-dir>/compiled\n```\n\nThe artifact is self-contained — copy or symlink the directory\nanywhere on the same machine and it runs without the source\ntree, the project's `langs/`, or the project's build environment.\n\n## Reference-counted artifacts\n\nA compiled directory carries its own reference log (`.refs`).\nOther programs that hold onto a build of a map across time\n(long-running runners, sibling tools that opened the artifact\nyesterday) **acquire** a reference on startup and **release** on\nshutdown. The compile pipeline checks the log before rebuilding:\n\n- If `compiled/` doesn't exist → build there fresh.\n- If `compiled/` exists with zero live references → wipe and\n  rebuild in place (the destructive case).\n- If `compiled/` exists with **one or more** live references →\n  fork to the next `compiled.N` sibling. The original stays\n  intact for its holders.\n\nEach fork's manifest carries a `forked_from` field naming its\nparent generation, so the lineage is recoverable.\n\nHelper:\n\n```bash\n# acquire a reference (prints the assigned id to stdout)\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir>\n\n# release when you're done\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\n\n# count live references\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh count <compiled-dir>\n\n# inspect — JSON array with per-entry validity\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh list <compiled-dir>\n\n# garbage-collect dead entries (stale PIDs, missing marker files)\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh reap <compiled-dir>\n```\n\nThe back pointer is PID + `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 (start\ntime in clock ticks). PID alone isn't enough — PIDs recycle —\nso the start-time match is what distinguishes \"the original\nholder is still alive\" from \"a different process has the same\nPID now.\" An optional marker file path supplies a second\nliveness signal.\n\nThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable** by design:\na crashing holder doesn't get to release. The back pointer is\nwhat lets `list` and `reap` independently verify whether any\ngiven entry is still meaningful.\n\n## Parallelism\n\nThe runner's thread pool fires independent boxes on different\nworkers. Two boxes whose inputs both become ready at the same\nmoment will run concurrently — there's no global lock on the\ngraph.\n\nSame-box concurrent fires are gated. A box that has been\nspawned but not yet completed won't get spawned again until it\nfinishes (single-spawn invariant). The exception is iterator\nrouting and any box downstream of an iterator: those boxes are\nmarked multi-spawn, and the dispatch re-fires them while their\ninput slots have queued values to drain.\n\nCross-language wires are atomic at the value level. The slot\nstore carries values as native bytes (when both sides share a\nlanguage) or JSON (when the sides differ); the dispatch picks\nthe right format per-wire. Each consumer sees a consistent\nsnapshot of the value, never a partial one.\n\n## Quiescence\n\nThe runner exits when the work queue is empty AND every\nin-flight task has completed AND no boxes have queued values\nwaiting to fire. Long-running maps (e.g., the timer-box design\nin issue 251) prevent quiescence by re-arming after each fire —\nthe runner stays up until you Ctrl-C.\n\n## Running tests\n\n- `make test` — full ship-it suite: builds + runs the C unit\n  tests, then runs the integration fixtures.\n- `make quicktest` — cheap iteration loop: runs only the\n  already-built C unit binaries. Add `ARGS=009` to filter to\n  binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\nSee [`docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`](006-test-coverage-map.md)\nfor the test inventory.\n",
    "type":"create",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-runtime.md"
  },

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Writing boxes\n\nThree languages ship with first-class support: Lua, C, and Bash.\nEach follows the same dataflow contract — a box function takes\ninput values, returns one output value — but the calling shape\ndiffers per language. This doc covers each language's\nquickstart plus the runtime self-construction API every spec\nexposes.\n\n## The contract, in plain english\n\nA box function receives values for each declared input port and\nmust produce exactly one output value. The output gets pushed to\nthe box's outgoing wires by the runtime — your function doesn't\npush or fan out anything itself; you just return.\n\nInput port names are declared on the box's JSON. Input order\nmatches the JSON's `inputs[]` order. The runtime delivers values\nin that order to your function.\n\n## Lua\n\n```lua\n-- src/greeter.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\n-- A box function: receives one string, returns one string.\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nWired up via the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greeter.lua\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a `lua_State` per worker, so consecutive\nfires of the same box reuse the same Lua state — module\nimports and closures persist across calls within a run.\n\n### Lua's runtime self-construction\n\nInside a Lua box's function, you can spawn new boxes and wire\nthem on the fly:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.planner(seed)\n    local id = soramech.create_box{\n        kind = \"call\",\n        lang = \"lua\",\n        ref  = \"src/worker.lua\",\n        fn   = \"process\",\n        inputs = { { name = \"x\", type = \"string\" } }\n    }\n    soramech.connect{\n        from_box = \"planner\",\n        to_box   = id,\n        to_input = \"x\"\n    }\n    return seed   -- the dispatch fans this to the new wire\nend\n```\n\nThe freshly-created box fires after the planner's return value\nhits its newly-attached connection. The new box's id (returned\nby `create_box`) is auto-generated unless you pass an explicit\n`id` field in the spec.\n\n### Lua values across wires\n\nThe Lua spec serialises return values to bytes for the wire.\nStrings pass through unchanged; numbers format as their JSON\nrepresentation; tables serialise to JSON; functions become a\n`$lang_opaque` sentinel that consumer Lua workers can\nreconstruct in their own state.\n\n## C\n\n```c\n// src/sqr.c\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\nint square(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n_inputs,\n           void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    (void)n_inputs; (void)out_capacity;\n    // First input is a string-encoded number.\n    char tmp[64];\n    int n = sizes[0] < 63 ? sizes[0] : 63;\n    memcpy(tmp, inputs[0], n);\n    tmp[n] = '\\0';\n    long x = strtol(tmp, NULL, 10);\n    long r = x * x;\n    int written = snprintf(out_buf, out_capacity, \"%ld\", r);\n    if (written < 0 || written >= out_capacity) return -1;\n    *out_size = written;\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"sqr\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/sqr.c\",\n  \"fn\":   \"square\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe C spec compiles `src/sqr.c` to `<map>/bin/sqr.so` at\ncompile-pipeline time (or to a `/tmp` artifact at first dispatch\nwhen no compile pipeline has run), then `dlopen`s it.\n\n### Compile hints per box\n\nTwo optional fields on the box JSON let you tune the build:\n\n```json\n{\n  ...\n  \"cflags\":    \"-O3 -DDEBUG_FLAG=1\",\n  \"link_libs\": [\"m\", \"crypto\"]\n}\n```\n\n`cflags` strings are split on whitespace and passed as\nindividual argv entries to gcc. `link_libs` produces `-l<name>`\nentries.\n\n### C's runtime self-construction\n\nC boxes can use the same `create_box` / `connect` primitives via\nthe bindings in `langs/c/soramech.h`:\n\n```c\n#include \"soramech.h\"\n\nint planner(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n            void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    char id_buf[SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE];\n    soramech_create_box(\n        \"{ \\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\", \\\"lang\\\":\\\"c\\\", \"\n        \"  \\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/worker.c\\\", \\\"fn\\\":\\\"process\\\",\"\n        \"  \\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}] }\",\n        id_buf, sizeof id_buf);\n    char conn[256];\n    snprintf(conn, sizeof conn,\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\",\n        id_buf);\n    soramech_connect(conn);\n    /* return the seed; the dispatch fans it to the new wire */\n    memcpy(out_buf, inputs[0], sizes[0]);\n    *out_size = sizes[0];\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n## Bash\n\n```bash\n# src/greet.sh\ngreet() {\n    local name=\"$1\"\n    echo \"Hello, $name!\"\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"bash\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greet.sh\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Bash spec runs a persistent helper bash process per worker\nand dispatches invocations over a socketpair using a small line\nprotocol. The function reads its inputs as positional args and\nwrites its output to stdout. Function source is loaded into the\nhelper's environment once per worker; subsequent invocations\nreuse the same helper.\n\nBash doesn't have a native dict, so the runtime\nself-construction API uses JSON-string arguments (same shape as\nthe C bindings):\n\n```bash\nplanner() {\n    local id=$(soramech_create_box \\\n        '{\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"bash\",\"ref\":\"src/worker.sh\",\n          \"fn\":\"process\",\"inputs\":[{\"name\":\"x\",\"type\":\"string\"}]}')\n    soramech_connect \\\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"$id\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\"\n    echo \"$1\"\n}\n```\n\n(The `soramech_create_box` and `soramech_connect` bash\nfunctions get pre-defined in every worker's helper environment\nby the spec.)\n\n## Choosing a language\n\n- **Lua** — easiest, fastest iteration. Source changes pick up\n  on the next worker init. Best for planner / glue logic and\n  anything where the box body is short.\n- **C** — fastest steady-state execution. Pays a compile on the\n  first dispatch (cached after); the compile pipeline can\n  precompile every C box so the runtime doesn't pay that cost.\n  Best for tight inner loops and anything you'd write in C\n  anyway.\n- **Bash** — for boxes that wrap external CLI tools. The\n  per-call overhead is real (process IPC), so don't use it for\n  hot inner work.\n\n## Cross-language wires\n\nA wire between two boxes of the same language carries values in\nthat language's native representation. A wire between two boxes\nof different languages crosses via JSON: the producer's spec\nserialises to JSON on the way out, the consumer's spec\ndeserialises on the way in. The dispatch handles the bookkeeping;\nyour box function never sees the boundary.\n\nThe slot store carries values dual-ring per wire — native and\nJSON cells side-by-side, with a per-cell tag picking which the\nconsumer reads. This is what makes a Lua function value sent on\na Lua → Lua wire survive as a callable function on the\nconsumer's side, while the same value sent on a Lua → C wire\narrives as a JSON sentinel the C side can pass back to Lua\nunchanged.\n\n## Adding a language\n\nIf you need a fourth language (Python, JavaScript, …), the\ncontract is the `lang_spec_t` struct in `langs/lang-spec.h`:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n    int  (*init)(int worker_idx);\n    int  (*invoke)(void *handle, ...);\n    void (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int  (*compile)(const char *src, const char *out, const box_t *box);\n    int  (*native_to_json)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    int  (*json_to_native)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    /* ... see the header for the full surface */\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\nShip a `langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` plus\nthe registration entrypoint, and the spec registry picks it up\non startup. The Lua / C / Bash specs are working references —\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is the most heavily-commented and the easiest\nstarting point.\n",

    "content":[{
        "content":"File created successfully at: /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/005-writing-boxes.md",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "structuredPatch":[],
    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# SoraMech — Writing boxes\n\nThree languages ship with first-class support: Lua, C, and Bash.\nEach follows the same dataflow contract — a box function takes\ninput values, returns one output value — but the calling shape\ndiffers per language. This doc covers each language's\nquickstart plus the runtime self-construction API every spec\nexposes.\n\n## The contract, in plain english\n\nA box function receives values for each declared input port and\nmust produce exactly one output value. The output gets pushed to\nthe box's outgoing wires by the runtime — your function doesn't\npush or fan out anything itself; you just return.\n\nInput port names are declared on the box's JSON. Input order\nmatches the JSON's `inputs[]` order. The runtime delivers values\nin that order to your function.\n\n## Lua\n\n```lua\n-- src/greeter.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\n-- A box function: receives one string, returns one string.\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nWired up via the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greeter.lua\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a `lua_State` per worker, so consecutive\nfires of the same box reuse the same Lua state — module\nimports and closures persist across calls within a run.\n\n### Lua's runtime self-construction\n\nInside a Lua box's function, you can spawn new boxes and wire\nthem on the fly:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.planner(seed)\n    local id = soramech.create_box{\n        kind = \"call\",\n        lang = \"lua\",\n        ref  = \"src/worker.lua\",\n        fn   = \"process\",\n        inputs = { { name = \"x\", type = \"string\" } }\n    }\n    soramech.connect{\n        from_box = \"planner\",\n        to_box   = id,\n        to_input = \"x\"\n    }\n    return seed   -- the dispatch fans this to the new wire\nend\n```\n\nThe freshly-created box fires after the planner's return value\nhits its newly-attached connection. The new box's id (returned\nby `create_box`) is auto-generated unless you pass an explicit\n`id` field in the spec.\n\n### Lua values across wires\n\nThe Lua spec serialises return values to bytes for the wire.\nStrings pass through unchanged; numbers format as their JSON\nrepresentation; tables serialise to JSON; functions become a\n`$lang_opaque` sentinel that consumer Lua workers can\nreconstruct in their own state.\n\n## C\n\n```c\n// src/sqr.c\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\nint square(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n_inputs,\n           void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    (void)n_inputs; (void)out_capacity;\n    // First input is a string-encoded number.\n    char tmp[64];\n    int n = sizes[0] < 63 ? sizes[0] : 63;\n    memcpy(tmp, inputs[0], n);\n    tmp[n] = '\\0';\n    long x = strtol(tmp, NULL, 10);\n    long r = x * x;\n    int written = snprintf(out_buf, out_capacity, \"%ld\", r);\n    if (written < 0 || written >= out_capacity) return -1;\n    *out_size = written;\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"sqr\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/sqr.c\",\n  \"fn\":   \"square\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe C spec compiles `src/sqr.c` to `<map>/bin/sqr.so` at\ncompile-pipeline time (or to a `/tmp` artifact at first dispatch\nwhen no compile pipeline has run), then `dlopen`s it.\n\n### Compile hints per box\n\nTwo optional fields on the box JSON let you tune the build:\n\n```json\n{\n  ...\n  \"cflags\":    \"-O3 -DDEBUG_FLAG=1\",\n  \"link_libs\": [\"m\", \"crypto\"]\n}\n```\n\n`cflags` strings are split on whitespace and passed as\nindividual argv entries to gcc. `link_libs` produces `-l<name>`\nentries.\n\n### C's runtime self-construction\n\nC boxes can use the same `create_box` / `connect` primitives via\nthe bindings in `langs/c/soramech.h`:\n\n```c\n#include \"soramech.h\"\n\nint planner(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n            void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    char id_buf[SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE];\n    soramech_create_box(\n        \"{ \\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\", \\\"lang\\\":\\\"c\\\", \"\n        \"  \\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/worker.c\\\", \\\"fn\\\":\\\"process\\\",\"\n        \"  \\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}] }\",\n        id_buf, sizeof id_buf);\n    char conn[256];\n    snprintf(conn, sizeof conn,\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\",\n        id_buf);\n    soramech_connect(conn);\n    /* return the seed; the dispatch fans it to the new wire */\n    memcpy(out_buf, inputs[0], sizes[0]);\n    *out_size = sizes[0];\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n## Bash\n\n```bash\n# src/greet.sh\ngreet() {\n    local name=\"$1\"\n    echo \"Hello, $name!\"\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"bash\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greet.sh\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Bash spec runs a persistent helper bash process per worker\nand dispatches invocations over a socketpair using a small line\nprotocol. The function reads its inputs as positional args and\nwrites its output to stdout. Function source is loaded into the\nhelper's environment once per worker; subsequent invocations\nreuse the same helper.\n\nBash doesn't have a native dict, so the runtime\nself-construction API uses JSON-string arguments (same shape as\nthe C bindings):\n\n```bash\nplanner() {\n    local id=$(soramech_create_box \\\n        '{\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"bash\",\"ref\":\"src/worker.sh\",\n          \"fn\":\"process\",\"inputs\":[{\"name\":\"x\",\"type\":\"string\"}]}')\n    soramech_connect \\\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"$id\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\"\n    echo \"$1\"\n}\n```\n\n(The `soramech_create_box` and `soramech_connect` bash\nfunctions get pre-defined in every worker's helper environment\nby the spec.)\n\n## Choosing a language\n\n- **Lua** — easiest, fastest iteration. Source changes pick up\n  on the next worker init. Best for planner / glue logic and\n  anything where the box body is short.\n- **C** — fastest steady-state execution. Pays a compile on the\n  first dispatch (cached after); the compile pipeline can\n  precompile every C box so the runtime doesn't pay that cost.\n  Best for tight inner loops and anything you'd write in C\n  anyway.\n- **Bash** — for boxes that wrap external CLI tools. The\n  per-call overhead is real (process IPC), so don't use it for\n  hot inner work.\n\n## Cross-language wires\n\nA wire between two boxes of the same language carries values in\nthat language's native representation. A wire between two boxes\nof different languages crosses via JSON: the producer's spec\nserialises to JSON on the way out, the consumer's spec\ndeserialises on the way in. The dispatch handles the bookkeeping;\nyour box function never sees the boundary.\n\nThe slot store carries values dual-ring per wire — native and\nJSON cells side-by-side, with a per-cell tag picking which the\nconsumer reads. This is what makes a Lua function value sent on\na Lua → Lua wire survive as a callable function on the\nconsumer's side, while the same value sent on a Lua → C wire\narrives as a JSON sentinel the C side can pass back to Lua\nunchanged.\n\n## Adding a language\n\nIf you need a fourth language (Python, JavaScript, …), the\ncontract is the `lang_spec_t` struct in `langs/lang-spec.h`:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n    int  (*init)(int worker_idx);\n    int  (*invoke)(void *handle, ...);\n    void (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int  (*compile)(const char *src, const char *out, const box_t *box);\n    int  (*native_to_json)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    int  (*json_to_native)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    /* ... see the header for the full surface */\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\nShip a `langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` plus\nthe registration entrypoint, and the spec registry picks it up\non startup. The Lua / C / Bash specs are working references —\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is the most heavily-commented and the easiest\nstarting point.\n",
    "type":"create",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/005-writing-boxes.md"
  },

}

For someone trying to build maps with\nSoraMech, that shape buries the practical answers under the\nnarrative of how the project got here.\n\nThis rewrite replaces the five user-facing docs with a guide\nordered around what a user actually needs to know:\n\n001-overview.md — what SoraMech is, when to reach for it, and\na quickstart that walks through installing, writing a tiny\ntwo-box map, and running it. The \"structural shell\" framing\nstays because it explains why box authors and the runtime have\ntheir respective scopes, but the apartment-building metaphor's\ndeeper philosophy collapses to a paragraph rather than the old\nlength.\n\n002-map-model.md — the box kinds (call / read / write / map /\ncreate_box / connect), the seven routing kinds (plain /\ncomparator including multi-band thresholds / iterator /\nrandomizer / weighted / distributor / nonlinearity), wire\nsemantics, input port states (wired / literal / optional), and\nencapsulation. Each routing kind gets a one-line \"what it does\"\nplus a minimal JSON example.\n\n003-editor.md — using the browser canvas: starting the server,\nthe three-region layout, working with boxes (create / move /\ninspect / delete), working with wires, the per-kind inspector\nsurface, the file browser, the map picker including the encap\nbutton, the compile button, keyboard shortcuts.\n\n004-runtime.md — running maps, the JSONL transcript (default\nevents plus the SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES / SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS opt-in\nverbosities), the compile pipeline that produces portable\nartifacts, the reference-counted-artifacts system that keeps\nlong-running holders safe across rebuilds, parallelism\nsemantics (single-spawn vs multi-spawn, cross-language wires),\nquiescence, and the test runners.\n\n005-writing-boxes.md — per-language quickstarts. Each language\ngets a tiny example box, the wiring JSON, the runtime\nself-construction API (Lua tables, C JSON-strings, Bash\nJSON-strings), and the slot-store native/JSON cross-language\ndetail. A \"choosing a language\" section helps a new user pick\nwhere to start; an \"adding a language\" section points at the\nlang_spec_t contract for anyone wanting a fourth language.\n\n006-test-coverage-map.md — kept as-is; already user-facing\nfrom the 232→docs conversion earlier in the session.\n\nThe old docs (001-architecture, 002-roadmap, 003-driver-system,\n004-ipc-and-threading, 005-language-specs) all delete.         "type":"text",
        "text":"Two commits land:\n\n```\nbe7ef4d docs: rewrite as a user-facing guide\nec274f9 tests/307: fix cflags test by giving each build its own .so path\n```\n\n**Docs now:**\n- `000-table-of-contents.md` — restructured with \"Start here\" reading order\n- `001-overview.md` — what SoraMech is + quickstart with a real two-box example\n- `002-map-model.md` — boxes, wires, all seven routing kinds, encapsulation\n- `003-editor.md` — canvas UI walkthrough + per-kind inspector + map picker + compile button\n- `004-runtime.md` — runtime mechanics, JSONL transcript, compile pipeline, refcounted artifacts, parallelism\n- `005-writing-boxes.md` — Lua / C / Bash quickstarts + runtime self-construction per language\n- `006-test-coverage-map.md` — kept as-is\n\n**307 fix:** distinct `.so` paths per build, stamped with both PID + timestamp; mirrors the production discipline of unique-per-box artifact paths. 179/179 unit, 33/33 integration, three consecutive 307 runs stable.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The 307 failure was a **test bug, not a runtime bug**. The C spec was correctly passing cflags through to gcc, the build was producing genuinely different `.so` files on disk, but `dlopen`'s same-path cache kept returning the previously-loaded mapping. Production code dodges this by deriving `.so` paths from box ids (each box gets a unique path), so the cache never returns wrong content. The test was the only place where two builds raced for one path. Fixing the test rather than the spec was the right call — the spec's behaviour is correct under the assumption production gives it, and changing the spec to defensively re-`dlopen` on every invoke would slow every dispatch for a hazard no real workflow hits.\n- The docs rewrite **deleted 5 files totalling ~1500 lines and replaced them with 5 files totalling ~750 lines**. The compression isn't because content was redundant — it's because the old docs were oriented around the project's development timeline (what each phase added, how features evolved). A user reading \"Phase 2 used driver scripts; Phase 3 uses language specs\" has to mentally compute \"so what do *I* use?\" The new docs answer that directly. The development-history information lives more honestly in the `issues/phase-*-progress.md` files where someone actually researching how the project got here would look.\n- The big risk in this kind of doc rewrite is **losing institutional context** — the \"structural shell\" / apartment-building framing was a load-bearing way to think about why the runtime is shaped the way it is. I preserved a compressed version of it in the overview rather than throwing it out, because it answers the \"why is X someone-else's-problem\" questions that any user eventually hits. The full philosophy can live in `notes/vision`, which the ToC still points at.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWorking tree leaves your inline 320 edits and the pre-existing untracked WIP (247, 249, 251, readme.md) where they were. Suite green: 179/179 unit + 33/33 integration."

```json
{
  "uuid":"a87f2556-00ac-4210-8649-70788d648d04",
  "type":"attachment",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-25T00:16:07.688Z",
  "parentUuid":"49e2e423-a3fb-4fc4-a976-c7f9d0133bac",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "slug":"goofy-noodling-torvalds",
  "userType":"external",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "attachment":{
    "filename":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/005-writing-boxes.md",
    "content":{
      "type":"text",
      "file":{
        "numLines":284,
        "startLine":1,
        "totalLines":284,
        "content":"# SoraMech — Writing boxes\n\nThree languages ship with first-class support: Lua, C, and Bash.\nEach follows the same dataflow contract — a box function takes\ninput values, returns one output value — but the calling shape\ndiffers per language. This doc covers each language's\nquickstart plus the runtime self-construction API every spec\nexposes.\n\n## The contract, in plain english\n\nA box function receives values for each declared input port and\nmust produce exactly one output value. The output gets pushed to\nthe box's outgoing wires by the runtime — your function doesn't\npush or fan out anything itself; you just return.\n\nInput port names are declared on the box's JSON. Input order\nmatches the JSON's `inputs[]` order. The runtime delivers values\nin that order to your function.\n\n## Lua\n\n```lua\n-- src/greeter.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\n-- A box function: receives one string, returns one string.\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nWired up via the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greeter.lua\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a `lua_State` per worker, so consecutive\nfires of the same box reuse the same Lua state — module\nimports and closures persist across calls within a run.\n\n### Lua's runtime self-construction\n\nInside a Lua box's function, you can spawn new boxes and wire\nthem on the fly:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.planner(seed)\n    local id = soramech.create_box{\n        kind = \"call\",\n        lang = \"lua\",\n        ref  = \"src/worker.lua\",\n        fn   = \"process\",\n        inputs = { { name = \"x\", type = \"string\" } }\n    }\n    soramech.connect{\n        from_box = \"planner\",\n        to_box   = id,\n        to_input = \"x\"\n    }\n    return seed   -- the dispatch fans this to the new wire\nend\n```\n\nThe freshly-created box fires after the planner's return value\nhits its newly-attached connection. The new box's id (returned\nby `create_box`) is auto-generated unless you pass an explicit\n`id` field in the spec.\n\n### Lua values across wires\n\nThe Lua spec serialises return values to bytes for the wire.\nStrings pass through unchanged; numbers format as their JSON\nrepresentation; tables serialise to JSON; functions become a\n`$lang_opaque` sentinel that consumer Lua workers can\nreconstruct in their own state.\n\n## C\n\n```c\n// src/sqr.c\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\nint square(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n_inputs,\n           void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    (void)n_inputs; (void)out_capacity;\n    // First input is a string-encoded number.\n    char tmp[64];\n    int n = sizes[0] < 63 ? sizes[0] : 63;\n    memcpy(tmp, inputs[0], n);\n    tmp[n] = '\\0';\n    long x = strtol(tmp, NULL, 10);\n    long r = x * x;\n    int written = snprintf(out_buf, out_capacity, \"%ld\", r);\n    if (written < 0 || written >= out_capacity) return -1;\n    *out_size = written;\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"sqr\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/sqr.c\",\n  \"fn\":   \"square\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe C spec compiles `src/sqr.c` to `<map>/bin/sqr.so` at\ncompile-pipeline time (or to a `/tmp` artifact at first dispatch\nwhen no compile pipeline has run), then `dlopen`s it.\n\n### Compile hints per box\n\nTwo optional fields on the box JSON let you tune the build:\n\n```json\n{\n  ...\n  \"cflags\":    \"-O3 -DDEBUG_FLAG=1\",\n  \"link_libs\": [\"m\", \"crypto\"]\n}\n```\n\n`cflags` strings are split on whitespace and passed as\nindividual argv entries to gcc. `link_libs` produces `-l<name>`\nentries.\n\n### C's runtime self-construction\n\nC boxes can use the same `create_box` / `connect` primitives via\nthe bindings in `langs/c/soramech.h`:\n\n```c\n#include \"soramech.h\"\n\nint planner(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n            void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    char id_buf[SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE];\n    soramech_create_box(\n        \"{ \\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\", \\\"lang\\\":\\\"c\\\", \"\n        \"  \\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/worker.c\\\", \\\"fn\\\":\\\"process\\\",\"\n        \"  \\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}] }\",\n        id_buf, sizeof id_buf);\n    char conn[256];\n    snprintf(conn, sizeof conn,\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\",\n        id_buf);\n    soramech_connect(conn);\n    /* return the seed; the dispatch fans it to the new wire */\n    memcpy(out_buf, inputs[0], sizes[0]);\n    *out_size = sizes[0];\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n## Bash\n\n```bash\n# src/greet.sh\ngreet() {\n    local name=\"$1\"\n    echo \"Hello, $name!\"\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"bash\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greet.sh\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Bash spec runs a persistent helper bash process per worker\nand dispatches invocations over a socketpair using a small line\nprotocol. The function reads its inputs as positional args and\nwrites its output to stdout. Function source is loaded into the\nhelper's environment once per worker; subsequent invocations\nreuse the same helper.\n\nBash doesn't have a native dict, so the runtime\nself-construction API uses JSON-string arguments (same shape as\nthe C bindings):\n\n```bash\nplanner() {\n    local id=$(soramech_create_box \\\n        '{\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"bash\",\"ref\":\"src/worker.sh\",\n          \"fn\":\"process\",\"inputs\":[{\"name\":\"x\",\"type\":\"string\"}]}')\n    soramech_connect \\\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"$id\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\"\n    echo \"$1\"\n}\n```\n\n(The `soramech_create_box` and `soramech_connect` bash\nfunctions get pre-defined in every worker's helper environment\nby the spec.)\n\n## Choosing a language\n\n- **Lua** — easiest, fastest iteration. Source changes pick up\n  on the next worker init. Best for planner / glue logic and\n  anything where the box body is short.\n- **C** — fastest steady-state execution. Pays a compile on the\n  first dispatch (cached after); the compile pipeline can\n  precompile every C box so the runtime doesn't pay that cost.\n  Best for tight inner loops and anything you'd write in C\n  anyway.\n- **Bash** — for boxes that wrap external CLI tools. The\n  per-call overhead is real (process IPC), so don't use it for\n  hot inner work.\n\n## Cross-language wires\n\nA wire between two boxes of the same language carries values in\nthat language's native representation. A wire between two boxes\nof different languages crosses via JSON: the producer's spec\nserialises to JSON on the way out, the consumer's spec\ndeserialises on the way in. The dispatch handles the bookkeeping;\nyour box function never sees the boundary.\n\nThe slot store carries values dual-ring per wire — native and\nJSON cells side-by-side, with a per-cell tag picking which the\nconsumer reads. This is what makes a Lua function value sent on\na Lua → Lua wire survive as a callable function on the\nconsumer's side, while the same value sent on a Lua → C wire\narrives as a JSON sentinel the C side can pass back to Lua\nunchanged.\n\n## Adding a language\n\nIf you need a fourth language (Python, JavaScript, …), the\ncontract is the `lang_spec_t` struct in `langs/lang-spec.h`:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n    int  (*init)(int worker_idx);\n    int  (*invoke)(void *handle, ...);\n    void (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int  (*compile)(const char *src, const char *out, const box_t *box);\n    int  (*native_to_json)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    int  (*json_to_native)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    /* ... see the header for the full surface */\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\nShip a `langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` plus\nthe registration entrypoint, and the spec registry picks it up\non startup. The Lua / C / Bash specs are working references —\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is the most heavily-commented and the easiest\nstarting point.\n",
        "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/005-writing-boxes.md"
      }
    },
    "type":"file",
    "displayPath":"docs/005-writing-boxes.md"
  },

}

The driver contract emits one JSON value, not an\n  array.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (210, complete): the old `branch`\n  box kind with named ports is removed. A box may carry a\n  `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `lt` / `eq` / `gt`.\n- **Iterator routing** (221): a box with `iterator_outputs` is a\n  pure routing primitive; the dispatch layer rotates through the\n  declared output names. A\nbox is the box it was born as.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\n**reconfigured** mid-run. A new configuration arrives as a\nJSON-shaped message inside the normal input stream, on any input\nport; the worker that's gathering inputs for the next fire\nencounters the reconfigure tag, applies it, and continues\ngathering under the new config before firing.\n\n## Concept\n\nEvery input slot grows a **third ring** alongside the native +\nJSON pair from issue 312. The third ring carries one kind of\nmessage only — a JSON object **exactly matching the box's own\nJSON schema**, the same shape a `boxes/<id>.json` file holds at\nload. Any input port can carry reconfigure messages; producers\npush to whichever port makes sense for their fan-in topology, and\nthe dispatch layer treats reconfigure cells as a peer to native\nand JSON cells.\n\nThe per-cell **ring-selector tag** (the bookkeeping that already\ntells the consumer \"this cell came in on the native ring, or the\nJSON ring\" — issue 312's dual-ring `which_ring` flag, extended\nthrough issue 318a's per-call ordering) grows a third value:\n**reconfigure**. When the consumer's input-gathering walks a port\nand sees the next cell tagged `reconfigure`, it doesn't push the\nbytes into an input buffer for the box function; it interprets\nthem as a re-parse of the box's own JSON.\n\n### The mixed-stream scenario\n\nImagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The\ndispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells\nin turn:\n\n```\nport_a → native value (popped, retained)\nport_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)\nport_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)\nport_c → RECONFIGURE\n```\n\n-- this actually will never happen. We only pop one value from each slot per box\n   execution cycle. We should do a quick audit to ensure the design reflects this,\n   updating current or re-opening closed issues if necessary.\n\nThe worker:\n\n1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.\n2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second\n   in worker-local stack buffers.\n3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails\n   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker\n   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;\n   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is\n   done.\n4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the\n   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory\n   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in\n   place.\n5. Releases the YARQ barrier.\n6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more\n   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port\n   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.\n7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained\n   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the\n   new config expects.\n\nThe fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure\nis a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering\nand the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.\n\n### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?\n\nThe retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the\nnew config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,\nremove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the\nretained values still map by port name. If the new config renames\na port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the\nrename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence\nrecorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port\nremoval mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get\ndropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.\n\n## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier\n\nA reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers\nfiring the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,\nno other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new\n`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.\n\nA spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing\ncaptures the intended shape exactly:\n\n> \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back\n> at the beginning of the queue please'\"\n\n**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this\nprimitive. Mechanism:\n\n- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).\n- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the\n  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker\n  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue\n  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.\n  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from\n  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately\n  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other\n  pending work runs first.\n- **Release**: atomic store of 0.\n\nThe cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each\ncontended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization\nprimitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than\n*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does\nbest (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the\nbox record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue\n319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own\ncopy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding\nthose into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't\ninterleave dangerously when both fire at once.\n\n-- workers who are just executing the box function should not claim the yarq.\n   they don't need it - they're just reading values, not mutating them.\n\n## Schema for the third-ring message\n\nA message on the third ring is a JSON object identical in shape\nto what `parse_box_file` parses today:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\":      \"my_box\",          // must match the target box\n    \"kind\":    \"call\",            // any kind, including a kind change\n    \"lang\":    \"lua\",\n    \"ref\":     \"lib/new_impl.lua\",\n    \"fn\":      \"new_handler\",\n    \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n    \"inputs\":  [\n        { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n        { \"name\": \"y\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true }\n    ],\n    \"connections\": [\n        { \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"value\" }\n    ]\n}\n```\n\nThe `id` field MUST match the target box (a safety check; mixed\nids hard-error). Every other field is the new state. Fields\nabsent get default treatment (same as a freshly-parsed box file).\nThe schema validator runs in full — a malformed reconfigure\ncan't half-apply.\n\n## Reconfigure semantics — what changes\n\n**Slice 1 supports every field comprehensively.** No \"cheap vs\nmedium vs expensive\" split; the same machinery that parses a box\nat load time runs against the in-memory reconfigure buffer and\napplies the result wholesale. Splitting the work into easy /\nhard tiers means coming back later to finish, and round-trips\nare where details get forgotten.\n\nThat means slice 1 has to handle, in one pass:\n\n- **Cheap-field rewrites** (lang / ref / fn / routing.kind /\n  routing.comparand / routing.weights / output_capacity /\n  returns / cflags / link_libs / headers) — pointer assignments\n  on the live record. The arena holds the strings; the rewrite\n  swaps pointers.\n- **Connections array swap** — uses the same copy-and-publish\n  pattern issue 319d established for `box_add_connection`,\n  except wholesale-replace instead of append. Old array goes to\n  the graph's stale list and is freed at graph_destroy.\n- **Input port shape changes** — adding, removing, renaming\n  ports. Triggers:\n  - Slot-store growth or shrink (issue 319b's slot growth in\n    the additive case; symmetric drain-and-release in the\n    removal case).\n  - Re-resolution of every producer's connection\n    `to_input_idx` against the new port names.\n  - Rebinding of retained pre-pop values via the old-name →\n    new-name correspondence (rename allowed; removal of a\n    retained port drops its values to the JSONL transcript).\n- **Kind changes** (BOX_CALL ↔ BOX_WRITE, etc.) — the dispatch\n  table is already keyed off kind; flipping the field flips\n  which branch runs next. BOX_MAP is the special case (would\n  re-trigger the encapsulation pass) — see open questions.\n\nA reconfigure that hands in an invalid spec is a hard error: the\nbox dies, the JSONL transcript records the failure with the\noffending JSON, the run terminates. No silent reject-and-continue\n— matches the project's \"errors over fallbacks\" rule.\n\n## How the third ring gets fed\n\nTwo complementary mechanisms, symmetric with issue 319's\ncreate_box / connect:\n\n1. **A `reconfigure` box kind** — one input port `spec` carries\n   the box-JSON, one field (or a second input port) names the\n   target box id and the target's input port to push the message\n   onto. On fire, the box pushes the reconfigure-tagged cell onto\n   the target slot's third ring.\n\n2. **A runtime API** —\n   `runtime_reconfigure(target_id, target_port, json, size, err)`\n   — that any language spec's invoke can call. Same shape as\n   `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` from issue 319d.\n\nA box can reconfigure itself by pushing onto its own third ring;\nthe next time the dispatch gathers inputs for this box, the\nreconfigure lands.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Extend the per-cell ring-selector tag** in\n   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. The dual-ring slot's `which_ring`\n   field grows a third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`).\n2. **Add the third ring to every input slot.** Same shape as the\n   JSON ring (variable-size cells, large-value-heap backed). Cell\n   capacity per slot is small (8? 16?) — reconfigures shouldn't\n   pile up faster than the box can apply them.\n3. **Add the YARQ barrier field** to `box_t`\n   (`src/010-graph-loader.h`). One `_Atomic int`;\n   acquire / release / yield-and-requeue helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.\n4. **Fold issue 319d's `box_add_connection` into YARQ.** Today\n   it has its own copy-and-publish atomic dance; sharing the\n   barrier keeps mutation paths from racing.\n5. **Refactor `parse_box_file`** so the JSON-parsing core\n   accepts an in-memory buffer (not just a file path). The\n   reconfigure path uses the same parser; one schema, one\n   validator, two entry points.\n6. **Add a `reconfigure_apply` function** in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c` that takes a parsed box record and\n   merges it into a live box, handling port-rename via name\n   correspondence, slot growth / shrink, connection array swap,\n   and producer re-resolution.\n7. **Teach the dispatch's input-gather loop** to peek the\n   ring-selector tag and, on `RING_RECONFIGURE`, acquire YARQ,\n   retain pre-popped values, apply the reconfigure, release\n   YARQ, then resume gathering under the new shape.\n8. **Implement the `reconfigure` box kind** in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c` and add parse-side support in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`.\n9. **Add `runtime_reconfigure`** to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.\n10. **JSONL event** for every reconfigure: full before / after\n    (or at least the changed fields), task id, worker id.\n    Reconfigures change behaviour mid-run; the audit log must\n    show them.\n11. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-routing/` — comparator routing\n      flipped to iterator routing mid-run; downstream\n      connections fire on the new branches.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn/` — same box, different\n      function on the same lang; output changes mid-stream.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape/` — input port\n      added (slot store growth) and renamed (producer\n      re-resolution); pre-popped retained values still land on\n      the right inputs.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind/` — BOX_CALL flipped to\n      BOX_WRITE; subsequent fires write to disk instead of\n      invoking a function.\n    - `tests/maps/320-yarq-contended/` — two reconfigure-feeders\n      race on the same target; both reconfigures land, neither\n      is lost, the box behaves correctly after both apply.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — ring-selector tag, third ring\n  storage per slot.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` refactor,\n  `reconfigure_apply`, YARQ field on box_t.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch input-gather changes, YARQ\n  acquire / release / yield-and-requeue, `reconfigure` box kind.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_reconfigure` entry\n  point for language specs.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` — reconfigure event emission.\n- `issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md` —\n  sister issue: create_box / connect are the additive\n  primitives, this is the mutative primitive.\n- `issues/318a-per-call-output-format-threads-to-push.md` and\n  `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the per-cell\n  ring-selector mechanism the third ring extends.\n- `issues/319b-slot-store-growth.md` — slot growth in the\n  additive port-add direction; symmetric shrink is new.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and reconfigure-pops.**\n  The mixed-stream scenario above shows reconfigure cells\n  interleaved with value cells on the same input port; the\n  consumer encounters them in producer-push order. Is that\n  ordering strict per port, or strict across all ports of the\n  box (so a reconfigure on port A blocks pops from port B until\n  it's applied)? The cleanest reading of \"ordered same as all\n  the other inputs\" is **strict per port**, with the consumer\n  applying reconfigures as it hits them. Across-port ordering\n  would need a per-box sequence number on every cell, which is\n  more bookkeeping than the user described.\n- **Slot growth and shrink for input port changes.** Issue 319b\n  defined slot growth in the create_box direction; this issue\n  extends it to the within-a-box direction (adding a new port\n  to an existing box). Shrink — releasing a slot when a port\n  goes away — is genuinely new and needs an issue of its own,\n  or rolled in here as part of slice 1.\n- **Port-rename correspondence.** When a reconfigure renames\n  port `x` to `y`, the rename is unambiguous if both\n  configurations declare the same number of ports in the same\n  position-order. When the port count or order changes too,\n  the correspondence isn't obvious — fall back to name match\n  (ports keeping their names get rebound by name; ports\n  whose names no longer exist get dropped). Worth documenting\n  precisely so the implementation behaves consistently.\n- **Recursive reconfigure / loop guard.** A box reconfigures\n  itself, the new config includes a producer that pushes\n  another reconfigure, etc. Cap per-box reconfigure depth per\n  run? Or trust the user and rely on integration tests to\n  surface infinite loops?\n- **BOX_MAP as a reconfigure target / source.** Changing a\n  BOX_CALL to a BOX_MAP would require re-running the\n  encapsulation pass on just this one box. The load-time pass\n  assumes single-pass flat-graph construction; running it\n  per-box at runtime is structurally awkward. Probably\n  out-of-scope unless a clear use case appears. Hard-error\n  the BOX_MAP transition in slice 1.\n- **Reconfigure visible in the compile artifact.** Issue 309's\n  compile pipeline bakes the box JSONs into the built program.\n  Reconfigure machinery is runtime-only by nature, but the\n  compile artifact needs to keep the YARQ barrier field, the\n  third ring per slot, and the in-memory parser path linked in\n  regardless. Probably means slice 1 ships always-on; the\n  per-box opt-out flag (`reconfigurable: false`) is a future\n  refinement if anyone needs the slot-store savings.\n- **JSONL event shape.** Full before/after JSON is the most\n  faithful audit trail; diff-only is smaller; \"just record\n  the new state\" loses the before. Default: full before/after\n  so the transcript is self-describing without cross-event\n  reasoning.\n- **Pre-popped retained values that don't fit the new schema.**\n  Reconfigure renames port `x` → `y` and adds port `z`; the\n  worker had already popped a value for `x` before hitting\n  the reconfigure cell. Rebind by name correspondence? If\n  the new config has no port `y` after a removal-rename\n  (effectively a delete), the retained value goes to the\n  JSONL transcript as a discard event and the box still fires\n  with whatever the new shape requires.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across two passes. The first\ndraft (now discarded) proposed a per-box config inbox treated as\na separate scheduling unit — i.e. reconfigure as its own task,\ndistinct from any fire. The user redirected to **per-port**\nplacement, with reconfigure cells riding the same ring-selector\ntag mechanism that already distinguishes native from JSON cells\non each port. The mixed-stream scenario described in the\n\"Concept\" section is the user's clarifying example.\n\nThe YARQ name landed in the same conversation. The user's\nphrasing:\n\n> \"yield and requeue works. yarq for short. YARQ what a weird\n> name!! I want to name my dog yarq. BARK BARK says yarq, haha\n> what a cute puppy ^_^\"\n\nSo: YARQ in the code, YARQ in the docs, and somewhere out there\na dog who answers to the same name. Both kinds of YARQ go where\nthe scheduler tells them — that's the joke and that's the\nmechanism.\n\nOn the YARQ requeue target (tail vs head of the pool queue),\nthe user's instruction was:\n\n> \"put it at the part of the queue that has the longest time\n> until running again. I think that's the end of the queue, but\n> you can decide. The tip of the tail maybe? snakes move\n> forward after all...\"\n\nEnd-of-queue (the \"tip of the tail\") is the chosen default.\nThe contended worker won't immediately re-collide with whoever\nis inside the barrier; the scheduler gets a chance to drain\nother pending work first.\n\nOn scoping, the user's direction was decisive:\n\n> \"they should all be configurable with the same interface,\n> so... don't split up the work in that way. Just do it\n> comprehensively the first time so we don't forget anything\n> on the return trip.\"\n\nSlice 1 covers every reconfigurable field — including the\nport-shape changes that require slot store growth / shrink and\nproducer re-resolution. No tiered \"cheap then medium then\nexpensive\" split; one comprehensive pass.\n",
