And the\n28\texisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\n29\tqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n30\t\n31\tThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\n32\twriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\n33\texercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n34\t\n35\t## Part A — Run output\n36\t\n37\t### Decoupling from the editor\n38\t\n39\tThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\n40\tdoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n41\t`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n42\t\n43\t- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n44\t  run did\n45\t- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n46\t  here) that pretty-prints the file\n47\t- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n48\t  written file against expected output\n49\t\n50\tDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\n51\tnot by editor rendering needs.\n52\t\n53\t### File format: JSON Lines\n54\t\n55\tThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\n56\tstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\n57\tJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\n58\tmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n59\t\n60\tEvent types:\n61\t\n62\t```jsonl\n63\t{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n64\t{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n65\t{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n66\t{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n67\t{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n68\t{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n69\t{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n70\t```\n71\t\n72\tJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\n73\tsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\n74\tline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n75\t(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n76\t\n77\tThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\n78\ttotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n79\t\n80\t### What gets logged\n81\t\n82\tPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\n83\tand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\n84\tproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\n85\tthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n86\t\n87\t- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n88\t  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n89\t- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n90\t\n91\tSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\n92\tverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\n93\tFor diagnosing memory issues.\n94\t\n95\t### Writer mechanism\n96\t\n97\tA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\n98\tfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\n99\tpush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\n100\twriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\n101\tfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\n102\tthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\n103\ton the producer side.\n104\t\n105\tAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\n106\tat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\n107\ttimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\n108\trunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n109\t\n110\tThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\n111\tbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\n112\tevent, including the final summary.\n113\t\n114\t### File location\n115\t\n116\t`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\n117\textension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n118\t\n119\tA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\n120\tUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n121\t\n122\t## Part B — Integration tests\n123\t\n124\t### Scope\n125\t\n126\tEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\n127\tEach test is:\n128\t\n129\t1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n130\t2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n131\t   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n132\t3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n133\t\n134\tThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n135\t`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\n136\tthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\n137\tdeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n138\t\n139\t### Test maps\n140\t\n141\tCoverage targets:\n142\t\n143\t| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n144\t|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n145\t| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n146\t| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n147\t| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n148\t| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n149\t| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n150\t| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n151\t| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n152\t| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n153\t| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n154\t| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n155\t| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n156\t\n157\tThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\n158\tto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\n159\texit code and stderr against expected.\n160\t\n161\t### Test driver\n162\t\n163\t```bash\n164\t# scripts/run-tests.sh\n165\tfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n166\t    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n167\t    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n168\t\n169\t    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n170\t    rc=$?\n171\t\n172\t    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n173\t        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n174\t        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n175\t    else\n176\t        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n177\t        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n178\t    fi\n179\tdone\n180\t```\n181\t\n182\t`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\n183\tslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\n184\tevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n185\t\n186\t### Phase 3 demo map\n187\t\n188\tA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\n189\tdemonstrates everything working together:\n190\t\n191\t- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n192\t- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n193\t- An iterator with a queued input\n194\t- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n195\t- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n196\t- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n197\t\n198\tRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\n199\tof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\n200\tvisible without a viewer utility.\n201\t\n202\tThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\n203\tphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n204\t\n205\t### Test infrastructure constraints\n206\t\n207\t- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n208\t- Tests must not depend on internet access\n209\t- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n210\t- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n211\t  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n212\t\n213\t## Open questions\n214\t\n215\t- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n216\t  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n217\t  default off.\n218\t- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n219\t  issues. Off by default.\n220\t- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n221\t  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n222\t  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n223\t- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n224\t  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n225\t  floats.\n226\t\n227\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n228\t\n229\t### Run output (Part A)\n230\t1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n231\t   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n232\t2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n233\t3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n234\t   appends a line to the output file.\n235\t4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n236\t   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n237\t   `run_end` after quiescence.\n238\t5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n239\t\n240\t### Tests (Part B)\n241\t6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n242\t7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n243\t8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n244\t   normalizer.\n245\t9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n246\t   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n247\t   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n248\t10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n249\t    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n250\t\n251\t## Relevant files\n252\t\n253\t- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n254\t- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n255\t- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n256\t- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n257\t- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n258\t- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n259\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n260\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n261\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n262\t- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n263\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n264\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n265\t  test design\n266\t\n267\t## Implementation log\n268\t\n269\t### JSON writer half — 2026-05-12\n270\t\n271\t`libs/json/json.c` had stub writer bodies left over from 314's\n272\tparser milestone; this pass filled them in. The writer maintains\n273\ta small depth stack (capped at 16) where each entry packs two\n274\tbooleans — \"next element is first\" and \"this level is an\n275\tobject.\" That's enough to handle comma placement and pick the\n276\tright close bracket. Overflow of the caller-supplied buffer is\n277\tsticky on `w->err`; `json_writer_finish` reports it.\n278\t\n279\tEight new writer tests in `tests/314-json-test.c` cover the\n280\tprimitives, escape encoding, empty and non-empty containers,\n281\tnesting depth, overflow detection, and a round-trip where the\n282\twriter emits an object that the parser then decodes and the test\n283\tverifies via the accessor API.\n284\t\n285\tStill ahead for 311: the JSONL event writer (a thin wrapper that\n286\tserializes `task_start` / `task_end` / `run_start` / `run_end`\n287\trecords using this writer), the MPSC ring buffer the worker\n288\tthreads push events into, and the dedicated writer thread that\n289\tdrains them.\n290\t\n291\t### Event emitters — 2026-05-12\n292\t\n293\t`src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` ships the per-event emit functions\n294\ton top of issue 314's bounded writer:\n295\t\n296\t- `jsonl_emit_run_start(w, ts, map, n_workers)`\n297\t- `jsonl_emit_task_submit(w, ts, task_id, box_id, worker_idx)`\n298\t- `jsonl_emit_task_start(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx)`\n299\t- `jsonl_emit_task_end(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx, duration_us, output_size)`\n300\t- `jsonl_emit_run_end(w, ts, duration_us, n_tasks)`\n301\t\n302\tEach emit serializes into a fixed 512-byte buffer, appends a\n303\tnewline, and writes to a `FILE *` under a per-writer mutex. The\n304\tMPSC ring + dedicated writer thread aren't there yet — the mutex\n305\tis a placeholder until dispatch is producing events fast enough\n306\tto justify the contention.\n307\t\n308\t`tests/013-jsonl-events-test.c` writes a full sequence, slurps\n309\tthe file back, and parses each line through 314's JSON parser to\n310\tverify the event shape. A concurrent-emit test runs 8 producer\n311\tthreads each emitting 200 events into the same writer and\n312\tverifies every line round-trips.\n313\t\n314\tStill ahead inside 311: slot-event opt-in\n315\t(`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`), inputs/outputs opt-in\n316\t(`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`), the MPSC ring + writer thread, and\n317\tthe integration-test harness map fixtures.\n318\t\n319\t### Multi-producer event queue + writer thread — 2026-05-12\n320\t\n321\t`src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` ships the producer-side queue and the\n322\tdedicated writer thread. Producers (worker threads + the main\n323\tthread) call `event_queue_run_start` / `task_submit` / `task_start`\n324\t/ `task_end` / `run_end`; each emit appends a small fixed-size\n325\tevent record under a brief mutex and signals a CV. The writer\n326\tthread sleeps on the CV, snapshots the queue head into a local\n327\tbatch under the lock, then drains the batch outside the lock —\n328\tJSON encoding + fwrite happen with zero producer contention.\n329\t\n330\tFour unit tests in `tests/014-event-queue-test.c` cover single\n331\tproducer / multi-thread burst (8 producers × 250 events each =\n332\t2000 lines, all round-trip through the JSON parser) / shutdown-\n333\tdrain / pending-count.\n334\t\n335\tThe dispatch action (issue 304) opt-in emits task_start and\n336\ttask_end events with monotonic-clock durations via the queue;\n337\tthe pool runner emits run_start and run_end. `soramech-pool`\n338\twrites to `map_dir/tmp/last-run.jsonl` when that directory\n339\texists, falling back to `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl`.\n340\t\n341\tWhat's still ahead inside 311:\n342\t- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n343\t  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n344\t  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n345\t- Opt-in slot events and per-task input/output dumps.\n346\t\n347\t### Integration test runner — 2026-05-12\n348\t\n349\t`scripts/run-tests.sh` runs every fixture map under `tests/maps/`\n350\tthrough `soramech-pool` and asserts the expected box-output\n351\tsubstrings show up in stderr. `make test` invokes the script\n352\tafter the unit tests so a full `make test` covers everything\n353\tfrom slot operations all the way through end-to-end Lua / C /\n354\tBash dispatch via JSONL logging.\n355\t\n356\tSix fixture checks at the moment:\n357\t- `calc`            — single Lua `add → 42`\n358\t- `hello`           — data → Lua, `greet → \"Hello, World!\"`\n359\t- `comparator`      — `high` fires, `low` / `mid` don't\n360\t- `iter-route`      — single-fire iterator picks `out_0` → `a`\n361\t- `pipeline`        — five-box multilang chain\n362\t- `pipeline file`   — verifies the file_write sink wrote\n363\t  `\"11!\"` to `/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt`\n364\t\n365\t### Runtime-mutation and per-push events — 2026-05-24\n366\t\n367\tThree new events extend the JSONL transcript to cover the\n368\truntime self-construction path from issue 319, which previously\n369\tleft no trace in the log even with `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`\n370\tbecause the events fire from inside a spec's invoke rather than\n371\tfrom the dispatch's task lifecycle.\n372\t\n373\t- **`box_create`** — fires from `runtime_create_box` after the\n374\t  new box is published into the graph.       "content":"# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)\n\n## Status\nin progress · JSONL writer, multi-producer event queue, dedicated\nwriter thread, optional value events (`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES`),\noptional slot events (`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS`), runtime-mutation\nevents (box_create / wire_add / runtime slot_alloc), per-push\nevents with skip-reason result field, the `scripts/run-tests.sh`\nintegration runner, and the phase-3 runtime-planner demo all\nshipped. The remaining open items are the lock-free MPSC ring\n(current mutex-based queue is a placeholder) and the JSONL\nnormaliser for diff-based fixture verification (current tests\nsubstring-match against stderr).\n\n## Current behavior\n\nPhase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-\nbox invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads\nit to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps\nin `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)\nthat the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor\nstill works.\n\nPhase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent\ninvocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,\nwritten from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 \"build a single\ntable at end of run\" approach does not survive that. And the\nexisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\nqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n\nThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\nwriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\nexercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n\n## Part A — Run output\n\n### Decoupling from the editor\n\nThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\ndoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n\n- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n  run did\n- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n  here) that pretty-prints the file\n- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n  written file against expected output\n\nDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\nnot by editor rendering needs.\n\n### File format: JSON Lines\n\nThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\nstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\nJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\nmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\nsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\nline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n\nThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\ntotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n\n### What gets logged\n\nPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\nand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\nproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\nthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n\nSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\nverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\nFor diagnosing memory issues.\n\n### Writer mechanism\n\nA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\nfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\npush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\nwriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\nfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\nthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\non the producer side.\n\nAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\nat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\ntimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\nrunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n\nThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\nbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\nevent, including the final summary.\n\n### File location\n\n`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\nextension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n\nA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\nUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n\n## Part B — Integration tests\n\n### Scope\n\nEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\nEach test is:\n\n1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n\nThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\nthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\ndeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n\n### Test maps\n\nCoverage targets:\n\n| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n\nThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\nto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\nexit code and stderr against expected.\n\n### Test driver\n\n```bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh\nfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n\n    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n    rc=$?\n\n    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n    else\n        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n    fi\ndone\n```\n\n`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\nslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\nevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n\n### Phase 3 demo map\n\nA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\ndemonstrates everything working together:\n\n- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n- An iterator with a queued input\n- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n\nRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\nof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\nvisible without a viewer utility.\n\nThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\nphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n\n### Test infrastructure constraints\n\n- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n- Tests must not depend on internet access\n- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n  default off.\n- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n  issues. Off by default.\n- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n  floats.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n### Run output (Part A)\n1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n   appends a line to the output file.\n4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n   `run_end` after quiescence.\n5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n\n### Tests (Part B)\n6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n   normalizer.\n9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n  test design\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### JSON writer half — 2026-05-12\n\n`libs/json/json.c` had stub writer bodies left over from 314's\nparser milestone; this pass filled them in. The writer maintains\na small depth stack (capped at 16) where each entry packs two\nbooleans — \"next element is first\" and \"this level is an\nobject.\" That's enough to handle comma placement and pick the\nright close bracket. Overflow of the caller-supplied buffer is\nsticky on `w->err`; `json_writer_finish` reports it.\n\nEight new writer tests in `tests/314-json-test.c` cover the\nprimitives, escape encoding, empty and non-empty containers,\nnesting depth, overflow detection, and a round-trip where the\nwriter emits an object that the parser then decodes and the test\nverifies via the accessor API.\n\nStill ahead for 311: the JSONL event writer (a thin wrapper that\nserializes `task_start` / `task_end` / `run_start` / `run_end`\nrecords using this writer), the MPSC ring buffer the worker\nthreads push events into, and the dedicated writer thread that\ndrains them.\n\n### Event emitters — 2026-05-12\n\n`src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` ships the per-event emit functions\non top of issue 314's bounded writer:\n\n- `jsonl_emit_run_start(w, ts, map, n_workers)`\n- `jsonl_emit_task_submit(w, ts, task_id, box_id, worker_idx)`\n- `jsonl_emit_task_start(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx)`\n- `jsonl_emit_task_end(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx, duration_us, output_size)`\n- `jsonl_emit_run_end(w, ts, duration_us, n_tasks)`\n\nEach emit serializes into a fixed 512-byte buffer, appends a\nnewline, and writes to a `FILE *` under a per-writer mutex. The\nMPSC ring + dedicated writer thread aren't there yet — the mutex\nis a placeholder until dispatch is producing events fast enough\nto justify the contention.\n\n`tests/013-jsonl-events-test.c` writes a full sequence, slurps\nthe file back, and parses each line through 314's JSON parser to\nverify the event shape. A concurrent-emit test runs 8 producer\nthreads each emitting 200 events into the same writer and\nverifies every line round-trips.\n\nStill ahead inside 311: slot-event opt-in\n(`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`), inputs/outputs opt-in\n(`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`), the MPSC ring + writer thread, and\nthe integration-test harness map fixtures.\n\n### Multi-producer event queue + writer thread — 2026-05-12\n\n`src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` ships the producer-side queue and the\ndedicated writer thread. Producers (worker threads + the main\nthread) call `event_queue_run_start` / `task_submit` / `task_start`\n/ `task_end` / `run_end`; each emit appends a small fixed-size\nevent record under a brief mutex and signals a CV. The writer\nthread sleeps on the CV, snapshots the queue head into a local\nbatch under the lock, then drains the batch outside the lock —\nJSON encoding + fwrite happen with zero producer contention.\n\nFour unit tests in `tests/014-event-queue-test.c` cover single\nproducer / multi-thread burst (8 producers × 250 events each =\n2000 lines, all round-trip through the JSON parser) / shutdown-\ndrain / pending-count.\n\nThe dispatch action (issue 304) opt-in emits task_start and\ntask_end events with monotonic-clock durations via the queue;\nthe pool runner emits run_start and run_end. `soramech-pool`\nwrites to `map_dir/tmp/last-run.jsonl` when that directory\nexists, falling back to `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl`.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- Opt-in slot events and per-task input/output dumps.\n\n### Integration test runner — 2026-05-12\n\n`scripts/run-tests.sh` runs every fixture map under `tests/maps/`\nthrough `soramech-pool` and asserts the expected box-output\nsubstrings show up in stderr. `make test` invokes the script\nafter the unit tests so a full `make test` covers everything\nfrom slot operations all the way through end-to-end Lua / C /\nBash dispatch via JSONL logging.\n\nSix fixture checks at the moment:\n- `calc`            — single Lua `add → 42`\n- `hello`           — data → Lua, `greet → \"Hello, World!\"`\n- `comparator`      — `high` fires, `low` / `mid` don't\n- `iter-route`      — single-fire iterator picks `out_0` → `a`\n- `pipeline`        — five-box multilang chain\n- `pipeline file`   — verifies the file_write sink wrote\n  `\"11!\"` to `/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt`\n\n### Runtime-mutation and per-push events — 2026-05-24\n\nThree new events extend the JSONL transcript to cover the\nruntime self-construction path from issue 319, which previously\nleft no trace in the log even with `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`\nbecause the events fire from inside a spec's invoke rather than\nfrom the dispatch's task lifecycle.\n\n- **`box_create`** — fires from `runtime_create_box` after the\n  new box is published into the graph. Records id, kind, lang,\n  ref, fn. Always emits when an event queue is open (rare and\n  load-bearing — no verbosity gate).\n- **`wire_add`** — fires from `runtime_connect` after the\n  connection is appended to the producer's array. Records\n  from_box, from_branch, to_box, to_input. Always emits.\n- **`slot_alloc`** (runtime variant) — fires from\n  `runtime_create_box`'s per-input-port slot allocation loop.\n  Same shape as the startup slot enumeration but for the\n  runtime path. Always emits.\n- **`push`** — fires from `push_one_connection` on every\n  attempt, with a `result` field carrying either `\"ok\"` or a\n  short skip reason (`no-to-box-idx`, `dst-null`,\n  `input-slots-null`, `to-input-out-of-range`, `push-failed`).\n  Opt-in via `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` — would be too noisy by\n  default. Crucial for diagnosing the latent visibility race\n  noted on 319's completed status: a `push` event with\n  `result=input-slots-null` is the immediately-recognisable\n  signature.\n\nThe runtime context that `dispatch_action` publishes via TLS\ngrew an `event_queue *` slot so the runtime builtins reach the\nsame writer the dispatch uses. The pool runner reads\n`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS` into a `ctx->log_slots` flag that gates\nboth the startup slot enumeration AND the per-push events —\none env var, one slot-level verbosity story.\n\nEnd-to-end check: running `319d-runtime-create` with\n`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` produces a transcript where the\nmutation timeline is fully visible — `task_start →\nslot_alloc → box_create → wire_add → push(result=ok) →\ntask_submit → task_end → task_start → task_end`. If the\nvisibility race resurfaces under some build layout, the push\nevent flips to `result=input-slots-null` and the diagnosis is\nin the log without a rebuild.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- JSONL normalizer for diff-based test verification (currently\n  the test harness uses substring matching against stderr).\n\n### Phase-3 demo — 2026-05-24\n\n`issues/completed/demos/phase-3-runtime-planner/` is the phase-3\ndeliverable: a Lua planner box receives a seed string and uses\n`soramech.create_box` + `soramech.connect` inside its invoke to\nspawn three downstream worker boxes mid-run (each running a\ndifferent transformation function from `src/worker.lua`), then\nfans the seed value into all three. The accompanying `run.sh`\nruns the map with `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES` and `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS`\non and extracts the story from the JSONL transcript: the seed\nvalue, the boxes that got created mid-run, the wires that got\nadded, each worker's distinct output, and a small statistics\nblock (tasks fired, runtime slots, runtime boxes, runtime wires,\ntotal duration).\n\nTop-level `demo.sh 3` invokes the demo's own `run.sh`, matching\nthe existing phase-1 pattern. The new demo proves end-to-end\nthat the C thread pool runner (301), the slot store (302), the\nLua spec (306), the dispatch (304), the runtime self-construction\nprimitives (319), and the JSONL transcript with the new\nruntime-mutation events all work together on a single map.\n",
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md"
    }

        "content":"1\t# 009-slot-store.c — public surface\n2\t\n3\tPer-input-port slot store. Allocated once at graph load; each box\n4\tinput port owns one slot, freed when the run ends. The dispatch\n5\tlayer reads and writes through this API; language specs never see\n6\tslot IDs (issue 303 keeps that boundary clean).\n7\t\n8\t## Lifecycle\n9\t\n10\t- `slot_store_t *slot_store_create(void)` — empty store; NULL on OOM.\n11\t- `void slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s)` — frees every slot.\n12\t\n13\t## Allocation\n14\t\n15\t- `slot_id_t slot_alloc(store, cell_capacity, n_cells, flags)`\n16\t  - Returns `SLOT_INVALID` on bad args / OOM.\n17\t  - Flags: `SLOT_FLAG_NONE`, `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED`, `SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER`.\n18\t  - `cell_capacity` and `n_cells` are ignored for atomic-counter slots.\n19\t\n20\t## Ring-buffer ops (push / peek / pop / has_value / fill_count)\n21\t\n22\t- `int slot_push(store, id, data, size, tag)` — 0 on success, -1 on\n23\t  full / wrong type / size too big.\n24\t- `int32_t slot_peek(store, id, buf, buf_size)` — returns the cell's\n25\t  filled_size on success; -1 on empty / wrong type / buf too small.\n26\t  Does not advance head. Used for 1-cell peek slots.\n27\t- `int32_t slot_pop(store, id, buf, buf_size)` — drains. Untagged\n28\t  pops head FIFO; tagged pops the lowest-tag filled cell.\n29\t- `int slot_has_value(store, id)` — 1 if a value is available.\n30\t- `int32_t slot_fill_count(store, id)` — number of filled cells.\n31\t\n32\t## Atomic-counter slot\n33\t\n34\t- `uint32_t slot_read_inc(store, id, mod)` — fetch-and-add. Returns\n35\t  the pre-increment counter value mod the supplied bound.\n36\t  `UINT32_MAX` on wrong type or `mod == 0`.\n37\t\n38\t## Thread safety\n39\t\n40\t- The atomic-counter slot uses `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`; no lock.\n41\t- Ring-buffer slots use a per-slot `atomic_flag` spinlock around\n42\t  header + cell mutations.\n43\t- The store itself is single-threaded for allocation (graph-load\n44\t  phase); after that, the slot array is read-only and per-slot\n45\t  operations run concurrently.\n46\t\n47\t## Variable-size payloads\n48\t\n49\tSlots allocated with `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` store payload bytes in\n50\tthe unified allocator (016) and keep only an opaque chunk handle in\n51\tthe cell. Push acquires a chunk (refcount 1, owned by the slot);\n52\tpop copies the bytes into the caller's buffer and drops the\n53\treference, returning the chunk to the allocator's free-lists with\n54\tan eager neighbor-merge. The reclamation test\n55\t(`tests/009-slot-store-test.c::large_value_reclamation`) is the\n56\tregression guard for the previous monotonic-growth path.\n57\t\n58\t`slot_store_large_value_bytes_in_use` exposes the allocator's\n59\t\"in use\" total for the regression test and for future telemetry.\n60\t\n61\t## What's NOT here (deferred)\n62\t\n63\t- Size-class free lists for the fixed-size cell arrays themselves —\n64\t  plain `malloc` per slot for now. Allocator-driven cell allocation\n65\t  is the next step in issue 302.\n66\t- Producer-declared output sizes are not yet piped through to\n67\t  `ua_create`, so the allocator starts with no pre-warmed classes\n68\t  and learns them by accretion. The number of bytes copied is min of\n *                   the cell's filled_size and buf_size.\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 if the slot is empty,\n * the buffer is too small, or the slot is the wrong type. The cell\n * remains filled and may be re-peeked by subsequent tasks (1-cell peek\n * mode). */\nint32_t       slot_peek(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                        void *buf, int32_t buf_size);\n\n/* Drain one cell from the slot.\n *\n *   buf, buf_size — destination.\n *\n * For untagged slots, returns the head cell and advances head FIFO.\n * For SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED slots, returns the cell with the lowest tag\n * among the filled cells and marks that cell empty (head advances as\n * front-of-ring cells empty).\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 on empty / wrong type\n * / buffer too small. */\nint32_t       slot_pop(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                       void *buf, int32_t buf_size);\n\n/* Dual-ring push: write `data` into the slot's native ring (issue 312)\n * and append the (NATIVE, idx) tuple to the ordering ring. The data\n * write and ordering write are atomic together — pops see them as a\n * pair or not at all.\n *\n * Only valid on SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING slots. On non-dual slots, aliases\n * to slot_push (the ordering ring isn't consulted; back-compat for\n * callers that want one entry point regardless of slot shape).\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 if the slot is full, arguments are\n * invalid, or the slot is the wrong type (e.g. ATOMIC_COUNTER). */\nint           slot_push_native(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                               const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag);\n\n/* Dual-ring push: write `data` into the slot's JSON ring and append\n * the (JSON, idx) tuple to the ordering ring. Atomicity is the same\n * as slot_push_native.\n *\n * Only valid on SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING slots. On non-dual slots returns\n * -1 — the caller has to use slot_push for the single-ring case.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on full / invalid / wrong type. */\nint           slot_push_json  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                               const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag);\n\n/* Dual-ring pop: read the next entry from the ordering ring,\n * then drain the indicated cell from the matching data ring.\n * `*out_which_ring` receives SLOT_RING_NATIVE or SLOT_RING_JSON.\n *\n * On non-dual slots, behaves like slot_pop and sets\n * `*out_which_ring = SLOT_RING_NATIVE`.\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 on empty / wrong\n * type / buffer too small. */\nint32_t       slot_pop_ordered(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                               void *buf, int32_t buf_size,\n                               int32_t *out_which_ring);\n\n/* Atomic read-and-increment on SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER slots.\n *\n *   mod — modulus for the returned value. Pass UINT32_MAX for \"no\n *         modulus\".\n *\n * Returns the pre-increment counter value mod the supplied bound.\n * Concurrent readers each get a distinct value (the underlying\n * counter is incremented atomically). Returns UINT32_MAX on type\n * mismatch — the dispatch layer is expected to call this op only\n * on slots it allocated with SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER. */\nuint32_t      slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n\n/* Check whether the slot has any filled cell available for read.\n * Used by the dispatch layer's spawn-on-input-ready rule (issue 304).\n *\n * Returns 1 if a value is available, 0 otherwise. Truncated at NUL or 4 KB. */\nvoid event_queue_task_input (event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                             int task_id, int port_index,\n                             const char *data, int size);\n\nvoid event_queue_task_output(event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                             int task_id, const char *data, int size);\n\n/* Slot allocator events (opt-in via SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1). Like\n * the value events, these bypass the queue and write directly so\n * the soramech-pool can emit them in a tight loop right after\n * graph_attach_runtime without inflating the queue with many\n * fixed-size records that all fire at the same instant. Issue 319\n * also emits one per slot when a runtime create_box allocates\n * input ports mid-run. */\nvoid event_queue_slot_alloc (event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                             int slot_id, int cell_capacity, int n_cells,\n                             const char *owner_box, const char *owner_port);\n\n/* Runtime graph mutation events (issue 319 / 248 self-construction).\n * Always emitted when an active queue is present — mutations are\n * rare enough that they don't need a verbosity gate. The trio\n * brackets every runtime-create + runtime-connect + per-push\n * fan-out so the JSONL transcript captures the full\n * mutate-then-dispatch timeline. The `result` field on push\n * carries either \"ok\" or a short skip reason — invaluable for\n * diagnosing visibility races where the new box's fields aren't\n * yet seen by the producer's fan-out (see 319's status note). */\nvoid event_queue_box_create (event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                             const char *box_id, const char *kind,\n                             const char *lang, const char *ref,\n                             const char *fn);\n\nvoid event_queue_wire_add   (event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                             const char *from_box, const char *from_branch,\n                             const char *to_box, const char *to_input);\n\n/* Per-push event (opt-in via SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1, since pushes\n * are slot-level activity). */\nvoid event_queue_push       (event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                             const char *from_box, const char *to_box,\n                             const char *to_input, int slot_id,\n                             int n_bytes, const char *result);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Inspection */\n/* Best-effort: returns the count of events currently queued\n * (between produce and drain). Mostly useful for diagnostics. */\nint event_queue_pending(const event_queue_t *q);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_EVENT_QUEUE_H */\n",

Drives the consumer's\n     * decoder choice on single-ring slots and seeds the\n     * `input_native[i]` flag that the spec's invoke consults.\n     *\n     * One bit per outgoing connection (not per output port — a\n     * single output may fan to consumers of different languages):\n     * true iff the consumer on the other end of that connection\n     * shares this box's language. When set, the producer pushes\n     * native bytes to the consumer slot's `ring_native`; when\n     * cleared, the producer calls `native_to_json` first and\n     * pushes JSON to `ring_json`. */\n    int           *input_edge_native;   /* n_inputs entries, or NULL              */\n    int           *output_edge_native;  /* n_connections entries, or NULL         */\n\n    /* 244 per-port read-box predecessor lists.\n     *\n     * A consumer's input port may be fed by one or more BOX_READ\n     * value sources. Under the pull-on-demand model these don't push\n     * at startup; instead, when the consumer fires and finds the\n     * slot empty, the dispatch layer pulls the next read box's\n     * cached value into the input buffer directly. With more than\n     * one predecessor on the same port the dispatch rotates via the\n     * counter slot (atomic increment, mod count).\n     *\n     * Allocated by graph_load: n_inputs entries each; entries with\n     * zero read predecessors hold NULL / 0 / -1. Freed by\n     * graph_destroy. */\n    int           *n_read_predecessors;    /* n_inputs entries     */\n    int          **read_predecessor_ids;   /* per-port box-index lists */\n    int           *read_pred_counter_slot; /* per-port; -1 unless >1 preds */\n} box_t;\n\n/* Slot mode constants used by box_t.input_slot_modes[]. */\n#define SLOT_MODE_PEEK 0\n#define SLOT_MODE_POP  1\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Graph */\ntypedef struct graph graph_t;\n\n/* Read a map directory and build the graph. Returns NULL on any\n * failure and sets *err to a malloc'd \"<file>:<line>: <message>\"\n * diagnostic. The caller frees *err. */\ngraph_t *graph_load(const char *map_dir, char **err);\n\n/* Free the graph and every byte it owns.           "old_string":"### The mixed-stream scenario\n\nImagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The\ndispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells\nin turn:\n\n```\nport_a → native value (popped, retained)\nport_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)\nport_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)\nport_c → RECONFIGURE\n```\n\n-- this actually will never happen. We only pop one value from each slot per box\n   execution cycle. We should do a quick audit to ensure the design reflects this,\n   updating current or re-opening closed issues if necessary.\n\nThe worker:\n\n1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.\n2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second\n   in worker-local stack buffers.\n3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails\n   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker\n   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;\n   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is\n   done.\n4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the\n   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory\n   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in\n   place.\n5. Releases the YARQ barrier.\n6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more\n   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port\n   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.\n7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained\n   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the\n   new config expects.\n\nThe fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure\nis a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering\nand the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.\n\n### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?\n\nThe retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the\nnew config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,\nremove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the\nretained values still map by port name. If the new config renames\na port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the\nrename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence\nrecorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port\nremoval mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get\ndropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"### The pre-gather scenario (post-audit)\n\nThe audit confirmed it: `read_inputs` in `src/012-dispatch.c`\nwalks each input port exactly once and does exactly one\npeek / pop per port per fire (line 459: `for (int i = 0; i <\nb->n_inputs; i++)`). There is no \"second pop on the same port\nin one fire\" — the original mixed-stream scenario was wrong, and\nthis section is the corrected design.\n\nBecause each fire consumes at most one cell per port, a\nreconfigure cell on any port's third ring will be observed at\nmost once per fire of the target box. The cleanest place to\nobserve it is **before any value-pop**: at the top of\n`read_inputs`, walk every input port once and check the third\nring's `slot_has_value` / peek. If any port has a reconfigure\nqueued, apply it (under YARQ) before any value cells are popped.\nThen drop into the regular gather loop under whatever shape\nexists after.\n\nThis means:\n\n1. The worker enters `read_inputs` for box B.\n2. **Pre-gather sweep**: for each port `i`, check the third ring.\n   For every port with a queued reconfigure:\n   - Try CAS-acquire YARQ. On fail, yield-and-requeue (see\n     below) and exit.\n   - On success, pop the reconfigure cell, run the JSON through\n     the same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the\n     in-memory buffer instead of a path), and rewrite the box\n     record in place via `reconfigure_apply`.\n   - Release YARQ.\n3. **Gather**: walk each input port (under the now-possibly-new\n   shape) and pop / peek values as usual.\n4. Fire the box under the now-current config.\n\nThe \"what about pre-popped values\" question dissolves: nothing is\npopped before reconfigures are applied, so there's nothing to\nretain or rebind. Port renames / additions / removals between\nreconfigure and gather are uneventful because the value-pop loop\nruns against whatever `box->inputs[]` / `box->input_slot_ids[]`\nthe reconfigured box now exposes.\n\n### What about reconfigures that arrive mid-gather?\n\nIf worker A starts gather (post-sweep), and worker B pushes a\nnew reconfigure cell while A is mid-value-pop, A doesn't notice\n— the sweep has already run. The reconfigure waits on the third\nring; the **next** fire of the box picks it up in its pre-gather\nsweep. This is fine: gathered values were collected under the\nshape A observed, and the box function runs under that same\nshape. The new reconfigure simply lands one fire later than\nstrictly possible. We trade tightness for simplicity, and the\ntrade is good because pre-gather application removes all the\nin-flight-snapshot bookkeeping.",

If a future slice allows port","-removal mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get","-dropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.","-"," ## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier"," "," A reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers"],
        "oldStart":46,

      }],
    "oldString":"### The mixed-stream scenario\n\nImagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The\ndispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells\nin turn:\n\n```\nport_a → native value (popped, retained)\nport_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)\nport_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)\nport_c → RECONFIGURE\n```\n\n-- this actually will never happen. We only pop one value from each slot per box\n   execution cycle. We should do a quick audit to ensure the design reflects this,\n   updating current or re-opening closed issues if necessary.\n\nThe worker:\n\n1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.\n2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second\n   in worker-local stack buffers.\n3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails\n   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker\n   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;\n   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is\n   done.\n4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the\n   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory\n   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in\n   place.\n5. Releases the YARQ barrier.\n6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more\n   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port\n   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.\n7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained\n   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the\n   new config expects.\n\nThe fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure\nis a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering\nand the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.\n\n### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?\n\nThe retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the\nnew config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,\nremove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the\nretained values still map by port name. If the new config renames\na port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the\nrename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence\nrecorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port\nremoval mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get\ndropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.",
    "newString":"### The pre-gather scenario (post-audit)\n\nThe audit confirmed it: `read_inputs` in `src/012-dispatch.c`\nwalks each input port exactly once and does exactly one\npeek / pop per port per fire (line 459: `for (int i = 0; i <\nb->n_inputs; i++)`). There is no \"second pop on the same port\nin one fire\" — the original mixed-stream scenario was wrong, and\nthis section is the corrected design.\n\nBecause each fire consumes at most one cell per port, a\nreconfigure cell on any port's third ring will be observed at\nmost once per fire of the target box. The cleanest place to\nobserve it is **before any value-pop**: at the top of\n`read_inputs`, walk every input port once and check the third\nring's `slot_has_value` / peek. If any port has a reconfigure\nqueued, apply it (under YARQ) before any value cells are popped.\nThen drop into the regular gather loop under whatever shape\nexists after.\n\nThis means:\n\n1. The worker enters `read_inputs` for box B.\n2. **Pre-gather sweep**: for each port `i`, check the third ring.\n   For every port with a queued reconfigure:\n   - Try CAS-acquire YARQ. On fail, yield-and-requeue (see\n     below) and exit.\n   - On success, pop the reconfigure cell, run the JSON through\n     the same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the\n     in-memory buffer instead of a path), and rewrite the box\n     record in place via `reconfigure_apply`.\n   - Release YARQ.\n3. **Gather**: walk each input port (under the now-possibly-new\n   shape) and pop / peek values as usual.\n4. Fire the box under the now-current config.\n\nThe \"what about pre-popped values\" question dissolves: nothing is\npopped before reconfigures are applied, so there's nothing to\nretain or rebind. Port renames / additions / removals between\nreconfigure and gather are uneventful because the value-pop loop\nruns against whatever `box->inputs[]` / `box->input_slot_ids[]`\nthe reconfigured box now exposes.\n\n### What about reconfigures that arrive mid-gather?\n\nIf worker A starts gather (post-sweep), and worker B pushes a\nnew reconfigure cell while A is mid-value-pop, A doesn't notice\n— the sweep has already run. The reconfigure waits on the third\nring; the **next** fire of the box picks it up in its pre-gather\nsweep. This is fine: gathered values were collected under the\nshape A observed, and the box function runs under that same\nshape. The new reconfigure simply lands one fire later than\nstrictly possible. We trade tightness for simplicity, and the\ntrade is good because pre-gather application removes all the\nin-flight-snapshot bookkeeping.",

          "old_string":"The YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the\nbox record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue\n319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own\ncopy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding\nthose into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't\ninterleave dangerously when both fire at once.\n\n-- workers who are just executing the box function should not claim the yarq.\n   they don't need it - they're just reading values, not mutating them.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"The YARQ barrier is acquired by **every path that MUTATES the\nbox record** — reconfigure_apply and runtime_connect (issue\n319d's wire attachment, which already does its own copy-and-\npublish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding those\ninto the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't\ninterleave dangerously when both fire at once.\n\n**Workers that only READ the box record (input-gather + box\nfunction invocation) DO NOT acquire YARQ.** They're not mutating\nanything; making them block on the mutator path would burn\nworker time for no consistency win. They read the box's mutable\nfields through the same atomic-load patterns issue 319d already\nuses for `connections` / `n_connections`.\n\n### Reader consistency under mutation — design knob\n\nToday, `n_connections` and `connections` are an `_Atomic` pair\nwith a \"pointer first, count second\" publish order so a reader\ndoing \"count first, pointer second\" sees either the old pair or\nthe new pair. That pattern relies on the connections array being\nappend-only — the new array's first `old_n` entries are\nidentical to the old array.\n\nReconfigure can SHRINK or REORDER the inputs array, so the same\ntrick doesn't work for `inputs[]` / `input_slot_ids[]` /\n`input_slot_modes[]` / `input_edge_native[]` / `n_inputs`.\nThree viable shapes:\n\n- **A — bundle into one atomic-swap struct**. Allocate an\n  `input_config_t` containing every per-port array + n_inputs;\n  reconfigure_apply allocates a new config and atomic-stores the\n  pointer; readers do ONE atomic load and use the snapshot.\n  Clean and contention-free, but restructures box_t.\n\n- **B — generation counter retry**. Add `_Atomic uint32_t\n  inputs_gen`. Reader reads gen, reads arrays, reads gen again;\n  on mismatch, retry. Less restructuring; small overhead per\n  read; the retry case is rare. Doesn't capture the \"snapshot\n  is internally consistent\" property as strongly as A — readers\n  rely on retry to catch torn reads.\n\n- **C — workers DO acquire YARQ for reads**. Simplest mechanism\n  but contradicts the user's stated preference and adds a CAS to\n  every fire.\n\nThis is a real fork in the road; the rest of the design\nproceeds the same way for any of the three. Defer the pick until\nthe user weighs in.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/320-box-reconfigure-via-third-input-ring.md"

    "id":"msg_01EwpaXk7UgjkNXALWrqy1Us",
    "role":"assistant",
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- The **one-pop-per-cycle invariant** has bigger consequences than just \"the issue's mixed-stream example was wrong.\" It collapses the whole design: a worker can't be mid-gather and discover a reconfigure on a later port, because each cycle visits each port exactly once with no re-entry. That means reconfigure can be applied as a **pre-gather sweep** with no retained values, no name-correspondence rebind, and no two-phase commit on the inputs array. The original design was twenty-step; the audited design is three-step.\n- **YARQ is a mutator-side primitive only.** Workers reading the box record don't take it. The clean reading of the user's note is: YARQ protects against two mutators racing each other (reconfigure vs. reconfigure, or reconfigure vs. runtime_connect). Readers get cheap atomic loads. This is exactly the asymmetry that RCU-style structures lean on — many readers, occasional writers, writers serialise themselves but never block readers.\n- **Reader consistency is the real design fork.** Today's `connections` array is append-only, so the publish order \"pointer first, count second\" + reader order \"count first, pointer second\" guarantees a safe snapshot. Reconfigure breaks append-only — inputs can shrink, rename, reorder. The three options I surfaced (atomic-swap bundle / generation counter retry / readers take YARQ) trade off restructure depth against per-read cost. I've left this open in the issue file because it's exactly the kind of decision that wants user input rather than my guess.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nAudit's now reflected in the issue file. Two design decisions for you before any code lands:\n\n**1. Where to start — 311 or 320?**\n311's two leftovers (MPSC ring + JSONL normaliser) are small, self-contained, and would benefit 320 (because 320 adds at least one new event type). 320 is the big one. My recommendation: 311's leftovers first as warm-up + infrastructure, then 320. Tell me if you'd rather flip it.\n\n**2. Reader-consistency shape for 320** — three options I sketched in the issue's new \"Reader consistency under mutation — design knob\" subsection:\n\n- **A. Atomic-swap bundle struct** — clean, contention-free, restructures box_t. Cleanest snapshot semantics.\n- **B. Generation-counter retry** — minimal restructure, small read overhead, retries are rare.\n- **C. Workers acquire YARQ on reads** — simplest mechanically, but contradicts your \"workers don't claim YARQ\" note.\n\nI'd rank these A > B > C. A matches the existing copy-and-publish discipline (just one level up — bundle the whole input shape, not just the connections array), and the per-read cost is one atomic load. Your call?\n\n● **Learn by Doing**\n\n**Context:** This is the foundational design decision for 320 — every other piece of the implementation depends on the reader-consistency shape. A is what I'd pick, but the choice has tradeoffs you might weigh differently (e.g., you might value keeping box_t's current layout flat over the cleanest snapshot semantics; or you might find generation counters more familiar from other systems). Whichever option you pick, the implementation pattern propagates everywhere else: `reconfigure_apply` lives or dies by it, the dispatch's pre-gather sweep code reads it, and runtime_connect's existing copy-and-publish either folds in (A) or stays separate (B / C).\n\n**Your Task:** Reply with which of A / B / C to use, and any rationale you want recorded in the issue file. I'll capture your reasoning verbatim in 320's \"Reader consistency under mutation\" subsection so the design history shows why the shape was chosen — both for future-you and for anyone reading the issue cold.\n\n**Guidance:** If you want a fourth option that's not on the list, propose it; the three I listed are the ones I could see, but the design space isn't closed. If you'd rather I just pick and proceed, say so. And on question 1 (311 leftovers before 320, or 320 first), your call there too — either order works."
      }],

  },

        "content":"1\t/* src/014-event-queue.c — multi-producer event queue with a\n2\t * dedicated writer thread.\n3\t *\n4\t * Design: singly-linked queue under one mutex; one CV the writer\n5\t * thread sleeps on when the queue is empty. Producers lock just\n6\t * long enough to append a node and signal the CV. The writer\n7\t * thread snapshots `head` (atomically swaps it with NULL) under\n8\t * the lock, then drains the snapshot outside the lock — so the\n9\t * serialization + fwrite work happens with zero producer\n10\t * contention.\n11\t *\n12\t * The architecture doc's MPSC ring with Vyukov-style sequence\n13\t * numbers is the next refinement once profiling shows the brief\n14\t * append-mutex contention is the bottleneck. The shape of the\n15\t * API stays the same.\n16\t *\n17\t * Designed in issue 311.\n18\t */\n19\t\n20\t#include \"014-event-queue.h\"\n21\t#include \"013-jsonl-events.h\"\n22\t\n23\t#include <pthread.h>\n24\t#include <stdatomic.h>\n25\t#include <stdio.h>\n26\t#include <stdlib.h>\n27\t#include <string.h>\n28\t\n29\t/* {{{ Event record */\n30\ttypedef enum {\n31\t    EV_RUN_START,\n32\t    EV_TASK_SUBMIT,\n33\t    EV_TASK_START,\n34\t    EV_TASK_END,\n35\t    EV_RUN_END,\n36\t} event_kind_t;\n37\t\n38\t#define MAP_BUF_SZ    128\n39\t#define BOX_ID_BUF_SZ 64\n40\t\n41\ttypedef struct event_node {\n42\t    struct event_node *next;\n43\t    event_kind_t       kind;\n44\t    double             ts;\n45\t    union {\n46\t        struct {\n47\t            char map[MAP_BUF_SZ];\n48\t            int  n_workers;\n49\t        } run_start;\n50\t\n51\t        struct {\n52\t            int  task_id;\n53\t            char box_id[BOX_ID_BUF_SZ];\n54\t            int  worker_idx;\n55\t        } task_submit;\n56\t\n57\t        struct {\n58\t            int task_id;\n59\t            int worker_idx;\n60\t        } task_start;\n61\t\n62\t        struct {\n63\t            int  task_id;\n64\t            int  worker_idx;\n65\t            long duration_us;\n66\t            int  output_size;\n67\t        } task_end;\n68\t\n69\t        struct {\n70\t            long duration_us;\n71\t            int  n_tasks;\n72\t        } run_end;\n73\t    } u;\n74\t} event_node_t;\n75\t/* }}} */\n76\t\n77\t/* {{{ Queue struct */\n78\tstruct event_queue {\n79\t    pthread_mutex_t  mtx;\n80\t    pthread_cond_t   cv;\n81\t    event_node_t    *head;\n82\t    event_node_t    *tail;\n83\t    _Atomic int      shutdown;\n84\t\n85\t    pthread_t        writer_thread;\n86\t    jsonl_writer_t  *writer;\n87\t\n88\t    _Atomic int      pending;\n89\t};\n90\t/* }}} */\n91\t\n92\t/* {{{ copy_str_bounded() — strncpy + always-NUL-terminate */\n93\tstatic void copy_str_bounded(char *dst, const char *src, size_t cap)\n94\t{\n95\t    if (cap == 0) return;\n96\t    if (!src) { dst[0] = '\\0'; return; }\n97\t    size_t n = strlen(src);\n98\t    if (n >= cap) n = cap - 1;\n99\t    memcpy(dst, src, n);\n100\t    dst[n] = '\\0';\n101\t}\n102\t/* }}} */\n103\t\n104\t/* {{{ enqueue() — append a node, signal the writer */\n105\tstatic void enqueue(event_queue_t *q, event_node_t *n)\n106\t{\n107\t    n->next = NULL;\n108\t    pthread_mutex_lock(&q->mtx);\n109\t    if (q->tail) q->tail->next = n;\n110\t    else         q->head       = n;\n111\t    q->tail = n;\n112\t Producers lock just\n * long enough to append a node and signal the CV. The writer\n * thread snapshots `head` (atomically swaps it with NULL) under\n * the lock, then drains the snapshot outside the lock — so the\n * serialization + fwrite work happens with zero producer\n * contention.\n *\n * The architecture doc's MPSC ring with Vyukov-style sequence\n * numbers is the next refinement once profiling shows the brief\n * append-mutex contention is the bottleneck. The shape of the\n * API stays the same.\n *\n * Designed in issue 311.\n */\n\n#include \"014-event-queue.h\"\n#include \"013-jsonl-events.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include *head;\n    event_node_t    *tail;\n    _Atomic int      shutdown;\n\n    pthread_t        writer_thread;\n    jsonl_writer_t  *writer;\n\n    _Atomic int      pending;\n};\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ copy_str_bounded() — strncpy + always-NUL-terminate */\nstatic void copy_str_bounded(char *dst, const char *src, size_t cap)\n{\n    if (cap == 0) return;\n    if (!src) { dst[0] = '\\0'; return; }\n    size_t n = strlen(src);\n    if (n >= cap) n = cap - 1;\n    memcpy(dst, src, n);\n    dst[n] = '\\0';\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ enqueue() — append a node, signal the writer */\nstatic void enqueue(event_queue_t *q, event_node_t *n)\n{\n    n->next = NULL;\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&q->mtx);\n    if (q->tail) q->tail->next = n;\n    else         q->head       = n;\n    q->tail = n;\n    pthread_cond_signal(&q->cv);\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&q->mtx);\n    atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&q->pending, 1, memory_order_relaxed);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ write_one() — serialize one event through }\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ writer_main() — drain loop */\nstatic void *writer_main(void *arg)\n{\n    event_queue_t *q = (event_queue_t *)arg;\n    while (1) {\n        pthread_mutex_lock(&q->mtx);\n Same\n * direct-write path as the verbose events — graph mutations are\n * infrequent and the payload is variable-length string data that\n * doesn't fit cleanly into a fixed-size queue record. */\nvoid event_queue_box_create(event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                            const char *box_id, const char *kind,\n                            const char *lang, const char *ref,\n                            const char *fn)\n{\n    if (!q) return;\n    jsonl_emit_box_create(q->writer, ts, box_id, kind, lang, ref, fn);\n}\n\nvoid event_queue_wire_add(event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                          const char *from_box, const char *from_branch,\n                          const char *to_box, const char *to_input)\n{\n    if (!q) return;\n    jsonl_emit_wire_add(q->writer, ts, from_box, from_branch, to_box, to_input);\n}\n\nvoid event_queue_push(event_queue_t *q, double ts,\n                      const char *from_box, const char *to_box,\n                      const char *to_input, int slot_id,\n                      int n_bytes, const char *result)\n{\n    if (!q) return;\n    jsonl_emit_push(q->writer, ts, from_box, to_box, to_input,\n                    slot_id, n_bytes, result);\n}\n/* }}} */\n",
