Subsequent calls would rotate via the\n# counter; this fixture exercises the first call only.\ncheck_map \"distributor-route\" \\\n    \"tagger_0 → got_0:hi\" \\\n    \"tagger_1 → (no output)\" \\\n    \"tagger_2 → (no output)\"\n\n# Issue 243 — multi-band comparator. Thresholds [3, 7] carve\n# three bands. Seed value 5 lands strictly between 3 and 7, so\n# only the between_3_7 branch fires (tagger_1). The picker also\n# proves the band-name formatter matches between dispatch and\n# the wire's from_branch string.\ncheck_map \"multi-band-comparator-route\" \\\n    \"tagger_0 → (no output)\" \\\n    \"tagger_1 → got_1:5\" \\\n    \"tagger_2 → (no output)\"\n\n# Issue 253 — nonlinearity refactor. The routing kind grew an\n# auto-calibrating ring buffer for bounds, dropped the variant\n# names in favour of a `range` toggle, and the output is now\n# v × score (gated linear unit) rather than score alone. Single-\n# fire fixtures cover the cold-start path: the buffer has only\n# the one observed value, n_filled < 2 triggers the neutral\n# score (0 for signed, 0.5 for unit), and the gated output is\n# v × neutral.\n#\n#   signed : tanh,   input v=5  → score 0 (cold start) → v×0 = 0\n#   unit   : sigmoid, input v=10 → score 0.5 (cold start) → v×0.5 = 5\ncheck_map \"nonlinearity-signed\" \\\n    \"tagger → 0\"\ncheck_map \"nonlinearity-unit\" \\\n    \"tagger → 5\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\ncheck_map \"319a-many-inputs\" \\\n    \"combine → count=20 sum=210\"\n\ncheck_map \"319d-runtime-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"auto_\" \\\n    \"echo_dyn-received:trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\ncheck_map \"319e-c-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → c-trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"c-echo-received:c-trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\ncheck_map \"246-c-shim\" \\\n    \"echo → seen:HELLO-FROM-SEED\"\n\ncheck_map \"246-lua-shim\" \\\n    \"echo → seen:REV-fedcba\"\n\n# Issue 318 — the producer's output proves the emit side works\n# end-to-end (Lua function → $lang_opaque sentinel in JSON). The\n# consumer's reconstruction needs the dual-ring slot to surface\n# \"I was written as JSON\" to the same-language consumer, which is\n# a deeper per-edge classification issue documented in 318's\n# closeout; the emit fixture stands today.\ncheck_map \"318-lang-opaque\" \\\n    '\"$lang_opaque\"' \\\n    '\"lang\":\"lua\"' \\\n    '\"shape\":\"function\"' \\\n    'consumer → doubled=42'\n\n# Language-agnostic create_box / connect box kinds (319\n# design-correction follow-on). A read box emits a box spec; a\n# create_box-kind box consumes it; the new box's id is captured\n# downstream. No per-language wrapper involved — same shape works\n# for Lua, C, and Bash producers.\ncheck_map \"319-box-kind-create\" \\\n    \"creator → auto_\"\n\n# 319 auto-init follow-on: a C trigger creates a Lua box at\n# runtime; the Lua spec wasn't in the static graph's language set,\n# so the worker's Lua handle was NULL at pool startup. The\n# dispatch's lazy-init populates the handle on demand and the new\n# box fires.\ncheck_map \"319-cross-lang-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → c-trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"lua-echo-from-runtime-init:c-trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\n# Issue 248 input-side encapsulation. The parent's read box wires\n# a value into a BOX_MAP whose sub-map has one externally-supplied\n# data box; the graph loader splices the parent's wire through to\n# the sub-map's write box at load time. Verification is split: the\n# stdout check confirms the renamed write box fires; the disk file\n# check confirms the parent's bytes actually arrived through the\n# splice (the only path that produces the file's content).\ncheck_map \"248-encap-input-only\" \\\n    \"encap__writer → true\"\n\n# Issue 248 output-side encapsulation. The encap declares an output\n# port; the sub-map's externally-consumed write box emits its\n# `value` bytes downstream (rather than the usual \"true\" success\n# string) and the encapsulation pass appends the parent's downstream\n# wire onto that write box's connections. The renamed sub-writer\n# emits the payload value, and the parent's writer then reports\n# \"true\" after writing that value to disk.\ncheck_map \"248-encap-output-only\" \\\n    \"encap__external_writer → round-trip-through-encap\" \\\n    \"parent_writer → true\"\n\n# Issue 248 recursion. A two-level nesting: the parent encapsulates\n# the outer sub-map, which itself encapsulates the inner sub-map.\n# The inline-encapsulations pass has to iterate twice (once per\n# nesting level), and both the input- and output-side splices have\n# to compose through the prefixed-twice ids. All three writes report\n# the same value, proving the splice carried it through both\n# boundaries.\ncheck_map \"248-encap-recursive\" \\\n    \"encap_outer__encap_inner__inner_writer → twice-nested-greeting\" \\\n    \"encap_outer__outer_writer → twice-nested-greeting\" \\\n    \"parent_writer → true\"\n\n# {{{ encap_input_only_file_check() — input-side encap reaches disk\nencap_input_only_file_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/248-encap-input-only\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"encap input-only write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"encapsulated-greeting\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected 'encapsulated-greeting', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"encap-input file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"encap-input: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ encap_recursive_file_check() — recursion exercises every disk\n# artifact across both nesting levels. The inner sub-map's writer\n# writes one file, the outer sub-map's writer writes another, and\n# the parent's writer writes a third — all three should hold the\n# same byte sequence, proving the value flowed from the parent\n# through both encapsulation boundaries.\nencap_recursive_file_check() {\n    local inner_file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-recursive-inner.txt\"\n    local outer_file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-recursive-outer.txt\"\n    local parent_file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-recursive-parent.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$inner_file\" \"$outer_file\" \"$parent_file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/248-encap-recursive\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"encap recursive write outputs\"\n    local detail=\"\"\n    local want=\"twice-nested-greeting\"\n    [[ -f \"$inner_file\"  && \"$(cat \"$inner_file\")\"  == \"$want\" ]] || \\\n        detail+=\"inner='$(cat \"$inner_file\" 2>/dev/null)' \"\n    [[ -f \"$outer_file\"  && \"$(cat \"$outer_file\")\"  == \"$want\" ]] || \\\n        detail+=\"outer='$(cat \"$outer_file\" 2>/dev/null)' \"\n    [[ -f \"$parent_file\" && \"$(cat \"$parent_file\")\" == \"$want\" ]] || \\\n        detail+=\"parent='$(cat \"$parent_file\" 2>/dev/null)' \"\n    if [[ -z \"$detail\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$detail\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"encap-recursive: $detail\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ refs_unit_tests() — issue 315: ref helper acquire/release/list/reap\n# Runs the dedicated 315-refs-test.sh and folds its overall pass/fail\n# into the suite's counters. The detailed per-scenario output goes\n# only on failure to keep the suite quiet on green.\nrefs_unit_tests() {\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"315-refs unit tests\"\n    local out\n    out=$(\"$DIR/tests/315-refs-test.sh\" --dir \"$DIR\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n    if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n        echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"315-refs unit: rc=$rc\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ refs_fork_on_live_check() — issue 315: compile forks on live refs\n# End-to-end integration. Compile the pipeline fixture, acquire a\n# reference on the result, compile again — the second run should\n# fork to a sibling generation (`compiled.1/`) and leave the original\n# untouched. The pinned generation must remain runnable after the\n# fork (its pool-runner / spec.so / sources are still where they\n# were). After the assertion the test releases the reference and\n# clears every generation directory so it doesn't interfere with the\n# compile_pipeline_check that runs alongside.\nrefs_fork_on_live_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local base=\"$map/compiled\"\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"315 compile fork on live refs\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$base\" \"$map\"/compiled.*\n    \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n\n    local id\n    id=$(\"$DIR/scripts/soramech-ref.sh\" acquire \"$base\")\n    \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n\n    local detail=\"\"\n    [[ -d \"$base\"        ]] || detail+=\"compiled/ missing; \"\n    [[ -d \"$map/compiled.1\" ]] || detail+=\"compiled.1/ missing; \"\n    grep -q '\"forked_from\"' \"$map/compiled.1/manifest.json\" 2>/dev/null \\\n        || detail+=\"forked_from missing from compiled.1; \"\n    # Pinned generation must still run. Capture stdout/err so a\n    # crash on the pinned dir surfaces clearly.\n    if ! (cd /tmp && \"$base/pool-runner\" \"$base\" >/dev/null 2>&1); then\n        detail+=\"pinned generation no longer runs; \"\n    fi\n\n    \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-ref.sh\" release \"$base\" --id \"$id\" >/dev/null\n    rm -rf \"$base\" \"$map\"/compiled.*\n\n    if [[ -z \"$detail\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$detail\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"315-refs fork: $detail\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ encap_output_only_file_check() — output-side encap reaches both\n# the sub-map's disk artifact AND the parent's disk artifact via the\n# spliced wire. The two files should be byte-identical because the\n# write box does its disk write THEN pushes the same value bytes\n# downstream to the parent's writer.\nencap_output_only_file_check() {\n    local sub_file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-output-sub.txt\"\n    local out_file=\"/tmp/soramech-248-encap-output-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$sub_file\" \"$out_file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/248-encap-output-only\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"encap output-only write outputs\"\n    local sub_ok=0 out_ok=0 detail=\"\"\n    if [[ -f \"$sub_file\" && \"$(cat \"$sub_file\")\" == \"round-trip-through-encap\" ]]; then\n        sub_ok=1\n    else\n        detail+=\"sub-file=${sub_file}:'$(cat \"$sub_file\" 2>/dev/null)' \"\n    fi\n    if [[ -f \"$out_file\" && \"$(cat \"$out_file\")\" == \"round-trip-through-encap\" ]]; then\n        out_ok=1\n    else\n        detail+=\"out-file=${out_file}:'$(cat \"$out_file\" 2>/dev/null)' \"\n    fi\n    if [[ $sub_ok -eq 1 && $out_ok -eq 1 ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$detail\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"encap-output: $detail\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\nencap_input_only_file_check\nencap_output_only_file_check\nencap_recursive_file_check\nrefs_unit_tests\nrefs_fork_on_live_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",
```json
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/scripts/run-tests.sh"
```
```json
    }
  },
  "userType":"external",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}
```

```json
    "userModified":false,
    "content":"#!/usr/bin/env luajit\n-- scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua — drop non-deterministic fields\n-- from a JSONL transcript so two runs of the same map produce\n-- identical output suitable for diff-against-expected fixture\n-- verification.\n--\n-- What this does, in one paragraph: each input line is parsed as\n-- JSON, the fields that vary across runs (timestamps, durations,\n-- worker indices, slot ids, task ids — anything timing or\n-- thread-id dependent) are removed, the remaining keys are\n-- re-emitted in alphabetical order, and then every line is\n-- sorted lexicographically against every other line. Two runs of\n-- the same map differing only in worker assignment / wall-clock\n-- timing will normalise to byte-identical output.\n--\n-- Usage:\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua < last-run.jsonl > normalised.jsonl\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua last-run.jsonl > normalised.jsonl\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua --dir DIR last-run.jsonl\n--\n-- Per the project convention: hard-coded ${DIR} path with an\n-- override argument; all paths inside are computed relative to\n-- ${DIR}.\n\n-- {{{ DIR resolution + argv parsing\nlocal DIR = \"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nlocal input_path = nil\nlocal i = 1\nwhile i <= #arg do\n    local a = arg[i]\n    if a == \"--dir\" then\n        DIR = arg[i + 1]\n        i = i + 2\n    else\n        input_path = a\n        i = i + 1\n    end\nend\n-- }}}\n\npackage.path = DIR .. \"/libs/?.lua;\" .. package.path\nlocal json = require(\"dkjson\")\n\n-- {{{ Fields stripped from every event.\n-- Each one varies across runs of the same map and would defeat a\n-- byte-equal diff:\n--   ts          — wall-clock seconds\n--   duration_us — measured elapsed time\n--   worker_idx  — which pool worker fired the task (changes per\n--                 schedule)\n--   slot_id     — the slot store assigns sequentially; growth /\n--                 ordering depends on registration order, which\n--                 can race\n--   task_id     — sequential dispatch counter; differs when\n--                 spawn order interleaves differently\nlocal STRIP_FIELDS = {\n    ts          = true,\n    duration_us = true,\n    worker_idx  = true,\n    slot_id     = true,\n    task_id     = true,\n}\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ read_input() — slurp from file or stdin\nlocal function read_input(path)\n    local fp\n    if path then\n        fp = io.open(path, \"r\")\n        if not fp then\n            io.stderr:write(\"normalise-jsonl: cannot open '\", path, \"'\\n\")\n            os.exit(1)\n        end\n    else\n        fp = io.stdin\n    end\n    local body = fp:read(\"*all\")\n    if path then fp:close() end\n    return body\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ normalise_object() — strip + sort keys in place\n-- Returns (sorted_keys_array, n_keys) so the caller can drive\n-- dkjson's keyorder serialisation parameter. Recurses into nested\n-- objects so a field like {\"old\": {...}, \"new\": {...}} also gets\n-- sorted-key emission on every level.\nlocal function normalise_object(obj)\n    if type(obj) ~= \"table\" then return nil, 0 end\n    for k in pairs(obj) do\n        if STRIP_FIELDS[k] then\n            obj[k] = nil\n        end\n    end\n    local keys = {}\n    for k, v in pairs(obj) do\n        keys[#keys + 1] = k\n        -- Recurse into nested objects (not arrays — arrays are\n        -- already positionally ordered).\n        if type(v) == \"table\" then\n            local is_array = (#v > 0)\n            if not is_array then\n                normalise_object(v)\n            end\n        end\n    end\n    table.sort(keys)\n    return keys, #keys\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ main\nlocal body = read_input(input_path)\n\n-- Split by newline; allow trailing blank line.\nlocal lines = {}\nfor line in body:gmatch(\"[^\\n]+\") do\n    lines[#lines + 1] = line\nend\n\nlocal out = {}\nfor idx, line in ipairs(lines) do\n    local obj, _, err = json.decode(line, 1, nil)\n    if err then\n        io.stderr:write(\"normalise-jsonl: line \", tostring(idx),\n                        \" parse error: \", tostring(err), \"\\n\")\n        os.exit(1)\n    end\n    local keys = normalise_object(obj)\n    -- Pass keyorder so dkjson emits fields in alphabetical order.\n    -- A line that originally read {\"ts\":1.2,\"event\":\"task_start\"}\n    -- normalises to {\"event\":\"task_start\"} regardless of source\n    -- ordering.\n    out[#out + 1] = json.encode(obj, { keyorder = keys })\nend\n\n-- Sort lines lexicographically. The combination \"alpha-keys per\n-- object + alpha-sort across lines\" makes the result invariant\n-- under both within-object reordering AND across-line reordering.\n-- A run that fires task_start then task_end vs. one that fires\n-- the same two events with slot_alloc interleaved will normalise\n-- to the same byte sequence after the slot_alloc field (with\n-- slot_id stripped) folds into its sorted spot.\ntable.sort(out)\n\nfor _, line in ipairs(out) do\n    io.write(line, \"\\n\")\nend\n-- }}}\n",
```

```json
    "content":[{
```

```json
        "input":{
          "content":"#!/usr/bin/env luajit\n-- scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua — drop non-deterministic fields\n-- from a JSONL transcript so two runs of the same map produce\n-- identical output suitable for diff-against-expected fixture\n-- verification.\n--\n-- What this does, in one paragraph: each input line is parsed as\n-- JSON, the fields that vary across runs (timestamps, durations,\n-- worker indices, slot ids, task ids — anything timing or\n-- thread-id dependent) are removed, the remaining keys are\n-- re-emitted in alphabetical order, and then every line is\n-- sorted lexicographically against every other line. Two runs of\n-- the same map differing only in worker assignment / wall-clock\n-- timing will normalise to byte-identical output.\n--\n-- Usage:\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua < last-run.jsonl > normalised.jsonl\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua last-run.jsonl > normalised.jsonl\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua --dir DIR last-run.jsonl\n--\n-- Per the project convention: hard-coded ${DIR} path with an\n-- override argument; all paths inside are computed relative to\n-- ${DIR}.\n\n-- {{{ DIR resolution + argv parsing\nlocal DIR = \"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nlocal input_path = nil\nlocal i = 1\nwhile i <= #arg do\n    local a = arg[i]\n    if a == \"--dir\" then\n        DIR = arg[i + 1]\n        i = i + 2\n    else\n        input_path = a\n        i = i + 1\n    end\nend\n-- }}}\n\npackage.path = DIR .. \"/libs/?.lua;\" .. package.path\nlocal json = require(\"dkjson\")\n\n-- {{{ Fields stripped from every event.\n-- Each one varies across runs of the same map and would defeat a\n-- byte-equal diff:\n--   ts          — wall-clock seconds\n--   duration_us — measured elapsed time\n--   worker_idx  — which pool worker fired the task (changes per\n--                 schedule)\n--   slot_id     — the slot store assigns sequentially; growth /\n--                 ordering depends on registration order, which\n--                 can race\n--   task_id     — sequential dispatch counter; differs when\n--                 spawn order interleaves differently\nlocal STRIP_FIELDS = {\n    ts          = true,\n    duration_us = true,\n    worker_idx  = true,\n    slot_id     = true,\n    task_id     = true,\n}\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ read_input() — slurp from file or stdin\nlocal function read_input(path)\n    local fp\n    if path then\n        fp = io.open(path, \"r\")\n        if not fp then\n            io.stderr:write(\"normalise-jsonl: cannot open '\", path, \"'\\n\")\n            os.exit(1)\n        end\n    else\n        fp = io.stdin\n    end\n    local body = fp:read(\"*all\")\n    if path then fp:close() end\n    return body\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ normalise_object() — strip + sort keys in place\n-- Returns (sorted_keys_array, n_keys) so the caller can drive\n-- dkjson's keyorder serialisation parameter. Recurses into nested\n-- objects so a field like {\"old\": {...}, \"new\": {...}} also gets\n-- sorted-key emission on every level.\nlocal function normalise_object(obj)\n    if type(obj) ~= \"table\" then return nil, 0 end\n    for k in pairs(obj) do\n        if STRIP_FIELDS[k] then\n            obj[k] = nil\n        end\n    end\n    local keys = {}\n    for k, v in pairs(obj) do\n        keys[#keys + 1] = k\n        -- Recurse into nested objects (not arrays — arrays are\n        -- already positionally ordered).\n        if type(v) == \"table\" then\n            local is_array = (#v > 0)\n            if not is_array then\n                normalise_object(v)\n            end\n        end\n    end\n    table.sort(keys)\n    return keys, #keys\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ main\nlocal body = read_input(input_path)\n\n-- Split by newline; allow trailing blank line.\nlocal lines = {}\nfor line in body:gmatch(\"[^\\n]+\") do\n    lines[#lines + 1] = line\nend\n\nlocal out = {}\nfor idx, line in ipairs(lines) do\n    local obj, _, err = json.decode(line, 1, nil)\n    if err then\n        io.stderr:write(\"normalise-jsonl: line \", tostring(idx),\n                        \" parse error: \", tostring(err), \"\\n\")\n        os.exit(1)\n    end\n    local keys = normalise_object(obj)\n    -- Pass keyorder so dkjson emits fields in alphabetical order.\n    -- A line that originally read {\"ts\":1.2,\"event\":\"task_start\"}\n    -- normalises to {\"event\":\"task_start\"} regardless of source\n    -- ordering.\n    out[#out + 1] = json.encode(obj, { keyorder = keys })\nend\n\n-- Sort lines lexicographically. The combination \"alpha-keys per\n-- object + alpha-sort across lines\" makes the result invariant\n-- under both within-object reordering AND across-line reordering.\n-- A run that fires task_start then task_end vs. one that fires\n-- the same two events with slot_alloc interleaved will normalise\n-- to the same byte sequence after the slot_alloc field (with\n-- slot_id stripped) folds into its sorted spot.\ntable.sort(out)\n\nfor _, line in ipairs(out) do\n    io.write(line, \"\\n\")\nend\n-- }}}\n",
```

```json
    "originalFile":"#!/usr/bin/env luajit\n-- scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua — drop non-deterministic fields\n-- from a JSONL transcript so two runs of the same map produce\n-- identical output suitable for diff-against-expected fixture\n-- verification.\n--\n-- What this does, in one paragraph: each input line is parsed as\n-- JSON, the fields that vary across runs (timestamps, durations,\n-- worker indices, slot ids, task ids — anything timing or\n-- thread-id dependent) are removed, the remaining keys are\n-- re-emitted in alphabetical order, and then every line is\n-- sorted lexicographically against every other line. Two runs of\n-- the same map differing only in worker assignment / wall-clock\n-- timing will normalise to byte-identical output.\n--\n-- Usage:\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua < last-run.jsonl > normalised.jsonl\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua last-run.jsonl > normalised.jsonl\n--   normalise-jsonl.lua --dir DIR last-run.jsonl\n--\n-- Per the project convention: hard-coded ${DIR} path with an\n-- override argument; all paths inside are computed relative to\n-- ${DIR}.\n\n-- {{{ DIR resolution + argv parsing\nlocal DIR = \"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nlocal input_path = nil\nlocal i = 1\nwhile i <= #arg do\n    local a = arg[i]\n    if a == \"--dir\" then\n        DIR = arg[i + 1]\n        i = i + 2\n    else\n        input_path = a\n        i = i + 1\n    end\nend\n-- }}}\n\npackage.path = DIR .. \"/libs/?.lua;\" .. package.path\nlocal json = require(\"dkjson\")\n\n-- {{{ Fields stripped from every event.\n-- Each one varies across runs of the same map and would defeat a\n-- byte-equal diff:\n--   ts          — wall-clock seconds\n--   duration_us — measured elapsed time\n--   worker_idx  — which pool worker fired the task (changes per\n--                 schedule)\n--   slot_id     — the slot store assigns sequentially; growth /\n--                 ordering depends on registration order, which\n--                 can race\n--   task_id     — sequential dispatch counter; differs when\n--                 spawn order interleaves differently\nlocal STRIP_FIELDS = {\n    ts          = true,\n    duration_us = true,\n    worker_idx  = true,\n    slot_id     = true,\n    task_id     = true,\n}\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ read_input() — slurp from file or stdin\nlocal function read_input(path)\n    local fp\n    if path then\n        fp = io.open(path, \"r\")\n        if not fp then\n            io.stderr:write(\"normalise-jsonl: cannot open '\", path, \"'\\n\")\n            os.exit(1)\n        end\n    else\n        fp = io.stdin\n    end\n    local body = fp:read(\"*all\")\n    if path then fp:close() end\n    return body\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ normalise_object() — strip + sort keys in place\n-- Returns (sorted_keys_array, n_keys) so the caller can drive\n-- dkjson's keyorder serialisation parameter. Recurses into nested\n-- objects so a field like {\"old\": {...}, \"new\": {...}} also gets\n-- sorted-key emission on every level.\nlocal function normalise_object(obj)\n    if type(obj) ~= \"table\" then return nil, 0 end\n    for k in pairs(obj) do\n        if STRIP_FIELDS[k] then\n            obj[k] = nil\n        end\n    end\n    local keys = {}\n    for k, v in pairs(obj) do\n        keys[#keys + 1] = k\n        -- Recurse into nested objects (not arrays — arrays are\n        -- already positionally ordered).\n        if type(v) == \"table\" then\n            local is_array = (#v > 0)\n            if not is_array then\n                normalise_object(v)\n            end\n        end\n    end\n    table.sort(keys)\n    return keys, #keys\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ main\nlocal body = read_input(input_path)\n\n-- Split by newline; allow trailing blank line.\nlocal lines = {}\nfor line in body:gmatch(\"[^\\n]+\") do\n    lines[#lines + 1] = line\nend\n\nlocal out = {}\nfor idx, line in ipairs(lines) do\n    local obj, _, err = json.decode(line, 1, nil)\n    if err then\n        io.stderr:write(\"normalise-jsonl: line \", tostring(idx),\n                        \" parse error: \", tostring(err), \"\\n\")\n        os.exit(1)\n    end\n    local keys = normalise_object(obj)\n    -- Pass keyorder so dkjson emits fields in alphabetical order.\n    -- A line that originally read {\"ts\":1.2,\"event\":\"task_start\"}\n    -- normalises to {\"event\":\"task_start\"} regardless of source\n    -- ordering.\n    out[#out + 1] = json.encode(obj, { keyorder = keys })\nend\n\n-- Sort lines lexicographically. The combination \"alpha-keys per\n-- object + alpha-sort across lines\" makes the result invariant\n-- under both within-object reordering AND across-line reordering.\n-- A run that fires task_start then task_end vs. one that fires\n-- the same two events with slot_alloc interleaved will normalise\n-- to the same byte sequence after the slot_alloc field (with\n-- slot_id stripped) folds into its sorted spot.\ntable.sort(out)\n\nfor _, line in ipairs(out) do\n    io.write(line, \"\\n\")\nend\n-- }}}\n",
    "oldString":"local STRIP_FIELDS = {\n    ts          = true,\n    duration_us = true,\n    worker_idx  = true,\n    slot_id     = true,\n    task_id     = true,\n}",
    "newString":"local STRIP_FIELDS = {\n    ts          = true,\n    duration_us = true,\n    worker_idx  = true,\n    slot_id     = true,\n    task_id     = true,\n    -- n_workers depends on the machine's CPU count (or\n    -- SORAMECH_WORKERS env); fixture tests are run on different\n    -- hardware so the worker count would flake even when the\n    -- map's behaviour is identical. Tests that genuinely care\n    -- about worker count should pin it via SORAMECH_WORKERS and\n    -- inspect the un-normalised log.\n    n_workers   = true,\n}",
```

```json
          "old_string":"# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"# {{{ check_jsonl() — JSONL transcript diff against an expected fixture\n# Stricter than check_map: runs the map, normalises the transcript\n# (drops ts / durations / worker_idx / slot_id / task_id / n_workers,\n# sorts events alphabetically), and diffs against tests/expected/<map>.jsonl.\n# A divergence here means the map's runtime behaviour changed in a way\n# that the substring-checks in check_map wouldn't catch — e.g. a new\n# event type appearing, a box firing an extra time, an output size\n# changing.\n#\n# Re-baselining: a fixture's expected file is updated by running the\n# map manually:\n#   ./soramech-pool tests/maps/<name> > /dev/null\n#   scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl \\\n#     > tests/expected/<name>.jsonl\n# and committing the result.\ncheck_jsonl() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    local expected=\"$DIR/tests/expected/$map.jsonl\"\n    local actual_raw=\"/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\"\n    local actual_norm=\"/tmp/soramech-norm-$map-$$.jsonl\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map (transcript diff)\"\n\n    if [[ ! -f \"$expected\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — expected fixture missing: %s\\n\" \"$expected\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map transcript: expected missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$actual_raw\"\n    local rc\n    if [[ -f \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers\" ]]; then\n        local workers_env\n        workers_env=$(cat \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers\")\n        SORAMECH_WORKERS=\"$workers_env\" \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n        rc=$?\n    else\n        \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" >/dev/null 2>&1\n        rc=$?\n    fi\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — pool exit=%d\\n\" \"$rc\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map transcript: pool exit=$rc\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    \"$DIR/scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua\" --dir \"$DIR\" \"$actual_raw\" > \"$actual_norm\"\n    if ! diff -u \"$expected\" \"$actual_norm\" >/tmp/jsonl-diff-$$.txt 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — transcript diverges\\n\"\n        sed 's/^/      /' /tmp/jsonl-diff-$$.txt\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map transcript: diff failed\")\n    else\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    fi\n    rm -f \"$actual_norm\" /tmp/jsonl-diff-$$.txt\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/scripts/run-tests.sh"
        },
        "caller":{
```

```json
          "old_string":"What's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- JSONL normalizer for diff-based test verification (currently\n  the test harness uses substring matching against stderr).\n\n### Phase-3 demo — 2026-05-24",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"What's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- JSONL normalizer for diff-based test verification (currently\n  the test harness uses substring matching against stderr).\n\n### Vyukov-style MPSC ring + transcript normaliser — 2026-05-24\n\nThe two open items above both landed.\n\nThe event queue's mutex + linked-list implementation became a\n4096-slot Vyukov-style ring with per-slot atomic sequence\nnumbers (`src/014-event-queue.c`). Producers do one CAS on\n`enqueue_pos` (no mutex on the hot path) and publish via a\nrelease-ordered store on the slot's seq counter; the consumer\nreads slots in order and frees them by bumping the seq forward\nby `EQ_RING_SIZE`. On full-ring contention, producers block on a\n`has_space` CV rather than dropping events — losing audit-trail\nevents is worse than briefly blocking a producer. Two new tests:\na 32-producer × 4000-event burst (128 k lines, per-thread\nmonotonicity preserved) and a single-producer 10 k-event overflow\nthat exceeds capacity by 2.4× and proves blocking-on-full lands\nevery line in the file.\n\nThe transcript normaliser is `scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua`. It\nparses each line with dkjson, drops the timing / scheduling\nfields that vary across runs (`ts`, `duration_us`, `worker_idx`,\n`slot_id`, `task_id`, `n_workers`), re-emits remaining keys in\nalphabetical order, and sorts the lines lexicographically. The\ncombination of within-object key-sort and across-line line-sort\nmakes the result invariant under both within-event reordering\nAND scheduling reordering. `scripts/run-tests.sh` grew a\n`check_jsonl <map>` helper that runs the map, normalises the\ntranscript, and diffs it against `tests/expected/<map>.jsonl`;\nre-baselining is the obvious sequence (`soramech-pool` →\n`normalise-jsonl.lua` → commit). Two fixtures opt in today —\n`hello` and `pipeline` — as proof; future fixtures snapshot\ntheir expected transcript at the same time the map lands.\n\n### Phase-3 demo — 2026-05-24",
```

```json
    "oldString":"What's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- JSONL normalizer for diff-based test verification (currently\n  the test harness uses substring matching against stderr).\n\n### Phase-3 demo — 2026-05-24",
    "newString":"What's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- JSONL normalizer for diff-based test verification (currently\n  the test harness uses substring matching against stderr).\n\n### Vyukov-style MPSC ring + transcript normaliser — 2026-05-24\n\nThe two open items above both landed.\n\nThe event queue's mutex + linked-list implementation became a\n4096-slot Vyukov-style ring with per-slot atomic sequence\nnumbers (`src/014-event-queue.c`). Producers do one CAS on\n`enqueue_pos` (no mutex on the hot path) and publish via a\nrelease-ordered store on the slot's seq counter; the consumer\nreads slots in order and frees them by bumping the seq forward\nby `EQ_RING_SIZE`. On full-ring contention, producers block on a\n`has_space` CV rather than dropping events — losing audit-trail\nevents is worse than briefly blocking a producer. Two new tests:\na 32-producer × 4000-event burst (128 k lines, per-thread\nmonotonicity preserved) and a single-producer 10 k-event overflow\nthat exceeds capacity by 2.4× and proves blocking-on-full lands\nevery line in the file.\n\nThe transcript normaliser is `scripts/normalise-jsonl.lua`. It\nparses each line with dkjson, drops the timing / scheduling\nfields that vary across runs (`ts`, `duration_us`, `worker_idx`,\n`slot_id`, `task_id`, `n_workers`), re-emits remaining keys in\nalphabetical order, and sorts the lines lexicographically. The\ncombination of within-object key-sort and across-line line-sort\nmakes the result invariant under both within-event reordering\nAND scheduling reordering. `scripts/run-tests.sh` grew a\n`check_jsonl <map>` helper that runs the map, normalises the\ntranscript, and diffs it against `tests/expected/<map>.jsonl`;\nre-baselining is the obvious sequence (`soramech-pool` →\n`normalise-jsonl.lua` → commit). Two fixtures opt in today —\n`hello` and `pipeline` — as proof; future fixtures snapshot\ntheir expected transcript at the same time the map lands.\n\n### Phase-3 demo — 2026-05-24",
    "userModified":false,
```

```json
        "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **Vyukov MPSC vs. mutex-list, on this codebase:** the mutex queue wasn't a correctness problem — it worked perfectly. It was a *future* contention problem that only shows up under bursty dispatch (every task fires 3+ events; under 16-worker contention each event went through one append-mutex). The ring isn't faster on average, but its tail latency is bounded — no producer ever waits for another producer holding the mutex during slow JSON encoding. The interesting design choice was the full-ring backpressure (block on `has_space` CV) vs. drop-and-warn. I chose block because the JSONL log exists for audit trails — a dropped event is a hole in the timeline that defeats the whole point.\n- **The normaliser's \"key-sort + line-sort\" trick:** if you sort just the lines, a re-ordered field in a single JSON object still diffs. If you sort just the keys per-object, a re-ordered event sequence still diffs. The combination kills both axes of nondeterminism. The same trick is what JSON canonicalisation (RFC 8785) does for cryptographic purposes — different reason, same shape.\n- **n_workers stripped:** machine-portable expected files require us to drop the worker count because it defaults to CPU count. The audit trade-off: a test that genuinely depends on worker-count behaviour (e.g. 318's per-worker lang state) has to pin `SORAMECH_WORKERS` *and* read the un-normalised log. The fixture file is a \"what is the same across machines\" snapshot; per-machine behaviour belongs in the env or in a dedicated check.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nBoth 311 tasks landed and committed. Suite still 181/181 unit + 35/35 integration green (the 35 reflects the two new `check_jsonl` checks). 320 is queued and waiting on your reader-consistency call (A / B / C from earlier). I'll pause here for you."
```

```json
        "text":"Yeah, you're right — I packed too much into the design knob and not enough explanation of what's actually moving through memory. Let me rewind and walk through it from the dataflow side.\n\n## The setup, slowly\n\nPicture a single box record sitting in memory. It has a bunch of fields hanging off it that the dispatch needs every time the box fires:\n- A **list of input ports** — names like \"x\", \"y\", \"z\" with types.\n- A **list of slot IDs** — one per input port, pointing at the slot where values for that port arrive.\n- The **count** of how many input ports there are.\n- A few other per-port arrays — the \"is this port pop or peek?\" modes, the \"is this port fed by a same-language wire?\" flags, etc.\n\nAll of these arrays are **the same length**, and they all change together. If you add a port, you grow all five arrays by one entry. If you rename a port, you change one entry in the names array but the slot ID stays put. They're a tight little cluster of stuff that describes \"what this box's input shape looks like right now.\"\n\nNow picture **two threads** trying to talk to this box at the same time:\n\n- **Worker A** is mid-fire. It's reading the port list to figure out what inputs to gather. It looks at `n_inputs`, then walks through `inputs[0]`, `inputs[1]`, etc., pulling values from the corresponding slots.\n\n- **Worker B** has just received a reconfigure message and is about to change the box's port shape. It needs to swap in a new port list — maybe one with three ports instead of two, maybe with port \"x\" renamed to \"x_renamed\", maybe with port \"y\" removed entirely.\n\n## What can go wrong\n\nIf Worker B writes the new fields one at a time, and Worker A happens to be reading at the same instant, Worker A can see a mid-flight state that never existed in any coherent version of the box.\n\nConcretely, imagine B writes the new `n_inputs` first, then the new `inputs[]` pointer. A might race in and see:\n- New count: 3\n- Old pointer (still pointing at the 2-entry array)\n\nNow A walks the array thinking there are 3 entries when there are only 2. The third \"entry\" is memory past the end of the array — garbage. A fires the box with garbage inputs, or segfaults reading past the array.\n\nOr imagine B writes the new pointer first, then the new count. A might see:\n- New pointer (3-entry array)\n- Old count: 2\n\nThat's actually safe! A processes 2 entries, ignores the third, fires the box with the first 2 inputs of the new shape. The reconfigure \"half lands\" but A doesn't crash.\n\nSo **the order of writes matters**, and one direction is safer than the other.\n\n## Why the existing pattern works for the connections array\n\nThe wires-going-out array (the `connections` field) has the same race story, and 319d already solved it by carefully picking the write order:\n\n1. Allocate a brand new array, copy the old entries, append the new entry.\n2. Atomically publish the new pointer.\n3. Atomically publish the new count.\n\nAnd readers do the opposite: read count first, then pointer. If count is the new value, the pointer is guaranteed to also be the new value (because writer's pointer-store happened before writer's count-store). If count is the old value, it doesn't matter what the pointer is — readers using the old count only touch entries 0..(old_count - 1), which exist in both arrays.\n\n**Why this works specifically for connections**: connections is **append-only**. The new array's first N entries are byte-identical to the old array's N entries. The new entries land at positions N, N+1, ... which old readers never look at. So even a reader holding the new pointer with the old count is reading completely valid data — just a subset.\n\nIt's an **apartment building where you can only add floors on top**. A visitor with an out-of-date map showing 10 floors can still navigate floors 1-10 just fine, because nobody renumbered them. The new 11th floor exists but visitors with old maps never go there.\n\n## Why this trick **stops working** for reconfigure\n\nReconfigure isn't append-only. It can:\n- **Remove** a port (the array shrinks).\n- **Rename** a port at the same position (the array changes in place).\n- **Reorder** ports (port \"x\" used to be at position 0, now it's at position 2).\n- **Insert** a port in the middle.\n\nSo now the apartment-building analogy breaks. After a reconfigure, the floors got rearranged. Floor 3 in the old building isn't floor 3 in the new building — it might be floor 5 now, or it might not exist at all. A visitor with the old map who reads \"go to floor 3\" using the new building's directory ends up at the wrong place.\n\nIn code: a reader with old count = 5 and new pointer (pointing at a 3-entry array) walks entries 0..4 of an array that only has 3 valid entries. Entries 3 and 4 are past the end → segfault, or worse, silently reading whatever happened to be next to that allocation in memory.\n\nSo **the staggered-publish trick we use for connections doesn't carry over**. We need something else.\n\n## The three options, explained as dataflow\n\nHere are A, B, C again, but now told as \"what happens at the level of memory accesses, step by step.\"\n\n---\n\n### Option A — Bundle everything that changes together into one swappable snapshot\n\n**The shape:** Instead of `n_inputs` + `inputs[]` + `input_slot_ids[]` + `input_slot_modes[]` + … all being separate fields hanging off the box record, collect them into one struct (call it the box's **port configuration**) and store just one pointer to it on the box.\n\n```\nbox.port_config → { n_inputs: 3,\n                    inputs: [name1, name2, name3],\n                    slot_ids: [5, 7, 9],\n                    modes: [POP, PEEK, POP],\n                    ... }\n```\n\n**What the mutator does:**\n1. Allocate a brand-new port configuration struct.\n2. Fill in all its fields with the new values.\n3. Atomically swap the `box.port_config` pointer to point at the new struct.\n4. Park the old struct on a free-later list (because some reader might still be holding the old pointer; can't free immediately).\n\nThat's it. The entire reconfigure is **one pointer swap**. Either readers see the old config or they see the new config — never a torn mix, because the writer never modifies the live struct, only swaps in a fresh one.\n\n**What a reader does:**\n1. Read `box.port_config` ONCE, save the pointer in a local variable.\n2. Use that local pointer for the entire fire. Don't re-read it mid-fire.\n3. When the fire is done, drop the reference (so the free-later list knows it's safe to reclaim).\n\nBecause the reader grabs a consistent snapshot at the start, it doesn't matter if the mutator swaps in a new config halfway through the reader's fire — the reader is using its local pointer to the OLD config, finishes its work cleanly, and the next fire of the same box will use the new config.\n\n**Dataflow picture:**\n```\nMutator side:          Reader side:\n  build new config       grab pointer to current config (one load)\n  swap pointer    ────►  ...keep using its snapshot through the whole fire...\n  (old config drifts     drop reference at end\n   on free-later list)\n```\n\n**What it costs us:** A medium-sized restructure of the box record. Today `n_inputs`, `inputs[]`, `input_slot_ids[]`, etc. are all separate fields directly on the box. To do option A, we'd lift them into a sub-struct and add the swap discipline. The dispatch code that reads them changes from `box->n_inputs` to `box->port_config->n_inputs`. Once-per-fire, one extra pointer dereference. Cheap to do, but it touches many call sites.\n\n---\n\n### Option B — A revision number, with readers retrying on mismatch\n\n**The shape:** Leave the box fields where they are. Add ONE new field: `version` (just an integer). Every time the mutator changes anything about the inputs, it bumps `version` by 1.\n\nThe trick is the mutator bumps `version` to an ODD number BEFORE making changes, makes the changes, then bumps it to an EVEN number AFTER. Odd means \"I'm in the middle of changing things, my data is torn.\" Even means \"I'm done, the data is coherent.\"\n\n**What the mutator does:**\n1. Bump `version` from 4 to 5. (Now odd → \"I'm working.\")\n2. Rewrite the `n_inputs` field, the `inputs[]` pointer, the `slot_ids[]` pointer, etc., one at a time.\n3. Bump `version` from 5 to 6. (Now even → \"I'm done.\")\n\n**What a reader does:**\n1. Read `version` into a local variable, call it `v1`.\n2. If `v1` is odd, the mutator is mid-write. Wait a tiny bit and retry.\n3. Read all the fields the reader needs (`n_inputs`, `inputs[]`, etc.) into local copies.\n4. Read `version` again, call it `v2`.\n5. If `v1 != v2`, the mutator changed something while the reader was reading → the local copies might be torn. **Throw them away and go back to step 1.**\n\n**Dataflow picture:**\n```\nMutator side:                  Reader side:\n  version: 4 → 5  (odd, \"go    read version = 4\n                  away\")        read n_inputs = 5\n  rewrite n_inputs               read inputs[] pointer\n  rewrite inputs[] pointer       read version again = 4? then OK, use the data\n  rewrite slot_ids[] pointer            = 5? throw out, retry\n  version: 5 → 6  (even, \"ok\")          = 6? throw out, retry\n```\n\n**What it costs us:** Minimal restructure — just add the `version` field. But every reader now does the read-data-read-version-check dance. And on contention, readers retry, which wastes work. Also, the \"odd/even\" trick relies on careful ordering — get the bump-before vs. bump-after wrong and you reintroduce the torn-read problem.\n\nThere's also a subtler problem with this approach: option B assumes the reader can detect a torn read after the fact and retry. But if the torn read causes the reader to crash mid-walk (e.g., walking past the end of a shrunken array and segfaulting), there's nothing to retry. So we'd need to be very careful that mid-flight states are safe to *attempt* to walk, even if we throw the result away. That's a stronger constraint than it sounds.\n\n---\n\n### Option C — Make every reader wait on the YARQ barrier\n\n**The shape:** Just lock. When the mutator wants to change things, it takes the YARQ barrier. When a reader wants to read things, it also takes the YARQ barrier. Only one party can hold it at a time.\n\n**What the mutator does:**\n1. Take YARQ. (If a reader holds it, wait.)\n2. Rewrite the fields in any order. Nobody else is looking.\n3. Release YARQ.\n\n**What a reader does:**\n1. Take YARQ. (If the mutator holds it, do the yield-and-requeue dance — drop yourself back at the end of the pool queue.)\n2. Read whatever you need.\n3. Release YARQ.\n\n**Dataflow picture:**\n```\nMutator side:                  Reader side:\n  take YARQ ──────────────►    (blocked, waiting for YARQ)\n  rewrite fields                ...\n  release YARQ ◄──────────────  take YARQ (now succeeds)\n                                read fields\n                                release YARQ\n```\n\n**What it costs us:** Simplest mechanism, but it goes against the \"workers don't take YARQ\" note you wrote. Every single box fire pays for a CAS-acquire and CAS-release, even though the mutator path runs maybe once a minute and the read path runs thousands of times a second. Most of those reads are paying a sync cost for a race that almost never happens.\n\n---\n\n## How they compare in dataflow terms\n\nThe thing I want you to notice is that **A and B are doing essentially the same thing in different shapes**. Both of them want the reader to get a self-consistent snapshot without blocking:\n\n- A says: \"the mutator builds the snapshot for you; just grab the pointer.\"\n- B says: \"the mutator changes things in place; you read, check the version, and confirm you got a coherent read.\"\n\nA pushes the consistency work onto the mutator (build the new struct, swap one pointer). B pushes the consistency work onto the reader (read everything twice, check it matches).\n\nA wins when mutations are rare and reads are frequent (which is exactly our case — boxes fire constantly, reconfigures land occasionally). B wins when you don't want to restructure the data layout. C is the brute-force option that works for any data layout but contradicts your stated preference.\n\n## My take, expanded\n\nFor this codebase, I'd pick **A**, and here's the dataflow reason: **we already have one example of this pattern working well.** The connections array's \"build a new array, copy + append, atomic-swap the pointer\" dance IS option A, just specialised to one field. We'd be generalising it from \"one field\" to \"all the per-port fields bundled together.\"\n\nThe cost is a one-time refactor: lift the per-port fields into a sub-struct and update the dispatch's reads to dereference through one extra pointer. That extra dereference happens once per fire and costs maybe 5 nanoseconds. The mutator gets slightly more work (allocate + populate a new struct instead of writing fields in place), but mutator work is rare.\n\nCompared to B, A is **less code to write and harder to get subtly wrong**. The version-counter dance is one of those patterns where if you mis-order an operation by one line, you reintroduce the bug you were trying to fix, and the bug only shows up under timing pressure that's hard to reproduce. A's \"build it complete, then publish\" pattern is structurally hard to mess up — there's no in-between state that can be observed.\n\nCompared to C, A is **kinder to the hot path**. Every box fire pays nothing for the consistency mechanism in option A (just one pointer load that would happen anyway). In option C, every box fire pays for a CAS that contended workers might lose.\n\nHopefully this is clearer? If you want me to draw out any of the three in even more detail, or work through a specific scenario (like \"what happens when a reconfigure arrives while two readers are mid-fire\"), just say which one."
```

```json
{
  "uuid":"9e57ea15-4a9e-47cd-96e5-5ed4b8a67e81",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-25T01:19:58.962Z",
  "slug":"goofy-noodling-torvalds",
  "parentUuid":"3831fac9-cbab-45fa-b5a8-4c07e06e5d86",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "promptId":"629f4bcd-6a38-4c2c-9c7f-d03e97d83e49",
  "userType":"external",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits",
  "message":{
    "content":"Okay so the connection box was never intended to be append only. It's supposed to be able to fully define all the output connections. And heck, now that we're adding json reconfiguring, do we even need it at all?\n\nI think the proper shape, what we need for the reconfigure system, is to basically have a double buffer - worker A is halfway through an input gathering task, and worker B decides to reconfigure. So what happens is worker B puts a flag on the box and sets it to 1. It's normally at 0. This flag says no new workers can start, and if they're requested to, that they should just put the task back on the task pool queue. Worker A is still in flight, so worker B then assembles a new box struct and... can you tell me, how are the ring buffers associated with the box? Also, do the task structs (the ephemeral instantiations of the box's task) store pointers back to the box, or just pointers to the function for the spec to invoke?\n\nanyway worker B assembles the box struct and reconfigures the ring pointers to point to the box, or the box to point to the old ring buffers. We should NOT move the ring buffers, because there could be a billion elements in one of them and we won't want to spend a lot of time moving them.\n\nonce the new box is fully constructed, the worker sets the original box's flag to 2, and this causes any workers that come in asking to run the original box to look at a pointer, that box B supplies, that points to the new box. From then on, newly created boxes *should* default to the new box, it's only the couple stale ones that are spinning through the queue while the new box is assembled that will ever touch the original again. And once it's ref count is zero, then we should be able to garbage collect the original box. Can you tell me how that reference count would apply? When is it modified? Will this system work? Any issues or edge-cases?",
    "role":"user"
  },
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}
```

```json
        "text":"Yes — your design is much cleaner. Let me answer your specific questions first, then walk through whether it works and where the rough edges are.\n\n## How the ring buffers are associated with the box\n\nGood news: **the ring buffers don't live inside the box at all.** They live in a separate place called the slot store, indexed by integer IDs. The box just holds an array of those IDs — one ID per input port — saying \"input port 0 reads from slot 5, input port 1 reads from slot 7, input port 2 reads from slot 9.\"\n\nThe slot is a handle, like a row number in a database table. The box doesn't own the row; it just knows which row to look at.\n\n```\nbox record:                  slot store (separate, shared):\n  input_port_0 → slot id 5     slot 5: [ring buffer with values for port 0]\n  input_port_1 → slot id 7     slot 7: [ring buffer with values for port 1]\n  input_port_2 → slot id 9     slot 9: [ring buffer with values for port 2]\n                               slot 12: [some other box's slot]\n                               slot 13: [some other box's slot]\n                               ...\n```\n\n**This is perfect for your design.** When you build the new box record, you copy the same slot IDs into it. Both boxes point at the same ring buffers — no copying, no moving, no \"billion elements\" problem. The ring buffers stay where they are; only the small metadata struct around them gets replaced.\n\nEven better: pushers (other boxes that send values into these slots) look up the slot by ID too — they don't reach through the box record. So when boxes upstream are firing, they're pushing into the same slot whether they look up the OLD box or the NEW box. The dataflow into the slot is completely independent of the box-pointer dance.\n\n## How task structs reference the box\n\nLooking at the code: a task carries the box's **index number into the graph's box array**, not a pointer to the box record. So:\n\n```\ndispatch_task_t:\n  box_id     = 7      ← the index, not a pointer\n  task_id    = 42\n  ctx        = pointer to the dispatch context (which holds the graph)\n```\n\nWhen the worker runs the task, it does `graph_box(graph, 7)` to resolve the index into the actual box record. That's the moment the worker grabs a pointer to the box. Until that moment, the task doesn't know anything about the box's memory address.\n\n**This is also good for your design** — it means when a worker dequeues a task and resolves the index, it'll get whatever box is currently at that index. If you've already swapped to the new box, the worker gets the new one. If the swap is in progress (flag = 1), the worker sees the old box with flag = 1 and yields. The lookup is the natural place to inspect the flag.\n\nThere's a subtlety: the function pointer the spec invokes (the \"lua_invoke\" or \"c_invoke\" callback) is reached *through* the box (`spec_registry[box->spec_idx]->invoke`). So once the worker has the box pointer, it walks through the box to find the function. It does NOT cache the function pointer in the task struct. So if the new box has a different spec, the worker that follows the redirect will naturally call the new spec.\n\n## Now for your design — does it work?\n\nYes, with one structural change and a few edge cases to think through.\n\n**The structural change:** today the graph holds boxes as an array of records (`box_t boxes[N]`), so each box's memory address is stable for the whole run. To do your swap-the-whole-box dance, we need to change the graph to hold an array of **pointers** to boxes (`box_t *boxes[N]`). That way the mutator can build a new box record, swap the pointer in the array entry, and the old box record stays at its original address with whatever workers are still using it.\n\nThis is a one-time refactor — wherever `graph_box(g, i)` is called, the implementation switches from \"return address of boxes[i]\" to \"return boxes[i]\" — but the public API stays the same.\n\n**The flag transitions:**\n```\nFlag state 0  ─►  normal. Workers proceed.\nFlag state 1  ─►  reconfigure in progress. Workers yield-and-requeue.\nFlag state 2  ─►  redirect. Workers follow box->next_box to the new box.\n```\n\nWorker arriving at a box:\n1. Increment the box's **refcount** (atomic fetch-add, +1).\n2. Check the flag.\n3. If flag = 0: proceed normally, do the fire, decrement refcount at the end.\n4. If flag = 1: decrement refcount, yield-and-requeue task to the back of the pool queue.\n5. If flag = 2: decrement refcount on OLD box, follow `next_box` pointer to NEW box, restart from step 1 on the NEW box.\n\nMutator (Worker B) arriving with a reconfigure message:\n1. Atomic CAS the flag from 0 → 1. If CAS fails (someone else is mutating, or someone already finished and we see flag = 2), yield-and-requeue our own task and exit.\n2. Build the new box record with new fields. Copy slot IDs from old to new (same ring buffers).\n3. Atomic store: `old_box->next_box = new_box_pointer`.\n4. Atomic store: graph's pointer-array entry → new_box_pointer.\n5. Atomic store: `old_box->flag = 2`. (Release-ordered, so anything we wrote before is visible.)\n6. Walk away. We don't free the old box; whoever decrements refcount to zero will.\n\n## Reference count — when modified, by whom\n\nThe refcount on a box is \"**how many workers are currently using this exact box record.**\" It's an atomic integer on the box.\n\n- **Incremented** at the top of `dispatch_action`, right after the worker resolves the box pointer and BEFORE it checks the flag. The increment serves as a registration: \"I'm here, don't free this box yet.\"\n- **Decremented** at the bottom of `dispatch_action`, whether the fire succeeded, failed, or got redirected. The decrement signals \"I'm done.\"\n\nThe worker that decrements the refcount to zero is responsible for the cleanup: if the decrement returned 0 AND the flag is 2 (meaning a redirect is in place, so no new workers will ever land here), that worker frees the old box record.\n\nThe \"flag is 2\" check matters because a freshly-created box with refcount briefly at 0 (between creations) shouldn't be freed — only a SUPERSEDED box should be. The flag = 2 says \"superseded; if you're the last one out, turn off the lights.\"\n\n## Will this system work — edge cases\n\nMostly yes. Here's my list of things to think through:\n\n**1. The redirect-chain problem.** What if you reconfigure the box ten times in quick succession? Worker A is using v1. While A is still running, B reconfigures to v2 (chain: v1 → v2). Before A finishes, C reconfigures to v3 (chain: v1 → v2 → v3). A new worker arrives at v1, sees flag = 2, follows to v2, sees flag = 2, follows to v3. That works — but if you have a thousand reconfigures faster than A can finish, the chain could grow large and walking it gets expensive.\n\nMitigation: the mutator (B, then C) can update `v1->next_box` to point directly at the freshest box, not the immediate next. So C does `old_box = v2, new_box = v3` but also rewrites `v1->next_box = v3`. Now the chain is flat: anyone arriving at v1 jumps straight to v3. Each box's `next_box` always points at the freshest, not just the next.\n\n**2. The graph pointer-array lookup race.** A new task gets dispatched on box index 7. By the time the worker resolves the index, the mutator has already swapped the pointer to the new box. The worker gets the new box, increments its refcount, runs normally. **This is fine** — the new box is the intended target. The old box was already superseded before the worker even looked.\n\nThe opposite case: a worker resolves the index, gets a pointer to the OLD box, and THEN the mutator swaps. The worker has the old pointer in a local variable, increments OLD's refcount, sees flag = 0 (because mutator hasn't flipped it yet), runs the fire on OLD. Mutator can't proceed past step 1 because the CAS would race — wait, no. The CAS on flag 0 → 1 succeeds regardless of refcount. The mutator flips OLD's flag to 1 while OLD's refcount is 1 (the worker). The mutator builds the new box. The worker, meanwhile, is mid-fire on OLD with the old config. The worker finishes, decrements refcount to 0. The mutator's flag transition 1 → 2 happens at some point. Free decision: the worker that decremented to 0 sees flag = 1 (not 2 yet) and DOESN'T free. The mutator finishes and sets flag = 2. Nobody is now decrementing, so the box leaks.\n\n**Fix for that:** the free check should be \"refcount == 0 AND flag = 2.\" But what if the mutator does its 1 → 2 transition and refcount is already 0? Nobody arrives to do the decrement-to-zero observation. So the mutator, after its 1 → 2 transition, should ALSO check refcount and free if 0. The rule becomes:\n- Whoever does an action (decrement OR flag transition) that results in \"refcount == 0 AND flag == 2\" frees the box.\n\nThis is the classic \"race to be the last actor\" problem in reference counting. The pattern is well-understood: use a CAS to atomically claim \"I am the freer,\" so only one party actually does the free.\n\n**3. The slot store grows / shrinks.** If the reconfigure adds an input port that wasn't there before, a new slot needs to exist. The new box would hold a new slot ID. Allocating the slot can happen while the new box is being built (mutator does `slot_alloc` before swap). Removing a port is trickier — the old box still references the slot, and the old box is still being used by some workers. The slot can't be freed until the OLD box is freed. So slot lifetime is naturally tied to box refcount: when the old box gets freed, any slots it referenced that aren't in the new box get released.\n\nBut — wait. The slot might still have unconsumed values in its ring buffer! Should those be drained? Or dropped? That's a real design question for \"remove a port mid-run.\" Probably worth a JSONL discard event for any leftover values.\n\n**4. Does this remove the need for the connections array's append-only dance?** Yes. Once we have the swap-the-whole-box mechanism, runtime_connect (which today builds a new connections array and atomic-swaps the pointer) becomes redundant. It can use the same mechanism: build a new box with the new connection, swap. Simpler one path for ALL box mutations. **Strong argument for unifying.** The connections-only dance was a special case of the general problem; the general solution subsumes it.\n\n**5. Reconfigure messages on the third ring.** The worker that pops a reconfigure cell from a slot's third ring is the one that becomes the mutator. It does the flag CAS, builds the new box, swaps. If the CAS fails (because someone else is already mutating), the worker yield-and-requeues with the message un-popped... actually no, the message IS popped. We'd need to either push it back (which violates the ring's normal semantics) or treat the mutator role as exclusive — if I can't grab the box, the reconfigure I just popped gets dropped and a JSONL event records it.\n\nHmm. Actually a cleaner shape: the worker that pops the reconfigure tag doesn't IMMEDIATELY apply it. It first CASes the flag. If CAS succeeds, THEN it pops the reconfigure and applies it. If CAS fails, leave the reconfigure on the ring and yield-and-requeue. The next worker that reaches the box and notices the reconfigure tag will retry.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The slot-as-handle decoupling is exactly what makes this design clean.** If the box owned its ring buffers directly (slot data inlined into the box struct), swapping the box would mean copying the rings — your \"billion elements\" worry. Because the box only holds integer IDs into the slot store, the box record is small and cheap to reallocate. The system's existing layered design earned this affordance — the people who built the slot store as a separate indexable thing in 302 didn't know they were enabling 320, but they were.\n- **Refcounting + flag transitions is the classic \"epoch-based reclamation\" pattern.** Linux's RCU (Read-Copy-Update) uses this exact shape for kernel data structures that get rewritten while running: replace the pointer, wait for all readers to finish, then free. The only thing we're adding on top is the explicit flag state to gate new readers, which RCU usually handles by other means (grace periods). Your design is essentially \"RCU with a per-object flag\" — simpler to reason about, costs a CAS per fire instead of a grace-period mechanism. For occasional reconfigures and frequent reads, it's the right shape.\n- **The \"swap the whole box\" pattern subsumes the connections-array pattern.** Once 320 lands, the special-case copy-and-publish on connections becomes a code smell — there's a more general mechanism that handles it. We'd retire the per-array dance in favor of \"all mutations go through the box swap.\" That's a nice consolidation: one mutation discipline for the whole runtime instead of one-per-field.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nSo my answers: yes this works, the structural prerequisite is converting the graph's box storage from \"array of records\" to \"array of pointers,\" and the main edges are (1) the chain-flattening trick on `next_box`, (2) the \"who frees\" race using a CAS to claim freer status, (3) slot lifetime tied to old-box lifetime so removed ports don't get yanked out from under in-flight readers, and (4) the reconfigure-message handling needs to NOT pop the message until the flag CAS succeeds.\n\nA question back to you: when a reconfigure changes the box's input port shape (removes a port that has values still queued in its slot), what should happen to those queued values? Drop them silently? Drop with a JSONL event? Drain them through a synthetic \"discarded inputs\" callback? This is the one bit I don't think the issue file has answered yet."
      }],
```

```json
        "text":"These refinements tighten the design significantly. Let me walk through each.\n\n## On flag = 2 — yes, you can collapse it\n\nYou're right; the third state isn't needed. Here's the cleaner two-state version:\n\n- **Flag 0:** nobody is mutating; readers proceed.\n- **Flag 1:** a mutator owns this box; new arrivals yield-and-requeue.\n\nWhat about the \"find the new box\" job that flag = 2 was doing? **The graph slot itself does that job.** Today the graph holds a pointer to each box at a numbered index. When the mutator atomically swaps that pointer from OLD-box-address to NEW-box-address, any worker that LATER looks up \"box #7\" gets the new box automatically. There's no need for OLD-box to know about NEW-box; OLD-box just sits there until its refcount expires.\n\nSo the dataflow becomes:\n\n```\nnew worker arriving at box #7:\n   1. look up graph slot #7 → get current box pointer (might be OLD or NEW\n                                depending on swap timing — either is fine)\n   2. increment refcount on whatever box you got\n   3. peek the input rings on that box\n   4. proceed (fire) or become-mutator or yield based on what you saw\n\nmutator wrapping up:\n   1. swap graph slot #7 → NEW\n   2. (NEW box's flag is already 0; new arrivals find it cleanly)\n   3. drop mutator's refcount on OLD\n   4. OLD box drifts toward refcount=0 as its in-flight users finish\n```\n\nThe \"stale, re-push and re-queue\" alternative you proposed for flag = 1 is also a valid shape, but it works at a finer granularity (mid-pop) than this design needs. Because we peek-everything-first before any pop (per your question 7), there's never a state where a worker has popped some values and then discovers the box is being mutated. The worker either knows about the reconfigure before any pops happen, or it commits to the whole fire under the current shape. No mid-fire bailout needed.\n\n## On your refcount worry — you're catching a real ambiguity\n\nYou're right to push on this. I described refcount as \"workers currently using\" and that's incomplete. The complete picture has TWO sources of \"still alive\":\n\n```\nA box is alive when:\n   (the graph slot still points at it)\n   OR\n   (refcount > 0 from in-flight workers + mutator)\n```\n\nA box is freeable only when BOTH:\n```\n   (graph slot points at something else, i.e. this box is superseded)\n   AND\n   (refcount has dropped to zero)\n```\n\nSo for an idle box late in the pipeline that nobody is currently running: the graph slot points at it, refcount is 0, and that's fine — it stays alive on the \"graph slot points at it\" leg. It's not freeable because it hasn't been superseded.\n\nOnce a reconfigure happens and the slot swap occurs, the old box loses that \"graph slot points at it\" leg. Now refcount alone keeps it alive. If refcount was already 0 at the swap moment (no current workers), the box is immediately freeable — and the mutator (which is the one that did the swap) holds a +1 it took at the start, so the actual decrement-to-0 happens when the mutator drops its +1. That decrement is what triggers the free. **Your \"mutator also holds a reference\" intuition is exactly the bridge that makes this work.**\n\nSo the rule the freer follows:\n\n```\nwhen my refcount-decrement returns 0:\n   if (graph slot points at me): do nothing. I'm still the live box.\n   else: I've been superseded AND nobody is using me. Free me.\n```\n\nThe mutator does that check when it drops its +1; if the old box had no other users, the mutator's decrement is the one that does the free.\n\n## On the chain — agreed\n\nYeah, your reasoning is right. Worker A finishes in bounded time (one fire's worth), and any reconfigure chain past that is naturally cleaned up by the next refcount-to-zero. The chain can transiently grow but doesn't accumulate. As long as the garbage collection logic above works, the chain self-shrinks.\n\n## On the orphaned-values question — confirmed, JSONL event\n\nI'll spec the event shape:\n\n```json\n{\"event\":\"reconfigure_discard\", \"box_id\":\"x\",\n \"port\":\"removed_port_name\",\n \"n_values_dropped\":3,\n \"first_value_bytes\":\"...truncated to 256...\",\n \"task_id\":42}\n```\n\nOne event per removed port (not one per value, to avoid log spam). First-value preview helps debugging without runaway log size.\n\n## On unifying the connections dance with the box swap — issue file incoming\n\nI'll write a new issue for \"retire the connections-array atomic-publish pattern; route all box mutations through the box-swap mechanism from 320\" and queue it for after 320 lands. The wrinkle is the \"push values back into the ring buffers\" step when the worker can't grab the CAS. Today's ring buffer doesn't have a \"push to head\" operation — it only pushes to the tail. So if Worker A pops value V from port 3's ring, then fails the CAS, then pushes V back, V goes to the BACK of the queue, behind any new values that arrived in the meantime. That breaks the arrival-order property.\n\nThere are three workable shapes here:\n\n**Shape 1 — Add a push-to-head operation to the ring.** Symmetric with pop-from-head. Used only on the recovery path. Implementation cost is small; the ring already has a head pointer.\n\n**Shape 2 — Peek instead of pop.** The worker peeks each port's next tag (looks at it without consuming). If no reconfigure, proceeds to actually pop. If any reconfigure, tries CAS. On CAS success, pops everything. On CAS fail, hasn't committed anything; just yields. Cleaner because there's nothing to put back.\n\n**Shape 3 — Hold values in worker-local memory until the decision is made.** The pop happens, but the values live in the worker's stack until either the fire commits or the worker becomes the mutator and decides what to do with them. On CAS-fail, the worker re-pushes (tail), accepting the reorder for that specific case.\n\nI'd vote **Shape 2** because it doesn't require any new ring operations and doesn't have a reorder edge case at all. Risk: infinite loop if mutators keep contending.\n   - **c)** C waits with peek-style semantics — leaves the message on the ring, requeues itself, retries naturally on next dispatch. Same as the general yield-and-requeue path.\n   - I'd vote (c) — same mechanism as everything else, no special case.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The graph slot acting as a refcount holder is the conceptually beautiful part of your design.** It naturally encodes \"the runtime considers this box current\" without needing a separate \"is_live\" flag. When a box gets superseded, its lifetime collapses from \"until the run ends\" to \"until in-flight users finish\" — that transition is captured entirely by the graph slot losing its pointer, no extra bookkeeping. The same pattern shows up in epoch-based reclamation and hazard pointers; you've reinvented a chunk of well-tested concurrent-GC theory by reasoning from first principles, which is the highest compliment a design pattern can pay you.\n- **Your pop-N-then-decide instinct catches a structural truth about reconfigure messages.** They aren't normal inputs — they're control plane masquerading as data. The reason they ride the same per-port slot system is convenience (the producer already knows how to reach a port), not because they ARE input values. So the \"decide whether to fire OR mutate based on what's queued\" pattern reflects the actual semantics: control-plane traffic preempts data-plane traffic. The peek-all-first design makes this preemption clean.\n- **The two-state flag + graph slot-as-liveness is structurally simpler than three states.** Every state machine should have as few states as it can get away with — fewer states = fewer transitions = fewer race conditions. Going from three states to two doesn't sound like much, but the THIRD state was the source of most of the \"what does free decision look like\" complexity in my version. Killing it killed half the edge cases.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nI'll update 320's issue file with this synthesised design (two-state flag, graph slot as liveness, refcount + mutator-holds-reference, peek-all-then-decide, JSONL discard event) and add a new issue file for the post-320 connections unification work, both after I hear your answers on the three questions above."
      }],
```
