    "content":"So, I'm thinking about the box freeing. Originally, before thinking about reconfiguring boxes and creating new ones and such, the box's were supposed to be garbage collected by refcount if-and-only-if they would never be able to run again. I was mostly thinking like, initialization steps and such. So the idea was, if there's nothing upstream that can call this box, then it will never receive inputs again, meaning it can never be called again. However, it needed to be that NOTHING upstream could call it - so long as one box could still provide input to it, it could plausibly be called again. However. If there's two upstream from the box we're considering deleting, and one of them can never run again and it has zero values pushed to the ring buffer, but there's lots of extra values in the second input ring buffer... I think, since the box will never run again, it should still be culled, even though there's values in the ring buffer. Though, now that I think of it, if we can add new boxes and make new connections with the reconfigure, then there COULD be new values added! Because a future box might connect and supply new values. So, can we ever actually feel safe and assume that a box will never be called again? I don't think so! But, what happens if we have too many boxes cluttering up memory? That's a memory leak! Hmmmmmmmmmmmmmmm...............\n\n  On your pop-N-then-decide pattern — works, with one wrinkle\n\n  Your design is sound. The wrinkle is the \"push values back into the ring buffers\" step when the worker can't grab the CAS. Today's ring buffer doesn't have a \"push to\n  head\" operation — it only pushes to the tail. So if Worker A pops value V from port 3's ring, then fails the CAS, then pushes V back, V goes to the BACK of the queue,\n  behind any new values that arrived in the meantime. That breaks the arrival-order property.\n\nokay so for this, if we pop the \"messages\" which is how I'm referring to the values in the ring buffer that decides which ring buffer to pop from (native/json) then if there's a reconfigure message, then we shouldn't have popped any values at all. Just the messages, which is okay because once the reconfiguring is done then we know we can pop an extra value from each of the slots that had reconfigure flags. Keep in mind... there might be multiple slots that have reconfigure! In such a case, while we're reconfiguring, we should first pop the reconfigure values. Then, we should pop from those slots again, and if there's any reconfigures (sigh) we repeat until we have an entire task-worth of actual native values. Then, we could apply the first reconfigure and create a task struct with those specific values. Then, we could repeat that for each subsequent reconfigure, each time popping off a new set of values. If we find any reconfigures, then we have to continue the process. Once we have our full set of task structs, we should put them in the ready pool. NOT execute them ourselves on the mutating thread. We must make sure they point to the \"old\" behavior (it's old because, if we had like 5 iterations of this, there'd be 5 different sets of box behavior) and they must also be run on different threads. This is a change from before where one reconfigure was expected maximum. I can see a system a user might make where there's like several boxes that add values to a box and then request to reconfigure it. Each time the box is run they'll want to reconfigure it, but the reconfigures might arrive all at once while the input values might arrive out of order. Actually... what do we do if there's say two reconfigures, and we have enough input values to start the first one but not the second one? Do we just, only apply the first reconfigure and then re-add to the task pool? This is complicated. >.<",
    "role":"user"
  },

        "text":"You're catching a really deep problem and proposing a really clever solution. Let me work through both halves separately.\n\n## On garbage collection paranoia\n\nYou've hit on something fundamental: **in a system that allows runtime creation and reconfiguration, you genuinely cannot prove a box will never run again.** Any currently-running box could call create_box-with-connection-to-Y, or reconfigure-some-existing-box-to-connect-to-Y. There's no finite analysis that says \"this box is unreachable forever.\"\n\nThis is the same problem Java's GC solves with mark-and-sweep, and it's the same problem the Linux kernel deals with via epoch-based reclamation. The general lesson: **you can't reason locally about reachability in a system that allows arbitrary mutation.** You either need a global walk (expensive) or you accept the leak.\n\nFor this codebase, I'd actually argue the right answer is: **don't try to GC live boxes at all.** Here's the reasoning chain:\n\n- The refcount system handles SUPERSEDED boxes (the reconfigure cleanup case). That's the only \"lifetime ends mid-run\" we genuinely need.\n- For boxes that just sit idle with no incoming values — they're not freed, they're just dormant. They consume metadata-sized memory (one box record + slot ids), which is tiny. The values that would otherwise pile up in their slot ring buffers aren't there, because no producer is feeding them.\n- For the case where a user genuinely wants a box destroyed during a run: add an explicit `runtime_destroy_box(id)` API. The user knows when their planner box is done planning. Trust them.\n- Runs are bounded. When the run ends (quiescence), everything gets cleaned up by graph_destroy.\n\nThe leak you're worried about — \"what if we have too many boxes cluttering up memory\" — would only show up in extremely long-running maps that constantly create new boxes without destroying old ones. Each box is ~200 bytes plus its slots. You'd need to create literally millions of boxes for this to matter on a workstation. Maps that long would have other architectural concerns anyway.\n\n**My proposal:** refcount handles superseded-box reclamation (automatic, transparent). Explicit destroy handles user-requested-destruction (rare, opt-in). Nothing tries to be clever about reachability. The leak case is real but practically negligible.\n\n## On the multi-reconfigure question\n\nOK so let me try to simplify what you described, because I think there's a cleaner shape hiding inside your description, and the cleaner shape eliminates the \"what if values for first but not second\" edge case entirely.\n\nYou're absolutely right that **peeking the ordering messages first (without popping any values) is the right move.** That part is the key insight. Let me re-state it in your terms: every input ring has, riding alongside the native and json rings, a third ring that's the **ordering ring** — it stores tags saying \"the next value on this slot is in the native ring\" or \"...is in the json ring\" or \"this is a reconfigure message, not a value.\" The ordering ring's head tells you what kind of thing is up next, without committing to consume the actual value or message yet.\n\nSo the worker's hot path becomes:\n\n```\nworker arrives at box:\n   1. for each input port, peek the head of its ordering ring (just the tag, no consume).\n   2. branch on what you saw:\n        no reconfigures anywhere AND all ports have a value waiting:\n           → pop one ordering tag from each port,\n             follow each tag to its native/json ring,\n             pop the value,\n             fire the box.\n\n        at least one port shows RECONFIGURE at its head:\n           → try CAS to become the mutator. yield if you lose.\n\n        no reconfigures, but some ports are empty:\n           → don't pop anything. nothing to fire yet. exit; the pool\n             will re-spawn this box when more values arrive.\n```\n\nNow for the multi-reconfigure case — here's where I want to push back on the \"build multiple tasks for multiple epochs\" idea. **I don't think we need it.** Let me show why with your scenario.\n\n### Walking through your hard case\n\nSetup: port X has `[R1, v1]`. Port Y has `[R2, v3]`. Two reconfigures (one per port), one fire's worth of values.\n\nWorker arrives. Peeks X → R1. Peeks Y → R2. Both reconfigures visible. Worker becomes mutator. What now?\n\nThe thing to notice: **R1 and R2 are on DIFFERENT ports.** They're not temporally ordered with respect to each other. The producer that pushed R1 onto X did so at some wall-clock moment; the producer that pushed R2 onto Y did so at some other wall-clock moment; the ring buffer system doesn't preserve cross-port ordering. So there's no \"right\" order for R1 vs R2 — apply them in any order, doesn't matter.\n\nMutator pops R1, applies it. Now the box has shape-after-R1. Mutator pops R2, applies it. Now the box has shape-after-R1-and-R2. Mutator releases.\n\nNext worker arrives. Peeks X → v1 (head of X now). Peeks Y → v3 (head of Y now). Both are values. Pops both, fires the box with v1 and v3 under the shape-after-R1-and-R2.\n\n**There's only one fire, and it happens after both reconfigures are applied.** The \"different epochs\" framing doesn't apply because the values v1 and v3 were queued BEHIND the reconfigure messages on their respective ports. So they were always meant for the post-reconfigure shape — that's what the producer signaled by ordering them that way on the ring.\n\nIf the producer had wanted v1 consumed under the pre-reconfigure shape, they would have pushed v1 FIRST, then R1. The ring would be `[v1, R1]`. Peek would show v1; a fire would happen with v1 under OLD shape; then peek would show R1; reconfigure applies; the next fire would be under NEW.\n\n### Now the harder case — back-to-back reconfigures\n\nSetup: port X has `[R1, R2, v1]`. Port Y has `[v3]`.\n\nWorker peeks X → R1. Peeks Y → v3. Has a reconfigure pending. Becomes mutator.\n\nThe mutator's loop:\n- Pop R1 from X. Apply it.\n- Peek X again. Head is now R2 (because R1 got popped). \n- Pop R2. Apply it.\n- Peek X again. Head is now v1. Not a reconfigure.\n- Release mutator role. Don't fire here; let a worker do that.\n\nNext worker arrives. Peeks X → v1, peeks Y → v3. Both values. Pop, fire.\n\n**One fire, after both R1 and R2 are applied.** No multi-task batching.\n\n### And the case you specifically asked about\n\nSetup: port X has `[R1, R2]`. Port Y has `[v3]`. Two reconfigures, only one port has a value.\n\nWorker peeks X → R1. Becomes mutator. Pops R1, applies. Peeks X → R2. Pops R2, applies. Peeks X → empty. Releases.\n\nNext worker arrives. Peeks X → empty. Peeks Y → v3. Mixed — some ports have values, some don't. Worker can't fire. Doesn't pop anything. Exits.\n\nThe next time someone pushes a value to X, the pool will spawn a task for the box. Next worker arrives, peeks X → (whatever's there now). If it's a value AND Y still has v3, fires. Otherwise waits.\n\n**No edge case to handle.** The \"we have enough values for the first reconfigure but not the second\" scenario doesn't actually exist, because reconfigures are NOT consumers of values. They're sideband messages that modify the box. Values are consumed by FIRES, and fires only happen when every required port has a value ready.\n\n### Why I think the multi-task batching isn't needed\n\nYour design described the mutator preparing multiple tasks for different box epochs. But under the simpler \"do one thing per worker visit\" model:\n\n- Reconfigure messages get drained (in batches if multiple are visible at peek time, but only one batch per mutator visit).\n- Fires happen separately, each one under the box's current shape at fire time.\n- A worker either fires once OR mutates once per visit; never both, never multiple of either.\n\nThe pool's natural re-spawning handles the back-and-forth. If there are 5 reconfigures and 5 fires worth of values queued, the workflow is:\n- Worker 1 visits: drains all visible reconfigures, releases.\n- Worker 2 visits: drains any reconfigures that became visible after the first batch (because they were behind the first batch on the rings), or fires if values are next up.\n- ...\n- Eventually all reconfigures are drained and fires proceed normally.\n\nThis is slightly more pool-queue traffic than the \"do everything in one mutator visit\" design, but each pool round-trip is cheap (microseconds). The complexity savings are large — no multi-task batching, no epoch tracking, no \"store this task pointing at the OLD box, submit it, store another pointing at NEW, submit that.\"\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The \"you can't prove a box won't run again\" realisation is the same as the halting problem in disguise.** In a Turing-complete dataflow system (which is what we are, since boxes can create boxes and connect them dynamically), you can't statically determine reachability. The Java GC people solved this with mark-sweep; Linux kernel people solved it with epoch-based reclamation; everybody else solves it with explicit destroy. Your project's vision is closer to \"explicit destroy\" because runs are bounded — when the run ends, everything frees. The leak you were worried about doesn't actually accumulate across runs, just within a single run, which is bounded.\n- **The \"epoch tasks\" idea is reinventing event sourcing.** Your instinct was: instead of mutating state and losing the history, capture the history (each reconfigure is an event) and replay tasks against each state in the history. That's exactly what event sourcing does in distributed systems. It's powerful but adds significant complexity. For this codebase, the \"ring buffer ordering IS the history\" framing is sufficient — values queued behind a reconfigure are implicitly \"for the post-reconfigure shape.\" The implicit ordering replaces explicit epoch tracking.\n- **The peek-don't-pop discipline solves the push-back problem entirely.** You arrived at this independently and correctly: if you commit nothing until you've inspected everything, there's nothing to put back if you bail. The same pattern shows up in database transactions (read-then-decide-then-commit), in optimistic concurrency control, and in modern parser combinators (peek-don't-consume until you know the production matches). It's a strong general pattern: in any concurrent system, prefer \"look first, commit later\" over \"commit first, undo if wrong.\"\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## Questions back\n\n1. **Do you buy the \"no multi-task batching, do one thing per worker visit\" simplification?** It dramatically simplifies the mutator's logic and eliminates the edge case you were worried about. The cost is more pool round-trips when many reconfigures are queued — but that cost is small.\n\n2. **Are you OK with \"no GC of live boxes, only superseded ones\"?** Plus an explicit `runtime_destroy_box(id)` API for users who want to actively clean up? That sidesteps the unreachability halting problem cleanly.\n\n3. **One subtle thing about the mutator's \"drain multiple visible reconfigures in one go\" loop** — should there be a cap on how many it'll drain before releasing? If a malicious or buggy producer keeps pushing reconfigures faster than the mutator can apply them, the mutator could be stuck draining forever. A cap (say, 100 reconfigures per mutator visit, then release and let someone else continue) would be a safety valve. Worth adding, or YAGNI?\n\nOnce you've signed off on these, I'll update 320's issue file with the consolidated design and start implementing."

    "content":"  2. What does the reconfigure tag carry in the case of an EMPTY box (no input ports)? Without input ports there's no third ring to put the message on. Does a box with\n  no inputs simply lose the ability to be reconfigured by message? Or do we add a \"control ring\" attached to the box itself, separate from input ports? My instinct: the\n  control ring is cleaner and generalizes (control messages aren't tied to a port, they're tied to the box). It also feels right because a reconfigure message isn't\n  conceptually an \"input value\" — it's a control plane thing.\n\n\nas far as I know there's only one type of box that would qualify for this, and it's the \"read\" boxes. For those, I think we just have to delete and re-create. Speaking of which... What if we made the \"create-a-box\" box take the same type of struct as the reconfigure process? And if it has the same box ID as an already existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure process.\n\n  3. Reconfiguring a box that's in the middle of being reconfigured — Worker B is mutating. Worker C arrives with a second reconfigure message in hand. C tries the CAS,\n  fails (flag = 1). What should C do?\n\nwe should check the CAS before popping values. That way, there's no way to know that we need to reconfigure - worker C could never arrive with a reconfigure message \"in hand\" because it can only receive such messages if the CAS is free.\n\n  You've hit on something fundamental: in a system that allows runtime creation and reconfiguration, you genuinely cannot prove a box will never run again. Any\n  currently-running box could call create_box-with-connection-to-Y, or reconfigure-some-existing-box-to-connect-to-Y. There's no finite analysis that says \"this box is\n  unreachable forever.\"\n\n\nOkay. Let's add an issue file to add a box delete functionality. Maybe in the \"create-a-box\" function we could rename it to just... box... and if we supply an ID and nothing else, no wires or anything (what's the minimum we'd need to supply?) then it would delete the box instead of creating a new one. The ID is already in use, and we want to \"clear\" it, and cleared boxes are just ID's floating in the void... so we can GC them then.\n\n  - The peek-don't-pop discipline solves the push-back problem entirely. You arrived at this independently and correctly: if you commit nothing until you've inspected\n  everything, there's nothing to put back if you bail. The same pattern shows up in database transactions (read-then-decide-then-commit), in optimistic concurrency\n  control, and in modern parser combinators (peek-don't-consume until you know the production matches). It's a strong general pattern: in any concurrent system, prefer\n  \"look first, commit later\" over \"commit first, undo if wrong.\"\n\n\nGot it... So what we're doing is peeking one value at a time until we get to the end, and if no reconfigures are found then we go back and pop them all, and continue the run. If a reconfigure is found, then we set the CAS (if impossible, then we just silently yarq ourselves) and apply the reconfigure. Question... Say two workers are peeking / popping values at once. They both peek and get the same set of peeked values, say [v1, v2, v3] for the three input slots. Then, the first worker pops the first values and gets [v1, v2, v3] and the second worker pops the values and gets [v4, v5, R1] - uh-oh, we found a reconfigure! Even though we didn't peek any! Gosh what to do, what to do... Should peeking be atomic? I don't think that'll help. Should peeking return a pointer to the value, and every peek increments the ring-buffer index? This is a genuinely hard problem...",

        "text":"You found a genuine race, and it's the deepest problem we've hit yet. Let me think through it carefully because the answer reshapes some of what we've decided.\n\n## Walking through what you just identified\n\nLet me restate to make sure I understand: two workers, A and B, both arrive at the same box at roughly the same time. Both peek every input port's head. Both see `[v1, v2, v3]`. Both decide \"no reconfigures, proceed to pop.\" A wins the pop race and gets `[v1, v2, v3]`. B's pops return `[v4, v5, R1]` — because v1, v2, v3 are gone, what B actually gets is whatever is NOW at the head of each ring.\n\nB has popped a reconfigure message it never saw during peek. B's choice is now: apply the reconfigure (but it already popped v4 and v5, which were meant for who?), or somehow undo. Both are bad.\n\n**Your three suggestions, evaluated:**\n\n- *Should peeking be atomic?* Atomic across what? Atomic peek of a single ring is already true. Atomic peek across THREE rings simultaneously is the hard part — it would essentially require locking all three rings at once, which is the very serialization we wanted to avoid.\n\n- *Should peek return a pointer and advance the index?* This is \"soft pop\" — reserve but don't release. The problem: if B bails (because it sees a reconfigure in its reserved set), the reservation has to be released. And once released, A might already have pop-committed past the reserved spot. We're in the same push-back problem we tried to avoid, just dressed up in different clothes.\n\nThe honest answer: **peek-then-pop cannot be made race-free across multiple rings without serializing the workers somewhere.** The race is inherent to \"two workers reading different rings at the same time.\"\n\n## When this race can actually happen\n\nHere's a saving grace: **the race only exists for boxes that allow multiple concurrent fires.** Most boxes in this system are single-spawn — only one task at a time gathers for them. For those, A and B can't both be gathering simultaneously, so the race doesn't appear.\n\nThe multi-spawn case (iterators, certain runtime-created boxes) is where this bites. The graph loader marks each box with whether it's multi-spawn-capable (the `multi_spawn` field on the box record).\n\nSo the cost of solving this only has to be paid by multi-spawn boxes. Single-spawn boxes get the simpler peek-then-pop dance for free.\n\n## Proposal — gather serialization on multi-spawn boxes only\n\nThe cleanest answer I can see: **on multi-spawn boxes, the gather phase is serialized through a per-box gather lock.** It's a CAS, brief (microseconds), and only contended when multiple workers genuinely want to fire the same box at the same time.\n\nThis means we'd revise your earlier principle slightly. The original framing was \"workers don't take YARQ — they're just reading values, not mutating them.\" But popping values from a shared ring IS a mutation; it changes the slot's head pointer and removes the value from the ring. When two workers pop from the same set of rings concurrently, they're racing on shared mutable state.\n\nSo a more precise version of your principle: **workers don't take YARQ for reading box METADATA (the input port list, the function pointer, the connections array). But for popping values from rings shared across multi-spawn fires, workers DO need brief serialization.**\n\nThis separates two different concerns:\n- **YARQ-for-mutation** (rare, taken by reconfigure / runtime_connect / box-swap operations).\n- **Gather-lock** (frequent on multi-spawn boxes, brief, just guards the peek-and-pop atomicity).\n\nThey could be the same atomic word with different semantics, or two separate words. I'd lean toward separate words: the gather lock is needed thousands of times per run; the YARQ is needed rarely. Conflating them means the rare reconfigure has to wait for every concurrent gather to finish, which is fine but loses some opportunity.\n\nOr — alternative — single-spawn boxes simply don't need a gather lock at all (because there's only one gatherer ever), so they skip it. Multi-spawn boxes take the gather lock for the duration of the peek-pop window.\n\n## On your other points\n\n**Read boxes have no inputs, so no ring for reconfigure messages.** Agreed — delete-and-recreate is the right answer. Read boxes are stateless cached values; rebuilding one is cheap.\n\n**\"create-a-box\" takes the same struct as reconfigure; same-ID means reconfigure.** YES, this is a great unification. The runtime mutation API collapses to one entry point: `runtime_apply_box_spec(spec_json)`. The dispatch reads the `id` field:\n- If the id is new → create.\n- If the id exists → reconfigure.\n\nThis is structurally honest: creating a box and reconfiguring a box are both \"express what this box should be.\" The implementation difference (allocate-then-publish vs swap-and-supersede) is a runtime detail, not a user-facing distinction.\n\n**\"check CAS before popping\"** — yes, exactly right. This is the same point as my proposed peek-first design, just stated more clearly: workers commit to nothing until they know the box is safe to operate on. If a worker sees a reconfigure message while peeking, it CASes first; if CAS fails, no values were touched, no rollback needed.\n\n**Box delete = \"create\" with just ID, nothing else.** Lovely. The minimum to supply is the ID and a flag like `\"delete\": true` (or some marker that distinguishes \"delete me\" from \"I forgot to fill in other fields\"). I'd suggest an explicit `\"action\": \"delete\"` field to avoid ambiguity. Deleted boxes get their refcount-driven cleanup via the same mechanism as superseded boxes. I'll write an issue file for this.\n\n## What I want to confirm with you before writing the design up\n\n1. **Are you OK with workers taking a brief gather lock on multi-spawn boxes?** This is the cleanest answer to the race you found. It's a CAS, uncontended in the common case (most boxes are single-spawn), brief in the contended case (microseconds). Your earlier principle was \"workers don't take YARQ\" — I'm proposing a refinement where \"workers don't take YARQ for METADATA reads, but DO take a brief gather-lock for popping values on multi-spawn boxes.\"\n\n2. **Separate locks or the same lock?** Option (a): one atomic word per box, used both for mutation and for multi-spawn gather. Simpler. Cost: rare reconfigures wait for any current gather to finish, which is fine. Option (b): two atomic words, one for each purpose. Slightly faster but more bookkeeping. I'd vote (a) for simplicity.\n\n3. **The unified `runtime_apply_box_spec` — should it also handle the delete case?** I.e., one entry point that does create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec's content?\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The race you found is a textbook example of \"linearizability across multiple objects.\"** Each ring buffer is independently atomic, but the CROSS-RING operation (peek every port, then pop every port) is not. This is the same problem distributed databases solve with two-phase commit: you can either serialize the cross-object operation, or you can accept that some operations might observe a transient inconsistent state and need to retry. Your project is small enough that serialization (per-box gather lock) is cheap. For larger systems, the trade-off shifts toward lock-free designs with retry loops.\n- **The \"single-spawn vs multi-spawn\" distinction is doing a LOT of work in this design.** Iterator boxes are basically the only multi-spawn case in normal use. By scoping the gather lock to multi-spawn boxes, we pay the synchronization cost exactly where it's actually needed — and the vast majority of fires (call boxes with simple inputs) cost nothing extra. The graph loader already computes this attribute, so we get the scoping for free.\n- **\"Workers don't claim YARQ\" was the right principle, with an important refinement: it applies to BOX-METADATA reads, not to RING POPS.** Reading the input port list is non-destructive; that's where the original principle applies — readers shouldn't pay for the writers' work. Popping a value is destructive; that genuinely needs some coordination among concurrent poppers. The refined principle preserves the original intent (no YARQ for metadata) while honestly acknowledging that popping is a different beast.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nIf you sign off on the gather-lock proposal, I'll consolidate everything we've discussed — two-state flag, graph-slot-as-liveness, refcount + mutator-holds-reference, peek-don't-pop, per-multi-spawn-box gather lock, unified runtime_apply_box_spec — into 320's issue file. Then we can start implementing."

```json
{
  "uuid":"4aec0c6c-695a-44c3-a11b-b8bfd761c29e",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-25T02:52:14.001Z",
  "slug":"goofy-noodling-torvalds",
  "parentUuid":"bbdbb501-cbd5-443d-9778-bfbd59edfcd5",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "promptId":"027a6419-848c-4a75-b737-b54f0f713a36",
  "userType":"external",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits",
  "message":{
    "content":"  When this race can actually happen\n\n  Here's a saving grace: the race only exists for boxes that allow multiple concurrent fires. Most boxes in this system are single-spawn — only one task at a time\n  gathers for them. For those, A and B can't both be gathering simultaneously, so the race doesn't appear.\n\n  The multi-spawn case (iterators, certain runtime-created boxes) is where this bites. The graph loader marks each box with whether it's multi-spawn-capable (the\n  multi_spawn field on the box record).\n\n  So the cost of solving this only has to be paid by multi-spawn boxes. Single-spawn boxes get the simpler peek-then-pop dance for free.\n\n\nactually this isn't true at all, all of the boxes are intended to have multiple tasks running in parallel at once.\n\nHow about this. What if we switch to pop-only semantics? The reason is, with multithreaded design, if you ever peek at something you can't be sure that someone isn't also looking at the same value. This is fine for read-only things, but if you ever need to pop that value later on... it might make problems.\n\nso here's a design, tell me what you think.\n\nWorker A arrives at a box and requests a set of inputs. Worker A's thread runs the gather_inputs() function or whatever. We could make this function be atomic - only one thread can be running it at once. If another thread attempts, then they get yarq'd. The gather_inputs() function will first peek at the first N values of the ordering ring. It's okay to peek here because we're in an atomic function. If any of them are reconfigure, it will immediately pop the reconfigure value (from where? the input ring buffers have a set size, and they're expecting like an integer or whatever. Do we have a separate ring buffer for the pointers to the reconfigure json? Or are we storing the reconfigure pointers inline with the integer inputs and such?) If any of the ordering messages are reconfigure, it will immediately apply the reconfiguration and swap the box pointer. I think this should resolve most of our issues. If none of the ordering messages are reconfigure, then it will pop them all and return them to the worker. So essentially a worker arriving at a box is \"either run this function, or reconfigure it\" - never both. Reconfigure yarq's itself after it's done. How does that sound?",
    "role":"user"
  },
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}

Reconfigure messages are variable-length JSON — could be a few hundred bytes, could be many kilobytes. They don't fit the same shape.\n\nThere are two ways to attach reconfigure messages to a box. We add a third \"reconfigure\" data ring per slot, storing the JSON payload via the large-value heap (so variable-size is handled cleanly).\n- The ordering ring's tags grow a third possible value — RECONFIGURE — telling the consumer \"the head of the ordering ring points at the reconfigure ring, not native or json.\"\n- Gather peeks every port's ordering ring as part of its scan.\n- Empty boxes (no input ports) can't receive reconfigure messages this way — they need delete-and-recreate (which you already agreed to).\n\n**Way 2 — A single per-box control queue, completely separate from any input port.**\n- Each box has its own small ring buffer attached directly to it (not to any port), specifically for control messages like reconfigure.\n- The runtime API `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, spec_json)` pushes onto the target box's control queue. Producer C pushes onto port Z. Three workers (W1, W2, W3) are spawned for box B (because all input ports are ready).\n\nW1 arrives first. CAS flag 0 → 1. Wins. Enters gather. Might win or lose depending on timing.\n- If wins: enters gather, finds rings empty (W1 just drained them), can't fire. Releases. The pool will respawn W2 if more values arrive.\n- If loses: yields. The runtime API pushes the spec onto box B's control queue.\n\nWorker W1 arrives. CAS flag 0 → 1. Wins. Enters gather. Checks control queue: non-empty. **Decision: mutate, not fire.** Pops the spec from the control queue. Builds a new box record (call it B'). Atomically swaps the graph slot's pointer from B to B'. Drops the mutator's refcount on B. Releases the flag (sets B's flag back to 0 — though it doesn't really matter, B is now superseded).\n\nWhat about the value that producer pushed onto port X? It's still in the ring buffer attached to slot ID for port X. **And here's the key — the new box B' carries the SAME slot IDs.** The slots themselves didn't move; they belong to the slot store, identified by integer IDs. This collapses the \"YARQ for mutation, separate gather lock for popping\" idea into one word. Simpler. The cost: a rare mutator waits for at most one in-flight gather to finish, which is microseconds.\n\n3. **Are we done with the design phase?** If you sign off on these two, I'll consolidate everything we've discussed into the 320 issue file, add the connections-unification follow-up issue, and the box-delete issue.   "message":{
    "content":"  - Any head is a reconfigure: pop the reconfigure message, apply it (build new box, swap the graph slot), release the flag. Don't fire. The worker either submits a new\n  task for the (now-new) box or just returns — the pool will naturally spawn fresh tasks when producers push more values.\n\nwe would need to yarq in this case. Otherwise, we'll have an extra set of values just sitting in the input buffer forever.\n\n  On your storage question\n\n  You're asking exactly the right question. The input ring buffers hold values, and a typical value is something like an integer or a short string. Reconfigure messages\n  are variable-length JSON — could be a few hundred bytes, could be many kilobytes. They don't fit the same shape.\n\n\nwhat if we just store a pointer to the reconfigure json that's been malloc'd somewhere? And after the reconfigure, we'd free it, because there's no reason to keep it afterwards. Or, even better, what if we just... pointed the box at the reconfigure input value? That way we wouldn't even have to create a new box and populate the values and such - it's already built, it's just sitting in memory somewhere.",
    "role":"user"
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Both of these corrections are right and the second one is genuinely elegant. Let me work through them.\n\n## On the YARQ-after-reconfigure correction\n\nYou're correct, and my earlier description had a bug. Here's the scenario:\n\nProducer pushes a value onto port X of box B. The pool spawns a task for box B (because B has inputs ready). Meanwhile, someone pushes a reconfigure onto B's control queue. Worker W1 arrives, wins the gather flag, checks the control queue, decides to mutate, applies the reconfigure, swaps the graph slot, releases the flag, and returns.\n\nBut the value on port X is still sitting in its ring. Nobody scheduled a fresh task — because no producer pushed anything new (producers don't push for nothing; the push that originally caused the spawn was already consumed by the spawn decision).\n\nThe value just sits there, orphaned. Eventually the run quiesces with this dangling value, and the box never fires.\n\nThe fix: **the mutator yields-and-requeues itself instead of just returning.** It tells the pool \"I'm not actually done; please put me back at the tail of the queue.\" The pool re-queues a task for box B. Eventually some worker picks it up, arrives at B (which now points at the NEW box struct via the graph slot), wins the gather flag, peeks the inputs, sees the value waiting, and fires under the new shape.\n\nThis is the same yield-and-requeue mechanism we already use when a worker can't grab the gather flag (because someone else has it). One unified path: any time a worker arrives at a box and doesn't actually fire, it yarqs.\n\n## On the \"point the box at the reconfigure input\" idea\n\nThis is wonderful. Let me make sure I'm reading you right: the reconfigure message doesn't need to be JSON that the mutator parses — it can already BE a fully-built box struct, sitting in memory, ready to use. The mutator's job is just to take that pointer and atomically substitute it into the graph slot.\n\nIf that's what you mean, then yes, this is the right design. Walking through the consequences:\n\n**Who builds the new box struct?**\n\nWhoever calls the runtime API. For an internal C caller, that's straightforward — they construct the struct directly. For a Lua box calling `soramech.reconfigure(target_id, {kind=\"call\", fn=\"new_fn\", ...})`, the Lua language bridge code does the build: it reads the Lua table, allocates a new box struct, fills in the fields, and hands the pointer to the runtime. The bridge does the same kind of work it already does today for `create_box` — it's the same shape.\n\nFor a \"reconfigure box\" kind (where some box receives a JSON spec on an input port and pushes a reconfigure), that box's spec invoke parses the JSON and builds the struct.\n\nIn all cases: by the time the message reaches the target box's control queue, it's already a pre-built struct pointer. No parsing happens inside the gather lock.\n\n**What does the control queue actually hold?**\n\nJust pointers. Each cell in the control queue is one pointer (8 bytes). A small ring — say, 8 cells per box — is enough to absorb bursts of reconfigures. If the ring fills up (which would require 8 reconfigures arriving in microseconds, faster than any worker can drain them), pushers block briefly waiting for space.\n\nNo JSON bytes ever live in a ring. No large-value heap involvement for control messages. The cells are tiny fixed-size pointer slots.\n\n**What does the mutator actually do?**\n\n```\nmutator wins the gather flag:\n   check control queue. it's non-empty.\n   pop one box-struct pointer (call it NEW).\n   resolve port mappings: for each port in NEW, find the matching\n       slot id from OLD (rename by name match), or allocate a new\n       slot if the port is brand new.\n   patch NEW's input_slot_ids[] with the resolved IDs.\n   atomically swap the graph slot pointer from OLD to NEW.\n   release the gather flag.\n   yarq.\n```\n\nThe slot-resolution step is the only non-trivial work. Ports that exist in both OLD and NEW (matched by name) share the same slot ID — the underlying ring buffer keeps all its queued values intact across the reconfigure. Ports that are new in NEW get freshly allocated slots. Ports that existed in OLD but not in NEW are abandoned — their slot IDs aren't in NEW, so nobody reads from them anymore; their remaining values get logged to the JSONL discard event you specified, and the slot itself can be released when OLD is freed.\n\n**What about the OLD box struct?**\n\nIt stays alive as long as any in-flight worker is using it (refcount > 0). The graph slot now points at NEW, so no new workers will land on OLD. When OLD's refcount hits zero, it's freed.\n\nThe free includes freeing the box struct's malloc'd memory (the struct itself) and releasing any per-box state that the new box doesn't share (like the slots for ports that were removed).\n\n## What this gives us\n\nThe reconfigure mechanism becomes structurally tiny:\n\n- The control queue is a fixed-size ring of pointers. Cheap.\n- The runtime API takes a box struct pointer. Caller builds it; runtime takes ownership.\n- The mutator's work is: resolve slots, swap graph pointer, release, yarq. No JSON parsing on the hot path. No variable-size storage. No \"where does the message live\" question because the message IS the new box.\n\nIt also means the **\"create\" and \"reconfigure\" operations converge even more cleanly** than we discussed before. Both are just \"here's a new box struct, please install it.\" Create: install at a fresh graph slot. Reconfigure: install at an existing graph slot, supersede the old occupant. Delete: install NULL at the graph slot, supersede the old occupant.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **\"The message IS the new box\" is the same pattern as immutable persistent data structures.** In Clojure or Haskell, you don't mutate a data structure in place — you produce a new version and let the runtime swap pointers. Old versions stick around as long as anyone references them. Your reconfigure design lands in the same place by reasoning about concurrent dataflow: the mutator builds a new immutable thing and atomically swaps in the new reference. Everyone holding the old reference finishes their work cleanly; the old thing eventually goes away. The pattern shows up independently in functional programming, in Linux RCU, and now in your dataflow runtime — three different domains converging on the same answer because the problem shape is the same.\n- **Putting the build work on the producer's side is a load-balancing move.** Parsing JSON, validating fields, allocating arrays — all of that happens in whoever called the runtime API, in their own time, on their own thread. The mutator's critical section (the gather lock hold) shrinks to \"swap pointer, resolve a few slot IDs.\" That's microseconds. The slower work (the parse) doesn't block anyone else's work on the same box.\n- **The slot-id stability across reconfigures is the unsung hero of the whole design.** Because port names map to stable slot IDs, the ring buffers don't need to move. A port \"x\" with 100 queued values stays exactly where it is across a reconfigure. The new box just keeps referencing the same slot ID. That's the cheapest possible transition: zero bytes copied.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## What I want to confirm\n\n1. **Control queue depth — 8 pointer cells per box?** Or do you want a different number? It's small fixed memory per box (64 bytes) and only matters under very bursty reconfigure traffic.\n\n2. **The runtime API surface — does it take a pre-built box struct directly, or does it take JSON and parse internally (with the parse happening in the caller's thread)?** Both are workable; \"takes a struct\" is faster and forces language bridges to do their job; \"takes JSON\" is more uniform across languages. My instinct: take a struct, provide a parse-JSON-to-struct helper for callers that want it.\n\n3. **Are we done designing?** If you sign off on these two, I'll consolidate the entire design into 320's issue file (replacing the older sketch), write the connections-unification follow-up issue, and write the box-delete-via-runtime-API issue. Then we move to implementation."
      }],

  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits",
  "message":{
    "content":"  Just pointers. Each cell in the control queue is one pointer (8 bytes). A small ring — say, 8 cells per box — is enough to absorb bursts of reconfigures. If the ring\n  fills up (which would require 8 reconfigures arriving in microseconds, faster than any worker can drain them), pushers block briefly waiting for space.\n\nwhy not just use a ring-buffer? They're such a versatile pattern...\n\n  The free includes freeing the box struct's malloc'd memory (the struct itself) and releasing any per-box state that the new box doesn't share (like the slots for ports\n   that were removed).\n\nhow does it know which slots to remove?\n\n  2. The runtime API surface — does it take a pre-built box struct directly, or does it take JSON and parse internally (with the parse happening in the caller's thread)?\n   Both are workable; \"takes a struct\" is faster and forces language bridges to do their job; \"takes JSON\" is more uniform across languages. My instinct: take a struct,\n  provide a parse-JSON-to-struct helper for callers that want it.\n\n\nwe should use json because it can be created cross-languages easier. The language specs we should try and make as lean as possible so people will actually want to create new ones.",
    "role":"user"
  },

  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"All three points push the design in good directions. Let me respond.\n\n## On using a ring buffer\n\nYou're completely right — I was overthinking the naming. The control queue IS a ring buffer; that's exactly the pattern. And we should use the same primitive we use everywhere else: the slot store. A box's control queue is just another slot allocated from the slot store, sized to hold pointer-cells.\n\nConcretely: at box creation time, the runtime allocates one extra slot per box flagged as the control slot. Cell capacity = sizeof(void*). Cell count = some small number (8 is plenty). The slot store's existing per-slot spinlock handles concurrent pushes for free, and pops use the same FIFO ordering the rest of the system already understands.\n\nThis is structurally honest about what the system is doing: every box has input slots for its incoming values plus one control slot for its incoming reconfigure messages. All slots, all rings, one mechanism. Reusing the primitive means no new code paths to maintain.\n\n## On knowing which slots to remove\n\nWalk through the algorithm:\n\nThe mutator has the OLD box in hand (with its input port names and the slot IDs they map to) and the NEW box just popped from the control queue (with input port names, but no slot IDs filled in yet).\n\nFor each port name in NEW: look that name up in OLD's port list.\n- **Found in OLD:** copy OLD's slot ID for that name into NEW. The ring buffer keeps all its queued values intact; the new box just keeps reading from the same place.\n- **Not found in OLD:** this is a brand-new port. Allocate a fresh slot from the slot store, put the new slot ID into NEW.\n\nFor each port name in OLD: look that name up in NEW's port list.\n- **Found in NEW:** already handled (shared slot).\n- **Not found in NEW:** this slot is abandoned. Add it to the OLD box's \"to-be-released\" list. When OLD is eventually freed (refcount hits zero), the to-be-released slots get released back to the slot store, and any leftover values in them get logged to the JSONL discard event.\n\nThe matching is by port name. Rename = effectively delete + add: if you change \"x\" to \"x_renamed\", \"x\" appears only in OLD (to release) and \"x_renamed\" appears only in NEW (to allocate). Any queued values on \"x\" get discarded.\n\nIf you wanted \"rename keeps the queued values,\" you'd need an explicit rename declaration in the spec — something like `{\"rename\": {\"old_name\": \"x\", \"new_name\": \"x_renamed\"}}`. Worth supporting? Maybe later. For now, rename-as-delete-plus-add is honest about what the message means: the producer who pushed onto \"x\" probably doesn't know about the rename, so dropping the values is conservative.\n\n## On JSON as the API contract\n\nSold. JSON it is — for exactly the reason you said: it keeps the language bridge work as small as possible. Every language can format JSON in a few lines. Asking each language bridge to know about C struct layouts would be a big lift, and would discourage adding new languages.\n\nSo the API shape becomes:\n\n```\nruntime_apply_box_spec(target_id, json_bytes, json_len, error_out)\n```\n\nThe runtime, in the caller's thread (whichever language called it), parses the JSON into a new box struct using the same parser the graph loader uses today (the refactored version that takes an in-memory buffer instead of a file path). Validates. Pushes the struct pointer to the target's control slot. Returns success or a parse error.\n\nThe mutator, when it eventually wins the gather flag, just pops the pointer and swaps. Pure pointer work.\n\nFor the JSONL transcript, we can keep the raw JSON bytes around long enough to log them. Either: copy the JSON into the JSONL event at push time (so the log records \"this is the spec that was queued\"), or re-serialize the box struct back to JSON at apply time (so the log records \"this is what actually applied\"). I'd vote the latter — it's the source of truth for what the box became, not just what was requested.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **Reusing the slot store for control messages is a design coherence win.** Every \"thing that moves through the system\" goes through the same ring-buffer primitive — input values, output values, now reconfigure messages. One mechanism, one set of edge cases to learn, one set of tests to maintain. The alternative would have been a special \"control plane\" mechanism just for reconfigure; that's exactly the kind of code that drifts away from the main code over time and grows its own subtle bugs.\n- **The port-name set-difference algorithm is what graphdiff libraries do.** When git compares two file trees, or when a UI framework diffs old-tree-of-elements vs new-tree-of-elements, the algorithm is identical to what we just sketched: match by stable identifier, ports-only-in-old get destroyed, ports-only-in-new get created, ports-in-both get preserved. You've reinvented React's reconciliation algorithm at the level of a single box's input ports.\n- **\"JSON as the API contract\" is the contract-as-text-not-binary principle.** Same reasoning that makes HTTP win over RPC frameworks for cross-system APIs: anyone with a string formatter can participate, no SDK required. By keeping the runtime API at the JSON layer, you make \"add a new language to SoraMech\" a smaller commitment — the new language only needs to learn JSON, which it almost certainly already knows.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## What I want to confirm\n\n1. **Use the slot store for the control queue, allocated as an extra slot per box?** Cell capacity = pointer size. Cell count = 8 (or whatever small number; tunable later).\n\n2. **Slot diffing by port name with rename-as-delete-plus-add?** And explicit `{\"rename\": ...}` declarations as a future enhancement if a use case appears.\n\n3. **JSONL records the post-apply state** (re-serialised from the resulting box struct), not the pre-apply spec?\n\n4. **Are we done designing?** If you sign off, I'll consolidate into the 320 issue file, write the connections-unification follow-up issue, and write the box-delete issue."

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via the runtime spec API\n\n## Status\nopen · design settled (consolidated through several discussion\nrounds), no code landed yet\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses\n`boxes/<id>.json` once, fills in every field — kind, language,\nfunction pointer, input port list, routing shape, outgoing\nconnections — and the dispatch layer reads that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes the box's record.\n\nThe two ways the runtime already has to \"modify the graph while\nrunning\" — the `create_box` and `connect` primitives from issue\n319, and the load-time encapsulation splice from issue 248 —\nboth **add** to the graph. Neither one **changes** a box that\nalready exists.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\nreplaced wholesale via a runtime API. Anyone holding a reference\nto the runtime can call `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id,\nspec_json)` and atomically swap a box's identity. The same API\ncovers create (target id is new), reconfigure (target id\nexists), and delete (spec asks for deletion).\n\n## Concept in one paragraph\n\nEvery box has a tiny atomic flag and a small per-box control\nqueue. A reconfigure request arrives as a fully-parsed\nreplacement box struct, pushed onto the target's control queue.\nWhen a worker arrives at the box to fire it, the worker first\ntries to claim the flag (CAS 0 → 1); if it wins, it checks the\ncontrol queue. A non-empty queue means there's a pending\nmutation — the worker becomes the mutator, pops the replacement\nstruct, atomically swaps the graph slot pointer from old to new,\nreleases the flag, and yields-and-requeues. An empty control\nqueue means the worker proceeds with a normal fire under the\ngather flag. Either way: a worker visit is exactly one of fire\nor mutate, never both. The flag holds for microseconds; in-flight\nfires don't take it. Old boxes drift toward freedom via a\nreference count once the graph slot stops pointing at them.\n\n## The five structural pieces\n\n### 1. The gather flag\n\nEach box record carries one atomic int — the gather flag — with\ntwo states:\n\n- **0 (free):** any worker may attempt to enter.\n- **1 (held):** exactly one worker is currently in the gather\n  section.\n\nWorkers entering a box do a CAS from 0 to 1. If the CAS wins,\nthe worker enters the gather section. If it loses, the worker\nyields-and-requeues — its task goes back to the tail of the\npool queue, the pool picks it up later. No spinning, no\nblocking.\n\nThe gather section is brief: peek a few input ports' ordering\nrings, decide fire-or-mutate, pop the appropriate cells, release\nthe flag. Microseconds. Workers on DIFFERENT boxes don't contend\n— the flag is per-box.\n\n### 2. The control queue\n\nEvery box has one slot dedicated to incoming control messages,\nallocated from the slot store at box-creation time. Cell capacity\nis sizeof(void*); cell count is small (8 is plenty). The cells\nhold pointers to pre-built replacement box structs.\n\nThe control queue is structurally identical to any other slot\nthe dispatch uses — same ring-buffer primitive, same per-slot\nspinlock for concurrent producers. The only thing that\ndistinguishes it is what's stored in the cells (pointers, not\nvalue bytes) and who reads it (the mutator inside the gather\nsection, not the spec's invoke).\n\n### 3. The graph slot as liveness indicator\n\nThe graph stores boxes as an array of pointers, one per box id.\nWorker lookup goes: `graph_box(graph, id) → returns the current\npointer at that index`. The mutator's job during a reconfigure\nis to atomically swap that pointer from the old box's address\nto the new box's address. Any worker that LATER looks up the\nsame id gets the new box; any worker that already grabbed the\nold pointer keeps it for the duration of its fire.\n\nA box is \"live\" when the graph slot points at it. A box is\n\"superseded\" when the graph slot points at something else (or at\nNULL, for the delete case).\n\nThe two-state flag doesn't need a third \"redirect\" state because\nthe graph slot itself is what new arrivals consult. Workers\narriving fresh get the current box via the graph slot; workers\nmid-fire on the old box finish on the old box. Both work cleanly.\n\n### 4. The reference count\n\nEach box record has an atomic refcount. Workers increment it at\nthe top of their fire (right after resolving the pointer through\nthe graph slot) and decrement at the bottom. The mutator\nincrements it when it becomes the mutator and decrements after\nthe swap.\n\nA box is freeable when BOTH:\n- The graph slot doesn't point at it (it's superseded), AND\n- The refcount has dropped to zero.\n\nThe worker whose decrement returns 0 checks both conditions. If\nboth hold, that worker frees the old box. If only refcount = 0\nbut graph slot still points at the box, the box is just\ntransiently idle — leave it alone.\n\nThe mutator's \"hold a +1 during the reconfigure\" discipline\nensures the refcount can only fall to zero AFTER the mutator\nhas finished its work. Without that, a race could decrement to\nzero while the mutator is still mid-swap.\n\n### 5. The replacement box struct\n\nA reconfigure message IS a fully-built box struct, sitting in\nmemory. The caller of `runtime_apply_box_spec` is responsible\nfor parsing the spec JSON into a `box_t` struct in their own\nthread. Once built, the caller pushes the struct's pointer to\nthe target's control queue.\n\nThis means the mutator's hot path doesn't include JSON parsing.\nThe mutator pops a pointer, does slot resolution (see below),\nand atomically swaps the graph slot. The slow work happens in\nproducer threads, in parallel with anything else going on.\n\n## The worker arrival flow\n\nWhen a worker is handed a task to fire box X:\n\n```\n1. look up the graph slot for X → get current box pointer (call it B).\n2. CAS the gather flag on B from 0 to 1.\n   - lose: yarq this task. exit.\n   - win: continue.\n3. increment B's refcount.\n4. peek B's control queue.\n   - non-empty: become MUTATOR (see below).\n   - empty: continue to gather inputs.\n5. for each input port i:\n     pop one ordering message from input slot i.\n     pop the corresponding value from the indicated data ring (native or json).\n6. release B's gather flag (set to 0).\n7. call the spec's invoke with the gathered values.\n8. push outputs to downstream slots per B's connections.\n9. decrement B's refcount.\n   - if refcount == 0 AND graph slot != B: free B.\n```\n\nImportant: pop is committed only AFTER the gather flag is held\nand the control queue is checked. There's no race window where\na popped value could be lost.\n\n## The mutator flow\n\nWhen a worker enters the gather section, finds the control queue\nnon-empty, and becomes the mutator:\n\n```\n1. pop one box-pointer (call it NEW) from the control queue.\n2. resolve NEW's input_slot_ids by port-name matching against OLD:\n     for each port in NEW:\n       if same name exists in OLD: copy that slot id into NEW.\n       else: allocate a fresh slot from the slot store; record the new id in NEW.\n3. record OLD's \"abandoned slots\" = ports in OLD but not in NEW.\n   these slots get released when OLD is freed; any remaining\n   queued values emit a discard JSONL event.\n4. NEW gets its own freshly-allocated control queue slot.\n5. atomically swap the graph slot for the box id from OLD to NEW.\n6. release B's (= OLD's) gather flag.\n7. yarq this task. (a fresh task will arrive later, find NEW\n   via the graph slot, and fire under the new shape.)\n8. decrement OLD's refcount.\n   - if refcount == 0: free OLD (along with its abandoned slots).\n```\n\nStep 7 is non-obvious but load-bearing: the values that were\nqueued on OLD's input slots are still there (the slot store\ndidn't change), but the worker that triggered the mutation\ndidn't fire. Without an explicit re-queue, the queued values\nwould sit unprocessed until the next producer push. Yarqing\nguarantees a fresh task gets scheduled so the queued values\nactually get fired under the new shape.\n\n## Slot diffing by port name\n\nThe slot resolution in mutator step 2 is the same algorithm used\nfor tree diffing in UI frameworks: match by stable identifier,\nports-only-in-old get abandoned, ports-only-in-new get freshly\nallocated, ports-in-both keep their slot id (and therefore keep\nall their queued values).\n\nRenames are NOT detected automatically — a port renamed from\n\"x\" to \"x_renamed\" looks like \"delete x, create x_renamed\" from\nthe algorithm's perspective. Any values queued on \"x\" get\ndropped to the JSONL discard event when OLD is freed. If a\nfuture use case calls for value-preserving renames, the spec\nJSON can grow a `\"rename\": [{\"from\":\"x\", \"to\":\"x_renamed\"}]`\nfield; for now, rename-as-delete-plus-add is the conservative\ndefault.\n\n## The unified runtime API\n\nOne entry point handles create, reconfigure, and delete:\n\n```c\nint runtime_apply_box_spec(const char *target_id,\n                           const char *spec_json, int spec_json_len,\n                           char **err_out);\n```\n\nThe runtime parses `spec_json` in the caller's thread, validates\nit, builds the replacement box struct, and dispatches based on\nthe spec's content:\n\n- **Spec describes a new box; target_id is not in the graph:**\n  install at a fresh graph slot. Equivalent to today's\n  `runtime_create_box`.\n- **Spec describes a box; target_id already exists:** push the\n  new struct's pointer onto the target's control queue. The\n  next worker that visits the target becomes the mutator and\n  swaps.\n- **Spec is `{\"action\":\"delete\", \"id\":\"target_id\"}`:** install\n  NULL at the graph slot via the same supersession path. Old box\n  drifts toward freedom via refcount.\n\nThe same shape works for any language. Lua's `soramech.apply_box`\nserializes the spec to JSON and calls in. Bash's\n`soramech_apply_box` is the same. The C bridge wraps the API\ndirectly. Adding a fourth language only requires the language\nto format JSON, which every language can do.\n\n## Reference counting policy — what gets freed when\n\n- **Box record:** freed when refcount = 0 AND graph slot ≠ this\n  box. Triggered by whoever decrements to 0.\n- **Slots used by both OLD and NEW:** kept alive (NEW still\n  references them).\n- **Slots in OLD but not in NEW (abandoned):** freed at the\n  same time OLD is freed; their remaining queued values get a\n  JSONL discard event per slot.\n- **The control queue's cells (pointers to replacement structs):**\n  if a producer pushed a replacement struct and the box was\n  deleted before any mutator ran, those pending replacement\n  structs are freed when the control queue is freed (which\n  happens when OLD is freed).\n- **Live boxes that nobody uses (idle):** not freed. The graph\n  slot still points at them; they're \"live, just waiting.\" This\n  is intentional — we cannot prove a box won't run again in a\n  system that allows runtime creation and connection, so we\n  don't try. Users who want to actively clean up call\n  `runtime_apply_box_spec(id, {\"action\":\"delete\"})`.\n\n## JSONL events\n\n- `box_reconfigure` — fires after the swap. Carries the box id,\n  the new spec (re-serialised from the post-apply struct so the\n  log records what actually applied, not what was requested),\n  task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n- `reconfigure_discard` — fires per abandoned port when a slot\n  has leftover queued values. Carries the box id, the port name,\n  the count of dropped values, and the first value bytes (up to\n  256, for debugging). Always emitted.\n- `box_delete` — fires after a delete supersedes a box. Carries\n  the box id, task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Add the gather flag and refcount to box_t.** Two atomic\n   ints, alongside the existing connections + n_connections\n   atomics in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.\n2. **Convert the graph's box storage from array-of-structs to\n   array-of-pointers.** `graph_box(g, i)` becomes a load from\n   the array. The graph still owns the storage; the array\n   entries become atomic pointers so the mutator can swap them.\n3. **Add the per-box control slot.** At box-creation time\n   (graph_load AND runtime_create_box), allocate one extra slot\n   per box, cell capacity = sizeof(void*), cell count = 8,\n   reachable via a new `box->control_slot_id` field.\n4. **Refactor `parse_box_file` to accept an in-memory JSON\n   buffer.** The file-path entry point becomes a thin wrapper.\n   The runtime API uses the buffer entry directly.\n5. **Add the gather lock acquire / release helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.** CAS 0 → 1 for acquire; store 0 for\n   release. Yield-and-requeue helper for the CAS-loss path:\n   push the task back to the pool's tail and return without\n   firing.\n6. **Wrap `dispatch_action`'s top-of-fire path with the gather\n   lock acquire.** On loss, yarq. On win, check the control\n   queue before doing the normal input gather.\n7. **Implement the mutator path inside `dispatch_action`.** Pop\n   the replacement struct from the control queue. Run the slot\n   resolution. Atomic-swap the graph slot pointer. Release the\n   gather flag. Yarq.\n8. **Add the unified `runtime_apply_box_spec` to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.** Parse JSON, build the\n   replacement struct, push the pointer to the target's control\n   queue. Same shape as the existing runtime_create_box /\n   runtime_connect entrypoints.\n9. **Update the language bridges (Lua, C, Bash) to expose\n   `soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec)`.** Each bridge\n   serialises its native spec representation to JSON and calls\n   the runtime API.\n10. **Add the JSONL events** (`box_reconfigure`,\n    `reconfigure_discard`, `box_delete`) to\n    `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` and\n    `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}`.\n11. **Implement reference-count-driven box GC.** Whoever\n    decrements to zero AND observes the graph slot doesn't\n    point at this box does the free.\n12. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn` — same lang, different\n      function on the same box. Fires once with old fn, then\n      reconfigures, then fires again with new fn.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape` — add a new\n      input port via reconfigure. Verifies new slot allocated\n      and slot diffing matches by name.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind` — flip a BOX_CALL to a\n      BOX_WRITE via reconfigure. Subsequent fires write to disk.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-delete` — reconfigure with\n      delete spec; box is gone, downstream still works (or\n      fails gracefully if it depended on the deleted box).\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-contended` — two reconfigure\n      pushers race on the same target. Both land in the control\n      queue; both apply in arrival order; final state reflects\n      the last one applied.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — already provides the ring-buffer\n  primitive the control queue reuses.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount fields\n  on `box_t`; `parse_box_file` refactor; graph array → array\n  of pointers; control slot allocation at box creation.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release wrapping\n  `dispatch_action`; mutator path; yarq helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_apply_box_spec`\n  unified entry point.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `apply_box`.\n\n## Open issues for after 320 lands\n\n- **Connections-array atomic-publish dance unification** —\n  today's `runtime_connect` does its own copy-and-publish on\n  the per-box connections array. Once 320 lands, that pattern\n  becomes redundant: a connection add can ride the same\n  box-swap mechanism. Tracked as a separate issue, to be\n  attended to after 320.\n- **Explicit value-preserving rename declaration in the spec\n  JSON** — currently rename-as-delete-plus-add is the default.\n  If a use case appears, add a `\"rename\": [...]` field that the\n  slot resolution honours.\n- **Tunable control queue depth** — currently 8 cells per box.\n  If bursty reconfigure traffic ever exceeds this, push back\n  to producers via the slot's existing fill-management.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across many discussion rounds.\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring** — reconfigure messages would have\n   ridden a third ring on every input slot, with the per-cell\n   ordering tag growing a RECONFIGURE value. Workers would peek\n   each port's ordering ring and apply reconfigures encountered\n   during gather. Discarded in favour of the per-box control\n   queue: control messages aren't conceptually input values,\n   and a per-box channel handles empty-input boxes cleanly.\n2. **In-place field rewrites with three-state flag (0 / 1 / 2)**\n   — the mutator would have rewritten the live box's fields in\n   place, with flag = 2 acting as a \"redirect to new box\"\n   indicator. Discarded in favour of the build-new-and-swap\n   pattern: the graph slot pointer naturally acts as the\n   liveness indicator, the third flag state was redundant, and\n   build-new avoids any \"torn read\" possibility because the old\n   box is never modified.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\" The\nmechanism is cooperative with the scheduler rather than\nadversarial — the scheduler keeps doing what it does best\n(managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe unification of create, reconfigure, and delete into one API\ncame from the user's observation: \"What if we made the\n'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process? And if it has the same box ID as an\nalready existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure\nprocess.\" Structurally honest about what these operations are:\nall three are \"express what this box should be now,\" and the\nruntime decides how to land that expression.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/320-box-reconfigure-via-runtime-spec-api.md"
