          "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via the runtime spec API\n\n## Status\nopen · design settled (consolidated through several discussion\nrounds), no code landed yet\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses\n`boxes/<id>.json` once, fills in every field — kind, language,\nfunction pointer, input port list, routing shape, outgoing\nconnections — and the dispatch layer reads that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes the box's record.\n\nThe two ways the runtime already has to \"modify the graph while\nrunning\" — the `create_box` and `connect` primitives from issue\n319, and the load-time encapsulation splice from issue 248 —\nboth **add** to the graph. Neither one **changes** a box that\nalready exists.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\nreplaced wholesale via a runtime API. Anyone holding a reference\nto the runtime can call `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id,\nspec_json)` and atomically swap a box's identity. The same API\ncovers create (target id is new), reconfigure (target id\nexists), and delete (spec asks for deletion).\n\n## Concept in one paragraph\n\nEvery box has a tiny atomic flag and a small per-box control\nqueue. A reconfigure request arrives as a fully-parsed\nreplacement box struct, pushed onto the target's control queue.\nWhen a worker arrives at the box to fire it, the worker first\ntries to claim the flag (CAS 0 → 1); if it wins, it checks the\ncontrol queue. A non-empty queue means there's a pending\nmutation — the worker becomes the mutator, pops the replacement\nstruct, atomically swaps the graph slot pointer from old to new,\nreleases the flag, and yields-and-requeues. An empty control\nqueue means the worker proceeds with a normal fire under the\ngather flag. Either way: a worker visit is exactly one of fire\nor mutate, never both. The flag holds for microseconds; in-flight\nfires don't take it. Old boxes drift toward freedom via a\nreference count once the graph slot stops pointing at them.\n\n## The five structural pieces\n\n### 1. The gather flag\n\nEach box record carries one atomic int — the gather flag — with\ntwo states:\n\n- **0 (free):** any worker may attempt to enter.\n- **1 (held):** exactly one worker is currently in the gather\n  section.\n\nWorkers entering a box do a CAS from 0 to 1. If the CAS wins,\nthe worker enters the gather section. If it loses, the worker\nyields-and-requeues — its task goes back to the tail of the\npool queue, the pool picks it up later. No spinning, no\nblocking.\n\nThe gather section is brief: peek a few input ports' ordering\nrings, decide fire-or-mutate, pop the appropriate cells, release\nthe flag. Microseconds. Workers on DIFFERENT boxes don't contend\n— the flag is per-box.\n\n### 2. The control queue\n\nEvery box has one slot dedicated to incoming control messages,\nallocated from the slot store at box-creation time. Cell capacity\nis sizeof(void*); cell count is small (8 is plenty). The cells\nhold pointers to pre-built replacement box structs.\n\nThe control queue is structurally identical to any other slot\nthe dispatch uses — same ring-buffer primitive, same per-slot\nspinlock for concurrent producers. The only thing that\ndistinguishes it is what's stored in the cells (pointers, not\nvalue bytes) and who reads it (the mutator inside the gather\nsection, not the spec's invoke).\n\n### 3. The graph slot as liveness indicator\n\nThe graph stores boxes as an array of pointers, one per box id.\nWorker lookup goes: `graph_box(graph, id) → returns the current\npointer at that index`. The mutator's job during a reconfigure\nis to atomically swap that pointer from the old box's address\nto the new box's address. Any worker that LATER looks up the\nsame id gets the new box; any worker that already grabbed the\nold pointer keeps it for the duration of its fire.\n\nA box is \"live\" when the graph slot points at it. A box is\n\"superseded\" when the graph slot points at something else (or at\nNULL, for the delete case).\n\nThe two-state flag doesn't need a third \"redirect\" state because\nthe graph slot itself is what new arrivals consult. Workers\narriving fresh get the current box via the graph slot; workers\nmid-fire on the old box finish on the old box. Both work cleanly.\n\n### 4. The reference count\n\nEach box record has an atomic refcount. Workers increment it at\nthe top of their fire (right after resolving the pointer through\nthe graph slot) and decrement at the bottom. The mutator\nincrements it when it becomes the mutator and decrements after\nthe swap.\n\nA box is freeable when BOTH:\n- The graph slot doesn't point at it (it's superseded), AND\n- The refcount has dropped to zero.\n\nThe worker whose decrement returns 0 checks both conditions. If\nboth hold, that worker frees the old box. If only refcount = 0\nbut graph slot still points at the box, the box is just\ntransiently idle — leave it alone.\n\nThe mutator's \"hold a +1 during the reconfigure\" discipline\nensures the refcount can only fall to zero AFTER the mutator\nhas finished its work. Without that, a race could decrement to\nzero while the mutator is still mid-swap.\n\n### 5. The replacement box struct\n\nA reconfigure message IS a fully-built box struct, sitting in\nmemory. The caller of `runtime_apply_box_spec` is responsible\nfor parsing the spec JSON into a `box_t` struct in their own\nthread. Once built, the caller pushes the struct's pointer to\nthe target's control queue.\n\nThis means the mutator's hot path doesn't include JSON parsing.\nThe mutator pops a pointer, does slot resolution (see below),\nand atomically swaps the graph slot. The slow work happens in\nproducer threads, in parallel with anything else going on.\n\n## The worker arrival flow\n\nWhen a worker is handed a task to fire box X:\n\n```\n1. look up the graph slot for X → get current box pointer (call it B).\n2. CAS the gather flag on B from 0 to 1.\n   - lose: yarq this task. exit.\n   - win: continue.\n3. increment B's refcount.\n4. peek B's control queue.\n   - non-empty: become MUTATOR (see below).\n   - empty: continue to gather inputs.\n5. for each input port i:\n     pop one ordering message from input slot i.\n     pop the corresponding value from the indicated data ring (native or json).\n6. release B's gather flag (set to 0).\n7. call the spec's invoke with the gathered values.\n8. push outputs to downstream slots per B's connections.\n9. decrement B's refcount.\n   - if refcount == 0 AND graph slot != B: free B.\n```\n\nImportant: pop is committed only AFTER the gather flag is held\nand the control queue is checked. There's no race window where\na popped value could be lost.\n\n## The mutator flow\n\nWhen a worker enters the gather section, finds the control queue\nnon-empty, and becomes the mutator:\n\n```\n1. pop one box-pointer (call it NEW) from the control queue.\n2. resolve NEW's input_slot_ids by port-name matching against OLD:\n     for each port in NEW:\n       if same name exists in OLD: copy that slot id into NEW.\n       else: allocate a fresh slot from the slot store; record the new id in NEW.\n3. record OLD's \"abandoned slots\" = ports in OLD but not in NEW.\n   these slots get released when OLD is freed; any remaining\n   queued values emit a discard JSONL event.\n4. NEW gets its own freshly-allocated control queue slot.\n5. atomically swap the graph slot for the box id from OLD to NEW.\n6. release B's (= OLD's) gather flag.\n7. yarq this task. (a fresh task will arrive later, find NEW\n   via the graph slot, and fire under the new shape.)\n8. decrement OLD's refcount.\n   - if refcount == 0: free OLD (along with its abandoned slots).\n```\n\nStep 7 is non-obvious but load-bearing: the values that were\nqueued on OLD's input slots are still there (the slot store\ndidn't change), but the worker that triggered the mutation\ndidn't fire. Without an explicit re-queue, the queued values\nwould sit unprocessed until the next producer push. Yarqing\nguarantees a fresh task gets scheduled so the queued values\nactually get fired under the new shape.\n\n## Slot diffing by port name\n\nThe slot resolution in mutator step 2 is the same algorithm used\nfor tree diffing in UI frameworks: match by stable identifier,\nports-only-in-old get abandoned, ports-only-in-new get freshly\nallocated, ports-in-both keep their slot id (and therefore keep\nall their queued values).\n\nRenames are NOT detected automatically — a port renamed from\n\"x\" to \"x_renamed\" looks like \"delete x, create x_renamed\" from\nthe algorithm's perspective. Any values queued on \"x\" get\ndropped to the JSONL discard event when OLD is freed. If a\nfuture use case calls for value-preserving renames, the spec\nJSON can grow a `\"rename\": [{\"from\":\"x\", \"to\":\"x_renamed\"}]`\nfield; for now, rename-as-delete-plus-add is the conservative\ndefault.\n\n## The unified runtime API\n\nOne entry point handles create, reconfigure, and delete:\n\n```c\nint runtime_apply_box_spec(const char *target_id,\n                           const char *spec_json, int spec_json_len,\n                           char **err_out);\n```\n\nThe runtime parses `spec_json` in the caller's thread, validates\nit, builds the replacement box struct, and dispatches based on\nthe spec's content:\n\n- **Spec describes a new box; target_id is not in the graph:**\n  install at a fresh graph slot. Equivalent to today's\n  `runtime_create_box`.\n- **Spec describes a box; target_id already exists:** push the\n  new struct's pointer onto the target's control queue. The\n  next worker that visits the target becomes the mutator and\n  swaps.\n- **Spec is `{\"action\":\"delete\", \"id\":\"target_id\"}`:** install\n  NULL at the graph slot via the same supersession path. Old box\n  drifts toward freedom via refcount.\n\nThe same shape works for any language. Lua's `soramech.apply_box`\nserializes the spec to JSON and calls in. Bash's\n`soramech_apply_box` is the same. The C bridge wraps the API\ndirectly. Adding a fourth language only requires the language\nto format JSON, which every language can do.\n\n## Reference counting policy — what gets freed when\n\n- **Box record:** freed when refcount = 0 AND graph slot ≠ this\n  box. Triggered by whoever decrements to 0.\n- **Slots used by both OLD and NEW:** kept alive (NEW still\n  references them).\n- **Slots in OLD but not in NEW (abandoned):** freed at the\n  same time OLD is freed; their remaining queued values get a\n  JSONL discard event per slot.\n- **The control queue's cells (pointers to replacement structs):**\n  if a producer pushed a replacement struct and the box was\n  deleted before any mutator ran, those pending replacement\n  structs are freed when the control queue is freed (which\n  happens when OLD is freed).\n- **Live boxes that nobody uses (idle):** not freed. The graph\n  slot still points at them; they're \"live, just waiting.\" This\n  is intentional — we cannot prove a box won't run again in a\n  system that allows runtime creation and connection, so we\n  don't try. Users who want to actively clean up call\n  `runtime_apply_box_spec(id, {\"action\":\"delete\"})`.\n\n## JSONL events\n\n- `box_reconfigure` — fires after the swap. Carries the box id,\n  the new spec (re-serialised from the post-apply struct so the\n  log records what actually applied, not what was requested),\n  task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n- `reconfigure_discard` — fires per abandoned port when a slot\n  has leftover queued values. Carries the box id, the port name,\n  the count of dropped values, and the first value bytes (up to\n  256, for debugging). Always emitted.\n- `box_delete` — fires after a delete supersedes a box. Carries\n  the box id, task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Add the gather flag and refcount to box_t.** Two atomic\n   ints, alongside the existing connections + n_connections\n   atomics in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.\n2. **Convert the graph's box storage from array-of-structs to\n   array-of-pointers.** `graph_box(g, i)` becomes a load from\n   the array. The graph still owns the storage; the array\n   entries become atomic pointers so the mutator can swap them.\n3. **Add the per-box control slot.** At box-creation time\n   (graph_load AND runtime_create_box), allocate one extra slot\n   per box, cell capacity = sizeof(void*), cell count = 8,\n   reachable via a new `box->control_slot_id` field.\n4. **Refactor `parse_box_file` to accept an in-memory JSON\n   buffer.** The file-path entry point becomes a thin wrapper.\n   The runtime API uses the buffer entry directly.\n5. **Add the gather lock acquire / release helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.** CAS 0 → 1 for acquire; store 0 for\n   release. Yield-and-requeue helper for the CAS-loss path:\n   push the task back to the pool's tail and return without\n   firing.\n6. **Wrap `dispatch_action`'s top-of-fire path with the gather\n   lock acquire.** On loss, yarq. On win, check the control\n   queue before doing the normal input gather.\n7. **Implement the mutator path inside `dispatch_action`.** Pop\n   the replacement struct from the control queue. Run the slot\n   resolution. Atomic-swap the graph slot pointer. Release the\n   gather flag. Yarq.\n8. **Add the unified `runtime_apply_box_spec` to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.** Parse JSON, build the\n   replacement struct, push the pointer to the target's control\n   queue. Same shape as the existing runtime_create_box /\n   runtime_connect entrypoints.\n9. **Update the language bridges (Lua, C, Bash) to expose\n   `soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec)`.** Each bridge\n   serialises its native spec representation to JSON and calls\n   the runtime API.\n10. **Add the JSONL events** (`box_reconfigure`,\n    `reconfigure_discard`, `box_delete`) to\n    `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` and\n    `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}`.\n11. **Implement reference-count-driven box GC.** Whoever\n    decrements to zero AND observes the graph slot doesn't\n    point at this box does the free.\n12. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn` — same lang, different\n      function on the same box. Fires once with old fn, then\n      reconfigures, then fires again with new fn.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape` — add a new\n      input port via reconfigure. Verifies new slot allocated\n      and slot diffing matches by name.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind` — flip a BOX_CALL to a\n      BOX_WRITE via reconfigure. Subsequent fires write to disk.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-delete` — reconfigure with\n      delete spec; box is gone, downstream still works (or\n      fails gracefully if it depended on the deleted box).\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-contended` — two reconfigure\n      pushers race on the same target. Both land in the control\n      queue; both apply in arrival order; final state reflects\n      the last one applied.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — already provides the ring-buffer\n  primitive the control queue reuses.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount fields\n  on `box_t`; `parse_box_file` refactor; graph array → array\n  of pointers; control slot allocation at box creation.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release wrapping\n  `dispatch_action`; mutator path; yarq helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_apply_box_spec`\n  unified entry point.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `apply_box`.\n\n## Open issues for after 320 lands\n\n- **Connections-array atomic-publish dance unification** —\n  today's `runtime_connect` does its own copy-and-publish on\n  the per-box connections array. Once 320 lands, that pattern\n  becomes redundant: a connection add can ride the same\n  box-swap mechanism. Tracked as a separate issue.\n- **Explicit value-preserving rename declaration in the spec\n  JSON** — currently rename-as-delete-plus-add is the default.\n  If a use case appears, add a `\"rename\": [...]` field that the\n  slot resolution honours.\n- **Tunable control queue depth** — currently 8 cells per box.\n  If bursty reconfigure traffic ever exceeds this, push back\n  to producers via the slot's existing fill-management.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across many discussion rounds.\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring** — reconfigure messages would have\n   ridden a third ring on every input slot, with the per-cell\n   ordering tag growing a RECONFIGURE value. Workers would peek\n   each port's ordering ring and apply reconfigures encountered\n   during gather. Discarded in favour of the per-box control\n   queue: control messages aren't conceptually input values,\n   and a per-box channel handles empty-input boxes cleanly.\n2. **In-place field rewrites with three-state flag (0 / 1 / 2)**\n   — the mutator would have rewritten the live box's fields in\n   place, with flag = 2 acting as a \"redirect to new box\"\n   indicator. Discarded in favour of the build-new-and-swap\n   pattern: the graph slot pointer naturally acts as the\n   liveness indicator, the third flag state was redundant, and\n   build-new avoids any \"torn read\" possibility because the old\n   box is never modified.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\" The\nmechanism is cooperative with the scheduler rather than\nadversarial — the scheduler keeps doing what it does best\n(managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe unification of create, reconfigure, and delete into one API\ncame from the user's observation: \"What if we made the\n'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process? And if it has the same box ID as an\nalready existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure\nprocess.\" Structurally honest about what these operations are:\nall three are \"express what this box should be now,\" and the\nruntime decides how to land that expression.\n",

The graph slot as liveness indicator"," ","-A reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers","-firing the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,","-no other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new","-`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.","+The graph stores boxes as an array of pointers, one per box id.","+Worker lookup goes: `graph_box(graph, id) → returns the current","+pointer at that index`. The mutator's job during a reconfigure","+is to atomically swap that pointer from the old box's address","+to the new box's address. Any worker that LATER looks up the","+same id gets the new box; any worker that already grabbed the","+old pointer keeps it for the duration of its fire."," ","-A spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing","-captures the intended shape exactly:","+A box is \"live\" when the graph slot points at it. A box is","+\"superseded\" when the graph slot points at something else (or at","+NULL, for the delete case)."," ","-> \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back","-> at the beginning of the queue please'\"","+The two-state flag doesn't need a third \"redirect\" state because","+the graph slot itself is what new arrivals consult. Workers","+arriving fresh get the current box via the graph slot; workers","+mid-fire on the old box finish on the old box. Both work cleanly."," ","-**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this","-primitive. Mechanism:","+### 4. The reference count"," ","-- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).","-- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the","-  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker","-  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue","-  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.","-  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from","-  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately","-  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other","-  pending work runs first.","-- **Release**: atomic store of 0.","+Each box record has an atomic refcount. Workers increment it at","+the top of their fire (right after resolving the pointer through","+the graph slot) and decrement at the bottom. The mutator","+increments it when it becomes the mutator and decrements after","+the swap."," ","-The cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each","-contended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization","-primitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than","-*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does","-best (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier","-just nudges contended workers to circle back later.","+A box is freeable when BOTH:","+- The graph slot doesn't point at it (it's superseded), AND","+- The refcount has dropped to zero."," ","-The YARQ barrier is acquired by **every path that MUTATES the","-box record** — reconfigure_apply and runtime_connect (issue","-319d's wire attachment, which already does its own copy-and-","-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding those","-into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't","-interleave dangerously when both fire at once.","+The worker whose decrement returns 0 checks both conditions. If","+both hold, that worker frees the old box. If only refcount = 0","+but graph slot still points at the box, the box is just","+transiently idle — leave it alone."," ","-**Workers that only READ the box record (input-gather + box","-function invocation) DO NOT acquire YARQ.** They're not mutating","-anything; making them block on the mutator path would burn","-worker time for no consistency win. They read the box's mutable","-fields through the same atomic-load patterns issue 319d already","-uses for `connections` / `n_connections`.","+The mutator's \"hold a +1 during the reconfigure\" discipline","+ensures the refcount can only fall to zero AFTER the mutator","+has finished its work.     "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via the runtime spec API\n\n## Status\nopen · design settled (consolidated through several discussion\nrounds), no code landed yet\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses\n`boxes/<id>.json` once, fills in every field — kind, language,\nfunction pointer, input port list, routing shape, outgoing\nconnections — and the dispatch layer reads that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes the box's record.\n\nThe two ways the runtime already has to \"modify the graph while\nrunning\" — the `create_box` and `connect` primitives from issue\n319, and the load-time encapsulation splice from issue 248 —\nboth **add** to the graph. Neither one **changes** a box that\nalready exists.\n\nThis issue introduces the third path: a running box can be\nreplaced wholesale via a runtime API. Anyone holding a reference\nto the runtime can call `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id,\nspec_json)` and atomically swap a box's identity. The same API\ncovers create (target id is new), reconfigure (target id\nexists), and delete (spec asks for deletion).\n\n## Concept in one paragraph\n\nEvery box has a tiny atomic flag and a small per-box control\nqueue. A reconfigure request arrives as a fully-parsed\nreplacement box struct, pushed onto the target's control queue.\nWhen a worker arrives at the box to fire it, the worker first\ntries to claim the flag (CAS 0 → 1); if it wins, it checks the\ncontrol queue. A non-empty queue means there's a pending\nmutation — the worker becomes the mutator, pops the replacement\nstruct, atomically swaps the graph slot pointer from old to new,\nreleases the flag, and yields-and-requeues. An empty control\nqueue means the worker proceeds with a normal fire under the\ngather flag. Either way: a worker visit is exactly one of fire\nor mutate, never both. The flag holds for microseconds; in-flight\nfires don't take it. Old boxes drift toward freedom via a\nreference count once the graph slot stops pointing at them.\n\n## The five structural pieces\n\n### 1. The gather flag\n\nEach box record carries one atomic int — the gather flag — with\ntwo states:\n\n- **0 (free):** any worker may attempt to enter.\n- **1 (held):** exactly one worker is currently in the gather\n  section.\n\nWorkers entering a box do a CAS from 0 to 1. If the CAS wins,\nthe worker enters the gather section. If it loses, the worker\nyields-and-requeues — its task goes back to the tail of the\npool queue, the pool picks it up later. No spinning, no\nblocking.\n\nThe gather section is brief: peek a few input ports' ordering\nrings, decide fire-or-mutate, pop the appropriate cells, release\nthe flag. Microseconds. Workers on DIFFERENT boxes don't contend\n— the flag is per-box.\n\n### 2. The control queue\n\nEvery box has one slot dedicated to incoming control messages,\nallocated from the slot store at box-creation time. Cell capacity\nis sizeof(void*); cell count is small (8 is plenty). The cells\nhold pointers to pre-built replacement box structs.\n\nThe control queue is structurally identical to any other slot\nthe dispatch uses — same ring-buffer primitive, same per-slot\nspinlock for concurrent producers. The only thing that\ndistinguishes it is what's stored in the cells (pointers, not\nvalue bytes) and who reads it (the mutator inside the gather\nsection, not the spec's invoke).\n\n### 3. The graph slot as liveness indicator\n\nThe graph stores boxes as an array of pointers, one per box id.\nWorker lookup goes: `graph_box(graph, id) → returns the current\npointer at that index`. The mutator's job during a reconfigure\nis to atomically swap that pointer from the old box's address\nto the new box's address. Any worker that LATER looks up the\nsame id gets the new box; any worker that already grabbed the\nold pointer keeps it for the duration of its fire.\n\nA box is \"live\" when the graph slot points at it. A box is\n\"superseded\" when the graph slot points at something else (or at\nNULL, for the delete case).\n\nThe two-state flag doesn't need a third \"redirect\" state because\nthe graph slot itself is what new arrivals consult. Workers\narriving fresh get the current box via the graph slot; workers\nmid-fire on the old box finish on the old box. Both work cleanly.\n\n### 4. The reference count\n\nEach box record has an atomic refcount. Workers increment it at\nthe top of their fire (right after resolving the pointer through\nthe graph slot) and decrement at the bottom. The mutator\nincrements it when it becomes the mutator and decrements after\nthe swap.\n\nA box is freeable when BOTH:\n- The graph slot doesn't point at it (it's superseded), AND\n- The refcount has dropped to zero.\n\nThe worker whose decrement returns 0 checks both conditions. If\nboth hold, that worker frees the old box. If only refcount = 0\nbut graph slot still points at the box, the box is just\ntransiently idle — leave it alone.\n\nThe mutator's \"hold a +1 during the reconfigure\" discipline\nensures the refcount can only fall to zero AFTER the mutator\nhas finished its work. Without that, a race could decrement to\nzero while the mutator is still mid-swap.\n\n### 5. The replacement box struct\n\nA reconfigure message IS a fully-built box struct, sitting in\nmemory. The caller of `runtime_apply_box_spec` is responsible\nfor parsing the spec JSON into a `box_t` struct in their own\nthread. Once built, the caller pushes the struct's pointer to\nthe target's control queue.\n\nThis means the mutator's hot path doesn't include JSON parsing.\nThe mutator pops a pointer, does slot resolution (see below),\nand atomically swaps the graph slot. The slow work happens in\nproducer threads, in parallel with anything else going on.\n\n## The worker arrival flow\n\nWhen a worker is handed a task to fire box X:\n\n```\n1. look up the graph slot for X → get current box pointer (call it B).\n2. CAS the gather flag on B from 0 to 1.\n   - lose: yarq this task. exit.\n   - win: continue.\n3. increment B's refcount.\n4. peek B's control queue.\n   - non-empty: become MUTATOR (see below).\n   - empty: continue to gather inputs.\n5. for each input port i:\n     pop one ordering message from input slot i.\n     pop the corresponding value from the indicated data ring (native or json).\n6. release B's gather flag (set to 0).\n7. call the spec's invoke with the gathered values.\n8. push outputs to downstream slots per B's connections.\n9. decrement B's refcount.\n   - if refcount == 0 AND graph slot != B: free B.\n```\n\nImportant: pop is committed only AFTER the gather flag is held\nand the control queue is checked. There's no race window where\na popped value could be lost.\n\n## The mutator flow\n\nWhen a worker enters the gather section, finds the control queue\nnon-empty, and becomes the mutator:\n\n```\n1. pop one box-pointer (call it NEW) from the control queue.\n2. resolve NEW's input_slot_ids by port-name matching against OLD:\n     for each port in NEW:\n       if same name exists in OLD: copy that slot id into NEW.\n       else: allocate a fresh slot from the slot store; record the new id in NEW.\n3. record OLD's \"abandoned slots\" = ports in OLD but not in NEW.\n   these slots get released when OLD is freed; any remaining\n   queued values emit a discard JSONL event.\n4. NEW gets its own freshly-allocated control queue slot.\n5. atomically swap the graph slot for the box id from OLD to NEW.\n6. release B's (= OLD's) gather flag.\n7. yarq this task. (a fresh task will arrive later, find NEW\n   via the graph slot, and fire under the new shape.)\n8. decrement OLD's refcount.\n   - if refcount == 0: free OLD (along with its abandoned slots).\n```\n\nStep 7 is non-obvious but load-bearing: the values that were\nqueued on OLD's input slots are still there (the slot store\ndidn't change), but the worker that triggered the mutation\ndidn't fire. Without an explicit re-queue, the queued values\nwould sit unprocessed until the next producer push. Yarqing\nguarantees a fresh task gets scheduled so the queued values\nactually get fired under the new shape.\n\n## Slot diffing by port name\n\nThe slot resolution in mutator step 2 is the same algorithm used\nfor tree diffing in UI frameworks: match by stable identifier,\nports-only-in-old get abandoned, ports-only-in-new get freshly\nallocated, ports-in-both keep their slot id (and therefore keep\nall their queued values).\n\nRenames are NOT detected automatically — a port renamed from\n\"x\" to \"x_renamed\" looks like \"delete x, create x_renamed\" from\nthe algorithm's perspective. Any values queued on \"x\" get\ndropped to the JSONL discard event when OLD is freed. If a\nfuture use case calls for value-preserving renames, the spec\nJSON can grow a `\"rename\": [{\"from\":\"x\", \"to\":\"x_renamed\"}]`\nfield; for now, rename-as-delete-plus-add is the conservative\ndefault.\n\n## The unified runtime API\n\nOne entry point handles create, reconfigure, and delete:\n\n```c\nint runtime_apply_box_spec(const char *target_id,\n                           const char *spec_json, int spec_json_len,\n                           char **err_out);\n```\n\nThe runtime parses `spec_json` in the caller's thread, validates\nit, builds the replacement box struct, and dispatches based on\nthe spec's content:\n\n- **Spec describes a new box; target_id is not in the graph:**\n  install at a fresh graph slot. Equivalent to today's\n  `runtime_create_box`.\n- **Spec describes a box; target_id already exists:** push the\n  new struct's pointer onto the target's control queue. The\n  next worker that visits the target becomes the mutator and\n  swaps.\n- **Spec is `{\"action\":\"delete\", \"id\":\"target_id\"}`:** install\n  NULL at the graph slot via the same supersession path. Old box\n  drifts toward freedom via refcount.\n\nThe same shape works for any language. Lua's `soramech.apply_box`\nserializes the spec to JSON and calls in. Bash's\n`soramech_apply_box` is the same. The C bridge wraps the API\ndirectly. Adding a fourth language only requires the language\nto format JSON, which every language can do.\n\n## Reference counting policy — what gets freed when\n\n- **Box record:** freed when refcount = 0 AND graph slot ≠ this\n  box. Triggered by whoever decrements to 0.\n- **Slots used by both OLD and NEW:** kept alive (NEW still\n  references them).\n- **Slots in OLD but not in NEW (abandoned):** freed at the\n  same time OLD is freed; their remaining queued values get a\n  JSONL discard event per slot.\n- **The control queue's cells (pointers to replacement structs):**\n  if a producer pushed a replacement struct and the box was\n  deleted before any mutator ran, those pending replacement\n  structs are freed when the control queue is freed (which\n  happens when OLD is freed).\n- **Live boxes that nobody uses (idle):** not freed. The graph\n  slot still points at them; they're \"live, just waiting.\" This\n  is intentional — we cannot prove a box won't run again in a\n  system that allows runtime creation and connection, so we\n  don't try. Users who want to actively clean up call\n  `runtime_apply_box_spec(id, {\"action\":\"delete\"})`.\n\n## JSONL events\n\n- `box_reconfigure` — fires after the swap. Carries the box id,\n  the new spec (re-serialised from the post-apply struct so the\n  log records what actually applied, not what was requested),\n  task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n- `reconfigure_discard` — fires per abandoned port when a slot\n  has leftover queued values. Carries the box id, the port name,\n  the count of dropped values, and the first value bytes (up to\n  256, for debugging). Always emitted.\n- `box_delete` — fires after a delete supersedes a box. Carries\n  the box id, task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Add the gather flag and refcount to box_t.** Two atomic\n   ints, alongside the existing connections + n_connections\n   atomics in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.\n2. **Convert the graph's box storage from array-of-structs to\n   array-of-pointers.** `graph_box(g, i)` becomes a load from\n   the array. The graph still owns the storage; the array\n   entries become atomic pointers so the mutator can swap them.\n3. **Add the per-box control slot.** At box-creation time\n   (graph_load AND runtime_create_box), allocate one extra slot\n   per box, cell capacity = sizeof(void*), cell count = 8,\n   reachable via a new `box->control_slot_id` field.\n4. **Refactor `parse_box_file` to accept an in-memory JSON\n   buffer.** The file-path entry point becomes a thin wrapper.\n   The runtime API uses the buffer entry directly.\n5. **Add the gather lock acquire / release helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.** CAS 0 → 1 for acquire; store 0 for\n   release. Yield-and-requeue helper for the CAS-loss path:\n   push the task back to the pool's tail and return without\n   firing.\n6. **Wrap `dispatch_action`'s top-of-fire path with the gather\n   lock acquire.** On loss, yarq. On win, check the control\n   queue before doing the normal input gather.\n7. **Implement the mutator path inside `dispatch_action`.** Pop\n   the replacement struct from the control queue. Run the slot\n   resolution. Atomic-swap the graph slot pointer. Release the\n   gather flag. Yarq.\n8. **Add the unified `runtime_apply_box_spec` to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.** Parse JSON, build the\n   replacement struct, push the pointer to the target's control\n   queue. Same shape as the existing runtime_create_box /\n   runtime_connect entrypoints.\n9. **Update the language bridges (Lua, C, Bash) to expose\n   `soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec)`.** Each bridge\n   serialises its native spec representation to JSON and calls\n   the runtime API.\n10. **Add the JSONL events** (`box_reconfigure`,\n    `reconfigure_discard`, `box_delete`) to\n    `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` and\n    `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}`.\n11. **Implement reference-count-driven box GC.** Whoever\n    decrements to zero AND observes the graph slot doesn't\n    point at this box does the free.\n12. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn` — same lang, different\n      function on the same box. Fires once with old fn, then\n      reconfigures, then fires again with new fn.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape` — add a new\n      input port via reconfigure. Verifies new slot allocated\n      and slot diffing matches by name.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind` — flip a BOX_CALL to a\n      BOX_WRITE via reconfigure. Subsequent fires write to disk.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-delete` — reconfigure with\n      delete spec; box is gone, downstream still works (or\n      fails gracefully if it depended on the deleted box).\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-contended` — two reconfigure\n      pushers race on the same target. Both land in the control\n      queue; both apply in arrival order; final state reflects\n      the last one applied.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — already provides the ring-buffer\n  primitive the control queue reuses.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount fields\n  on `box_t`; `parse_box_file` refactor; graph array → array\n  of pointers; control slot allocation at box creation.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release wrapping\n  `dispatch_action`; mutator path; yarq helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_apply_box_spec`\n  unified entry point.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `apply_box`.\n\n## Open issues for after 320 lands\n\n- **Connections-array atomic-publish dance unification** —\n  today's `runtime_connect` does its own copy-and-publish on\n  the per-box connections array. Once 320 lands, that pattern\n  becomes redundant: a connection add can ride the same\n  box-swap mechanism. Tracked as a separate issue.\n- **Explicit value-preserving rename declaration in the spec\n  JSON** — currently rename-as-delete-plus-add is the default.\n  If a use case appears, add a `\"rename\": [...]` field that the\n  slot resolution honours.\n- **Tunable control queue depth** — currently 8 cells per box.\n  If bursty reconfigure traffic ever exceeds this, push back\n  to producers via the slot's existing fill-management.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across many discussion rounds.\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring** — reconfigure messages would have\n   ridden a third ring on every input slot, with the per-cell\n   ordering tag growing a RECONFIGURE value. Workers would peek\n   each port's ordering ring and apply reconfigures encountered\n   during gather. Discarded in favour of the per-box control\n   queue: control messages aren't conceptually input values,\n   and a per-box channel handles empty-input boxes cleanly.\n2. **In-place field rewrites with three-state flag (0 / 1 / 2)**\n   — the mutator would have rewritten the live box's fields in\n   place, with flag = 2 acting as a \"redirect to new box\"\n   indicator. Discarded in favour of the build-new-and-swap\n   pattern: the graph slot pointer naturally acts as the\n   liveness indicator, the third flag state was redundant, and\n   build-new avoids any \"torn read\" possibility because the old\n   box is never modified.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\" The\nmechanism is cooperative with the scheduler rather than\nadversarial — the scheduler keeps doing what it does best\n(managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe unification of create, reconfigure, and delete into one API\ncame from the user's observation: \"What if we made the\n'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process? And if it has the same box ID as an\nalready existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure\nprocess.\" Structurally honest about what these operations are:\nall three are \"express what this box should be now,\" and the\nruntime decides how to land that expression.\n",
    "type":"update",

}

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# 321 — Unify connections-array mutation through the 320 box-swap path\n\n## Status\nopen · waits on 320 landing first; design is straightforward\nonce the box-swap mechanism exists\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 319d added the ability to attach new outgoing connections\nto an existing box at runtime via `runtime_connect`. The way it\ndoes this today is a special-case atomic dance directly on the\nbox's `connections` field: allocate a new connections array,\ncopy the old entries, append the new entry, atomic-store the\npointer, then atomic-store the new count. Readers that walk\nthe connections array use the order \"read count first, then\npointer\" so they always observe either the old pair or the new\npair, never a torn mix.\n\nThis works because the connections array is append-only —\nruntime_connect only ever adds, never removes or reorders.\nThat's the reason the staggered-publish pattern doesn't break\nexisting readers.\n\nOnce issue 320 lands, the runtime has a more general mechanism:\nbuild a fully replacement box struct, push its pointer to the\ntarget's control queue, let the next worker visit do the\natomic graph-slot swap. This mechanism is strictly more\npowerful than the connections-only dance — it can change\nanything about the box, not just append to one field.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nRetire the special-case copy-and-publish on the connections\nfield. Re-implement `runtime_connect` as a thin wrapper over\n`runtime_apply_box_spec`:\n\n1. Look up the current box for the target id.\n2. Build a new box struct that is a copy of the current one,\n   with the new connection appended to its connections array.\n3. Call `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, new_spec_json)` (or\n   the underlying push-pointer-to-control-queue equivalent).\n\nThe atomic discipline collapses to one path. The connections\nfield on `box_t` can become a plain pointer + plain int (no\n`_Atomic` qualifiers needed) because the only way to mutate it\nis via the box-swap mechanism, which never modifies a live box\nin place.\n\n## Why bother\n\n- **One mutation discipline instead of two.** Every change to\n  a box's identity — adding a connection, changing the function\n  pointer, renaming a port, deleting the box — uses the same\n  build-new-and-swap pattern. Less code to maintain, fewer\n  edge cases to learn.\n- **The connections-only dance is structurally fragile.** It\n  relies on append-only semantics that nobody enforces at the\n  type level. A future change that wanted to remove or reorder\n  connections would silently introduce torn-read bugs. Removing\n  the path removes the trap.\n- **Smaller box_t.** The `_Atomic` qualifiers on\n  `n_connections` and `connections` can come off. Plain int +\n  plain pointer is fine because mutation only happens during\n  the build-new step, before the new box is published.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Re-implement `runtime_connect` as a wrapper over\n   `runtime_apply_box_spec`.** Caller still sees the same\n   signature; internals route through the box-swap path.\n2. **Remove the `_Atomic` qualifiers on `n_connections` and\n   `connections` in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.** Plain types\n   suffice now.\n3. **Remove the copy-and-publish helper in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`** that runtime_connect used to\n   call.\n4. **Verify the existing 319d fixture (`319d-runtime-create`,\n   `319e-c-create`, etc.) still passes under the new path.**\n   The behavioural contract for runtime_connect is unchanged;\n   the internal mechanism changes.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — drop atomic qualifiers; drop\n  copy-and-publish helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — rewrite runtime_connect\n  to call into runtime_apply_box_spec.\n- Existing 319d/319e/319f fixtures act as the regression\n  guard; no new fixtures needed.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Does the language bridges need any change?** Lua's\n  `soramech.connect`, Bash's `soramech_connect`, C's\n  `soramech_connect` all currently call straight into\n  runtime_connect. If runtime_connect's signature stays the\n  same, no bridge changes. Confirm during implementation.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/321-unify-connections-mutation-through-box-swap.md"
        },

    "userModified":false,
    "content":"# 321 — Unify connections-array mutation through the 320 box-swap path\n\n## Status\nopen · waits on 320 landing first; design is straightforward\nonce the box-swap mechanism exists\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 319d added the ability to attach new outgoing connections\nto an existing box at runtime via `runtime_connect`. The way it\ndoes this today is a special-case atomic dance directly on the\nbox's `connections` field: allocate a new connections array,\ncopy the old entries, append the new entry, atomic-store the\npointer, then atomic-store the new count. Readers that walk\nthe connections array use the order \"read count first, then\npointer\" so they always observe either the old pair or the new\npair, never a torn mix.\n\nThis works because the connections array is append-only —\nruntime_connect only ever adds, never removes or reorders.\nThat's the reason the staggered-publish pattern doesn't break\nexisting readers.\n\nOnce issue 320 lands, the runtime has a more general mechanism:\nbuild a fully replacement box struct, push its pointer to the\ntarget's control queue, let the next worker visit do the\natomic graph-slot swap. This mechanism is strictly more\npowerful than the connections-only dance — it can change\nanything about the box, not just append to one field.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nRetire the special-case copy-and-publish on the connections\nfield. Re-implement `runtime_connect` as a thin wrapper over\n`runtime_apply_box_spec`:\n\n1. Look up the current box for the target id.\n2. Build a new box struct that is a copy of the current one,\n   with the new connection appended to its connections array.\n3. Call `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, new_spec_json)` (or\n   the underlying push-pointer-to-control-queue equivalent).\n\nThe atomic discipline collapses to one path. The connections\nfield on `box_t` can become a plain pointer + plain int (no\n`_Atomic` qualifiers needed) because the only way to mutate it\nis via the box-swap mechanism, which never modifies a live box\nin place.\n\n## Why bother\n\n- **One mutation discipline instead of two.** Every change to\n  a box's identity — adding a connection, changing the function\n  pointer, renaming a port, deleting the box — uses the same\n  build-new-and-swap pattern. Less code to maintain, fewer\n  edge cases to learn.\n- **The connections-only dance is structurally fragile.** It\n  relies on append-only semantics that nobody enforces at the\n  type level. A future change that wanted to remove or reorder\n  connections would silently introduce torn-read bugs. Removing\n  the path removes the trap.\n- **Smaller box_t.** The `_Atomic` qualifiers on\n  `n_connections` and `connections` can come off. Plain int +\n  plain pointer is fine because mutation only happens during\n  the build-new step, before the new box is published.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Re-implement `runtime_connect` as a wrapper over\n   `runtime_apply_box_spec`.** Caller still sees the same\n   signature; internals route through the box-swap path.\n2. **Remove the `_Atomic` qualifiers on `n_connections` and\n   `connections` in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.** Plain types\n   suffice now.\n3. **Remove the copy-and-publish helper in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`** that runtime_connect used to\n   call.\n4. **Verify the existing 319d fixture (`319d-runtime-create`,\n   `319e-c-create`, etc.) still passes under the new path.**\n   The behavioural contract for runtime_connect is unchanged;\n   the internal mechanism changes.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — drop atomic qualifiers; drop\n  copy-and-publish helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — rewrite runtime_connect\n  to call into runtime_apply_box_spec.\n- Existing 319d/319e/319f fixtures act as the regression\n  guard; no new fixtures needed.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Does the language bridges need any change?** Lua's\n  `soramech.connect`, Bash's `soramech_connect`, C's\n  `soramech_connect` all currently call straight into\n  runtime_connect. If runtime_connect's signature stays the\n  same, no bridge changes. Confirm during implementation.\n",

        "input":{
          "content":"# 322 — Box delete: the user-facing experience\n\n## Status\nopen · the underlying mechanism is part of 320; this issue\ncovers the user-facing API and the explicit-vs-implicit-deletion\ndesign decision\n\n## Current behavior\n\nOnce issue 320 lands, the runtime has a unified\n`runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, spec_json)` entry point that\nhandles create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec's\ncontent. The delete path is: install NULL at the graph slot\nvia the same supersession mechanism, let the refcount drive\nthe old box's eventual free.\n\nWhat 320 does NOT cover, and what this issue is for:\n\n- The user-facing spec shape that triggers deletion.\n- A convenience wrapper for the common case.\n- Validation that catches \"I forgot to fill in fields\"\n  accidents from masquerading as deletes.\n- The downstream effects when consumers wired to a deleted box\n  try to push values into the now-gone graph slot.\n\n## Why deletion needs more than just \"any minimum spec\"\n\nThe natural shortcut would be: \"if the spec only has an id and\nno other fields, treat it as a delete.\" Compact and elegant.\n\nBut it's also dangerous: a user who forgets to populate fields\nin their reconfigure spec accidentally deletes the box. Defaults\nshould fail-closed (do nothing surprising) rather than fail-open\n(do something destructive). The minimum-spec-means-delete shape\nfails open.\n\nThe safer alternative is an explicit marker in the spec:\n\n```json\n{\"action\": \"delete\", \"id\": \"target_box_id\"}\n```\n\nThe runtime parses the spec, sees `action == \"delete\"`, and\nroutes through the delete path. Specs without an explicit\n`action` field default to create-or-reconfigure (the inferred\naction based on whether target_id exists). Explicit beats\nimplicit; destructive operations are always explicit.\n\n## Convenience wrapper\n\nFor the common case where a user just wants to delete a box\nthey know the id of, add a sugar function:\n\n```c\nint runtime_destroy_box(const char *target_id, char **err_out);\n```\n\nInternally, this constructs the delete spec JSON and calls\n`runtime_apply_box_spec`. Same code path, friendlier signature.\n\nSame shape per language bridge:\n\n- Lua: `soramech.destroy_box(target_id)`\n- C:   `soramech_destroy_box(target_id, err_buf, err_cap)`\n- Bash: `soramech_destroy_box \"$target_id\"`\n\n## Downstream effects of deletion\n\nA box X is deleted. Some other box Y has a connection pointing\nat X. Y fires, produces an output, attempts to push to X's\ninput slots — but X is gone from the graph slot.\n\nTwo possible behaviours:\n\n- **Silent drop:** the push fails because the target lookup\n  returns NULL. Producer continues; output is lost. A push\n  event with `result=target-gone` records the loss in the\n  JSONL transcript.\n- **Hard error:** the push fails and the producer's fire is\n  treated as a failure. The run aborts (or the producer's\n  spec returns an error code).\n\nThe user's stated preference throughout the project is \"errors\nover fallbacks.\" So hard error is the strict reading. But\ndeletion is a deliberate user action — if they deleted X, they\nprobably know Y depended on it. Hard-error-on-every-push would\nmean a single deleted leaf-box could crash the entire run.\n\nA middle path: silent drop by default, with the JSONL event\nmaking the loss observable, AND a runtime knob (env var or\nspec field) to upgrade the drop to a hard error for users who\nwant strict behaviour.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Define the spec shape for delete.** `{\"action\": \"delete\",\n   \"id\": \"...\"}`. Document that the `action` field defaults to\n   \"apply\" (which means create-or-reconfigure based on target\n   existence) and the only other recognised value is \"delete\".\n2. **Implement the delete path inside\n   `runtime_apply_box_spec`.** Already part of 320's\n   implementation; this is just adding the action dispatch.\n3. **Add `runtime_destroy_box` as the sugar wrapper.** Three\n   language bridges plus the C entry point.\n4. **Add the push-target-gone JSONL event.** Same shape as\n   other push events; `result=target-gone` is the new value.\n5. **Add an opt-in strict mode** for users who want push-to-\n   deleted-box to hard-error rather than silent-drop. Env var\n   `SORAMECH_STRICT_DELETE=1` or per-call flag, TBD.\n6. **Fixtures:**\n   - `tests/maps/322-delete-then-orphaned-push` — A box X is\n     created; B is wired to X; X is deleted; B fires once more;\n     the push fails with `result=target-gone` in the JSONL.\n   - `tests/maps/322-delete-and-recreate` — A box X is created,\n     deleted, then created again with the same id and different\n     behaviour. The recreate succeeds at the now-NULL graph\n     slot; subsequent fires use the new behaviour.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_destroy_box`\n  sugar wrapper.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` extended to\n  recognise the `action` field on the spec.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  `target-gone` as a new push result.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `destroy_box`.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Strict-mode default.** Should `SORAMECH_STRICT_DELETE=0`\n  (silent drop default) or `=1` (hard error default) be the\n  shipped default? Silent drop matches \"don't crash the run on\n  a leaf-box deletion\"; hard error matches \"errors over\n  fallbacks.\" Lean toward silent-drop-by-default + JSONL event\n  + opt-in strict; revisit if a project disagrees.\n- **Implicit recreation.** A delete followed by a create at\n  the same id — should this work seamlessly, or require an\n  explicit timing barrier? My instinct: works seamlessly. The\n  graph slot transitions NULL → new-box-pointer atomically;\n  any worker that arrives at the in-between state (graph slot\n  is NULL) just exits gracefully.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/322-box-delete-via-runtime-spec-api.md"

    "content":"# 322 — Box delete: the user-facing experience\n\n## Status\nopen · the underlying mechanism is part of 320; this issue\ncovers the user-facing API and the explicit-vs-implicit-deletion\ndesign decision\n\n## Current behavior\n\nOnce issue 320 lands, the runtime has a unified\n`runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, spec_json)` entry point that\nhandles create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec's\ncontent. The delete path is: install NULL at the graph slot\nvia the same supersession mechanism, let the refcount drive\nthe old box's eventual free.\n\nWhat 320 does NOT cover, and what this issue is for:\n\n- The user-facing spec shape that triggers deletion.\n- A convenience wrapper for the common case.\n- Validation that catches \"I forgot to fill in fields\"\n  accidents from masquerading as deletes.\n- The downstream effects when consumers wired to a deleted box\n  try to push values into the now-gone graph slot.\n\n## Why deletion needs more than just \"any minimum spec\"\n\nThe natural shortcut would be: \"if the spec only has an id and\nno other fields, treat it as a delete.\" Compact and elegant.\n\nBut it's also dangerous: a user who forgets to populate fields\nin their reconfigure spec accidentally deletes the box. Defaults\nshould fail-closed (do nothing surprising) rather than fail-open\n(do something destructive). The minimum-spec-means-delete shape\nfails open.\n\nThe safer alternative is an explicit marker in the spec:\n\n```json\n{\"action\": \"delete\", \"id\": \"target_box_id\"}\n```\n\nThe runtime parses the spec, sees `action == \"delete\"`, and\nroutes through the delete path. Specs without an explicit\n`action` field default to create-or-reconfigure (the inferred\naction based on whether target_id exists). Explicit beats\nimplicit; destructive operations are always explicit.\n\n## Convenience wrapper\n\nFor the common case where a user just wants to delete a box\nthey know the id of, add a sugar function:\n\n```c\nint runtime_destroy_box(const char *target_id, char **err_out);\n```\n\nInternally, this constructs the delete spec JSON and calls\n`runtime_apply_box_spec`. Same code path, friendlier signature.\n\nSame shape per language bridge:\n\n- Lua: `soramech.destroy_box(target_id)`\n- C:   `soramech_destroy_box(target_id, err_buf, err_cap)`\n- Bash: `soramech_destroy_box \"$target_id\"`\n\n## Downstream effects of deletion\n\nA box X is deleted. Some other box Y has a connection pointing\nat X. Y fires, produces an output, attempts to push to X's\ninput slots — but X is gone from the graph slot.\n\nTwo possible behaviours:\n\n- **Silent drop:** the push fails because the target lookup\n  returns NULL. Producer continues; output is lost. A push\n  event with `result=target-gone` records the loss in the\n  JSONL transcript.\n- **Hard error:** the push fails and the producer's fire is\n  treated as a failure. The run aborts (or the producer's\n  spec returns an error code).\n\nThe user's stated preference throughout the project is \"errors\nover fallbacks.\" So hard error is the strict reading. But\ndeletion is a deliberate user action — if they deleted X, they\nprobably know Y depended on it. Hard-error-on-every-push would\nmean a single deleted leaf-box could crash the entire run.\n\nA middle path: silent drop by default, with the JSONL event\nmaking the loss observable, AND a runtime knob (env var or\nspec field) to upgrade the drop to a hard error for users who\nwant strict behaviour.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Define the spec shape for delete.** `{\"action\": \"delete\",\n   \"id\": \"...\"}`. Document that the `action` field defaults to\n   \"apply\" (which means create-or-reconfigure based on target\n   existence) and the only other recognised value is \"delete\".\n2. **Implement the delete path inside\n   `runtime_apply_box_spec`.** Already part of 320's\n   implementation; this is just adding the action dispatch.\n3. **Add `runtime_destroy_box` as the sugar wrapper.** Three\n   language bridges plus the C entry point.\n4. **Add the push-target-gone JSONL event.** Same shape as\n   other push events; `result=target-gone` is the new value.\n5. **Add an opt-in strict mode** for users who want push-to-\n   deleted-box to hard-error rather than silent-drop. Env var\n   `SORAMECH_STRICT_DELETE=1` or per-call flag, TBD.\n6. **Fixtures:**\n   - `tests/maps/322-delete-then-orphaned-push` — A box X is\n     created; B is wired to X; X is deleted; B fires once more;\n     the push fails with `result=target-gone` in the JSONL.\n   - `tests/maps/322-delete-and-recreate` — A box X is created,\n     deleted, then created again with the same id and different\n     behaviour. The recreate succeeds at the now-NULL graph\n     slot; subsequent fires use the new behaviour.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_destroy_box`\n  sugar wrapper.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` extended to\n  recognise the `action` field on the spec.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  `target-gone` as a new push result.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `destroy_box`.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Strict-mode default.** Should `SORAMECH_STRICT_DELETE=0`\n  (silent drop default) or `=1` (hard error default) be the\n  shipped default? Silent drop matches \"don't crash the run on\n  a leaf-box deletion\"; hard error matches \"errors over\n  fallbacks.\" Lean toward silent-drop-by-default + JSONL event\n  + opt-in strict; revisit if a project disagrees.\n- **Implicit recreation.** A delete followed by a create at\n  the same id — should this work seamlessly, or require an\n  explicit timing barrier? My instinct: works seamlessly. The\n  graph slot transitions NULL → new-box-pointer atomically;\n  any worker that arrives at the in-between state (graph slot\n  is NULL) just exits gracefully.\n",
    "type":"create",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/322-box-delete-via-runtime-spec-api.md"
  },
  "userType":"external",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}

New design:\n\n- Per-box control queue (a regular slot allocated from the slot\n  store, cell capacity = pointer size) carries pre-built\n  replacement box-struct pointers.\n- Two-state gather flag (held / not-held); the graph slot\n  pointer acts as the liveness indicator, eliminating the\n  three-state flag's redirect mode.\n- Mutator builds nothing in place; it swaps the graph slot from\n  old box to new box atomically. Old box drifts toward freedom\n  via refcount + \"graph slot doesn't point at me\" check.\n- Pop-only ring semantics inside the gather flag's brief atomic\n  section, eliminating the peek-vs-pop race that plagued the\n  earlier design.\n- One unified runtime API for create / reconfigure / delete:\n  the spec's content decides which path runs.\n\nRenamed the issue file from \"via-third-input-ring\" to\n\"via-runtime-spec-api\" to reflect the actual mechanism.\n\nTwo follow-up issues track work that becomes natural after 320\nlands but doesn't belong inside it:\n\n- 321: retire the runtime_connect copy-and-publish dance on the\n  connections array; route it through the same box-swap path.\n- 322: the user-facing box-delete experience — explicit\n  \"action\": \"delete\" marker (fail-closed defaults), a sugar\n  destroy_box wrapper, push-to-deleted-box handling.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -8",

        "text":"Design phase committed. Three issue files in place. Task list updated to reflect the new design (10 implementation tasks for 320).\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The design discussion collapsed roughly 25 design decisions into 5 structural pieces.** The gather flag, the control queue, the graph slot as liveness, the refcount, the replacement box struct. Every other detail in the issue file follows from these five — slot diffing is \"how to handle ports across the swap,\" the unified API is \"what does the spec mean,\" refcount-driven GC is \"when is OLD freeable.\" Identifying the load-bearing primitives and letting the rest fall out is how complex designs become tractable.\n- **The \"design history\" section preserves the rejected designs concisely.** Future readers (including future-you) will benefit from knowing what was tried and discarded, but the body of the issue should describe the final design. The history paragraph at the bottom is small enough to skip if you don't care, and substantive enough to ground you if you do. This is a different shape from a changelog — it's \"here are the dead ends,\" not \"here's how this evolved.\"\n- **Splitting 320 from 321 and 322 reflects scope discipline.** All three could have lived as one massive issue, but they have different blast radii: 320 introduces the core mechanism; 321 is a refactor that depends on 320; 322 is user-facing polish that depends on 320. Each can land independently with its own commit history. A single-issue design encourages monster PRs; a properly-split-issue design encourages focused work.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nReady to implement. With 10 implementation tasks queued, the natural starting points are:\n\n- **#11 (parse_box_file refactor)** — no dependencies, smallest blast radius, prerequisite for the API.\n- **#10 (gather flag + refcount fields)** — pure data layout addition, prerequisite for the gather lock.\n- **#12 (graph as array-of-pointers)** — biggest structural change; everything else easier once this lands.\n\nI'd start with **#12 (array of pointers)** because it's the most invasive and easiest to get wrong; landing it first gets the painful part out of the way while other code paths are still simple. Then #10 + #11 in any order, then the gather lock + control queue + mutator + API stack. Sound good, or do you want a different sequence?"

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Good question — I've been sloppy with \"API.\" Let me clarify the dataflow, because there are actually two different channels involved.\n\n## Two distinct channels\n\n**Channel 1 — wires (the dataflow plane):** boxes connected to other boxes by connections. Producer fires, pushes its output bytes into the consumer's input slot's ring buffer. The consumer's worker pops from the ring. This is what you've been thinking of as \"input ports.\"\n\n**Channel 2 — direct function calls into the runtime (the control plane):** any code running inside a box's invoke can call C functions like `runtime_create_box(...)`, `runtime_connect(...)`, and now `runtime_apply_box_spec(...)`. These are NOT wire-based — they're plain function calls that the language bridge exposes to box code.\n\nWhen I said \"API,\" I meant **Channel 2.** The reconfigure JSON does NOT ride the wire system to reach the target box. It travels via a direct function call from whichever box wants to do the reconfiguring.\n\n## Walking through a concrete example\n\nSuppose you have a Lua box called `planner` that wants to reconfigure a box called `worker`. The planner's Lua function looks something like:\n\n```lua\nfunction planner.run(some_input)\n    -- decide we want to change how worker behaves\n    local new_spec = {\n        kind = \"call\",\n        lang = \"lua\",\n        ref  = \"src/worker.lua\",\n        fn   = \"new_implementation\",\n        inputs = { { name = \"x\", type = \"string\" } }\n    }\n    soramech.apply_box(\"worker\", new_spec)\n    return some_output\nend\n```\n\nWhen `planner` fires, its Lua function calls `soramech.apply_box(\"worker\", new_spec)`. That's the language bridge. Inside the bridge:\n\n1. It serializes `new_spec` (a Lua table) to JSON bytes.\n2. It calls the C function `runtime_apply_box_spec(\"worker\", json_bytes, json_len, &err)`.\n3. That C function parses the JSON, builds a fresh `box_t` struct in memory, and pushes the struct's pointer onto **worker's control queue** (the per-box slot we talked about).\n\nThe reconfigure JSON never touched a wire. It came into existence inside planner's invoke, got passed through the bridge as a function argument, and ended up as a struct pointer in worker's control queue.\n\n## Why the control queue and not an input port?\n\nTwo reasons:\n\n**First, control messages aren't input values.** An input value on port \"x\" is a piece of data that the box's function consumes. A reconfigure message is metadata about the box's identity. They're different in kind, and mixing them on the same channel led to all the peek-vs-pop race conditions we struggled with for a while.\n\n**Second, the producer of the reconfigure isn't a graph-wired box.** It's whatever code happens to be running that decided to reconfigure something. Could be a Lua box's invoke. Could be a C function called from anywhere. Could even be a future REST endpoint someone wires up to let an external system reconfigure boxes. None of these are connected to the target box by a wire — they all just call the same C function.\n\n## What about the \"reconfigure box kind\" we discussed early on?\n\nThat idea — a box whose JOB is to receive a JSON spec on an input port and apply it as a reconfigure — still works in this design, but it's no longer a special box kind. It's just a normal box with a regular function that happens to call `soramech.apply_box(...)` internally.\n\nSo if you DO want reconfigure messages to flow through your map's wire system (e.g., one box produces a spec, another consumes and applies it), you'd build it like this:\n\n```\n[spec_producer] --wire (carries JSON)--> [reconfigure_relay_box]\n                                              |\n                                              | (its invoke calls\n                                              |  soramech.apply_box)\n                                              v\n                                         (control queue of \"worker\")\n```\n\nThe wire carries the JSON to `reconfigure_relay_box`. That box's function reads the JSON from its input port and calls the runtime API. The runtime API pushes the struct pointer to worker's control queue.\n\nThe wire is still there for users who want the dataflow style. But the runtime mechanism underneath is the same direct function call.\n\n## What the control queue actually receives\n\nThe control queue stores **already-parsed box-struct pointers**, not raw JSON. The parsing happens in the caller's thread (wherever `runtime_apply_box_spec` was called from), so the mutator on the target box doesn't have to do any JSON work — it just pops a pointer and swaps.\n\nIf multiple reconfigures are pushed in quick succession (say, planner_a and planner_b both call `soramech.apply_box(\"worker\", ...)` at nearly the same time), both struct pointers land in worker's control queue. The mutator processes them in FIFO order — first one wins the swap, second one swaps over the first, etc.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The \"control plane vs data plane\" distinction is the same one networking made decades ago.** TCP carries data; ICMP carries control. They share the wire but are conceptually separate, and confusing them creates exactly the kind of edge case we wrestled with for several rounds of design. Your runtime made the same split: input slots carry data, control queue carries control, runtime API is the function-call entry point that bridges between \"code running in a box\" and \"the control plane mechanism.\" Once the split is named, the design clarifies.\n- **\"API\" in this codebase always means C functions callable from any thread, not wire-based message passing.** Same as create_box and connect today. The convention is: anything that mutates the graph at runtime is a function call, not a dataflow. Dataflow is for values; function calls are for graph changes. Keeping these orthogonal means box authors don't have to invent ad-hoc protocols for \"how do I tell the runtime to add a wire\" — they just call a function.\n- **The relay box pattern is the bridge between wires and the runtime API.** If you want a dataflow-style reconfigure, you build a normal box whose function happens to call the runtime API on each fire. The runtime doesn't know or care; it just sees another invocation of `runtime_apply_box_spec`. This means \"dataflow reconfigure\" is composable — you can have multiple producers feeding one relay box, or one producer feeding multiple relay boxes, all expressible with normal wires.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nDoes this clear up where the JSON travels and what \"API\" means? Once you're comfortable with this picture, the implementation tasks should make more sense — task #15 (the API entry point) and task #18 (the language bridges) are the two pieces of the function-call path; task #17 (control queue) is the per-box slot that receives the resulting pointers; tasks #10/#12/#13/#14 are the gather/mutator mechanics that read from the control queue."
      }],
