        "type":"text",
        "text":"Good clarifying questions — let me untangle the layers.\n\n## Where the code lives\n\nThe function `soramech.apply_box` is registered by the **language bridge**, not added as a file in libs/. It's the same shape as the existing `soramech.create_box` and `soramech.connect` — those aren't libs/ files either; they're functions the Lua spec exposes to every Lua box.\n\nTo make this concrete: when the Lua spec initialises a worker thread, it pushes a table called `soramech` into the global Lua state. The table has entries for create_box, connect, and (after 320) apply_box. Any Lua box's function can call any of these without importing anything — they're just available.\n\nSo the answer to \"are we adding a file to libs/?\" is no, not for the foundational mechanism. **The mechanism is bridge code.** libs/ is reserved for higher-level helpers — for example, if a pattern emerges where users keep building call-box specs by hand (`{kind=\"call\", lang=\"lua\", ref=\"...\", fn=\"...\", inputs={...}}`), we could add `libs/box-builder.lua` that exposes `box.call(\"src/foo.lua\", \"process\", {\"x\", \"y\"})` and returns a populated spec table. That's optional polish that lands when there's a clear use case, not part of 320.\n\n## How a box reconfigures a different box\n\nInside a box's function (in any language), the box code calls `soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec)`. The target_id is just a string — the id of whichever box you want to reconfigure.\n\nWhere does the target_id come from? Three patterns, all valid:\n\n**Pattern A — hardcoded in the box's source.**\n```lua\nfunction controller.run(input)\n    soramech.apply_box(\"worker\", { kind=\"call\", fn=\"new_fn\", ... })\n    return input\nend\n```\nThe literal string `\"worker\"` is in the source. Fine when the controller box always reconfigures the same target. Simple, no extra wires needed.\n\n**Pattern B — supplied as an input value.**\n```lua\nfunction controller.run(target_id, spec_json)\n    soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec_json)\nend\n```\nThe controller has two input ports: target_id and spec_json. Upstream boxes push values onto these ports. When controller fires, its function reads the values and calls apply_box. Useful when the target depends on data.\n\n**Pattern C — id captured from a previous create_box call.**\n```lua\nfunction planner.run(seed)\n    local new_id = soramech.create_box({ kind=\"call\", ... })\n    -- ...later...\n    soramech.apply_box(new_id, { kind=\"call\", fn=\"updated_fn\", ... })\nend\n```\nThe id was generated when the box was created. The planner remembers it and uses it later for reconfigure. This is \"I'm managing a fleet of boxes I created\" territory.\n\nAll three patterns work with the same mechanism. The runtime doesn't care how the controller decided which target to talk to — it just gets a string and a spec.\n\n## Thread-pool interaction, step by step\n\nThis is the bit that's most worth walking through carefully, because the timing has some non-obvious moments.\n\n**Step 1 — Controller fires.** Upstream boxes push values into controller's input slots. The dispatch spawns a task for controller. The pool picks a worker, say W1. W1 enters `dispatch_action` for controller.\n\n**Step 2 — Controller's invoke runs on W1.** W1 holds controller's gather flag briefly during the input gather, then releases the flag and calls the Lua spec's invoke. The invoke runs controller's function. Inside the function: `soramech.apply_box(\"worker\", spec_table)` is called.\n\n**Step 3 — apply_box runs on the SAME thread (W1).** The Lua bridge serialises the spec_table to JSON. It calls the C function `runtime_apply_box_spec(\"worker\", json, len, &err)`. The C function parses the JSON, allocates a new box struct, fills in the fields. All of this happens on W1.\n\n**Step 4 — The new struct's pointer is pushed onto worker's control queue.** This is a slot operation, thread-safe via the slot's spinlock. The push is fire-and-forget — it doesn't wait for any worker on the target. If worker's control queue is full (8 cells already taken), W1 briefly waits for space. In practice it's always empty.\n\n**Step 5 — apply_box returns.** Control returns to controller's Lua function, which returns its output value. W1 finishes controller's fire — pushes controller's output to downstream slots, decrements controller's refcount, etc. W1 is done with controller and goes back to the pool to pick up another task.\n\n**Step 6 — Eventually a worker arrives at the target box.** This is the decoupled-in-time part. Some time later — could be microseconds, could be longer — a worker (say W2, could be the same as W1 or different) arrives at worker box. W2 enters dispatch_action, tries to acquire worker's gather flag, succeeds, checks worker's control queue, sees the pending pointer. W2 becomes the mutator: pops the pointer, resolves slot mappings, atomically swaps the graph slot, releases the gather flag, yarqs.\n\n**Step 7 — The reconfigure has landed.** From now on, anyone looking up \"worker\" via the graph slot gets the new box struct. Subsequent fires of worker run under the new shape.\n\n## What triggers W2 to arrive at the target?\n\nThis is the subtle bit. The thread pool doesn't proactively schedule work for the target box just because a reconfigure was pushed to its control queue. The pool only schedules tasks for boxes whose inputs are ready (or boxes that were explicitly spawned via dispatch_spawn).\n\nSo if no producer pushes values to worker's inputs after the reconfigure, no worker arrives at worker, and the reconfigure sits unread in the control queue forever. This is fine semantically — reconfigure means \"next time you fire, fire as this new shape.\" If worker never fires, the reconfigure is moot.\n\n**But** if you want the reconfigure to take effect EAGERLY — even when no inputs are queued — the runtime API should automatically dispatch_spawn the target after pushing to its control queue. The spawned task arrives at worker, finds the control queue non-empty, becomes mutator (the mutator path doesn't need any input values — it just does the swap), applies the reconfigure, yarqs.\n\nMy proposal: **apply_box automatically spawns a task for the target.** Cost is one task in the pool queue (cheap). Benefit is eager application — the reconfigure lands quickly even if no producer is pushing to the target. Workers that arrive at the target but find nothing to do beyond the reconfigure just process the reconfigure and exit. No fire happens unless inputs are also available.\n\n## Putting it all together — the dataflow picture\n\n```\nupstream values ──wire──> controller's input slots\n                              │\n                              ▼\n                       (W1 fires controller)\n                              │\n                       controller.run() called\n                              │\n                       calls soramech.apply_box(\"worker\", spec)\n                              │\n                       (still W1) parse JSON, build struct,\n                       push struct pointer onto:\n                              │\n                              ▼\n                       worker's CONTROL QUEUE (not its inputs!)\n                              │\n                       apply_box returns\n                              │\n                       controller.run() returns its output\n                              │\n                       (W1 done with controller)\n\n         ...later, separately...\n\n                       (W2 arrives at worker, e.g. because a\n                        producer pushed an input, or because\n                        apply_box auto-spawned a task)\n                              │\n                       W2 acquires worker's gather flag\n                              │\n                       W2 checks worker's control queue → non-empty\n                              │\n                       W2 becomes mutator\n                              │\n                       atomic graph slot swap: worker → new struct\n                              │\n                       W2 yarqs\n                              │\n                       (next worker to visit \"worker\" runs under new shape)\n```\n\nThe wire system (upstream → controller) is the data plane. The function call (controller → apply_box → control queue) is the control plane. The mutator path (W2 → graph slot swap) is the application. Three distinct phases, decoupled in time, each one running on whatever thread the pool happened to assign.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The \"language bridge exposes runtime APIs\" pattern is a thin layer with deep consequences.** Boxes get to participate in graph modification without knowing anything about graph internals — they just call functions. The bridge is the only piece that knows both the language's calling conventions AND the C function signatures. New languages added later only need to learn one shape: \"expose these N functions in your soramech namespace.\" Everything downstream stays the same.\n- **The \"decoupled in time\" property of pushing to the control queue is what makes this safe to call from anywhere.** The caller doesn't have to know whether the target is currently busy, whether other reconfigures are pending, whether the target even has inputs queued. The push is fire-and-forget; the application happens when it can. Same pattern as posting to a message queue in a distributed system — the producer never blocks on the consumer's state.\n- **Auto-spawn after apply_box is the small piece of glue that makes the API feel responsive.** Without it, reconfigures could land arbitrarily late, depending on when the next input arrives at the target. With it, the runtime guarantees the reconfigure is processed within \"one trip through the pool queue\" — typically microseconds. The cost is one extra task in the queue; the benefit is predictable timing for users.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## Question back\n\nDo you want **apply_box to auto-spawn a task on the target after pushing to the control queue**, so reconfigures land eagerly even when no inputs are queued? Or do you prefer the lazy \"applies whenever the target next fires\" semantic? My instinct is auto-spawn — feels right for an API that users will reach for — but it's your call.\n\nAnd: should `soramech.apply_box` return immediately after pushing (fire-and-forget), or should it return some kind of \"confirmation that the reconfigure landed\" — a way for the caller to wait for the swap to happen? Fire-and-forget is simpler; the confirmation pattern would require a callback or a future, which is more complex but might be useful for \"I want to know my reconfigure landed before I continue.\""
      }],

```json
{
  "uuid":"88c80e53-0680-44e9-808b-646bb78dcf4e",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-25T03:55:42.961Z",
  "slug":"goofy-noodling-torvalds",
  "parentUuid":"384e130e-c2da-40cc-b86c-2c1f16fcfd13",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "promptId":"73c74486-702c-4cc9-b525-0560c47231e9",
  "userType":"external",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits",
  "message":{
    "content":"  The function soramech.apply_box is registered by the language bridge, not added as a file in libs/. It's the same shape as the existing soramech.create_box and soramech.connect — those aren't libs/ files either; they're functions the Lua spec exposes to every Lua box.\n\nwhoa whoa whoa, that doesn't sound right. We shouldn't have the box creation and connection utilities be part of the language bridge, that'd require the user to write code that used those functionalities. Actually, what the heck is a language \"bridge\" anyway? We have language specs, and those are for taking input values and running values in their own thread's languages / runtimes, and then returning outputs. But this is the first I've heard of a language \"bridge\". If all it does is create a box and connect boxes (the connecting we're superseding with reconfiguring) then it doesn't belong in the language spec. It's sora-mech specific, it doesn't have anything to do with lua! We need to build it as it's own box type, like the iterator / non-linear / comparator etc.\n\n  How a box reconfigures a different box\n\n  Inside a box's function (in any language), the box code calls soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec).\n\nyeah see this is what we want to avoid. We don't want to have to make soramech includable as a library - we include other libraries, we don't expect them to include us. If the user wants to use soramech's functionality, then they must use soramech to do so - whether that means using the editor or creating json at runtime, that's up to them. But we shouldn't have them create that sort of thing in language.\n\nI figured we had the \"create-a-box\" box which I'm considering renaming to just \"utility-box\" or something. That box will create a json structure that can be parsed by the graph loader. It will apply itself to whichever box it's output wire points to, on any of it's input slots - this is how we target which box to reconfigure, and also this is why we were planning on interleaving the pointer to the new box json with the input values in the input slot ring buffers - they can never be confused for actual values because the gather_inputs() process is atomic, and handles the reconfiguring. Frankly I don't see the benefit of the control queue?",
    "role":"user"
  },

  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"You're right and I was off in the weeds. Let me recalibrate, because I had the wrong mental model and was steering toward a design that doesn't match your architectural intent.\n\n## What I got wrong\n\nI was treating \"the runtime API\" as a thing users would call from their language code — like Java's reflection API, where user code reaches into the runtime to manipulate it. That's the function-call-as-a-library pattern, and you're right that it pulls in the wrong direction: it makes SoraMech-the-system depend on being importable from arbitrary user code, which is exactly the inversion you don't want.\n\nYour model is the opposite: **users express what they want by building boxes and wires, and the runtime interprets that.** If you want to reconfigure a box, you don't write code that calls reconfigure — you put a reconfigure-utility-box in your map, wire its output to the target, and let the dataflow do the work. The runtime never gets called as a library; it's always the substrate.\n\nThe phase 3 progress file confirms this — 319f's `BOX_CREATE_BOX` and `BOX_CONNECT` are already dispatch primitives (box kinds), language-agnostic. The Lua bridge functions from 319d still exist but they're the legacy path; the box-kind pattern is the project's current direction. I should have spotted this and stayed consistent with it.\n\n## The corrected architecture\n\nLet me re-walk what we're actually building, all the way through:\n\n**The utility-box (renaming from \"create-a-box\"):** a dispatch primitive box kind that handles create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec it receives. It has:\n- One input port — the JSON spec\n- One output wire — points to the target\n\nWhen the utility-box fires, it doesn't produce a normal value. Instead, it parses the JSON into a fully-built box struct (in the firing worker's thread), then pushes a **pointer to that struct** onto its output wire's destination — which is one of the target box's input slots. The push is tagged so the target's gather knows \"this isn't a value; this is a reconfigure.\"\n\n**The wire system carries everything:** values, reconfigure messages, anything. The same slot, same ring buffer infrastructure. The ordering ring tag distinguishes what's in each cell. The user builds reconfigure topologies with the same wires they use for everything else, visible in the editor, expressible in JSON.\n\n**The target box's gather is atomic.** When a worker arrives at the target, it tries to CAS the box's gather flag from 0 to 1. Wins → enters gather, peeks each port's ordering ring (safe because nobody else can be in gather right now). If any port shows a RECONFIGURE tag, the worker becomes the mutator: pops the reconfigure messages, swaps the graph slot to the new box, releases the gather flag, yarqs. If all ports show value tags, the worker pops values normally and fires.\n\n**The race I was so worried about doesn't happen** because the gather lock is the serialization point. Two workers can't both be in gather at the same time on the same box, so peek-then-pop is honest within the lock.\n\n**No separate control queue.** The reconfigure message lives in the same slot the values do. The ring buffer's ordering tag is what carries the kind discrimination.\n\n## Walking through a fire-then-reconfigure scenario\n\n```\nupstream JSON producer ──wire──> utility_box ──wire──> target_box (input \"x\")\n                                                  │\n                                                  ▼\n                                         pushes a struct pointer\n                                         with RING_RECONFIGURE tag\n                                         onto target_box's input \"x\"\n```\n\nWhen utility_box fires:\n1. It pops a JSON spec from its input port.\n2. It parses the JSON into a `box_t` struct (in the worker's thread).\n3. It pushes the struct pointer onto its output wire's target — which lands in target_box's input slot for port \"x\", tagged as RECONFIGURE.\n\nSome time later, when target_box is fired:\n4. A worker arrives at target_box, CASes the gather flag.\n5. Inside gather: peeks each input port's ordering ring. Port \"x\" shows RECONFIGURE at its head.\n6. Worker becomes mutator. Pops the struct pointer from port \"x\". Resolves slot mappings between OLD and NEW (port-name set-diff). Atomically swaps target_box's graph slot from OLD to NEW. Releases gather flag. Yarqs.\n7. Next worker to fire target_box gets NEW via the graph slot. NEW's input slots are the same physical slots (matched by port name), so any queued values on the unaffected ports are still there.\n\n## Why this is simpler than what I was proposing\n\n- **No new infrastructure.** No separate control queue, no per-box control slot. Just the existing input slots with an extra ordering tag value.\n- **Visible in the editor.** A reconfigure wire IS a wire. Users see it on the canvas, drag it like any other wire.\n- **Composable with existing patterns.** A read box can feed a static spec to a utility-box. A planner box can generate dynamic specs. A fan-in topology can feed multiple producers' specs to one utility-box.\n- **No language bridge bloat.** Languages don't expose runtime mutation as library functions. They only have to know how to fire box functions and serialise their outputs.\n\n## What this changes about the issue files\n\nThe 320 issue I just wrote is wrong — it's based on the control-queue + bridge-function design. I need to rewrite it to reflect the box-kind + per-port-third-ring approach. Tasks #15 (runtime API entry point) and #18 (language bridges) should be replaced with tasks for the BOX_RECONFIGURE (or unified utility) box kind and the per-port RECONFIGURE tag handling. Task #17 (control slot) goes away.\n\nBefore I rewrite, let me ask the right questions this time:\n\n## Questions back\n\n1. **Naming the box kind.** You floated \"utility-box\" — is that what you want? It's a fairly broad name; a more specific alternative would be \"spec-applier\" or \"reconfigure-box\" or just \"box-control.\" If utility-box is going to absorb everything (create, reconfigure, delete), the broad name fits. If it's specifically for reconfigure-style operations with create and delete as separate kinds, a narrower name is better. My instinct: **utility-box** with the spec's `action` field deciding what it does (create / reconfigure / delete based on whether target exists and what the spec asks for). One box kind, three meanings, dispatched by content.\n\n2. **What does \"target\" mean — the box at the wire's other end?** I assumed the utility-box's output wire goes to a specific input slot of the target box, and the target is identified by being at the wire's other end. Is that right? The alternative is the utility-box has TWO inputs — one for the JSON spec, one for the target_id string — and its output goes... nowhere? Or it has no output? My read of your description is: the wire end IS the target, no separate target-id field needed.\n\n3. **Does 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX get folded into the new utility-box, or stay separate?** They're the same operation if utility-box handles create. Folding means one box kind for all graph mutation; staying separate means we have BOX_CREATE_BOX (existing) + BOX_RECONFIGURE (new) + later BOX_DELETE (or fold delete into reconfigure). My instinct: fold them all. One mutation primitive, one mental model.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **\"The runtime is the substrate; the user expresses through it\" is a clean architectural inversion.** Most systems put themselves in the import path; users have to learn the system's API to use it. SoraMech goes the other way: the user builds boxes and wires; the runtime makes sense of them. This is the same inversion that visual programming languages (Scratch, Max/MSP, Pure Data) made decades ago — the IDE isn't a window into the code, it IS the code. Sticking to this discipline matters because every concession to the \"import us as a library\" pattern weakens the visual-programming nature of the system.\n- **The per-port third ring really was the right design** — the gather lock makes the peek-pop race I was worried about disappear. I was solving a problem that didn't exist within the architecture you laid out. The control queue solution I proposed was elegant in isolation, but it was a layer-mismatch: I was trying to keep \"control\" out of the data plane when your design explicitly wants them in the same plane, distinguished by ordering tag rather than by channel. The reason it's safe to mix them is the gather lock, not channel separation.\n- **319f already proved the box-kind pattern works for graph mutation.** I should have built directly on that precedent rather than pulling in a different shape. When a project has an established mutation primitive pattern (BOX_CREATE_BOX as a dispatch kind), the new mutation primitive should match — same shape, same expectations, same composability with the editor. Consistency at this level pays dividends in user mental load.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nI'll rewrite 320 once you've answered the three questions above. The implementation tasks need a similar overhaul — the box-kind tasks should match what 319f already established for BOX_CREATE_BOX, just with the reconfigure semantics swapped in."
      }],

  "message":{
    "content":"  Your model is the opposite: users express what they want by building boxes and wires, and the runtime interprets that. If you want to reconfigure a box, you don't write code that calls reconfigure — you put a reconfigure-utility-box in your map, wire its output to the target, and\n  let the dataflow do the work. The runtime never gets called as a library; it's always the substrate.\n\nyes that's true, but I should mention that users CAN build the json manually if they want. Say they have a long-running function that builds up json about how it wants to reconfigure it's box for the next time it's run - that's fine! They should be able to do that. So long as they store the json in shared memory, then it's perfectly okay for them to build the json manually. But we're not going to help them, the manual path is supported but the box-and-wire path is intended.\n\n  1. Naming the box kind. You floated \"utility-box\" — is that what you want? It's a fairly broad name; a more specific alternative would be \"spec-applier\" or \"reconfigure-box\" or just \"box-control.\" If utility-box is going to absorb everything (create, reconfigure, delete), the broad\n   name fits. If it's specifically for reconfigure-style operations with create and delete as separate kinds, a narrower name is better. My instinct: utility-box with the spec's action field deciding what it does (create / reconfigure / delete based on whether target exists and what\n  the spec asks for). One box kind, three meanings, dispatched by content.\n  2. What does \"target\" mean — the box at the wire's other end? I assumed the utility-box's output wire goes to a specific input slot of the target box, and the target is identified by being at the wire's other end. Is that right? The alternative is the utility-box has TWO inputs —\n  one for the JSON spec, one for the target_id string — and its output goes... nowhere? Or it has no output? My read of your description is: the wire end IS the target, no separate target-id field needed.\n  3. Does 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX get folded into the new utility-box, or stay separate? They're the same operation if utility-box handles create. Folding means one box kind for all graph mutation; staying separate means we have BOX_CREATE_BOX (existing) + BOX_RECONFIGURE (new) + later\n   BOX_DELETE (or fold delete into reconfigure). My instinct: fold them all. One mutation primitive, one mental model.\n\n\nyep these are right",
    "role":"user"
  },
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sessionId":"1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa"
}

The single input port is named\n * `connection` and carries one connection-entry shape (the same\n * JSON object that goes inside a box JSON's `connections[]`\n * array). On success the box emits the literal string \"true\"\n * so downstream consumers can chain off the side effect. */\nstatic int do_connect_box(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b, int task_id,\n                          char *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    int n = b->n_inputs;\n    if (n < 0 || n > DISPATCH_MAX_INPUTS_PER_BOX) return -1;\n    size_t n_arr = (n > 0) ? (size_t)n : 1;\n    char        *bufs[n_arr];        memset(bufs,       0, sizeof bufs);\n    ua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[n_arr];  memset(buf_chunks, 0, sizeof buf_chunks);\n    const void  *datas[n_arr];       memset(datas,      0, sizeof datas);\n    int          sizes[n_arr];       memset(sizes,      0, sizeof sizes);\n    int failed = 0;\n    int n_present = read_inputs(ctx, b, bufs, buf_chunks, datas, sizes,\n                                NULL, ctx->default_out_capacity, &failed);\n    emit_input_events(ctx, task_id, bufs, sizes, n_present);\n    if (failed || n_present < 1) {\n        release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    char *err = NULL;\n    int rc = runtime_connect((const char *)datas[0], sizes[0], &err);\n    release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"connect box '%s': %s\\n\",\n                b->id, err ? err : \"(no message)\");\n        free(err);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (out_capacity >= 4) {\n        memcpy(out_buf, \"true\", 4);\n        *out_size = 4;\n    } else {\n        *out_size = 0;\n    }\n    return 0;",

        "text":"Good news: 319f's existing pattern matches what we want for create. The hard part is unifying the three operations cleanly. Let me lay out what I see and ask one specific question.\n\n## How 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX works today\n\nReading the code: a BOX_CREATE_BOX has one input port (`spec`) carrying JSON bytes. When fired, it parses the JSON, allocates a new box at a fresh graph slot, and emits the new box's id as a string on its output wire. Downstream consumers receive the id as a normal string value and can use it (e.g., a BOX_CONNECT downstream takes the id and wires the new box to something).\n\nThe key thing: BOX_CREATE_BOX's output wire carries the NEW box's id, not control traffic. The output is just a normal string.\n\n## What changes with the unification\n\nFor reconfigure, the user's model is different: the utility-box's output wire points AT the target box's input port, and the message that flows on the wire is a control-tagged pointer (the new box struct) rather than a normal value. The target's gather sees the RECONFIGURE tag and handles it.\n\nFor delete, same shape: a delete-marker flows on the output wire to the target, with a DELETE tag.\n\nSo the three operations have **different output semantics**:\n\n- **Create:** output is a normal string value (the new id); wire goes wherever a consumer wants the id.\n- **Reconfigure:** output is a RECONFIGURE-tagged pointer; wire MUST go to the target box that's being reconfigured.\n- **Delete:** output is a DELETE-tagged marker; wire MUST go to the target box that's being deleted.\n\nThe utility-box, on each fire, has to decide which of these three to do. Two ways to decide:\n\n**Option A — decide by the spec's `action` field.**\n```json\n{ \"action\": \"create\", \"spec\": { ...box JSON... } }\n{ \"action\": \"reconfigure\", \"spec\": { ...box JSON... } }\n{ \"action\": \"delete\" }\n```\nExplicit action field; the utility-box reads it and dispatches. Default action is \"create\" (matches today's BOX_CREATE_BOX behaviour). The wire endpoint validation depends on the action:\n- create: wire endpoint is treated as a normal value consumer of the id string.\n- reconfigure / delete: wire endpoint must be the target box; runtime errors if there's a mismatch with anything else.\n\n**Option B — decide by looking up the spec's id field in the graph.**\n- If the id exists → it's a reconfigure; push tagged message to target.\n- If the id is new → it's a create; emit id string.\n- If the spec is empty / has only an action: delete marker → it's a delete; push tagged message to target.\n\nImplicit, content-driven. Cleaner JSON but more \"magic.\"\n\nI lean toward **Option A** — explicit beats implicit, especially for destructive operations like delete. A user who fat-fingers an id and accidentally hits a real box's id would trigger a reconfigure they didn't intend. Explicit `action` makes the operation visible.\n\n## The wire endpoint mismatch problem\n\nFor reconfigure and delete, the wire endpoint IS the target. So you might think the spec doesn't need an `id` field — the wire already says where to apply. But there's a wrinkle: what if the user wires a utility-box to box A but the spec's content describes box B?\n\nThree options:\n- **Trust the wire, ignore the spec's id.** Wire endpoint = target, full stop. Spec's id field is informational only (or required to match for safety checks).\n- **Trust the spec, ignore the wire endpoint.** Whatever the spec says is the target. Wire endpoint just receives an ack.\n- **Both must agree; mismatch is a hard error.** Wire endpoint MUST point at the box the spec describes.\n\nThird option is the safest — it catches mistakes at runtime and forces the user to be consistent. The wire is the visible truth (you can see it in the editor); the spec's id is the textual truth. Requiring them to match means the visual and textual representations stay aligned.\n\n## Question back\n\n**For the unification:** Option A (explicit `action` field) or Option B (content-driven)? And do you want wire-endpoint-must-match-spec-id as a safety check, or is the wire endpoint authoritative (spec's id is just informational)?\n\nMy instinct after all this back-and-forth:\n- **Option A** for the action field — explicit beats implicit.\n- **Wire endpoint is authoritative for reconfigure/delete; spec's id field is optional but if present must match.** This gives the user a single source of truth (the wire) and an optional safety net (the redundant id).\n- **Default action is \"create\"** — matches today's BOX_CREATE_BOX behaviour, so existing maps using BOX_CREATE_BOX continue to work unchanged.\n\nIf you sign off on this, I'll rewrite 320 to match. Then I want to ask one more practical question about how the JSON is built (the \"users CAN build manually\" path you mentioned) so the issue file documents both the supported-but-not-assisted manual path and the intended box-and-wire path.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n- **The \"explicit action field\" pattern shows up everywhere in API design.** REST APIs use HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) as explicit actions. SQL uses INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE as explicit operations. Git uses add/commit/reset as explicit verbs. The reason: destructive operations need to be loud. Implicit \"the system figures out what you meant\" is fine for reads, dangerous for writes. Your utility-box is a write operation, so explicit action is the safe default.\n- **Wire endpoint as authoritative ties the visual representation to the runtime behaviour.** A user looking at the editor canvas should be able to see exactly what each utility-box affects by following its output wire. If the spec's id could override the wire, the canvas would be lying. By making the wire authoritative, the canvas is always honest — what you see is what happens.\n- **The \"matches today's BOX_CREATE_BOX behaviour by default\" piece preserves backwards compatibility for free.** Existing maps with create_box-kind boxes (and there are several fixtures already) keep working without any changes, because the default action when the spec doesn't specify one IS create. This is the kind of small consideration that avoids a \"we have to update every fixture\" migration headache later.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`"

    "content":"I'm leaning option B - if the ID exists, it's a reconfigure. If we finish reconfiguring and we find that there are no values provided to the box, then it must have been a delete, and we can GC it. If the ID is new or not present, then we create a box and emit the ID as a string.\n\nHmmmmm... Actually, maybe we shouldn't take an ID as input at all. That way, we only have the wire for targeting - if the user wants to change targets, they should change the utility-box's connections.\n\nOkay. Lemme think through this. so let's say we have a utility-box function that creates a JSON spec for a box. It can either fill out the values or not - if empty, it's a delete signal. When applying, we essentially clear the box's fields one by one until we reach the end and realize \"hey this box isn't attached to anything, doesn't have a function, and has a refcount of 0 - it's obviously meant to be deleted\" and we can GC it. When reconfiguring a box, which the delete path would flow down, we increment the refcount because the reconfigurer has a reference and is modifying it. Then we swap the pointer to the new box. I... ugh... I can't think... It's too late at night... Can you update 320 and we can just, come back in the morning? My head hurts...",

        "input":{
          "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via the utility-box kind\n\n## Status\nopen · design substantially settled; a few naming / mechanical\ndetails still need a fresh-morning pass (see \"Open items for\nlater\" at the bottom)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses\n`boxes/<id>.json` once, fills in every field — kind, language,\nfunction pointer, input port list, routing shape, outgoing\nconnections — and the dispatch layer reads that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes a box's record.\n\nIssue 319f already added a language-agnostic way to **create**\nnew boxes at runtime: the BOX_CREATE_BOX kind. A box of that\nkind takes a JSON spec on a `spec` input port; when it fires, it\nparses the spec, allocates the new box at a fresh graph slot,\nand emits the new id as a string on its output wire. Downstream\nconsumers can take the id and wire the new box up further (via\nBOX_CONNECT).\n\nThis issue extends that pattern to **reconfigure** and\n**delete** — also via a box kind, not via library functions in\nthe language bridges. The new mechanism is the utility-box: a\nsingle box kind that subsumes create / reconfigure / delete by\ninspecting the spec it receives.\n\n## Architectural ground rules (from the design discussion)\n\n1. **Graph mutation is a box-kind operation, not a language-\n   bridge function.** Users express mutations by placing\n   utility-boxes in their maps and wiring them, not by writing\n   code that imports the runtime as a library. The runtime is\n   the substrate; users express through it.\n2. **Manual JSON construction is supported but not assisted.**\n   A user who wants to build a long-running Lua box that\n   accumulates JSON for its own future reconfigure can do so —\n   the manual path works as long as the bytes end up on a wire\n   that feeds a utility-box. We don't provide convenience\n   helpers for this path; the box-and-wire path is the intended\n   one.\n3. **The wire endpoint is the target.** When a utility-box's\n   output wire points at box X's input port, that wire IS the\n   declaration of \"this utility-box operates on box X.\" No\n   separate target_id input.\n4. **One unified box kind.** create / reconfigure / delete are\n   all the same kind, dispatched by the spec's content. Folds\n   in 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX.\n5. **Reconfigures ride the regular input slots, tagged with\n   RING_RECONFIGURE.** No separate control queue. The gather\n   lock makes peek-then-pop honest within the lock, so the\n   peek-vs-pop race that would have plagued an unsynchronised\n   design doesn't appear.\n\n## The five structural pieces\n\n### 1. The utility-box kind\n\nOne box kind absorbs 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX. The behaviour\ndepends on the spec's content:\n\n- **Spec describes a box with no existing target** (or target\n  doesn't exist in the graph): CREATE. Allocate at a fresh\n  graph slot. Emit the new id as a string on the output wire.\n- **Spec describes a box with an existing target id** (the\n  wire's endpoint matches an existing box): RECONFIGURE.\n  Build a replacement box struct. Push the struct pointer to\n  the target box's input slot (whichever port the wire ends\n  at), tagged RING_RECONFIGURE.\n- **Spec is empty / minimal** (no fields, no function): DELETE\n  signal. Push a delete-marker to the target box's input slot,\n  tagged RING_DELETE (or maybe just RING_RECONFIGURE with a\n  null struct — see open items).\n\n### 2. The gather flag\n\nEach box record carries one atomic int — the gather flag — with\ntwo states:\n\n- **0 (free):** any worker may attempt to enter.\n- **1 (held):** exactly one worker is currently in the gather\n  section.\n\nWorkers entering a box CAS from 0 to 1. Win → enter gather.\nLose → yield-and-requeue (push task back to pool tail and\nreturn). No spinning, no blocking. Per-box, so workers on\ndifferent boxes don't contend.\n\n### 3. The graph slot as liveness indicator\n\nThe graph stores boxes as an array of pointers, one per box id.\n`graph_box(graph, id)` returns the current pointer. The mutator\natomically swaps that pointer from OLD to NEW. Workers that\nLATER look up the same id get NEW; workers mid-fire on OLD\nfinish on OLD.\n\nA box is **live** when the graph slot points at it. **Superseded**\nwhen the graph slot points at something else (or NULL, for\ndelete). The two-state flag doesn't need a third \"redirect\"\nstate because the graph slot itself is the source of truth for\n\"is this still the current box.\"\n\n### 4. The reference count\n\nEach box record has an atomic refcount. Workers increment at\nthe top of their fire (just after resolving the pointer through\nthe graph slot) and decrement at the bottom. The mutator\nincrements when it becomes the mutator, decrements after the\nswap.\n\nFreeable when BOTH:\n- Graph slot doesn't point at this box (superseded), AND\n- Refcount has dropped to zero.\n\nWhoever decrements to zero AND observes the graph-slot\nmismatch frees the box. Mutator's \"hold a +1\" discipline\nensures the refcount only reaches zero AFTER the mutator\nfinishes its work.\n\n### 5. The reconfigure tag on input slots\n\nEach input slot's ordering ring grows a RING_RECONFIGURE value\nalongside the existing RING_NATIVE and RING_JSON. When a worker\nenters gather and peeks each input port's ordering ring, a\nRING_RECONFIGURE tag at any port's head means \"this is a\ncontrol message, not a value.\" The cell holds a pointer to a\npre-built box_t struct (built by the utility-box during its\nfire, in the utility-box's worker thread — no parsing happens\ninside the target's mutator path).\n\n## The worker arrival flow\n\n```\n1. look up the graph slot for X → get current box pointer (B).\n2. CAS B's gather flag from 0 to 1.\n   - lose: yarq this task. exit.\n   - win: continue.\n3. increment B's refcount.\n4. peek each of B's input ports' ordering rings.\n5. branch on what's there:\n     all heads are values:\n        pop one ordering message + value from each port.\n        release gather flag.\n        call spec's invoke with the gathered values.\n        push outputs to downstream slots per B's connections.\n        decrement B's refcount; free if it qualifies.\n\n     any head is RING_RECONFIGURE:\n        pop the struct pointer from that port.\n        run mutator path (see below).\n\n     some ports empty:\n        don't pop anything. release gather flag. exit.\n        the pool will respawn this box when more values arrive.\n```\n\n## The mutator flow\n\n```\n1. with B's gather flag held and refcount +1:\n2. pop the replacement struct pointer (call it NEW) from the\n   RING_RECONFIGURE-tagged cell.\n3. resolve NEW's input_slot_ids by port-name matching:\n     for each port in NEW:\n       if same name exists in B (= OLD): copy that slot id.\n       else: allocate a fresh slot.\n4. record OLD's abandoned slots (in OLD but not in NEW). They\n   get released when OLD is freed; remaining queued values\n   emit a discard JSONL event per slot.\n5. atomically swap the graph slot for the box id from OLD to NEW.\n6. release B's gather flag.\n7. yarq this task. (queued values on B's slots — still there,\n   slot store didn't change — get fired under the new shape\n   when the requeued task runs.)\n8. decrement OLD's refcount; free OLD + abandoned slots if 0.\n```\n\nThe yarq in step 7 is load-bearing — without it, queued values\non B's input slots sit unprocessed until the next producer\npush.\n\n## Slot diffing by port name\n\nSame algorithm as UI framework tree diffing: match by stable\nidentifier (port name), only-in-old gets abandoned, only-in-new\ngets freshly allocated, in-both keeps its slot id (and its\nqueued values).\n\nRenames are NOT auto-detected — \"x\" → \"x_renamed\" looks like\n\"delete x, create x_renamed.\" Any queued values on \"x\" get\ndropped to JSONL. Value-preserving rename via explicit\n`{\"rename\":[...]}` field is a possible future addition.\n\n## JSONL events\n\n- `box_reconfigure` — fires after the swap. Carries box id,\n  post-apply spec (re-serialised from the new struct), task id,\n  worker idx. Always emitted.\n- `reconfigure_discard` — fires per abandoned port with leftover\n  values. Carries box id, port name, count of dropped values,\n  first value bytes (up to 256). Always emitted.\n- `box_delete` — fires when the spec resolves to a delete.\n  Carries box id, task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n\n## Open items for later (the things to think about with a fresh head)\n\nThese are settled enough in shape that implementation can\nstart, but the exact mechanics want one more pass:\n\n1. **How exactly does \"empty spec → delete\" detection work?**\n   The user's framing: \"we essentially clear the box's fields\n   one by one until we reach the end and realize 'hey this box\n   isn't attached to anything, doesn't have a function, and\n   has a refcount of 0 — it's obviously meant to be deleted.'\"\n   Two possible mechanics:\n   - **Wholesale replace then check:** apply the entire new\n     spec, then look at the resulting struct. If function\n     pointer is null, no connections, no inputs — interpret as\n     delete, swap graph slot to NULL instead of NEW.\n   - **Explicit DELETE tag:** the utility-box decides up\n     front based on spec content and pushes RING_DELETE\n     (separate tag from RING_RECONFIGURE) so the mutator\n     doesn't have to do the emptiness check after applying.\n   Lean toward the explicit tag — keeps the mutator's\n   decision simple — but the implicit \"fields-equal-zero\n   means delete\" is closer to the user's stated intuition.\n2. **For CREATE specifically: where does the wire endpoint\n   point?** Reconfigure and delete both target an existing\n   box (the wire endpoint). Create has no existing target —\n   the box is born when the spec is applied. Today's\n   BOX_CREATE_BOX emits the new id as a string output, and\n   downstream consumers receive that string normally. We\n   should keep that shape: for create, the output wire\n   carries the new id as a value, not a control message.\n3. **Should the wire endpoint be the only target indicator?**\n   The user leaned \"yes, no id input at all\" — but then said\n   \"lean option B\" (content-driven by id field). These two\n   are in tension. Probably the right answer is:\n   - The wire endpoint is the only target for reconfigure and\n     delete.\n   - The spec's id field, if present, is used only for create\n     (since there's no existing target to wire to).\n   - For reconfigure/delete: if the spec has an id field, it\n     must match the wire endpoint's box (safety check).\n4. **Detecting \"reconfigure vs create\" from the spec alone.**\n   Without explicit action field, the utility-box has to look\n   up the spec's id (if present) in the graph: found = this\n   is a reconfigure (or delete); not found = this is a create.\n   This needs care because the lookup races with concurrent\n   creates / deletes. Probably needs the lookup + decision +\n   apply to happen under some kind of brief lock.\n5. **Should the utility-box have a name change?** \"utility-\n   box\" was the user's tentative rename. Alternatives floated:\n   \"spec-applier\", \"box-control\", \"reconfigure-box.\" Lean\n   utility-box because it absorbs three operations.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps (subject to open-item resolution)\n\n1. Add the gather flag and refcount to box_t in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.h`.\n2. Convert the graph's box storage from array-of-structs to\n   array-of-pointers so the mutator can swap.\n3. Refactor `parse_box_file` to accept an in-memory JSON\n   buffer (the utility-box's invoke will call this on the\n   spec it received).\n4. Add RING_RECONFIGURE (and possibly RING_DELETE) as\n   ordering-ring tag values in `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`.\n   Each input slot's existing ring system grows the new tag\n   variants.\n5. Wrap `dispatch_action`'s top with the gather-flag CAS;\n   yarq on loss, continue on win.\n6. Add the mutator path inside `dispatch_action`: pop the\n   tagged cell, resolve slot mappings, swap the graph slot,\n   release the flag, yarq.\n7. Add the utility-box kind in `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}`\n   and `src/012-dispatch.c`. Folds in 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX\n   behaviour for the create path; adds the reconfigure /\n   delete paths.\n8. Add the JSONL events (box_reconfigure, reconfigure_discard,\n   box_delete).\n9. Fixtures under `tests/maps/`:\n   - `320-utility-create` — same shape as 319f's create test\n     (regression that the unified utility-box still creates).\n   - `320-utility-reconfigure-fn` — fires once with old fn,\n     reconfigures, fires again with new fn.\n   - `320-utility-reconfigure-port-shape` — adds a port,\n     verifies new slot allocated.\n   - `320-utility-reconfigure-kind` — flips BOX_CALL to\n     BOX_WRITE.\n   - `320-utility-delete` — deletes a box; downstream\n     gracefully handles the now-gone target.\n   - `320-utility-contended` — two utility-boxes race on the\n     same target; both reconfigures apply in arrival order.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — extend ordering ring tag with\n  RING_RECONFIGURE (and possibly RING_DELETE).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount on\n  box_t; parse_box_file refactor; graph array → array of\n  pointers.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release; mutator\n  path; utility-box kind dispatch.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — runtime_create_box stays;\n  no new bridge functions added.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n\n## Design history\n\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring with three-state flag (0/1/2)** — the\n   original sketch. Discarded once we recognised the graph\n   slot pointer can act as the liveness indicator, eliminating\n   the third state.\n2. **Per-box control queue + language-bridge `apply_box`\n   function** — proposed as a way to keep control messages\n   separate from data messages. Discarded once the user\n   clarified the architectural principle: graph mutation is a\n   box-kind operation, not a library function. The control\n   queue was a layer mismatch — the existing input slots with\n   the RING_RECONFIGURE tag (atomic gather makes peek-then-pop\n   safe inside the lock) work fine.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\"\n\nThe unification of create / reconfigure / delete into one\nutility-box kind came from the user's observation: \"What if we\nmade the 'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process?\" The architectural principle that drove\nthe final shape: graph mutation is a box-kind, the wire\nendpoint is the target, and the runtime is the substrate, not\nthe library.\n",

    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# 320 — Box reconfigure via the utility-box kind\n\n## Status\nopen · design substantially settled; a few naming / mechanical\ndetails still need a fresh-morning pass (see \"Open items for\nlater\" at the bottom)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's identity is frozen at graph-load. The loader parses\n`boxes/<id>.json` once, fills in every field — kind, language,\nfunction pointer, input port list, routing shape, outgoing\nconnections — and the dispatch layer reads that record on every\nfire. Nothing in the running program changes a box's record.\n\nIssue 319f already added a language-agnostic way to **create**\nnew boxes at runtime: the BOX_CREATE_BOX kind. A box of that\nkind takes a JSON spec on a `spec` input port; when it fires, it\nparses the spec, allocates the new box at a fresh graph slot,\nand emits the new id as a string on its output wire. Downstream\nconsumers can take the id and wire the new box up further (via\nBOX_CONNECT).\n\nThis issue extends that pattern to **reconfigure** and\n**delete** — also via a box kind, not via library functions in\nthe language bridges. The new mechanism is the utility-box: a\nsingle box kind that subsumes create / reconfigure / delete by\ninspecting the spec it receives.\n\n## Architectural ground rules (from the design discussion)\n\n1. **Graph mutation is a box-kind operation, not a language-\n   bridge function.** Users express mutations by placing\n   utility-boxes in their maps and wiring them, not by writing\n   code that imports the runtime as a library. The runtime is\n   the substrate; users express through it.\n2. **Manual JSON construction is supported but not assisted.**\n   A user who wants to build a long-running Lua box that\n   accumulates JSON for its own future reconfigure can do so —\n   the manual path works as long as the bytes end up on a wire\n   that feeds a utility-box. We don't provide convenience\n   helpers for this path; the box-and-wire path is the intended\n   one.\n3. **The wire endpoint is the target.** When a utility-box's\n   output wire points at box X's input port, that wire IS the\n   declaration of \"this utility-box operates on box X.\" No\n   separate target_id input.\n4. **One unified box kind.** create / reconfigure / delete are\n   all the same kind, dispatched by the spec's content. Folds\n   in 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX.\n5. **Reconfigures ride the regular input slots, tagged with\n   RING_RECONFIGURE.** No separate control queue. The gather\n   lock makes peek-then-pop honest within the lock, so the\n   peek-vs-pop race that would have plagued an unsynchronised\n   design doesn't appear.\n\n## The five structural pieces\n\n### 1. The utility-box kind\n\nOne box kind absorbs 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX. The behaviour\ndepends on the spec's content:\n\n- **Spec describes a box with no existing target** (or target\n  doesn't exist in the graph): CREATE. Allocate at a fresh\n  graph slot. Emit the new id as a string on the output wire.\n- **Spec describes a box with an existing target id** (the\n  wire's endpoint matches an existing box): RECONFIGURE.\n  Build a replacement box struct. Push the struct pointer to\n  the target box's input slot (whichever port the wire ends\n  at), tagged RING_RECONFIGURE.\n- **Spec is empty / minimal** (no fields, no function): DELETE\n  signal. Push a delete-marker to the target box's input slot,\n  tagged RING_DELETE (or maybe just RING_RECONFIGURE with a\n  null struct — see open items).\n\n### 2. The gather flag\n\nEach box record carries one atomic int — the gather flag — with\ntwo states:\n\n- **0 (free):** any worker may attempt to enter.\n- **1 (held):** exactly one worker is currently in the gather\n  section.\n\nWorkers entering a box CAS from 0 to 1. Win → enter gather.\nLose → yield-and-requeue (push task back to pool tail and\nreturn). No spinning, no blocking. Per-box, so workers on\ndifferent boxes don't contend.\n\n### 3. The graph slot as liveness indicator\n\nThe graph stores boxes as an array of pointers, one per box id.\n`graph_box(graph, id)` returns the current pointer. The mutator\natomically swaps that pointer from OLD to NEW. Workers that\nLATER look up the same id get NEW; workers mid-fire on OLD\nfinish on OLD.\n\nA box is **live** when the graph slot points at it. **Superseded**\nwhen the graph slot points at something else (or NULL, for\ndelete). The two-state flag doesn't need a third \"redirect\"\nstate because the graph slot itself is the source of truth for\n\"is this still the current box.\"\n\n### 4. The reference count\n\nEach box record has an atomic refcount. Workers increment at\nthe top of their fire (just after resolving the pointer through\nthe graph slot) and decrement at the bottom. The mutator\nincrements when it becomes the mutator, decrements after the\nswap.\n\nFreeable when BOTH:\n- Graph slot doesn't point at this box (superseded), AND\n- Refcount has dropped to zero.\n\nWhoever decrements to zero AND observes the graph-slot\nmismatch frees the box. Mutator's \"hold a +1\" discipline\nensures the refcount only reaches zero AFTER the mutator\nfinishes its work.\n\n### 5. The reconfigure tag on input slots\n\nEach input slot's ordering ring grows a RING_RECONFIGURE value\nalongside the existing RING_NATIVE and RING_JSON. When a worker\nenters gather and peeks each input port's ordering ring, a\nRING_RECONFIGURE tag at any port's head means \"this is a\ncontrol message, not a value.\" The cell holds a pointer to a\npre-built box_t struct (built by the utility-box during its\nfire, in the utility-box's worker thread — no parsing happens\ninside the target's mutator path).\n\n## The worker arrival flow\n\n```\n1. look up the graph slot for X → get current box pointer (B).\n2. CAS B's gather flag from 0 to 1.\n   - lose: yarq this task. exit.\n   - win: continue.\n3. increment B's refcount.\n4. peek each of B's input ports' ordering rings.\n5. branch on what's there:\n     all heads are values:\n        pop one ordering message + value from each port.\n        release gather flag.\n        call spec's invoke with the gathered values.\n        push outputs to downstream slots per B's connections.\n        decrement B's refcount; free if it qualifies.\n\n     any head is RING_RECONFIGURE:\n        pop the struct pointer from that port.\n        run mutator path (see below).\n\n     some ports empty:\n        don't pop anything. release gather flag. exit.\n        the pool will respawn this box when more values arrive.\n```\n\n## The mutator flow\n\n```\n1. with B's gather flag held and refcount +1:\n2. pop the replacement struct pointer (call it NEW) from the\n   RING_RECONFIGURE-tagged cell.\n3. resolve NEW's input_slot_ids by port-name matching:\n     for each port in NEW:\n       if same name exists in B (= OLD): copy that slot id.\n       else: allocate a fresh slot.\n4. record OLD's abandoned slots (in OLD but not in NEW). They\n   get released when OLD is freed; remaining queued values\n   emit a discard JSONL event per slot.\n5. atomically swap the graph slot for the box id from OLD to NEW.\n6. release B's gather flag.\n7. yarq this task. (queued values on B's slots — still there,\n   slot store didn't change — get fired under the new shape\n   when the requeued task runs.)\n8. decrement OLD's refcount; free OLD + abandoned slots if 0.\n```\n\nThe yarq in step 7 is load-bearing — without it, queued values\non B's input slots sit unprocessed until the next producer\npush.\n\n## Slot diffing by port name\n\nSame algorithm as UI framework tree diffing: match by stable\nidentifier (port name), only-in-old gets abandoned, only-in-new\ngets freshly allocated, in-both keeps its slot id (and its\nqueued values).\n\nRenames are NOT auto-detected — \"x\" → \"x_renamed\" looks like\n\"delete x, create x_renamed.\" Any queued values on \"x\" get\ndropped to JSONL. Value-preserving rename via explicit\n`{\"rename\":[...]}` field is a possible future addition.\n\n## JSONL events\n\n- `box_reconfigure` — fires after the swap. Carries box id,\n  post-apply spec (re-serialised from the new struct), task id,\n  worker idx. Always emitted.\n- `reconfigure_discard` — fires per abandoned port with leftover\n  values. Carries box id, port name, count of dropped values,\n  first value bytes (up to 256). Always emitted.\n- `box_delete` — fires when the spec resolves to a delete.\n  Carries box id, task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n\n## Open items for later (the things to think about with a fresh head)\n\nThese are settled enough in shape that implementation can\nstart, but the exact mechanics want one more pass:\n\n1. **How exactly does \"empty spec → delete\" detection work?**\n   The user's framing: \"we essentially clear the box's fields\n   one by one until we reach the end and realize 'hey this box\n   isn't attached to anything, doesn't have a function, and\n   has a refcount of 0 — it's obviously meant to be deleted.'\"\n   Two possible mechanics:\n   - **Wholesale replace then check:** apply the entire new\n     spec, then look at the resulting struct. If function\n     pointer is null, no connections, no inputs — interpret as\n     delete, swap graph slot to NULL instead of NEW.\n   - **Explicit DELETE tag:** the utility-box decides up\n     front based on spec content and pushes RING_DELETE\n     (separate tag from RING_RECONFIGURE) so the mutator\n     doesn't have to do the emptiness check after applying.\n   Lean toward the explicit tag — keeps the mutator's\n   decision simple — but the implicit \"fields-equal-zero\n   means delete\" is closer to the user's stated intuition.\n\n2. **For CREATE specifically: where does the wire endpoint\n   point?** Reconfigure and delete both target an existing\n   box (the wire endpoint). Create has no existing target —\n   the box is born when the spec is applied. Today's\n   BOX_CREATE_BOX emits the new id as a string output, and\n   downstream consumers receive that string normally. We\n   should keep that shape: for create, the output wire\n   carries the new id as a value, not a control message.\n\n3. **Should the wire endpoint be the only target indicator?**\n   The user leaned both ways in the discussion: \"we shouldn't\n   take an ID as input at all\" AND \"lean option B\" (content-\n   driven by id field). These are in tension. Probably the\n   right resolution:\n   - For reconfigure/delete: wire endpoint is the only target;\n     no id in spec needed.\n   - For create: the spec's id field IS required (since\n     there's no existing target to wire to). The output wire\n     carries the new id.\n   - If spec for reconfigure/delete includes an id, it must\n     match the wire endpoint's box id (safety check).\n\n4. **Detecting \"reconfigure vs create\" from the spec / wire.**\n   - If the wire endpoint exists → it's a reconfigure or delete\n     (decided by spec content emptiness).\n   - If there's no wire endpoint (or it points at something\n     invalid) → it's a create.\n   Mechanically: the utility-box, on fire, looks at where its\n   output wire is going. If the endpoint exists, push the\n   struct pointer with a control tag. If not, allocate a new\n   graph slot, install, emit the new id.\n\n5. **Should the utility-box have a name change?** \"utility-\n   box\" was the user's tentative rename. Alternatives floated:\n   \"spec-applier\", \"box-control\", \"reconfigure-box.\" Lean\n   utility-box because it absorbs three operations.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps (subject to open-item resolution)\n\n1. Add the gather flag and refcount to box_t in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.h`.\n2. Convert the graph's box storage from array-of-structs to\n   array-of-pointers so the mutator can swap.\n3. Refactor `parse_box_file` to accept an in-memory JSON\n   buffer (the utility-box's invoke will call this on the\n   spec it received).\n4. Add RING_RECONFIGURE (and possibly RING_DELETE) as\n   ordering-ring tag values in `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`.\n   Each input slot's existing ring system grows the new tag\n   variants.\n5. Wrap `dispatch_action`'s top with the gather-flag CAS;\n   yarq on loss, continue on win.\n6. Add the mutator path inside `dispatch_action`: pop the\n   tagged cell, resolve slot mappings, swap the graph slot,\n   release the flag, yarq.\n7. Add the utility-box kind in `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}`\n   and `src/012-dispatch.c`. Folds in 319f's BOX_CREATE_BOX\n   behaviour for the create path; adds the reconfigure /\n   delete paths.\n8. Add the JSONL events (box_reconfigure, reconfigure_discard,\n   box_delete).\n9. Fixtures under `tests/maps/`:\n   - `320-utility-create` — regression that the unified\n     utility-box still creates (matches 319f's existing\n     create test).\n   - `320-utility-reconfigure-fn` — fires once with old fn,\n     reconfigures, fires again with new fn.\n   - `320-utility-reconfigure-port-shape` — adds a port,\n     verifies new slot allocated.\n   - `320-utility-reconfigure-kind` — flips BOX_CALL to\n     BOX_WRITE.\n   - `320-utility-delete` — deletes a box; downstream\n     gracefully handles the now-gone target.\n   - `320-utility-contended` — two utility-boxes race on the\n     same target; both reconfigures apply in arrival order.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — extend ordering ring tag with\n  RING_RECONFIGURE (and possibly RING_DELETE).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount on\n  box_t; parse_box_file refactor; graph array → array of\n  pointers.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release; mutator\n  path; utility-box kind dispatch.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n\n## Design history\n\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring with three-state flag (0/1/2)** — the\n   original sketch. Discarded once we recognised the graph\n   slot pointer can act as the liveness indicator, eliminating\n   the third state.\n2. **Per-box control queue + language-bridge `apply_box`\n   function** — proposed as a way to keep control messages\n   separate from data messages. Discarded once the user\n   clarified the architectural principle: graph mutation is a\n   box-kind operation, not a library function. The control\n   queue was a layer mismatch — the existing input slots with\n   the RING_RECONFIGURE tag (atomic gather makes peek-then-pop\n   safe inside the lock) work fine.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\"\n\nThe unification of create / reconfigure / delete into one\nutility-box kind came from the user's observation: \"What if we\nmade the 'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process?\" The architectural principle that drove\nthe final shape: graph mutation is a box-kind, the wire\nendpoint is the target, and the runtime is the substrate, not\nthe library.\n",

Both land in the control","-      queue; both apply in arrival order; final state reflects","-      the last one applied.","-"," ## Relevant files"," ","-- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — already provides the ring-buffer","-  primitive the control queue reuses.","-- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount fields","-  on `box_t`; `parse_box_file` refactor; graph array → array","-  of pointers; control slot allocation at box creation.","-- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release wrapping","-  `dispatch_action`; mutator path; yarq helper.","-- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_apply_box_spec`","-  unified entry point.","+- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — extend ordering ring tag with","+  RING_RECONFIGURE (and possibly RING_DELETE).","+- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount on","+  box_t; parse_box_file refactor; graph array → array of","+  pointers.","+- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release; mutator","+  path; utility-box kind dispatch."," - `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —","   three new event types.","-- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —","-  one new bridge function per language for `apply_box`."," ","-## Open issues for after 320 lands","-","-- **Connections-array atomic-publish dance unification** —","-  today's `runtime_connect` does its own copy-and-publish on","-  the per-box connections array. Workers would peek","-   each port's ordering ring and apply reconfigures encountered","-   during gather. And if it has the same box ID as an","-already existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure","-process.\" Structurally honest about what these operations are:","-all three are \"express what this box should be now,\" and the","-runtime decides how to land that expression.","+The unification of create / reconfigure / delete into one","+utility-box kind came from the user's observation: \"What if we","+made the 'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the","+reconfigure process?\" The architectural principle that drove","+the final shape: graph mutation is a box-kind, the wire","+endpoint is the target, and the runtime is the substrate, not","+the library."],
